11506-the-old-bell-of-independence-or-ph:
Henry C. Watson's 1851 Old Bell of Independence, or Philadelphia in 1776, in the Young American's Library, aims to awaken veneration for Revolutionary patriots and emulation of their example. Its preface warns that freedom's enjoyment makes Americans underrate the toils and sufferings that secured it, and argues knowledge of the fathers is the best cure for falling off. War's horrors are condemned, but generous devotion, resolution, and skill are commended wherever displayed.

Stories of Washington, a spy's fate, a sermon, a prayer, Lydia Darragh, and a dead man's lake cluster around the old bell as rallying point for veteran story-tellers. Watson, author of Camp-Fires of the Revolution, writes for young readers. The book shows mid-century patriotic education in story form.
23174-a-good-for-nothing-1876:
Hjalmar Hjorth Boyesen published A Good for Nothing in 1876, a work of fiction centred on a boy named Ralph. The opening follows Ralph from babyhood into early childhood. His mother reads deep meaning into small habits, taking his thumb-sucking and quiet corner-sitting as signs of a poet's brooding mind.

By age five, Ralph has become the ruling force in his own home. Boyesen tells this with gentle irony, letting the mother's proud reading sit beside the plain facts of a spoiled small child. Readers get a wry portrait of family pride, early character, and how adults can build large hopes on very small evidence.
25536-history-of-the-english-people-volu:
John Richard Green closes his History of the English People with this eighth volume, Modern England from 1760 to 1815, in the 1896 Eversley edition. The full index to the eight volumes once stood at its end, and now circulates as a separate volume.

Chapters cover the independence of America from 1767 to 1782, industrial England, England and revolutionary France, and England and Napoleon. Green follows a nation remade by lost colonies, new mills, and long wars, in the readable narrative style that made his history popular. Macmillan issued the volume in London and New York.
28010-bacon-s-rebellion-1676:
Thomas J. Wertenbaker published Bacon's Rebellion, 1676 as Jamestown 350th Anniversary Historical Booklet Number 8, issued by the Virginia 350th Anniversary Celebration Corporation in Williamsburg in 1957, with later printings in 1959 and 1964. The booklet also opens with omens: a great comet, vast flights of pigeons, and swarms of cicadas.

Wertenbaker also traces the disaster to Charles I naming Sir William Berkeley Governor of Virginia, a member of the Privy Chamber whose intense loyalty shaped his rule. The booklet still remains a clear, concise, plain account today of the greatest catastrophe in the colony's history, written for the Jamestown anniversary audience.
30557-lilrc-interlibrary-loan-manual-jan:
The Long Island Library Resources Council publishes its Interlibrary Loan Manual in January 1976, from Box 31, Bellport, New York. Eight sections cover introduction, loan policies and procedures, direct access to other libraries, the INS system, request forms, good borrowing, good lending, and appendices.

Loan procedures detail what may be borrowed, placing requests, form of request, verification, photocopying, and expenses. Direct access adds location service and a research loan program, while INS covers billing, cancellations, delivery, pickup, microforms, recalls, renewals, and returns. The manual serves librarians and borrowers who share books across Long Island libraries. Staff can use it day to day to move books, check forms, and keep loans on track.
32222-felicitas-a-tale-of-the-german-mig:
Felix Dahn's Felicitas, a tale of the German migrations in the year 476, translated from the German by M. A. C. E., was published in London by Macmillan in 1883. Its introduction places the author in Salzburg, studying old records and Roman antiquities. His studies concerned the fifth century, when Germanic tribes invaded those regions and Roman garrisons retired, with or without resistance.

Many settlers, Dahn writes, remained in the land: peasants, tradespeople, and mechanics who would not forsake their homes, lucrative occupations, or valued, long-cherished plots of ground. They stayed under the rule of the barbarian, who, once conquest's storm and battle had ended and the country was divided, did not molest them. Readers get a migration-era romance grounded in Salzburg records, about ordinary settlers under a new rule.
4824-the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volu:
This twenty-second volume of The Rise of the Dutch Republic covers 1574 to 1576. Its file header numbers it as the twenty-fourth Gutenberg volume. Chapter three opens with latter days of the Blood Council, and informal, insincere negotiations for peace. Characteristics of negotiators and their diplomatic correspondence are weighed, with Dr. Junius prominent among them.

Secret conferences between Dr. Leoninus and Orange follow, with steadfastness of the Prince amid shifting talks. Changes in internal government of the northern provinces, generosity and increasing power of municipalities, and incipient jealousies among them shape the chapter's second half. Peace talks that neither side trusts, a prince who will not bend, and towns growing strong enough to govern themselves carry the narrative on. Readers get Motley's account of diplomacy without trust, in the years before the provinces united.
4825-the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volu:
By 1576 the revolt has outgrown single provinces, and John Lothrop Motley shows Orange pulling them into closer union. A new act joins Holland and Zealand, defines the prince's authority, and sets out a provincial polity built around towns that now fund and govern much of the war.

At Brussels, a state council tries to run affairs while Madrid hesitates, and Orange watches every move with care. Letters from the king, talks with Elizabeth of England, and secret dealings with France and Alencon fill the background. The volume explains how a rebellion became a state, held together by law, money, and Orange's steady leadership.
66607-story-of-the-automobile-its-histor:
H. L. Barber wrote this tale of the car, printed at Chicago in 1917. He was a man of funds and wrote on how funds are made. The full head of the book sets its span: the tale of the car and its growth from 1760 to 1917. To the tale is added a look at the stand and the hopes of the trade of the car. A plate at the front names three men of the theme: Franklin, Duryea, and Ford.

Franklin is called the first great teach of thrift in America. Duryea is named as the maker of the first car of America that ran on the fumes of oil. Ford is named the sire of the make of cars in great count. The word at the front states the gap the book fills.
9072-life-of-johnson-volume-2-1765-1776:
This second volume of Boswell's Life of Johnson, in the Hill edition, covers the years 1765 to 1776. Johnson, now famous for his Dictionary, works on his edition of Shakespeare and writes for friends, while Boswell records his talk, letters, and quarrels with care. The volume adds notes on Johnson's views of America and his own records.

Readers meet Johnson in his prime: witty, learned, dogmatic, and kind in turns, holding court in London coffee houses and clubs. Boswell's eye for small detail makes the man live on the page. For lovers of biography, this stretch of the Life is among its richest, full of talk that still sparks.
9112-the-dare-boys-of-1776:
Stephen Angus Cox wrote this boys' adventure novel, published in New York in 1910. It opens on July 4, 1776, as Philadelphia weighs the Declaration of Independence. Two brothers, Dick and Tom Dare, join the patriot cause and take on dangerous work as spies. Their deeds soon please General Washington himself.

Chapters move from road ambushes and night attacks to camps of the foe, a haunted house, and the Battle of Long Island. The pace is swift and the heroes brave. The book is a fine sample of the patriotic dime-novel spirit that once fired young readers.
a-general-history-and-collection-of-voya: Volume eleven of Robert Kerr's voyages continues George Shelvocke's voyage round the world from 1719 to 1722. Its sections follow Shelvocke from California to Canton in China and his residence there. The voyage then returns from China to England. Kerr's volume adds a lively privateering circumnavigation to his collection. The tale is lively, bold, and full of the sea and strange lands.
abridgement-of-elements-of-phrenology-18: Abridgement of Elements of Phrenology, dated 1876 and credited to B H Webb, is a shortened version of a phrenology textbook's elements. By the eighteen seventies phrenology had a long shelf of elementary treatises. An abridgement served readers who wanted the system in brief: the faculties, the organs on the skull, and the rules for reading them. The record for this entry gives little beyond its title, author, and date. The piece survives as a late, small brick in the large popular literature of head reading.
account-of-an-alchemical-roll-on-parchme: Account of an Alchemical Roll on Parchment, dated 1876, describes a remarkable object: a parchment roll presented by the Earl of Cromarty in 1707 to the Royal College of Physicians of Edinburgh. Alchemical rolls carry the work of the philosophers in pictures and text along a long strip. This account records the Edinburgh roll for learned readers. The copy preserved here comes through the University of Glasgow Library and the Ferguson collection, whose name stands on the record.
allen-encyclopedia-pure-materia-medica-v:
Volume V of the Encyclopaedia of Pure Materia Medica appeared in 1876, the halfway point of Allen's ten. The symptoms of each remedy stand in strict anatomical order, a habit that lets a busy reader land on the right page fast. Sources are cited, so claims can be traced.

Some entries run for pages, proof of how often a drug was tested in that busy age of provings. Others stay brief. All of it feeds the same craft: choosing one remedy whose proved picture matches the sick person's signs. The volume keeps the archive's standard of full record over fine writing.
arxiv-2412-00676:
The XRISM Collaboration presents a 2024 astronomy paper on the supernova remnant Sagittarius A East, which sits beside the Milky Way's central black hole. The remnant's X-ray glow was suspected to come from overionized plasma, gas whose atoms were stripped further than its current temperature allows, hinting at a strange history. The team's new space telescope paired a high-resolution spectrometer with a wide-field imager for the first detailed look.

Iron emission lines were resolved into fine structure for the first time. Their intensity pattern strongly confirms overionized plasma. Before the shift, the gas must have been hotter than four kiloelectronvolts, and the change happened fast. The iron ions move slowly, ruling out violent expansion now. The authors weigh two triggers: rapid cooling as the gas expanded out of dense surrounding material, or a past blaze of radiation from the black hole next door.
arxiv-2412-02076:
Bo Wen, Haochen Zhang, Dirk-Uwe Bartsch, William Freeman, Truong Nguyen, and Cheolhong An wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-four. It keeps the topology of tube-like forms true when software cuts them out of biomedical images.

A cut that breaks a vessel or drops a loop can ruin later work, even if most pixels are right. Past loss rules match lasting features in a pure topology space, which can pair the wrong features. The new loss also uses where features sit in the image, so matches are guided by place. Tests on many kinds of tube images beat top rivals on topology accuracy. Code is public.
arxiv-2412-02276:
Mbewe, Mekuria, Sahlu, and Abebe study a cosmology where the cosmic fluids are slightly sticky, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-four. With the right conditions, their viscous interacting model mimics the standard ΛCDM universe at the background level, expanding the same way while telling a different microphysical story.

The authors derive the background equations for the multifluid system. They then fit the model to Type Ia supernova data using Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling. Best-fit parameters are compared against the standard picture. Next they perturb the model in a dust-dominated frame, using a covariant formalism that tracks how inhomogeneities grow. The perturbation results carry a warning: bound structures in the late universe tend to disintegrate in this model. That prediction gives observers a handle to test viscous cosmologies against the large-scale structure we actually see.
arxiv-2412-02676:
Li and five co-authors teach two robot arms touch-rich tasks from plan-made drills in this twenty twenty-four paper. Two-arm work needs fine sync of grips, pushes, and turns on one thing. Real drill sets for such work are scant and hard to grow by hand.

Inside, a plan tool breeds drill paths in a rich fake world for the arms. Those paths span things of all shapes, sizes, and stuff traits in the set. A spread-style net then learns the drill paths by copy in the lab. Craft picks in marks, task code, and drill mix help cross to real arms. Tests in fake and real rooms show the arms work on new things well.
arxiv-2412-03076:
Francesc Wilhelmi and four co-authors tackle Wi-Fi crowding in this two thousand twenty-four paper. Nearby networks often talk over each other. A method called spatial reuse lets devices send at the same time if they tune their power and sensing levels well. The authors let each network learn its own settings through trial and reward. They call this a multi-agent multi-armed bandit setup.

The agents act under a coordination scheme planned for future Wi-Fi. The team tested several learning rules and ways to share rewards. They ran the tests in Komondor, a known Wi-Fi simulator. Their results show that learned settings can beat fixed ones. The work speaks to engineers shaping the next Wi-Fi standards, where smart control will be built in.
arxiv-2412-03176:
León-Paul Schaub Torre, Pelayo Quirós, and Helena García-Mieres wrote this research paper, published in 2024. It builds a system that reads Spanish clinical notes and names the skin disease a patient likely has, by pairing a large language model with medical reference structures.

The hybrid system learns in a set order: first the type of skin problem, then its severity, then where on the body it sits. Teaching the model that order, and grounding it in medical ontologies, lifted accuracy a great deal. The system reached precision of 0.84 on disease classification, with strong balance scores. The authors report the best results to date for this task. They release both the method and the dataset, so other teams can test and extend the approach for Spanish medical text.
arxiv-2412-03676:
Francesco Innocenti and five co-authors set out JPC, a library for training networks that learn by foretelling their own input, built on a fast code base. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four.

Such networks, drawn from how the brain may work, learn by a flow of error through their layers. The library gives a plain, fast, and loose face for many forms: sorting, making, and mixed nets. In place of the plain step rule past libraries used, it solves the flow with true equation solvers. A second-order solver runs far faster, at like scores, across tasks and depths. The library adds theory tools to study such nets. The code is shared.
arxiv-2412-03776:
Stephen Lack and Shay Tobin characterize the category of Hilbert spaces using only abstract category theory, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-four. Hilbert spaces are the stage of quantum mechanics, and knowing that a category must consist of them, from structural clues alone, is a deep kind of recognition.

Earlier characterizations by Heunen and Kornell leaned on a monoidal structure, and that assumption shut out quaternionic Hilbert spaces. The new approach drops the monoidal assumption entirely. Behind it stands Solèr's theorem, which forces a space satisfying certain symmetry conditions to be a Hilbert space over the reals, the complexes, or the quaternions. Lack and Tobin recover the real and complex cases and gain the quaternionic one as well. Their result widens the categorical fingerprint of Hilbert spaces. It also speaks to the foundations of quantum theory, where such recognition theorems matter.
arxiv-2412-05476:
Carlos Budde, Pedro D'Argenio, and Arnd Hartmanns model an open-pit mine in their 2024 case study. They want to find the best way to run trucks and loaders so the mine earns the most in a set time. Their model treats each choice and delay as a chance event in a formal network.

Exact checking of the model proved hopeless, since the number of states explodes even for a small mine. So the team sampled strategies at random and also tried a learning method that builds a score table. They added a way to turn the best strategies into decision trees, which people can read and trust. Tests showed the learning method has limits, but the trees made the winning plans clear.
arxiv-2412-08876:
Jakob Robnik, Reuben Cohn-Gordon, and Uroš Seljak make a fast sampling method practical by removing its guesswork, in a 2024 paper. The head title calls it practical and scalable Hamiltonian Monte Carlo without the usual acceptance test. That test removes the small bias caused by rough numerical steps, but it also slows mixing and raises noise.

Skipping the test trades a little bias for much lower variance, yet few used the shortcut because picking the step size was an art. The authors tie the size of energy errors to the bias, then tune the step automatically to meet a bias limit the user sets. On hard test problems, including one with over a million parameters, the tuned shortcut beat the standard method clearly.
arxiv-2412-09476:
Lee Mitchell and four co-authors report how the SIRI-2 instrument caught the extraordinary gamma-ray burst GRB 221009A without being blinded by it. Most detectors saturated on this record-breaking burst and needed pile-up corrections. SIRI-2, a set of strontium iodide detectors in geosynchronous orbit, stayed clean.

Its measured energetics agree with other instruments, and its spectral fits match the unsaturated Insight and GECAM results. The total fluence came out lower than elsewhere, likely because rising background forced a shorter counting window. Extrapolating from known bursts, the authors estimate events this bright should occur roughly once every four thousand years. The paper documents a rare unsaturated record of an extreme event.
arxiv-2412-09576:
Irakli Giorgadze and four co-authors study how to gauge the entanglement of states of many fermions, the class of parts that make up matter. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four.

Such states sit at the heart of quantum chemistry, a top use case for near-term quantum machines. Plain qubits pay a high cost to hold fermion traits. New fermion-based gear may cost less. The team reads entanglement through trimmed states, for cuts of the full space at many sizes. One gauge, the von Neumann disorder of the trimmed state, needs no base choice. It stretches the old one-part gauge of chemistry. They map the top bounds such gauges can reach.
arxiv-2412-09676:
A large survey team reports a planet smaller than Jupiter around a very light star or brown dwarf. Their paper, from twenty twenty-four, rests on a microlensing event from twenty fifteen. In such events, a front star's gravity bends light from a back star and briefly brightens it. A planet near the front star adds a short extra blip.

Two survey telescopes, OGLE and MOA, each caught the blip cleanly. That double catch makes the planet claim firm, which is rare for survey-only finds. The host is so light that it may not be a true star at all. Such finds help count planets around the smallest hosts.
arxiv-2412-10476:
Tao Li and seven colleagues survey, in a 2024 preprint, a decade of research on testing web applications. Web apps run in browsers and build pages on the fly from user actions. Their mix of shifting content, background operations, and varied user setups makes testing hard. Yet quality matters more as user counts grow. The survey gathers what the field has produced over twelve years of fast change.

It walks through the main steps of testing: making test cases, running them, and judging the results. Tools built for each step are catalogued and compared. The authors sort the many approaches by the web traits they target. They close with open problems, such as keeping tests valid as apps change weekly. The paper aims to give new researchers a map of the area and veterans a view of where it should go next.
arxiv-2412-10876:
Weinan Lin, Guozhen Wang, and Zhouli Xu report machine proofs for Adams differentials in two thousand twenty-four. Adams computations decide deep facts about stable homotopy groups. Their dataset covers forty nine CW spectra and many maps. Sixty one cofiber sequences enter the records as well.

The document explains how the machine results were obtained. Detailed proofs back the computed differentials and extensions. Human insight adds ad hoc steps where the machine stops. Together they settled the Last Kervaire Invariant Problem in dimension one two six. The dataset sits on Zenodo for others to inspect.
arxiv-2412-11376:
Chengsen Wang and co-authors build ChatTime, a base model that treats time series as a foreign tongue, in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. Human experts blend numbers with text when reading series, but most forecast tools take numbers alone. Fixed windows and one-set training also cramp older tools.

ChatTime takes both series and text in, and returns both as well. It forecasts on fresh sets with no new training. The team built four mixed datasets to close data gaps and ran wide task checks. Results back the model's range across tasks and scenes. Readers get one model for series work where words and numbers meet.
arxiv-2412-13376:
Christian Green, Mehmet Ergezer, and Abdurrahman Zeybey present a 2024 paper on attacks that fool systems which recognize three-dimensional objects. Such systems often view an object from many angles. A weak spot is a small, crafted noise pattern that makes the system name the wrong object.

Their method, called VIAP, builds one noise pattern that works from many viewpoints. It can also be aimed, forcing the system to output a chosen wrong label. They tested it on 1,210 images of 121 rendered objects. The untargeted version held up under rotations and other changes of view. The targeted version reached top accuracy above 95 percent in their tests. The work offers a way to stress-test vision systems before real-world use.
arxiv-2412-13776:
Kaihong Lu, Huanshui Zhang, and Long Wang study games where the shared aggregate that players react to is itself chosen by an inner optimization. In these aggregative games with bilevel structure, a virtual leader's objective sets the aggregation. Each player sees only a local piece of that objective.

The authors propose a distributed algorithm using second-order gradient information, including Hessian matrices of the leader's costs. Players update their actions while jointly estimating the aggregation through neighbor communication on a connected graph. Under mild assumptions, the actions converge to the Nash equilibrium. A second part of the paper treats the case where Hessian information is unavailable.
arxiv-2412-14876:
Kevin Marc Seja, Niclas Wall-Wennerdal, Tomas Löfwander, Annica Black-Schaffer, Mikael Fogelström, and Patric Holmvall wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-four, with fuller names in its text. It maps how dirt, in the form of impurities, fights a phase crystal state at the edge of a nodal d-wave superconductor.

Phase crystals are ground states with built-in phase slopes that drive rings of current and break time symmetry. The team uses a t-matrix method with full self-consistency to chart the state against impurity strength and heat. The crystal holds up to a large share of the strength that would kill superconductivity outright, in both weak and strong scattering. In small samples a rival edge state with even currents competes.
arxiv-2412-15176:
Lukas Aichberger, Kajetan Schweighofer, and Sepp Hochreiter rethink uncertainty scores for language models in this 2024 paper. Knowing when a model is unsure is key to trusting its text. Leading methods sample many outputs and compare them, which is costly at scale. The authors inspect the theory behind those methods.

Proper scoring rules point to a simpler measure. The negative log likelihood of the most likely output is itself a principled uncertainty score. Their method, G-NLL, estimates it from one greedy output sequence. No repeated sampling is needed. Tests across varied scenarios matched the best prior methods. The result challenges the need for complex multi sample scoring in routine use.
arxiv-2412-15476:
Iiro Kumpulainen, Sebastian Dalleiger, Jilles Vreeken, and Nikolaj Tatti ask, in a 2024 paper, how to find structure shared across many networks at once. The classic stochastic block model sorts a graph's nodes into blocks with similar linking patterns. Real work, though, often hands us several graphs of different sizes whose nodes do not line up. The authors define the shared version of the problem.

They prove that fitting such a shared model exactly is NP-hard, then give two workable routes. One searches directly with a sampling algorithm. The other fits each graph on its own and then picks which blocks to share, by exact optimization or by a fast greedy rule. On synthetic and real data, both routes recovered shared structure well. The work serves anyone comparing networks across sites or times.
arxiv-2412-16676:
Yihui Tong and co-authors study, in a 2024 math paper, a family of diffusion equations proposed to clean a speckled form of noise from images. Multiplicative noise, common in radar and medical scans, is harder to remove than plain grain. Their equations flow forward in some places and backward in others, with an added source term.

Using a step-by-step time method, a relaxation result, and a fixed-point theorem, the authors prove that solutions of a generalized kind exist for the model. They also show results on how solutions depend on the starting image. Computer tests then compare the model's cleaning power with rival methods, showing clear gains on test images.
arxiv-2412-17176:
Md Mahmuddun Nabi Murad, Mehmet Aktukmak, and Yasin Yilmaz wrote a 2024 paper on forecasting long stretches of time series data. Forecasts of weather, power demand, and prices all depend on spotting patterns at several scales at once. Recent mixer models, built from simple layers, rival fancy attention models at this task but had not reached their full strength.

Their model, WPMixer, splits the series with wavelets into layers of detail, from slow trends to fast wiggles. It then cuts the series into patches and mixes information within and across patches. Tests showed it beat leading mixer and attention models on long-range forecasts. The design keeps the cost low, which matters when forecasts run every few minutes.
arxiv-2412-17776:
Davide Bilò and co-authors design data structures that answer network questions fast after links fail. A network may lose a few nodes or links, and planners still need sound answers at once. Such a structure pre-reads the network and a failure bound. It then answers for any small set of failures without a full re-run.

Three questions are covered: short paths with few links, paths of a set length, and tight groups of a set size. The core tool is a family of backup subnetworks that keep at least one good path. The new build queries that family far faster than past builds, at near the same size. Oracles for all three questions flow from it, with a clear speed gain for path queries.
arxiv-2412-17876:
Elgammal reads the spin of a proposed Z-prime boson from the angles of muon pairs in simulated collider data. The paper from twenty twenty-four uses electron-positron runs at the planned International Linear Collider. Low-mass muon pairs there come mostly from the Drell-Yan process, which leans forward-backward in a set way. New physics models bend that angular shape in their own ways.

The study tracks one angle in the Collins-Soper frame. A mono-Z-prime model, with fermionic dark matter in tow, interprets the mock data. No new signal is assumed found. Upper limits at a set confidence level then bound the masses of the model's particles. The spin-one nature of the Z-prime is the trait under the lens. The work shows how angular shapes can sort rival models before any discovery lands.
arxiv-2501-02676:
Penrose and Yang count parts in chance shape graphs at the dense edge. Points fall at chance in a tight zone with a smooth rim. A set span ties which points join by line in the graph. Three counts lead: whole parts, off-giant points, and lone points. Picks of the span make one count grow but at a slow pace. Mean lone counts grow vast in that pick frame as well.

All three counts then run near one mark in chance terms. That mark takes a closed form for flat zones of two parts. For three or more parts, a rim term joins the closed form. Spread and bell claims cap the counts for the high case. A Poisson in-feed case gets the same care in the work. Off-flat point spreads join the claim set in the close.
arxiv-2501-03076:
Levine and Friedman test in 2025 a deep idea about how quantum systems settle into balance. The eigenstate thermalization hypothesis says a small part of an excited system should look thermal on its own. They study free fermions linked to a reservoir through only a few narrow channels, called quantum point contacts.

With so few links, the small system's entanglement grows only with its edge length, not its volume, unlike a normal thermal system. At low energies the entropy followed the pattern of a one-dimensional system. Each added channel contributed a fixed, quantized share. The result shows that connection geometry can change even equilibrium properties, not just the time needed to reach them.
arxiv-2501-03676:
Zheng Chun builds on an offline reinforcement learning method, TD7, by adding ensemble Q-networks and a gradient diversity penalty drawn from another method. Offline learning trains from logged data alone, where out of sample acts can skew values. The work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The base method learns state action codes and replays key past steps first. Ensembles punish the actor for stray acts, which keeps it near the data. The diversity penalty spreads Q gradients, which further damps over high values for stray acts. A cloning term guides early training, then fades as the ensemble sharpens. Tests on robot control benchmarks beat past methods in speed and score.
arxiv-2501-04376:
Xinghe Fu and colleagues investigated why deepfake detectors fail on new material in 2025. The usual explanation blames differences between forgery techniques. Their investigation showed failures also appear when factors unrelated to forgery change, and they traced the problem to two biases detectors pick up during training.

The first bias is positional: detectors lean on where a suspicious region sits in the image, even in spots with no forgery. The second is content bias: detectors use irrelevant details such as background or hair to decide. To fight both, the authors add two branches that shuffle and mix the image tokens inside a transformer's hidden space, scrambling positions and content while keeping local structure. The aim is a detector that judges the forgery itself and generalizes more honestly.
arxiv-2501-05876:
Leandro Arosio and Matteo Fiacchi wrote a survey in two thousand twenty-five on a property of paths in curved spaces. In a well-behaved space, shortest paths that head toward the boundary should approach each other in a controlled way. That approaching geodesics property links the geometry of a space to maps of its edge at infinity.

The authors gather recent results and open questions on the property. They cover its use in studying two ways of adding a boundary to a space, and new results on how symmetries of the space move. They also give an example of a well-behaved complex domain where the property fails.
arxiv-2501-06476:
Xing Li, Ying-ying Sun, and Da-jun Zhang build a direct route to solutions of a classic wave equation. Their 2025 paper treats the Kadomtsev-Petviashvili equation, a model for shallow water waves. Their scheme is elliptic, built around the Lamé function from the theory of elliptic curves. It pairs an integral equation with a formula for wave solutions.

They check the scheme against the equation's known symmetry pairs. Careful study of real-valuedness leads to a Marchenko equation for the elliptic waves. A mechanism in the scheme yields smooth, real wave trains on a repeating background. Reductions then carry the results to two cousin equations, for water waves and long waves. Pictures of the solutions show solitons crossing on the periodic swell.
arxiv-2501-08276:
Pulkit Arora, Akbar Karimi, and Lucie Flek wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five on whether language models handle reworded text evenly across social groups. Models can be thrown off by small changes to their input. Most robustness work twists single words, while real variation follows the style of whole communities.

The team extended a question data set with paraphrases shaped by age and gender. They tested both whether models can write such paraphrases and whether they still understand the results. Checks covered word variety, fluency scores, and human judgment. Rewriting by demographic style changed model performance markedly, which the authors flag as a fairness concern.
arxiv-2501-08476:
Kuban, Nemitz, and Chahine build a simulation of quantum key distribution to check NASA's quantum communications software, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Sharing entangled particles over long distances could power future air and space links. NASA's analysis suite models such systems, but little measured data exists to confirm its predictions.

Key distribution experiments, by contrast, offer a rich published record. The team's simulation takes the suite's own input parameters and produces a link budget: key rates, error rates, and a correlation measure. Early comparisons with published experiments line up well, supporting the model's soundness. A verified suite will guide experiments at NASA's Glenn laboratory and possible future missions.
arxiv-2501-08676:
Anant Khandelwal published this study in 2025. It introduces FlexiClip, a tool for animating clipart characters with smooth, faithful motion. Earlier tools warp clip art well in single frames but stumble across time, giving jerky moves and bent shapes. Video generators trained on real footage also mishandle the flat clipart style. FlexiClip starts from curve-based motion paths, then adds three fixes.

Temporal corrections adjust the motion step by step to keep it smooth. Continuous-time modeling with flow equations cuts timing noise. A flow-matching loss, borrowed from generative network theory, polishes the transitions. Tests across many clipart types, people and animals included, show clean, natural movement. The author claims a new quality bar for free-form clipart animation, especially in fast or stretchy scenes.
arxiv-2501-09276:
The IceCube Collaboration reports a search for closely timed neutrino pairs and triples in a 2025 paper. IceCube is a huge detector buried in Antarctic ice that watches for neutrinos from space. Pairs or triples arriving close together could signal brief cosmic events, such as flares from distant objects.

The search uses eleven point four years of IceCube data, the longest run applied to this question by the team. Events are checked for clustering in time and direction beyond what random background would produce. A huge author list reflects the scale of running the observatory. Such searches test whether any cosmic sources flash repeatedly on short time scales in neutrinos.
arxiv-2501-10376:
Waleed El-Geresy, Christos Papavassiliou, and Deniz Gündüz study how to store data on memristors whose resistance drifts over time, in work the text dates to 2024. The catalog lists 2025. Memristors promise dense analog memory, but their stored values wander. The team proves a basic trade-off: longer-lived states cost more energy to write. They then treat storage as sending a message over a noisy, power-limited channel.

Their scheme codes images jointly for source and channel, trained end to end with a learned model of the drift. A new normalization layer lets the coder adapt to the starting resistance and the expected delay. The delay-aware network learned to spend energy wisely, keeping image quality high and even across delays. The authors frame the result as a design rule for analog memory.
arxiv-2501-11076:
Christopher Atherfold wrote a 2025 mathematics paper on random number-theoretic functions. A Rademacher random multiplicative function assigns each whole number a value built from fair coin flips at the primes. Analysts study weighted sums of such a function to understand how cancellation behaves. The paper pins down how large those sums can typically grow.

For almost every such random function, the author proves the sum up to any point stays below a modest power of a slowly growing log term. Yet he also shows that somewhere along the way, the sum must sometimes exceed a smaller threshold in the other direction. This mix differs from a cousin case studied before, because here a product over primes dominates the behavior. A sharper bound is proved for sums restricted to numbers with a large prime factor. The results refine the theory of random models for arithmetic functions.
arxiv-2501-11376:
Marko Pesut, a solo author, presents a study from twenty twenty-five on a twist to the standard model of particle physics. In his take, force groups act in unlike ways on light quarks and on the heavy third family. The Higgs boson is not a basic field here. It forms as a light relic of a new strong force that breaks a larger symmetry.

He shows how the Higgs field's energy shape can arise from loops of the new particles. That shape holds the tuning needed to split the weak scale from the strong scale. New flavoured force carriers must sit near the TeV scale. Colliders in the near term can hunt for their marks.
arxiv-2501-11676:
Tristan Daus and Elena Kozlikin computed the growth of cosmic structure in twenty twenty-five. They used Newtonian particle dynamics. They ran no simulation to do it. Their analytical framework treats gravitating particles in phase space as a field theory. It is a perturbative solution of the kinetic hierarchy. Its loop expansion has a natural truncation rule built in. From it they derived the nonlinear power spectrum of density fluctuations.

On big scales the analytic spectrum matches numeric simulations to very high precision. On mid and small scales it is off by about ten percent. The pair argue the gap is diagnostic, not fatal. If the perturbation theory is restructured, the fit on small scales should get much better. A firm analytic grip on how structure forms would add to brute-force cosmology simulations. It would show which physics drives each scale of the cosmos.
arxiv-2501-11976:
Michal Bizzarri, Miroslav Lávička, Rafael Sendra, and Jan Vršek ask when a spun surface admits a polynomial description. A surface of revolution comes from rotating a plane curve around an axis. Modelers want parametrizations built from polynomials, not messier functions. The team ties the surface's polynomiality to that of its generating curve.

When the curve qualifies, the surface does too, and the paper gives formulas to compute its polynomial parametrization over the complex numbers. Real parametrizations are harder, and the authors take first steps on existence and computation there. Quadrics, the simplest curved surfaces, get a complete real classification as a payoff. A conjecture covers the general case. The work serves geometric modeling, where polynomial patches are the currency of design tools.
arxiv-2501-12076:
Jacopo Nudo, Matteo Cinelli, Andrea Baronchelli, and Walter Quattrociocchi study how community size shapes talk on social media in a 2025 paper. Platforms now host public debate at a huge scale. The team asks whether the size of a platform or a thread changes how people join in and how long they stay.

They tracked user behavior across six platforms over more than three decades. Smaller platforms held richer, longer exchanges, while larger ones drew wider but briefer input. As communities grew, users were less likely to return to a thread. Niche spaces broke that rule, keeping strong repeat input. The authors link these patterns to how each platform is built.
arxiv-2501-12576:
Yunshu Liu and Lingjie Duan studied blockchain order books in twenty twenty-five, where miners match trades and may act selfishly. In these systems, buyers and sellers post trades with fees, and miners choose which to include in blocks. Selfish miners chase high fees and skip matches that would help overall welfare.

The authors give the first analytic study of fee choices and miner strategies here, proving the welfare loss can be unboundedly bad. Their fix is an adjustable block size mechanism that needs no change to the decentralized protocol and leaves fees and matching free. Despite missing information and mixed strategies, the mechanism keeps welfare loss well bounded, and hits the optimum for uniform-quantity trades like NFTs. Tests on a local Ethereum setup and real data confirm the gains.
arxiv-2501-13576:
Majid Rafiei, Mahsa Pourbafrani, and Wil van der Aalst tackle process checking across firms in a 2025 paper. Process mining compares how work actually runs against a model of how it should run. Doing that across company borders can expose miscommunication, but firms guard their data. Their method checks the shared process while keeping each firm's records private.

They test the idea on a simulated supply chain with three firms. Each firm runs one part, from buying to shipping, and fake event logs are made for each part and the whole chain. The method finds planted miscommunications and puts a cost on them, showing the approach can work without pooling raw data.
arxiv-2501-14176:
Micah Rentschler and Jesse Roberts show that a pre-trained Transformer, fine-tuned with reinforcement learning, can learn to solve new problems on its own, in a paper from 2025. The model practices across many episodes of varied tasks. Over time it gains a skill the authors call in-context reinforcement learning.

The trained model solved tasks it had never seen, using few attempts. It also did well on tasks outside its training range. Its gains did not depend much on the quality of its training examples. It could stitch together behaviors shown in its context and adapt when the rules of a task changed mid-stream. The authors present it as a general-purpose problem solver that improves its own answers.
arxiv-2501-15176:
Tristan van der Vlugt studies a counting question about infinite series in a 2025 mathematics paper. A conditionally convergent series can be thinned to a subseries that diverges, a classic fact. The subseries numbers ask how few index sets one must choose in advance so that every such series diverges on at least one of them.

Van der Vlugt turns the question around. Taking only index sets that are endless in both directions, he asks how the answer changes when the chosen sets must make every such series converge instead. That number turns out to be a cardinal characteristic of the continuum, one of the standard gauges of infinity's fine structure. He links his new numbers to several known ones and proves matching dual results.
arxiv-2501-15676:
Tuhin Paul, Aishee Chakraborty, Souvik Ghose, and Tapas Das study how matter falling into a black hole can mimic gravity itself. When gas streams steadily onto a black hole, small ripples in the flow travel like sound waves in a medium. Under the right conditions those ripples face their own horizon, a point they cannot cross, much like light at a real black hole.

The team builds steady, faster-than-sound inflow solutions for a hot, multi-species gas, using stand-in potentials for the black hole's pull, then nudges the flow to test stability. The nudges reveal an acoustic metric, a geometry for sound, with horizons they map using causal diagrams. They also track how the analogue surface gravity of that horizon shifts as the flow's settings change. The work feeds analogue gravity, the effort to study black hole physics through look-alike systems.
arxiv-2501-16176:
Tyler Sterling explains the physics of light from snapping shrimp in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. When these shrimp snap, they make bubbles that collapse and flash with light. The effect is a shrimp version of sonoluminescence, the light emitted by a collapsing bubble in a fluid.

Sterling studies the dynamics of such a bubble in detail. The collapse is so fast that no heat escapes, and the trapped gas grows hot enough to ionize. Light then comes from electrons striking ions and atoms, and from electrons rejoining ions. He shows how to compute the spectrum of the emitted light. That calculation explains the physical steps behind the shrimp's flash.
arxiv-2501-17576:
Patricia Bouyer, Srivathsan, and Vaishnavi Vishwanath wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It revisits model-checking for real-time systems through alternating timed automata, machines that track clocks and can flip between states in a game-like way.

Timed logics such as Metric Temporal Logic can be turned into one-clock versions of these automata, and checking a formula comes down to checking if the automaton is empty. Past emptiness tests rest on region builds that suit theory more than code. The authors add a deactivation move that switches a clock off in plain sight, sharpen the logic swap, and build zone-based tests. They give a fast entailment check and show the general check is NP-hard.
arxiv-2501-18176:
Chen-Xun Weng and eight co-authors test asymmetric relativistic zero knowledge proofs in two thousand twenty-five. Such proofs build trust with privacy, with no assumptions on compute limits. Past quantum sound forms needed too many rounds to run. Their cost in time and randomness blocked real use.

The new protocol uses relativistic bit commitments for its base. Its soundness ties to a known nonlocal game, CHSH. Rounds grow in a line with the edge count of the graph. A lab run finished all rounds in a flash of time. Randomness cost was large but far more sane than past forms.
arxiv-2501-18476:
Aditya Banerjee (2025) asks whether part of an isolated quantum system forgets its past as it settles. The standard picture treats each part as an open system bathed by the rest. If that bath erased memory steadily, the part's motion would be Markovian. Banerjee tested this on a mixed-field Ising chain pushed far from equilibrium. He followed the distances between a small subsystem's states at different times.

The distances did not decay in the clean, memory-free way. They carried clear signatures of memory, meaning the surroundings feed information back. The effect depended on the direction of the sudden change that started the motion. Jumps from the disordered side into the ordered side showed much stronger memory than the reverse. The classical distance measure behaved in a strikingly regular way. Banerjee offers rough arguments for the asymmetry. The work warns against assuming simple forgetting inside closed quantum systems.
arxiv-2502-01276:
Marcel Wever and co-authors wrote a paper from 2025 on explaining the tuning knobs of a learning algorithm with fair-share math. Tuning those knobs, called hyperparameters, decides much of a model's skill. Yet which knob matters, and how knobs interact, stays opaque, and black-box tuners give users little reason to trust them. The team borrows Shapley values from game theory, which split a team's payoff fairly among its players.

Their frame, named HyperSHAP, splits a model's score among the knobs that produced it. It also prices how pairs of knobs amplify or cancel each other. The split works knob by knob for one run, or pooled across many runs. Users can read it as an ablation guide, a measure of how much tuning headroom an algorithm holds, or a window on the tuner's own behavior. Tests across tuning benchmarks showed the readings are stable and usable.
arxiv-2502-01576:
Malik and co-authors test whether image encoders hardened on large datasets can shield multi-modal language models from visual attacks. Such models answer questions about images, but tiny crafted changes can fool them. Attacks can trigger false claims or slip past safety checks. Current defenses fine-tune the vision part on modest data with limits that cap gains. The team instead borrows classifiers already hardened at large scale.

Large, diverse attack training gave these encoders stronger resistance across many threat types. They held up where narrower defenses thinned out. The analysis weighs robustness against keeping general vision skill. Borrowing proven parts may beat training small defenses from scratch.
arxiv-2502-01676:
Man Luo and seven co-authors create the first benchmark for detecting toxic language in scientific peer review. Harsh feedback discourages authors and slows science, yet toxicity in reviews had no agreed definition or dataset. The team split the concept into four categories and had experts annotate reviews from the OpenReview platform.

They then benchmarked a dedicated toxicity model, a sentiment model, open-source language models, and two commercial ones. Prompt detail mattered enormously: leading models aligned poorly with human judgments under simple instructions but improved with detailed ones. Model confidence proved a useful filter, raising agreement when only confident calls were kept. The dataset and findings give the community a starting point.
arxiv-2502-02176:
Juma Kamulali, Benard Nsamba, and their colleagues introduce MAISTEP, a machine learning tool for dating stars, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. The tool reads a star's age, mass, and size from its air alone. Knowing host star ages matters because the census of planets depends on the stars they orbit.

Most planet hosts come with only atmospheric measures: surface heat, iron content, and brightness. MAISTEP trains four tree-based learning methods on a grid of star models, then blends their answers. Fed those three measures, it infers radius, mass, and age together. The authors run a detailed statistical check of how trustworthy the inferences are. They then apply the tool to stars that host giant planets and study how those ages spread out. The work offers planet hunters a sturdier way to date the stars behind their finds.
arxiv-2502-02576:
Mun Jung Jung and three co-authors propose a rare neutrino reaction as a yardstick for the DUNE experiment, in a 2025 physics paper. DUNE will shoot neutrinos through the Earth to study their shifts. Knowing the beam's strength well is key, and the muon neutrino share is the hardest part. In the reaction they study, a neutrino knocks a pion out of a nucleus in one clean piece, so the beam energy can be read back from the debris.

The cross section for the reaction can be tied to pion-argon scattering data by a known relation. That data could even be taken in DUNE's own near detector at the same time. Their fits suggest the beam peak could be pinned to within a few percent. The authors list the lab and theory work still needed to make the yardstick trustworthy.
arxiv-2502-04276:
Xin Li, Markus Lange-Hegermann, and Bogdan Raiţă present a study from twenty twenty-five on solving inverse tasks for linear partial differential equations with Gaussian processes. A Gaussian process can serve as a prior guess for the unknown field. Here the prior is built from deep algebra, not from a plain smooth kernel. That build is turned into code with an algebra package.

Their test task reads the wave speed from noisy data for the classic wave equation. The method hits high truth while it runs fast. The authors frame the gain as a blend of system theory and algebra based priors. Such tasks are core in physics, where the rules are known but key dials hide.
arxiv-2502-04576:
So Yeon Min and six co-authors teach AI agents to ask for help at the right time. Their twenty twenty-five paper starts from a human trait: we know our limits and seek aid only when needed. Language model agents lack that sense, and they either fail boldly or ask so often that they waste time.

The team trains a helper policy offline, with a fixed budget of interventions, like calls to a stronger model. Process reward models score the best moments to step in, using past trajectories. Tabular reinforcement learning then trains the helper on those labels. The offline design avoids costly calls during training and holds up on off-policy data.
arxiv-2502-05276:
Dennis Sweeney presents a 2025 math paper on the shapes hidden inside small semigroups. A semigroup is a set with an associative combining rule, like numbers under addition. Each finite one has a classifying space, a shape whose holes encode its algebra.

Sweeney built software that computes the integral homology of finite ones quickly, by using structure in projective resolutions. Running it over semigroups and monoids of small orders gave a trove of counterexamples. One finite aperiodic one carries large torsion in its homology. Two have Moore spaces as classifying shapes. Another has nonzero rational homology in infinitely many dimensions, which refutes conjectures by William Nico. The set of such shapes is also closed under suspension.
arxiv-2502-06276:
Kasun Weerasekara and co-authors simulate how uneven dust spread changes explosion strength in the standard twenty-liter test sphere, in this 2025 paper. Labs worldwide use this sphere to rate dust explosion hazards for industry. Inflow eddies push dust toward the wall before ignition, breaking the assumed even spread. The team modeled lycopodium dust blasts and checked the model against real data.

They define a simple score, Phi, for wall crowding, from zero for all-at-wall to one for perfectly even. As Phi drops from one, blast pressure first dips, then climbs. With heavy wall crowding, peak pressure rose slightly and its rise rate jumped a tenth over the even case. Middling crowding gave the weakest blasts. The authors warn test standards should account for distribution.
arxiv-2502-07476:
Shiquan Ren wrote a 2025 mathematics paper on bundles that persist over spaces of hard spheres. A configuration space lists all ways a set of spheres can sit in a region without overlap. As the spheres grow, some layouts vanish, and the space changes in steps.

Ren builds bundle structures that survive across these steps. Classic markers of such bundles, called characteristic classes, then give tests for embedding problems. One use is deciding when a space can sit inside another in a regular way. The Stiefel-Whitney and Chern classes serve as the main tools. The work links topology with hard questions in geometry and robotics paths.
arxiv-2502-07776:
Chenchen Gu, Xiang Lisa Li, Rohith Kuditipudi, Percy Liang, and Tatsunori Hashimoto audit commercial language model APIs for a side channel hiding in their speed. Prompt caching makes repeated prompts answer faster. If a cache is shared across users, timing becomes a leak: an attacker can probe what others asked by watching response times. The team built statistical audits to detect caching in the wild.

Seven providers, including the largest, show evidence of globally shared caches. The privacy implication is direct: strangers' prompts leave timing fingerprints. Timing also betrayed architecture: one provider's embedding model shows the signature of a decoder-only transformer, previously undisclosed. The authors press for transparency about caching policies. Efficiency features, they show, are never merely efficiency features when a service is shared.
arxiv-2502-07876:
Sean Benevedes, Ameen Ismail, and Thomas Steingasser propose solving the Higgs hierarchy problem by letting cosmology delete the universes that get it wrong. In their landscape, regions scan over Higgs mass values. Where the mass takes its natural large value, the Higgs potential has only a deep negative-energy minimum, and that region crunches out of existence.

Where the mass falls below a critical value, a metastable minimum with an ordinary cosmic history survives. The critical value is set by where the quartic coupling runs negative. The mechanism needs new TeV-scale physics, such as vector-like fermions, to work. Two example models are worked out, and proposed colliders could probe the relevant parameter space.
arxiv-2502-08476:
The five authors introduce low rank MSO, a fragment of monadic second-order logic in which set quantification is limited to vertex sets of bounded cutrank. They compare its expressive power with several other logics built for graph properties. Separator logic extends first-order logic with connectivity checks, while flip-connectivity and flip-reachability logic are analogues suited to dense graphs, proposed in this work.

Three results anchor the paper. On weakly sparse graph classes, low rank MSO matches separator logic, though not on all graphs. On classes of bounded VC dimension, it matches flip-connectivity logic, again not everywhere. On all graphs, it matches flip-reachability logic. That last result implies every undirected graph property expressible in low rank MSO can be decided in polynomial time, a concrete payoff for pinning down what the logic can say.
arxiv-2502-08976:
Robin Bowers, Elias Lindgren, and Bo Waggoner study costly search over many options in a theory paper from 2025. A decision maker can spend resources probing options, then pick one or a feasible set and collect the rewards. Each option hides its value behind a step-by-step search process modeled as a Markov chain on a graph.

Even simple cases of this problem are provably hard in the worst case. Still, the authors prove prophet-style guarantees for a simple sequential rule: probe each option fully as it arrives, keep it or drop it, then move on. For matroid limits the rule secures about half the best possible reward, and it yields fair mechanisms.
arxiv-2502-09276:
Carlos Melo and nine co-authors modeled transaction flow in a club-run blockchain to tune its speed, in a paper published in 2025. Such chains, run by known clubs, serve banks and trade, but waste and pace worry their keepers. Their model is a chance-based net that tracks each transaction step. It gives reply time bands at high confidence for a known chain build, Fabric.

Change tests show which dials move pace most. Block size alone could swing pace and reply times by up to three times. Keepers can thus test a change in the model before they touch the live network. The authors stress pace with lean resource use. The network serves as a what-if laboratory for chain administrators.
arxiv-2502-10076:
Samrik Chowdhury and co-authors present a 2025 method for sorting graphs that change over time. The hosted text lays out a way to layer such a graph by patterns that repeat across time, called temporal motifs. That layering turns a moving graph into a stack of still views at many scales, from fine to broad.

With that stack in place, tools built for still graphs can be used on time-based ones. The tools include persistent homology, which tracks how shapes in the data appear and vanish across scales, and recent kernel methods for layered graphs. The team shows the approach works on tasks that ask which class a time-based graph belongs to. The frame opens a new path for studying networks such as message traffic or contact patterns.
arxiv-2502-11776:
Koki Yanagida's paper from 2025 defines a new invariant for links, loops of knotted string sitting in the three-sphere. An invariant is a value that stays fixed while the link is bent, so it can tell links apart. The new one, the parabolic Dijkgraaf-Witten invariant, widens a reduced form set out earlier by Karuo.

Yanagida computes it for several links whose double covers match lens spaces, a well-known family of shapes. The paper also gives a way to read part of the invariant straight from a link diagram, the flat drawing of the knot. That shortcut makes the new tool usable without heavy machinery, and it ties knot theory to gauge-style counting methods.
arxiv-2502-13176:
Gulhan and co-authors wrote a paper in 2025 on BaKlaVa, a budgeted allocation approach for the key-value cache used by large language models processing long texts. The cache stores past computations so the model need not redo them, but it grows linearly with the length of the input, consuming scarce graphics memory. Earlier shortcuts treated the cache's many attention heads uniformly, clearing or compressing them by a single fixed rule.

BaKlaVa instead estimates the importance of each cache individually. A one-time profiling step then assigns each cache a share of a total memory budget. Important caches retain more of their data, while unimportant ones are trimmed harder. The team tested the approach on two widely used open models. It compressed the cache by up to seventy percent while keeping baseline performance, and at higher compression rates it improved accuracy by as much as tenfold over uniform methods.
arxiv-2502-14976:
Nastaran Darabi and colleagues shielded vision-language models from adversarial images in a 2025 paper. These models read pictures and text together, and tiny crafted changes to a picture can flip their answers. Older defenses cost heavy retraining, depend on one model's shape, or break when attackers adapt, so the team sought a filter that runs at use time with no retraining.

Their EigenShield uses random matrix theory to spot structured distortions in the model's internal features. A scoring rule separates feature directions that carry real meaning from those prone to carry attack noise, and the input is projected onto the clean directions. Attack success dropped sharply in tests, with no model changes needed. The method works across model designs.
arxiv-2502-15076:
Five authors wrote a computer vision paper in two thousand twenty-five on training self-driving systems with fake data. Real road data are costly to label, so simulators make scenes instead. The catch is that models trained on fake scenes often fail on real streets, a gap between the virtual and real worlds.

Using the CARLA simulator, the team built a pipeline that makes LiDAR point cloud scenes for finding objects in three dimensions. Random variation in the scenes helped the model transfer. A detector trained only on fake data did well on the real KITTI benchmark. A little real data for fine-tuning nearly matched full real training.
arxiv-2502-15876:
Michael Unger and Glennys Farrar wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five, per the author line in its text. It studies how our galaxy's magnetic field bends the paths of the most energetic cosmic rays, a bend that must be undone to find where they were born.

The authors first sum up how unsure the back-tracked paths are under a recent set of field models. They then give a fresh fit that adds glow from the Local Bubble, a nearby cavity, using a shell model for its field. They also show why two well-known field maps differ, tracing it to the halo part. Last, they back-track the top events seen by two big observatories. None points to a clear steady source, which hints that some came from brief, one-off blasts.
arxiv-2502-15976:
Luca Battaglia and Francisco Reyes-Sánchez published a 2025 mathematics paper on shaping surfaces to order. A classic problem asks: given a surface, can it be stretched so its curvature matches a prescribed pattern? Their version is knottier: the surface has a boundary, cone-like singular points, and corners. Both the surface's own curvature and the boundary's bending are prescribed at once.

The authors solve it with a variational method, recasting the geometry as the search for a best function, an approach built for smooth surfaces and extended here to the singular case. They state this is the first result of its kind for surfaces with singularities. Prescribed-curvature problems sit at the junction of geometry and partial differential equations, with uses from materials to relativity. Handling cones and corners matters because surfaces are rarely perfectly smooth. The paper widens the map of what can be shaped to order.
arxiv-2502-16276:
Vu Hong Quan and two co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on best choices when goals clash and data is unsure. Their problem has many aims at once, range based values, and rough, non-smooth terms. Facts in the rules may also be off. They work with the robust twin of the problem, the form that guards against the worst data shifts.

They set out kinds of near best answers for that twin, in near and near regular forms. With a penalty trick, they show one kind exists and meets a key set of terms to a set level of truth. They then give terms that suffice for such answers. A dual form of the problem is built and its links to the primal are checked.
arxiv-2502-18276:
Pinaki Mondal revisits a classic counting problem in algebra in a solo twenty twenty-five paper. When a system of polynomial equations has more solutions bunched together than expected, we must assign each bunch a weight, called a multiplicity. Old fixes by Severi and Lazarsfeld treated all bunches alike.

Mondal breaks that symmetry and defines an ordered multiplicity, where the order in which equations are used matters. He gives an explicit form for this new weight. The payoff is a step-by-step route to count lone solutions, with bounds in the style of Bernstein and Kushnirenko. As a test, he counts the lines that touch four general spheres in space, and gets the known count of twelve.
arxiv-2502-18576:
Jaemarie Solyst and seven co-authors study teens as AI auditors in twenty twenty-five. Young people use AI daily yet are shut out of responsible AI practice. Auditing, the hunt for problematic system behavior, is one place their perspective is missing. The authors ran a workshop study with seventeen teens.

The teens audited AI tools they actually meet: image generators, search autocomplete, and image search. Support came from critical AI literacy scaffolding. Guided discussion of AI ethics and a dedicated auditing tool backed their work. The teens produced quality insights, the authors found. Their hobbies, identities, and age-specific experience shaped what they caught. Readers in responsible AI get proof that youth can audit meaningfully, not just be studied.
arxiv-2502-20176:
Xinran Liu, Zhenhua Feng, Diptesh Kanojia, and Wenwu Wang wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It makes full-body dance from music with a diffusion model fed by a music foundation model.

Past dance makers lean on hand-made music traits. The new method blends the deep traits of a foundation model with the hand traits, so high sense and fine timing both guide the steps. The team checks four foundation models and two hand trait sets. Their blend makes the most true-to-life dance and the best match to the beat and mood of the track. The work was shown at a NeurIPS workshop.
arxiv-2503-00776:
Yun Min Song, Kangmin Lee, and Jae Kyoung Kim review a shortcut in cell modeling in this 2025 paper. Modelers of chemical networks inside cells often shrink big models with a steady-state shortcut. The total version of that shortcut is trusted for its accuracy in smooth, average models. Random, molecule-by-molecule models are another matter.

The review shows the shortcut can warp behavior in random models. The warp appears even where the shortcut is strictly valid in the smooth setting. False conclusions about cell dynamics can follow. The authors urge modelers to check the shortcut case by case in random simulations. Ease of use, they argue, is no proof of safety.
arxiv-2503-02076:
Shanting Wang, Panagiotis Typaldos, and Andreas Malikopoulos present CorrA for obstacle avoidance in two thousand twenty-five. Self driving cars must dodge moving blocks in real time. CorrA pairs a large language model with model predictive control. The model sets the bounds of a safe corridor around each block.

Sigmoid shaped bounds define that corridor in a smooth way. Real time car data reshape the bounds as the scene shifts. That trims the state space the controller must search. An optimal control solver then finds a crash free, near best path. Tests in simulation and real runs beat a plain control baseline.
arxiv-2503-02176:
Kaoru Teranishi and Takashi Tanaka designed a way in 2025 to outsource control calculations without revealing them. A dynamic controller, the algorithm steering a machine in real time, may be run on remote servers for power or convenience, but its parameters, state, and signals can be sensitive. Their protocol splits the computation between two servers using secret sharing, so neither server ever sees the secrets it helps compute with.

Earlier encrypted control schemes worked with a single server and needed periodic decryption of the controller state or re-encryption of inputs, which caps how long they can run. The two-party design runs indefinitely with no such resets. The authors show its control performance can be made arbitrarily close to an unencrypted controller's, present refinements that cut communication costs, and demonstrate the protocol numerically on proportional-integral-derivative and observer-based controllers.
arxiv-2503-02676:
Park, Cho, Kim, and Lee assess the Electron-Ion Collider as a facility for pentaquark measurements, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Pentaquarks are exotic particles made of five quarks. The collider offers high energy plus polarized beams for precision study. One heavy pentaquark, Pc forty-three twelve, serves as the test case.

Production rates are computed under different spin-parity guesses. A vector meson dominance model keeps the approach parameter-free. Beam spin asymmetry and decay polarization can pin down spin and parity. The ePIC detector can measure both quantities accurately. Other heavy pentaquarks and nuclear matter studies extend the program.
arxiv-2503-03076:
The Raychaudhuri equation tracks how a bundle of paths through spacetime spreads or focuses, and it anchors much of cosmic evolution theory. The five authors extend it with a non-affine parametrization inside the k-essence framework, which lets the flow curves stray from geodesics. Working with a DBI-type k-essence Lagrangian, they derive a modified equation that produces emergent repulsive effects in the expansion of the universe.

Their Bayesian analysis, checked against cosmological data, supports the scaling link between the k-essence field's rate of change and the cosmic scale factor. The modified equation can address the Hubble tension and predicts a naturally evolving dark energy equation of state. Read as an anti-damped harmonic oscillator, it shows a caustic avoidance signature that may hint at classical or quantum-like effects. The authors present the work as a bridge between scalar field dynamics and modified gravity.
arxiv-2503-03276:
Jiayi Zhang and seven co-authors present a hybrid neural model for city traffic in a paper from 2025. Classic routing algorithms work on static maps but struggle with the shifting, tangled flow of real streets. Their model joins graph convolutional networks, which learn the street network's shape, with Kolmogorov-Arnold networks, which flex to fit curved patterns in the flow data.

Tests used real traffic data from the Baltimore area. The model matched rival methods on accuracy and handled noisy, irregular data better. It also rerouted flow in ways that eased congestion and adapted to a shock event, the collapse of a major bridge.
arxiv-2503-04276:
Julius Reinhard, Felix Wiesner, and co-workers showed soft X-ray depth imaging driven by a tabletop light source in a 2025 paper. High-harmonic making produces coherent extreme ultraviolet light in the lab, but its speed falls toward higher photon energies. Blocking use in the soft X-ray water window. The band where carbon absorbs strongly and water stays transparent, ideal for imaging living and layered samples. The team pushed a high-flux harmonic source across that whole band anyway.

With it they performed soft X-ray coherence tomography, adapted from the optical technique, reading depth shapes inside a layered heterostructure without destroying it. The broadband, noise-resistant method reached an axial resolution of about twelve nanometers. Lab-scale sources that image in the water window could bring such analysis to plain facilities.
arxiv-2503-05176:
Shuxiang Xu and a team of co-authors study a nickel-based material under high pressure, in two thousand twenty-five. The material belongs to a rare family that can carry current with no resistance. Pressure is applied with diamond tools, which makes close study of its states hard.

The team used fast light pulses to watch the material as pressure rose. A wave pattern in the material faded with pressure and vanished near a point where its structure changed. Two forms of that wave stayed locked together as pressure grew. Past that point, a small energy gap appeared at low heat, in line with pairing for the no-resistance state. The two states seem to compete strongly.
arxiv-2503-11076:
Pinghui Huang and Xue-Ning Bai wrote a 2025 astronomy paper on how dust clumps in the outer parts of planet-forming disks. Clumping dust is the first step toward building planetesimals, the seeds of planets, yet the process is uncertain. A famous mechanism, the streaming instability, can gather dust, but the outer disk stirs its gas with other instabilities.

The authors ran a three-dimensional global simulation with a leading fluid code, refined enough to hold all four instabilities at work. Shear in the gas set the overall motion, with a breathing pattern strengthened by the dust itself. Dust settled into a thin midplane layer crowded with small vortices. Strong clumps appeared, likely where the streaming effect and a wavy instability acted together. Only a small share of vortices held clumps dense enough to form planetesimals. Finer grids made clumping stronger still, so the process had not settled.
arxiv-2503-11276:
Edward Pearce-Crump builds neural networks whose outputs respect the symmetries of symmetric tensors. The paper from twenty twenty-five notes that such tensors fill statistics, machine learning, and graph theory. They also serve physics, chemistry, and materials work. Past symmetry-aware models chased Euclidean motions and skipped symmetric tensor inputs. Permutation symmetry, where swapping indices changes nothing, is the trait here.

Pearce-Crump gives two full accounts of all linear maps with this trait between symmetric power spaces. No other linear maps qualify. Tests on two tasks show the maps learn from far less data than plain multilayer networks. They also hint at skill transfer to tensors of new sizes. The work hands modelers a complete parts list for this symmetry class.
arxiv-2503-11376:
Panggih Kusuma Ningrum and co-authors present a system for spotting uncertainty in science writing in a 2025 paper. Scientists often hedge claims with words that show doubt, and finding those spots helps search and text mining. Their system, called UnScientify, uses a weakly supervised method, so it needs little hand-labeled data.

The system matches word patterns, parses complex sentences, and checks who a claim is tied to. In tests, it scored higher on accuracy than modern large language models, reaching a score of about zero point eight one. The authors stress the trade-offs in the result. A plain rule-based tool can be cheap, clear, and easy to adapt to a field. For this narrow task, they argue, the older style still has real strengths.
arxiv-2503-11776:
Paula Benaglia and five co-authors present radio observations of a rare pair of giant stars in a 2025 paper. The two stars in HD 93129A blow strong winds that crash into each other. That crash zone glows at radio wavelengths and speeds up tiny particles. The pair recently passed their closest point in a very long orbit.

The team watched the system for over a year at three radio bands, and added older data. Brightness rose about fourfold over fifteen years, then fell again. Their fits suggest the magnetic field grew stronger near the closest pass. They also measured radio glow from other giant star pairs in the same field.
arxiv-2503-11976:
Patrick Martin and Radmila Sazdanović study hidden twists, called torsion, inside two related algebraic tools for measuring the shape of networks, in a 2025 paper. The tools are magnitude homology and its Eulerian variant, which sort the paths in a graph into algebraic groups. Torsion in those groups signals subtle structure that plain counting misses.

Building on three lines of earlier work, the authors give two proofs that torsion does occur in the Eulerian version. They also describe what kinds of torsion appear and what orders it can take. Worked computations for several families of graphs make the abstract claims concrete. The paper ties the two homology theories closer together and gives researchers a sharper picture of what these invariants can detect in a finite graph.
arxiv-2503-13176:
Rui Wang, Quentin Lohmeyer, Mirko Meboldt, and Siyu Tang rebuild clean three-dimensional scenes from messy real captures in a 2025 computer vision study. People walking through a scan, objects that move, and other clutter end up baked into ordinary reconstructions, ruining them for design or measurement. Their framework separates the scene into a static part and a dynamic part inside a Gaussian splatting representation, the current fast standard for photo-real scenes.

The split is learned self-supervised, without hand labels for what moves. Distractor-free models from ordinary walkthrough videos suit product design review and robot mapping.
arxiv-2503-13576:
Ziqiang Li and four co-authors survey how researchers teach image generators specific visual concepts, in a 2025 paper. Text prompts alone cannot pin down a particular face, style, or object. So a field has grown around mining concepts from reference images and feeding them to diffusion models alongside words.

The survey sorts the field into four pursuits. Concept learning captures a new idea from a few pictures. Concept erasing removes unwanted notions, from copyrighted styles to unsafe content. Decomposition splits a pictured concept into parts, and combination merges several learned concepts into one scene. For each, the authors explain the core techniques. They close with open challenges, offering newcomers a map of a fast-moving corner of generative AI.
arxiv-2503-14376:
Maximilian Beck and co-authors present faster software kernels for linear recurrent networks in this 2025 paper. Such networks scale gently with sequence length and now rival transformers at language modeling. In practice, though, speed needs hand-tuned kernels like the famous Flash Attention. A prior kernel for linear networks split sequences into chunks, but small chunks forced many states into memory.

Their Tiled Flash Linear Attention adds a second level of splitting inside each chunk. That lifts chunk size limits and keeps the chip's math units busy.
