They apply it to the xLSTM network with matrix memory, plus a slimmed variant with a simpler gate. Benchmarks beat Flash Attention, plain linear attention, and Mamba kernels. The authors claim a new speed mark for long-context building blocks.
arxiv-2503-14776:
Parameshwar Pasnoori, Ari Mizel, and Patrick Azaria solve a one-dimensional model in twenty twenty-five. The massive Thirring model is equivalent to the sine-Gordon model, a classic pair in quantum physics. They solve it under two kinds of Dirichlet boundary conditions: open, and twisted open. A duality symmetry links the two setups.

The symmetry swaps the sign of the bare mass while swapping the boundary type. For negative mass with open boundaries, the system sits in a trivial phase with a unique ground state. With twisted boundaries at the same mass, it enters a topological phase. That phase hosts zero energy modes pinned at each end. Positive mass reverses the pairing, as the duality demands. Readers get a full boundary spectrum for a textbook model.
arxiv-2503-15076:
Lynnyngs Kelly Arruda and Dmitry E. Pelinovsky wrote a math paper in two thousand twenty-five on wave patterns in a nonlinear equation. The equation is the defocusing modified Korteweg-de Vries equation, used for waves in some physical settings. They study a wave that travels and repeats as it moves.

The authors describe that wave with special functions based on theta functions, and they derive the linked functions for the Lax system behind the equation. Their main result is a new solution. It describes a kink breather, a sharp step joined to a pulsing wave, moving on the traveling wave background. The work adds exact forms for a class of complex wave motion.
arxiv-2503-15776:
Alice Chen, Phil Halper, and Niayesh Afshordi surveyed physicists about black holes and fundamental physics in two thousand twenty-five. The poll was taken at a two thousand twenty-four conference in Copenhagen called Black Holes Inside and Out. It aimed to snapshot expert attitudes for historians and sociologists of science.

Eighty-five completed surveys came back from one hundred fifty-one registered participants. Questions covered contested topics like black holes and dark energy. Leading ideas such as the cosmological constant, inflation, and string theory each won less than a majority. The only majority view, at sixty-eight percent, was that the Big Bang means the universe evolved from a hot dense state, not an absolute beginning.
arxiv-2503-16476:
Tsvetomila Mihaylova and colleagues staged traffic conflicts between self-driving cars and human drivers in a 2025 paper. Shared roads force automated and human drivers to negotiate, and misunderstandings at that interface cause the riskiest moments. Using the CARLA driving simulator, the team built a set of exemplary conflict scenarios that arise under shared autonomy.

The scenarios probe how driver behavior and split-second decisions affect safety and traffic flow when both kinds of driver must react. The toolkit is deliberately simple and extendable, so other groups can add conflicts and rerun them. Situation awareness researchers gain a shared stage for testing how machines and people read each other's intentions.
arxiv-2503-17376:
Douglas Plummer and five co-authors review brain-like computing hardware in twenty twenty-five. Demand for computing keeps rising fast with AI, machine learning, and connected devices. That growth calls for new building blocks that save energy and scale well. Neuromorphic computing, modeled on the brain, is one such path.

The review covers two-dimensional spintronics, which uses electron spin in atom-thin materials. Methods discussed include spin-orbit torque, magnetic tunnel junctions, and skyrmions. New layered materials can join memory and logic at the atomic scale. The authors stress both how far the field has come and what still blocks real use. Readers get a survey aimed at scale and energy efficiency above all.
arxiv-2503-17576:
Zeynab Aghabazaz, Michael Daniels, Donald Lloyd-Jones, and Juned Siddique build a joint statistical model of cardiovascular risk in a two thousand twenty-five biostatistics paper. Risk factors, medications, and fatal events evolve as one, and modeling them apart loses information.

Their Bayesian approach links longitudinal trajectories of risk factors with medication use over time and with time-to-death results. It handles missing medication status and treatment switching as explicit uncertainties rather than nuisances. Applied to a cardiovascular cohort study, the model captures detailed temporal dynamics and improves prediction of events. The authors aim at personalized intervention plans grounded in how risk and treatment in fact unfold.
arxiv-2503-17776:
Zewen Zhang, Qinyuan Zheng, and colleagues study a lattice model with three internal flavors in a 2025 physics study. Ultracold alkaline-earth atoms in optical lattices let experimenters tune such models closely. The Fermi-Hubbard model describes particles that hop between sites and repel when sharing one, and extra symmetry across flavors enriches its behavior.

Most theory assumes equal flavor populations and strong coupling limits. Real experiments drift from both, so the authors examine flavor imbalance away from those limits. Their ground-state results show how the model's phases respond to imbalance. That response tells experimenters which effects are robust and which are artifacts of ideal settings.
arxiv-2503-18076:
Somnath Roy and co-authors adapt, in twenty twenty-five, speculative decoding from text generation to classification. Speculative decoding uses small draft models to propose answers that a big model checks. Their framework flips that idea: up to three lightweight worker models predict class labels independently. When a majority agree, the label is accepted, skipping the expensive judge model. When they disagree, the judge decides. This balances efficiency and accuracy, they argue.

They found small three-billion-parameter chat models align with judges about as well as larger seven-billion models after tuning. The best small worker pair agreed with judges on eighty to eighty-three percent of sentiment cases. Harder ticket-similarity cases ranged from fifty to eighty percent. The design confines costly judging to hard cases.
arxiv-2503-19476:
Chuqin Geng, Ziyu Zhao, Zhaoyue Wang, Haolin Ye, Yuhe Jiang, and Xujie Si explain graph neural networks with logical rules that stay tied to real data, in a 2025 paper. Rule-based explanations promise global clarity about a model. Many are scored in an abstract concept space, though. Their final form, a highlighted subgraph, may mislead users. The team's framework builds rules from predicates matched to message passing. That structure keeps explanations grounded by design.

They also define a grounded fidelity score. It judges explanations in their final graph form, not the abstract one. Coverage and validity measures join it. Across experiments, the method beat rivals on grounded fidelity by over twenty percent. It also ran ten to one hundred times faster. Scaling held up on larger graphs. The authors release their code openly. They argue faithfulness must be checked where users actually look. The work targets explainable AI practice.
arxiv-2503-21176:
Machine learning potentials are usually built in Python, but most molecular dynamics software is written in lower-level languages, which makes the two awkward to combine. Learning potentials also tend to skip long-range electrostatics, a gap that hurts accuracy when flexible charges matter. Charge equilibration models fix that, yet they need iterative solvers with tight convergence, which costs time and threatens stability.

The five authors present a scalable Python version of a shadow molecular dynamics scheme built on charge equilibration. It avoids the convergence problem while keeping long-term energy stability and accurate properties. They add a fast neighbor list, Particle Mesh Ewald, and classic Ewald summation, powered on GPUs by Triton and PyTorch. The library runs fast charge equilibration for systems with hundreds of thousands of atoms, aiming to be friendly for users building learning potentials.
arxiv-2503-21376:
Sangeeta Sharma and four co-authors show that saddle points in the electronic structure of graphene can be used to write information with laser light. Their paper came out in 2025. Graphene is a single layer of carbon atoms, and its energy landscape has both valleys and saddle points, which are passes between peaks.

Valleys were already known as carriers of binary information states. The team shows that light with a set polarization excites two of the three saddle points, creating three possible excited configurations. Which configuration appears depends on the direction of the light's polarization. The effect proved robust, working both for very short strong pulses and for longer pulse trains. The same idea should apply to related single-layer materials.
arxiv-2503-21876:
Edward Zhang and a large mission team forecast what the SPHEREx space telescope will reveal about a key dust molecule family in nearby galaxies. Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons glow at specific infrared wavelengths, and their shortest band sits inside SPHEREx's all-sky spectrophotometric survey range. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team simulated galaxy spectra to test how well the mission can measure the band. Galaxies out to moderate redshifts are covered. Detectability depends on stellar mass and star formation rate.

For massive, actively star-forming galaxies nearby, the band flux should be measurable to about thirty percent accuracy. More distant systems need to be bigger and busier to register. The thresholds are tabulated across redshift slices. The work tells the mission team which galaxy populations will yield dust chemistry, and where stacking or follow-up will be needed.
arxiv-2503-23176:
Adiesha Liyanage and co-authors wrote a 2025 computer science paper on the hard core of feature matching for malware hunting. Low level malware checks can be cast as a search for a pattern of colored blocks inside a program. Each block holds one key instruction, and a match must line up colors while the key signs form a reshuffle of each other.

The authors name three forms of the problem, from the loose general one to a strict form that demands a full pattern match. The strict form, they prove, is NP-complete, and so is the general one. Even ruling that no part of a pattern shows up is hard in a dual sense. Their upshot is blunt: feature matching tools face hard limits in theory.
arxiv-2503-23476:
Janmejoy Sarkar and a large team of co-authors describe the testing and tuning of a solar telescope flown on India's Aditya-L1 mission, in a 2025 paper. The telescope takes pictures of the Sun in ultraviolet light, a band that reveals the Sun's lower atmosphere. Ground and in-flight checks were needed before its data could be trusted.

The team compares test results with the design targets and explains how raw readings are turned into clean data. Nearly every target was met. The one miss was sharpness: fine detail came out at a scale a bit coarser than hoped, which limits only the finest brightness measures. Even so, the authors say the telescope opens a fresh window on the Sun.
arxiv-2504-00176:
Marco Canducci and six co-authors ask which traits split two groups in twenty twenty-five. A class task is hard when the training set is small, the traits are many, and the class scores overlap a lot. When two split groups share the same task, the aim of the work shifts. What counts most is which traits best split how the task plays out in each group.

Their tool, Discriminative Subspace Emersion, grows subspace learning into a broad trait rank plan. It finds the traits that count most to tell how the two groups make their class calls. The plan builds on clear learners with near straight cut lines. Careful tuning and trait rank scores do most of the hard work. The tool lets you set side by side how a choice is made in each group, and not just how right that choice is.
arxiv-2504-01076:
Chiu and co-authors weigh galaxy clusters found by an X-ray sky survey and study their central galaxies, in a research paper from 2025. The clusters come from the first data release of the eROSITA survey, taken with a telescope aboard the SRG space observatory. The team used images from the Hyper Suprime-Cam program on the Subaru telescope.

Weak lensing, the slight bending of light by mass, let the team weigh 96 clusters from the shape changes in background galaxies. They also fit the light of the brightest central galaxy in 101 clusters to get its star mass. The central galaxy's star mass at a fixed cluster mass has grown only modestly since early times, by about 20 percent. That pattern fits a view where most of those stars formed very early.
arxiv-2504-01176:
Krzysztof Szczygielski, writing alone in two thousand twenty-five, spells out covariant decomposable maps between C-star algebras. Such maps are the math backbone of quantum moves that respect a symmetry.

The main result is a dilation theorem for covariant positive decomposable maps, building on a classic nineteen seventy-nine result of Scutaru. As a case study, Szczygielski spells out the operator sum form of maps on complex matrix algebras that commute with the maximal commutative subgroup of the unitary group. The paper then links to how quantum systems change over time, giving needed and enough settings for decomposably divisible quantum evolution families to be covariant.
arxiv-2504-02476:
Nativ Ben-Yeda, Kfir Blum, and Inbar Havilio wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It uses the spread of globular clusters, dense balls of stars, as a probe of the dark matter halos around their host galaxies.

Clusters are heavy test particles that plow through the halo. Drag from the halo matter, called dynamical friction, shrinks their orbits over time, which gives a test of cold dark matter past mean-field checks. The team ran body simulations and quick models across many starts. Data from two diffuse galaxies and the Fornax dwarf show halos are there, in line with star motion data. One galaxy is too spread out to bind the answer.
arxiv-2504-02676:
Tong introduces Snow, a broadcast protocol that lets cloud computers share messages without a fixed tree of senders. Tree broadcasts wobble when machines join or leave, and gossip methods waste bandwidth while only promising probable delivery. Cloud clusters churn constantly, so both flaws bite.

Snow lets each node forward messages based on its own view of the membership. A balanced multi-way tree then forms on its own, with leaf depths differing by at most one. Tests under churn showed reliable delivery and steady delay. The protocol adds no redundant copies to get there. Tong offers Snow as a fit for large distributed applications that cannot pause for repairs.
arxiv-2504-04876: Peter Danchev, Brendan Goldsmith, and Patrick Keef characterize two recently defined classes of abelian groups in a 2025 math paper. The classes, co-Bassian groups and their generalized form, were introduced by the third author in 2024. The paper asks which of these groups keep their defining property in two stronger senses: hereditarily, under subgroups, and in the super form. The authors find necessary and sufficient conditions for both cases. The result sharpens the picture of how these classes are structured.
arxiv-2504-05676:
William Hutchins and co-authors predict a new route by which heat can cross the border between a metal and a non-metal, in a 2025 paper. When a metal film is driven hard, its electrons can run far hotter than its lattice. In that state, the team argues, heat may leap the border as faint near-field radiation stirred by the hot electrons, without passing through the lattice at all.

Using the standard theory of fluctuating fields, they compute the radiated heat flow across a tungsten film on a boron nitride base. At an electron temperature of 5,000 degrees, the radiated conductance passed 300 units and rivaled the normal conducted flow. The size of the effect depends on how the electrons scatter. The authors say heat models for fast, hot electronics should count this channel alongside the usual ones.
arxiv-2504-06076:
Dhruv Mubayi and Nicholas Spanier pin down a Ramsey number for triple systems, confirming a conjecture posed by six researchers. Ramsey numbers measure how large a structure must be before a chosen pattern or its complement's pattern becomes unavoidable. Here the pattern is a small four-vertex triple system with three edges, and the complement pattern is a star: many triples sharing one common vertex.

The team proves the Ramsey number grows like the square of the star's size divided by its logarithm. The result generalizes a famous bound for the graph Ramsey number of a triangle against a star. That link is structural: fixing one vertex in a triple system avoiding the small pattern leaves a triangle-free graph. The proof adapts a pseudorandom refinement of the classic graph argument, following a route opened by Guo and Warnke.
arxiv-2504-07576:
Bernard Julia wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five as the sole author, per its byline. It traces the road from general relativity to maximal supergravity, and the web of symmetry and duality that links them.

The tale runs through ten and eleven dimensions and down again by torus cuts. At each stage large exceptional duality groups appear, in a strikingly even pattern. Plain general relativity sits as the plainest case, tied to the real world. Shrunk to two dimensions, affine Kac-Moody groups rule and the theory turns integrable. At one dimension, hyperbolic groups bring chaos. Borcherds forms then let all matter laws be written as twisted self-duality. Seven open challenges close the piece.
arxiv-2504-09676:
Jaya Maithil and eleven colleagues study jets of matter blasting from two quasars seen as they were when the universe was young, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Jets with clear X-ray extent are well studied nearby but barely explored at such distances.

Using data from the Chandra X-ray telescope, the team confirms extended jets, thousands of light-years long, in both quasars. Radio follow-up observations then pin down how fast and how angled the jets are. Those details let the authors estimate the energy the jets carry. The main goal is to test what makes the jets glow in X-rays. One candidate is X-rays produced when fast electrons in the jet bounce photons of the cosmic microwave background up to high energies. Distant jets, where that background was denser, are the natural place to check.
arxiv-2504-09876:
Tran Quoc Khanh Le and seven co-authors present a 2025 paper on segmenting fetal ultrasound images when labeled examples are scarce. Outlining the cervix in these scans is hard: contrast is low, shadows intrude, and borders blur. Fully supervised networks need large annotated sets that clinics rarely have. Their framework, HDC, learns from unlabeled scans too, using a single teacher model rather than several.

A hierarchical distillation scheme guides the student with two losses. One aligns feature representations between teacher and student. The other uses mutual information to steady the student against noisy guidance. The design cuts computing cost while fighting the confirmation bias that plagues teacher-student setups. On two fetal ultrasound data sets the method matched multi-teacher rivals with less overhead. The authors target practical semi-supervised segmentation for clinical imaging.
arxiv-2504-10276:
Lauren Olson and colleagues surveyed who carries the flag for ethics in software teams in 2025. Ethical concerns compete with profit-first market pressures inside companies, and the industry's demographic imbalance makes it important to know whether a practitioner's own background changes what they notice and push for. The team surveyed over two hundred software practitioners across roles, industries, and countries about the concerns they see, rank, and try to address.

The results show sharp demographic disparities. Practitioners from marginalized groups, including women, Black, Indigenous, and people of color, and disabled practitioners, reported ethical concerns more often than their peers. They also showed heightened sensitivity to how ethics is implemented in practice. The authors use these findings to identify the critical barriers to weaving ethics into development and to assess how much capacity practitioners actually have to push back.
arxiv-2504-11876:
Giacomo Colombo proves smoothness results for the Stefan problem, a classic model of melting and freezing. The paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. The model tracks a moving boundary between phases, such as ice and water. That free boundary can have singular points where it kinks. Colombo asks how bad those points can be over time. The setting here is four space dimensions plus time.

He shows the boundary is a smooth three-dimensional surface at almost every time. The singular set splits into two parts with distinct shapes. One part lies on a single smooth surface whose bad times form a tiny set. The other part is thin in a parabolic counting sense. The proof extends known results to this higher dimension. It sharpens the picture of phase change geometry.
arxiv-2504-12476:
Andreas Jungherr and Adrian Rauchfleisch survey what people in Germany and the United States expect from AI moderation. Their 2025 paper asks how well AI systems should match public values. Generative AI has raised public hopes and worries alike. Little was known about which alignment goals people actually back.

About eighteen hundred Germans and seventeen hundred fifty-six Americans answered. They rated four goals: accuracy, safety, bias reduction, and uplifting visions of society. Americans used AI more and backed every goal more strongly. Accuracy and safety won the widest support in both lands. Fairness and vision goals drew cooler backing, above all in Germany, where speech attitudes split views.
arxiv-2504-12876:
XinXin Qi and Hao Sun present a 2025 paper on a dark matter model with two kinds of dark particles. One is a scalar particle and the other a heavy neutral fermion, held apart by a combined symmetry rule. An extra scalar field gives the fermion its mass when the symmetry breaks, and brings a new Higgs-like particle. The team scans the model's options under the known cosmic dark matter amount.

The order of the new particles' masses changes which reactions matter. When the fermion is lightest, its creation runs through normally forbidden channels. Combining limits from Higgs decays, cosmic abundance, and direct detection searches narrows the space. Direct detection gives the tightest squeeze overall. The authors map which mass ranges survive all checks. Their work guides searches for multi-part dark sectors.
arxiv-2504-13176:
Fei Shen and five co-authors present a framework for generating clothing images in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Fashion designers want fine control over a garment's shape, color, and logo placement. Earlier generators took only one condition at a time, which limits design work. Their system, IMAGGarment, accepts several conditions at once. It trains in two stages to handle global look and local detail apart.

The first stage models the overall silhouette and color with a mixed attention design. The second stage adds user logos and spatial constraints with care. The two stages join into one end-to-end tool. Output images aim for high fidelity to the brief. The work serves digital apparel and personalized fashion design.
arxiv-2504-13376:
Aitor Gómez-Tejedor, Eneko Osaba, and Esther Villar-Rodriguez wrote this computer science paper, published in 2025. It studies the unglamorous step that decides whether quantum annealers succeed: squeezing a problem's variables onto the machine's fixed wiring.

Annealers solve problems shaped like their hardware easily, but foreign shapes must be embedded, chaining several physical qubits per variable. The authors first measured how embedding quality drives results on D-Wave machines. Longer average chains clearly tracked worse solution errors. They then graded the standard embedding tool, Minorminer, on random graphs for quality, robustness, and speed. A deterministic clique embedder served as the worst-case yardstick. The verdict: the standard tool leaves significant room for improvement, and embedding deserves research attention equal to the hardware itself.
arxiv-2504-13476:
Jiadong Lou, Bingqing Liu, Yuanheng Xiong, Xiaodong Zhang, and Xu Yuan use a generative model to read plankton levels in coastal water from satellite color, in a 2025 paper. Tiny floating plants tint the sea in subtle ways that sensitive space sensors can catch. Two NASA missions now gather such rainbow-rich data, but coastal water is optically messy, and one spectrum can match several plankton mixes.

Their framework is built on a variational autoencoder, a model suited to one-to-many puzzles. Tailored designs let it recover both the plankton's light absorption and its green pigment amount from reflected spectra. Against real observations, the models scored high precision with low bias, beating a leading rival approach above all on the richer data. The authors see a path to tracking coastal ecosystems from orbit.
arxiv-2504-13576:
Weiqi Qin, Yuxin Liu, Dongze Wu, Zhenkai Qin, and Qining Luo propose a traffic prediction model in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Traditional traffic flow models lose accuracy and fluctuate badly when flows show patterns at several time scales at once. Their model, MSTIM, is built on the MindSpore framework. It combines long short-term memory networks, convolutional networks, and an attention mechanism to model multi-scale temporal information.

Experiments used the Metropolitan Interstate Traffic Volume dataset. MSTIM was compared against typical hybrid baselines pairing attention with recurrent or convolutional models in various combinations. On mean absolute error, mean square error, and root mean square error, MSTIM came out ahead. The authors conclude the integrated design significantly improves both the accuracy and the stability of traffic volume prediction for transportation planning.
arxiv-2504-17376:
Maoyang Xiang, Ramesh Fernando, and Bo Wang show how to run a small language model directly on an edge device. Their paper appeared in 2025. Large models strain small hardware through heavy computing, memory traffic, and power use. The team deployed a half-billion-parameter model on a chip board that pairs a modest processor with programmable logic. They shrank the model with a compression method that weighs which weights matter most.

Their setup splits work between the two halves of the board. Heavy operations go to the programmable logic, and light tasks stay on the processor. The model shrank by about 55 percent. Output speed rose to about five tokens per second, nearly double the baseline rate. The work shows that direct on-device language models are practical without a data center.
arxiv-2504-17776:
Amir Carmel, Debarati Das, Evangelos Kipouridis, and Evangelos Pipis study clustering methods for streaming data in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Fitting distances to tree metrics and ultrametrics backs hierarchical clustering and numerical taxonomy. The input is a distance function over elements. The goal is a tree whose distances near-match the ones given. In the semi-streaming model, distances come in any order. Memory is tight.

For the zero-norm, the team gives a method that runs in polynomial time, uses near-linear space, and gives a near call for ultrametrics. They prove no exact single-pass method is there, even with no time cap. Their zero-norm result gives a near call for the one-norm too, matching the offline bound in a parameter regime. For the infinity-norm they mark out ultrametric fitting: a two-approximation in one pass, best, improving with one more pass.
arxiv-2504-18476:
Leonid Antipov and Stefan Kratsch wrote this theoretical computer science paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on shrinking hard problems before solving them. Kernelization is the art of trimming an input down to a small core with the same answer, but classic kernels demand a lot of global structure.

The authors propose boundaried kernelization, which trims local patches of a graph instead. The idea grows out of protrusion replacement, where a well-behaved lump of the input is swapped for a smaller stand-in. They show polynomial-size local kernels exist for a number of problems, and prove none can exist for others. The local tool also feeds back into the classic game: they use it to improve the kernel for Vertex Cover under a distance measure. The paper reframes preprocessing as a local craft.
arxiv-2504-21176: Wang wrote a solo math study in twenty twenty-five on a sum that flips sign term by term, built from factorials and a kind of Stirling count. He finds a neat rule that makes the whole set of such sums at once, and shows the sums are never below zero. The sums count a class of trees read as game trees won by the second player. He also gives plain maps among three kinds of trees and match lists.
arxiv-2505-01176:
Massimo Bilancioni and Massimiliano Esposito extend, in a 2025 paper, the theory of how energy is transduced from one process to another inside chemical reaction networks. In the classic view, one input drives one output against its spontaneous direction. Real networks, such as the core pathways of cell life, juggle many inputs and outputs through shared steps, which blurs which process drives which.

Their fix starts from elementary processes, steps that cannot be decomposed further. From those, they pick out the true set of processes at play in transduction. The method mirrors how efficiency is defined for heat engines working between several heat baths. Choosing a reference equilibrium environment shows that efficiency is relative, tied to a stored quantity called exergy. Waste outputs can be left out of the count. Applied to core cell pathways, the framework separates true efficiency from plain output share.
arxiv-2505-01876:
Artur Sidorenko presents a 2025 study of when singular stochastic control problems are well-posed. In such problems, the control can push the system in jumps of bounded total variation, a style that fits storage management and investing with transaction costs. Sidorenko builds an abstract framework and proves that an optimal strategy exists among randomized controls, for a broad range of goal functions.

The goals include cumulative prospect theory preferences, which weight gains and losses the way real people do. The storage result is, he notes, the first treatment of behavioral storage management with that goal. For portfolios, a topology suited to irregular paths simplifies the proofs. The framework separates what the market model must provide from what the goal must satisfy.
arxiv-2505-02376:
Ekaterina Shemetova and seven co-authors let language models write the annotations that static analyzers need to catch memory leaks. Their paper from twenty twenty-five presents LAMeD. Tools like CodeQL, Infer, and Cooddy track data flow through functions marked as sources or sinks. Hand-writing those marks for big or third-party libraries is slow and error-prone.

LAMeD drafts function-specific marks on its own. Plugged into the Cooddy analyzer, the marks sharpen leak detection in their tests. Search paths that once exploded in count stay in bounds. The gain is scale: whole codebases become tractable without weeks of manual tagging. The authors sketch how the same trick could serve wider code analysis. It is a pragmatic bridge between model fluency and rigid program checking.
arxiv-2505-02576:
Sergio Hernández-Gutiérrez and co-authors published a 2025 paper on a divide-and-conquer method for hard reasoning problems. Language models reason step by step, but long chains scale poorly: accuracy and speed both suffer on complex tasks, and each new task tends to demand fresh examples. The authors' method breaks a problem into subproblems recursively, tracking the dependencies between them, so partial results combine in the right order.

The decomposition needs little supervision and can be applied to an entirely new class of problems without task-specific guidance. Where chain-of-thought wanders linearly, this structure branches and rejoins like a work plan. The authors present the method as generic reasoning infrastructure, in science and engineering especially, where problems naturally nest. If it holds, one solver could face many problem families without retraining for each.
arxiv-2505-02676:
Yuhan Zhao and Jun Jiang compute how often heavy quark states decay into bound lepton pairs. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, concerns leptonium, atoms made of two leptons. Such pairs bind through electric forces alone. Factories churn out huge numbers of J/psi particles, a heavy quark-antiquark state.

Decays can spit out positronium, muonium, or dimuonium plus light or extra leptons. Future facilities will make trillions of J/psi events each year. Rates for one prized channel, ortho-dimuonium, are tiny but perhaps reachable. The authors map both spin forms of the bound pairs. A first sighting of true dimuonium motivates the hunt.
arxiv-2505-03076:
Zhenyu Xu and co-authors work out the odds math for radar-style direction detectors in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The task is to spot a signal with known row and column spaces inside matrix data, while its exact coordinates stay unknown. Many detectors exist, but their hit and false-alarm rates lacked formulas.

Focusing on two adaptive detectors with a known spatial steering vector, the team derives their statistical distributions. Closed-form expressions follow for both the chance of detection and the chance of a false alarm. Computer simulations matched the theory well. The authors say the formulas let designers set thresholds on paper rather than by trial.
arxiv-2505-03676:
Arthur Satouf, Gabriel Ben Zenou, Benjamin Piwowarski, Habiboulaye Amadou Boubacar, and Pablo Piantanida present a 2025 paper on improving sparse search with ideas from linguistics. Sparse retrievers score documents term by term, ignoring how the rest of the collection shapes what a term means. The Rational Speech Acts framework asks how a speaker trims features to single out one object among many.

Adapted to search, the framework reweights each token by contrast with other documents. Representations become sharper, since common tokens count less and distinctive ones more. Added to several sparse models, the method improved results every time. On out-of-domain tests from the BEIR benchmark it reached top performance. Code is publicly available.
arxiv-2505-04876:
Tianyu Wu, Baohua Sun, and colleagues derive how protons are distributed inside stable atomic nuclei in a 2025 nuclear physics study. Elastic electron scattering measures a nucleus's charge distribution; stripping away the proton's own size yields the point-proton density, the map of where proton centers sit. The authors work through well over one hundred stable nuclei, from lithium up to thorium.

Results appear in several standard model shapes, from harmonic oscillator and Fermi forms to a Fourier-Bessel expansion that stays close to the data. A uniform proton map library feeds reaction calculations and tests of nuclear structure theory.
arxiv-2505-05276:
Adam Kisiel worked out how to extend a measurement technique called femtoscopy from one dimension to three. He applied it to pairs of protons created in heavy-ion collisions. Femtoscopy reads the size and motion of the fireball made when heavy nuclei crash, by tracking how pairs of particles move together. For pions and kaons the full three-dimensional analysis is routine. For protons only simpler one-dimensional versions existed, because protons are rarer and the theory was incomplete.

Kisiel names the specific problems that arise for proton pairs and builds both the mathematics and the practical fitting methods to handle them. Tests on simulated collisions from a standard model show the approach recovers the source properties. He warns, though, about care needed when reading the fitted radii.
arxiv-2505-05576:
Gonchar and colleagues argue that current world trade models cannot justify fair trade relations. Their twenty twenty-five economics paper starts from the classic comparative advantage model. That model explains gains from trade, but not how income gets shared. The authors propose a method for building balanced trade instead.

Their ideal state gives every country a zero trade balance. Prices and export mixes are built to reach that state together. The paper proves such a price set exists when supply matches demand. It also shows tariff limits push traded goods prices upward. In a balanced system, tariff wars would have no room to start. The work is theory, aimed at reshaping trade debate.
arxiv-2505-06176:
Niladri Shekhar Dutt, Duygu Ceylan, and Niloy Mitra teach multimodal models the craft of photo retouching through puzzles in a 2025 computer vision study. Generative editors follow words or strokes but often warp the identity of objects in the photo, an unacceptable surprise in professional work. Traditional procedural edits, the sliders in standard tools, are safe but demand skill to sequence well.

Training on retouching puzzles, where the model must find the edit steps that transform one image into another, builds procedural skill. The resulting system aims for edits that are expressive yet conservative, keeping the photograph itself intact.
arxiv-2505-06276:
Liang Shi and co-authors build a public fake data set of crashes and near-crashes for driving research. Real crash data is rare and bound by privacy rules, so few teams can use it. The source is the largest natural driving study to date, with thousands of such events. Their set holds over 1,800 crashes and 6,900 near-crashes drawn from that study.

Faces and plates were replaced by AI-made keyframes that keep the safety facts of each scene. Notes mark event type, road and traffic states, and motion data for five seconds around the event. Synced text tales aid scene reading by machines. Two benchmark tasks show how the set can test event sorting and scene sense. The authors aim to open safety work to more labs.
arxiv-2505-07376:
Junji Yu and co-authors test how well language models find security flaws in code written in many programming languages, in a 2025 study. Older deep learning detectors were trained per language, which limits real-world use. Large language models promise one tool for all languages. The team benchmarked pre-trained models and top large models across seven popular languages.

A pre-trained code model, CodeT5P, won overall, above all at catching the most critical flaws. The big general models did not dominate as expected. The authors discuss where large models might still help in practice and call the study a first step. Their results give future cross-language detection work a measured baseline to beat.
arxiv-2505-08876:
Jin Koda and five co-authors map molecular gas in the barred spiral galaxy M83 in two thousand twenty-five. They use the ratio of two carbon monoxide lines as their probe. Fine data from the ALMA array show how the ratio shifts across the galaxy. Low values sit between the arms, high values in the bar and arms.

The shifts sync with the galaxy's rotation and its large shapes. Star forming zones push the ratio higher still in spots. The center starts very high, the bar dips, and the disk varies again. Big gas blocks with no star birth show low values. The team says bulk gas is ruled more by galaxy dynamics than by star feedback.
arxiv-2505-09376: Hyunyoung Han, Jongwon Jang, Kitaeg Shim, and Sang Ho Yoon present AfforDance, an augmented reality system for learning dance, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The system turns a dance video a user picks into an interactive lesson. It builds a 3D reference avatar from the video, syncs the music, and adds adaptive visual cues that steer the learner's moves. The authors offer the design as a step toward personal, user-centered dance teaching that adjusts to each student.
arxiv-2505-09476:
Yanbing Zhou and co-authors probe the magnetism of infinite-layer nickelates, in a 2025 paper. These compounds superconduct when doped and resemble the famous cuprates. Their charge gap is larger, though, which should weaken magnetic links through oxygen. The team measured oxygen-17 nuclei in two samples with nuclear magnetic resonance.

The signals showed glassy spin behavior from the nickel-oxygen planes, placing the material near magnetic order. Their analysis found the standard nickel-to-nickel exchange through oxygen about ten times weaker than in cuprates, too weak to explain the observed magnetism. Heavy calculations point to an extra orbital near the Fermi level that boosts the coupling. The authors say nickelate magnetism runs on a different engine than cuprate magnetism.
arxiv-2505-09876:
Takuma Isobe, Tsuneya Yoshida, and Yasuhiro Hatsugai review topology in light systems that break the standard mold. Most such work rests on the Schrödinger equation, which reduces to a plain eigenvalue problem. Some real light systems instead obey generalized or nonlinear versions of that problem. Bands there can take complex values even for well-behaved matrices.

The first part covers the generalized case, which explains odd light spread in hyperbolic materials. It also predicts guarded crossing points in crystals made of negative-index media. The second part adds helper bands to set up a bulk-edge rule under weak nonlinearity. That rule explains why edge light modes stay sturdy when material traits shift with frequency. The review ties both cases into one frame.
arxiv-2505-11476:
Runze Zuo and colleagues presented a wearable soft robotic arm in 2025 that carries its own air supply and control hardware. Pneumatic soft arms bend safely around people and clutter, but they usually trail bulky external pressure regulators and offer limited strength and precision. The team's design, called UMArm, mounts many modified McKibben artificial muscles on a lightweight rigid spine. Each muscle hides its own valves and controller inside, so no separate regulator box is needed.

The hybrid rigid-soft structure aims to combine the compliance of soft robots with the force and accuracy of rigid ones. Because the arm is modular and untethered, sections can be rearranged and the whole device worn on the body. The paper presents the design as a step toward soft arms that work in unstructured places, where rigid robots struggle and human contact is likely.
arxiv-2505-11576:
Wu, Alaniz, Karthik, Dayan, Schulz, and Akata argue in twenty twenty-five that neural networks are not true black boxes: their inner activity mirrors patterns in their training data. Borrowing the mind's trick of chunking, they slice the chatter of many neurons into recurring units that stand for concepts. Three extractors cover different cases, from labelled data to none, and from low to high dimensions.

The chunks captured concrete words, grammar tags, and even story schemas, across small recurrent nets and large language models alike. Pasting a chunk into a network shifted its behaviour in controlled, predictable ways, showing the units do causal work. The authors offer chunking as a fresh route to interpretability grounded in how people themselves parse streams.
arxiv-2505-11776:
Jiali Chen and Avijit Mukherjee wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It joins the two great schools of graph self-supervised learning, generative and contrastive, in one frame that uses community shape to pick its pairs.

Contrastive methods shine at node sorting, generative ones at link calls. The new build adds community-aware node contrast, graph-level contrast for broad sense, and a rich tweak plan that masks traits, stirs nodes, and drops edges. On open benchmarks it beats top rivals across sorting, grouping, and link tasks, by small but steady lifts. The frame is meant for graphs with few or no labels.
arxiv-2505-12076:
Ali Akbar Septiandri and four co-authors fill gaps in intensive care data by treating the patient's many measurements as one connected stream. Monitors record different signals at irregular times, and the timing itself can carry clinical meaning. Standard imputation usually handles each signal separately and gives no uncertainty for its guesses.

Their method adapts deep Gaussian process emulation with stochastic imputation, borrowing strength across related measurements and across time. Each filled value comes with an uncertainty estimate, which matters when clinicians act on the numbers. On a clinical dataset the approach beat common alternatives, including chained-equation multiple imputation and last-value carry-forward. The authors stress the value of modeling cross-signal relationships explicitly.
arxiv-2505-12576:
Kiran Kokilepersaud, Mohit Prabhushankar, and Ghassan AlRegib study how representation size evolves during self-supervised learning in a 2025 study. A known failure is dimensional collapse, where features use only part of the space they are given. Higher effective dimension usually means richer features and better transfer to new tasks.

The authors focus on the stage where a projection head maps core features into an embedding space. Recent work casts that head as a filter removing noisy or irrelevant features. Their method adapts dimensionality during training in response to the dynamics they measure. The goal is to keep feature diversity high without wasting capacity on noise.
arxiv-2505-13276:
Sebastian Barzaghi, Arianna Moretti, Ivan Heibi, and Silvio Peroni wrote a 2025 paper on CHAD-KG, a knowledge graph for cultural heritage objects. Museums and exhibitions increasingly digitize their objects, producing both descriptive metadata and paradata, records of how the digitization itself was done. Storing both in a structured, linked form makes them reusable.

CHAD-KG converts two tabular data sets into RDF, the web's linked data format, following an application profile built on standards such as CIDOC-CRM and the Getty thesaurus. A reproducible pipeline generates the graph automatically. It now serves as the main metadata source for a digital twin of a temporary exhibition, a virtual copy that mirrors the physical show.
arxiv-2505-13876:
Yu-Sik Kim and Jae-Young Kim (2025) tracked the jet of the blazar PKS 0735+178 around the time of a high-energy neutrino event. Blazars are galaxies whose jets point near Earth, and some may fire neutrinos across the universe. Radio telescopes with continent-wide baselines imaged this jet at two frequencies from 2020 to 2024. The data resolve features less than a parsec from the core. A neutrino recorded in December 2021 falls inside the window.

After the neutrino, the core region brightened in radio waves, grew hotter in apparent terms, and became more opaque. A new jet knot had left the core shortly before the event. It raced downstream at about four times light speed in apparent terms. Right at the neutrino's arrival, within the timing uncertainty, the knot passed a slower feature about 0.77 parsecs out. The authors propose that crossing point as the likely birthplace of the neutrino.
arxiv-2505-16376:
Zijia Lu, Gaurav Mittal, and their colleagues find moments in long videos from text queries without paying full price for every second, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. The task, temporal grounding, asks a system to point to the exact span a description refers to, and long videos make the naive approach ruinously expensive.

The naive approach cuts the video into clips and runs a heavyweight encoder on each one. DeCafNet instead delegates the first pass to a light sidekick encoder. The sidekick scans all clips cheaply and draws a saliency map of likely matches. Only the most promising clips go to the full expert encoder for careful processing. Features from the two passes are then combined for the final answer. The delegate-and-conquer split aims to keep accuracy while slashing compute. It targets search and retrieval over the long videos that dominate real collections.
arxiv-2505-16776:
Vladislav Popkov, Xin Zhang, Carlo Presilla, and Tomaž Prosen set out the firm state of spin chains that can be solved in full. Strong loss at the ends drives those chains. They bring in grains whose spread law is re set, or dressed, by the loss it self. The firm state's range then comes from Bethe rules for a kin set that sings in tune. That set shares the same base states.

The team works out clear dressed strength scores for the XXX and XXZ chains. Those chains have loss led end fields that run straight. They grow the finds to XXZ and XYZ chains with end fields that do not run straight. In each case the dress adds a sharp point to the spread law. That point by much re shapes the firm state range next to the tune model.
arxiv-2505-17176:
João D Álvares and Alex Vaño-Viñuales present a 2025 arXiv paper on simulating Einstein's equations together with electromagnetic and scalar fields. Their setup uses hyperboloidal slices, surfaces that reach future null infinity, the one place where radiation such as gravitational waves is sharply defined. The team reports the first run of this system under a standard common formulation.

Tests in spherical symmetry cover a charged scalar field perturbing calm spacetime and one near a charged black hole. A third run follows the collapse of a charged scalar field into a Reissner-Nordström black hole. The work shows the code can extract clean signals at infinity.
arxiv-2505-19176:
Zhuo Liu and four colleagues wrote a 2025 paper on a flaw in how AI judges are trained. Many labs use a strong model to grade answers, then train a cheaper judge on those grades. The authors name a hidden catch in this plan: teacher preference bias.

A judge trained this way learns to favor answers from its own teacher model. That skew makes scores unfair for other models. The team adds an assistant model that has no tie to the teacher. Its grades balance the training data. Tests check whether the fix cuts the bias while keeping the judge sharp. The work matters wherever cheap AI judges stand in for human review.
arxiv-2505-19376:
Ying and a team of colleagues studied in twenty twenty-five how people attribute beliefs to others. Explaining someone's actions often means guessing what they believe. Yet people could attribute many possible beliefs, and the team asked which ones they actually pick.

They built a computer model scoring a belief statement on three factors: accuracy, how much it tells, and causal relevance to the action. People watched an agent collect keys hidden in boxes to reach a goal. They then ranked statements about the agent's beliefs. Accuracy and informativeness together predicted the rankings fairly well. Causal relevance alone predicted them best. The results suggest people favor beliefs that actually explain why the agent acted.
arxiv-2505-21276:
Wang, Guo, and Zhou show that axion interactions with kaons heat axions in the early universe far faster than past estimates said. The axion heating rate sets the hot dark matter limit on axion mass. Standard rates counted only the channel where an axion and a pion trade into two pions. Above 100 MeV, that channel alone badly understates the rate. The team computed axion scattering with light mesons in a chiral framework. The kaon channel, axion plus kaon to pion plus kaon, proved much larger.

Resonances inside that channel swell its cross section. Near 130 MeV its share dominates the total rate. Dark matter bounds built on the old rate need revisiting.
arxiv-2505-21676:
Yufeng Yang and five co-authors report real trials of a cloud-based driving system for driverless vehicles, in a 2025 study. Cars that sense only for themselves can miss hazards hidden by crowds or walls. The system adds fixed sensor posts at key spots, each with cameras, laser scanners, and small computers. The posts send tidy summaries to a cloud hub over fast 5G links. The hub merges the views into one shared scene picture.

Two field sites tested the setup: a busy urban roundabout and an indoor space like a hospital. Shared sensing helped the vehicles keep track of people and other movers around blind spots. The authors report gains in safety and smooth coordination between vehicles. They present the design as a general frame for indoor and outdoor fleets.
arxiv-2505-22076:
Stahl, Ziegenbein, Park, and Wachsmuth present a study from twenty twenty-five on training language models for argumentation tasks. General instruction tuning leaves models weak on tasks that need domain knowledge. Argumentation, with tasks like claim and fallacy checks, is one such domain. The team craft plain instructions for one hundred five argumentation tasks from past research. They build a benchmark to grade models across those tasks. They then synthesize tens of thousands of training instructions by a self-instruct method.

Fine-tuning on that set lifts scores on both seen and unseen argumentation tasks. General language task scores stay stable in parallel checks. The authors say domain instruction sets can specialize models safely. Their benchmark gives the field a shared yardstick.
arxiv-2505-22176:
Vihang Pancholi and colleagues grade machine-made tables the way a careful teacher would: first check the structure, then read the content, then explain the grade. Standard metrics miss small structural and factual slips that make a table misleading. Writing in twenty twenty-five, their framework begins with a rubric mixing multi-level structural descriptors with fine-grained contextual signals. A first phase aligns the candidate table against the reference table's layout; a second compares meaning and wording cell by cell, producing interpretable, detailed feedback rather than one opaque score.

The system was tested on a new benchmark spanning many domains, with realistic table corruptions and human annotations. A sensitivity and specificity analysis backed its robustness across table tasks. Code and data are public. The work targets the growing pipeline of generated reports and data summaries, where tables carry the facts readers trust most.
arxiv-2505-22576:
Qing-He Ni and seven co-authors present ExoPhoto, a store of data on how molecules break apart in ultraviolet light at a range of heat levels. Such data are a must to model the air of planets round other stars, and of stars too, with care. One gap has been the short end of the ultraviolet band.

ExoPhoto grows out of the known ExoMol frame. It pulls in theory from three data stores built on computers, plus tests done by lab groups. It now holds twenty molecules, from water and carbon dioxide to ones that bear metals. For each heat level, its files give cross sections by wavelength, set out in the ExoMol way, with ExoMol names. For some sets it adds branching ratios and quantum yields. Growth plans call for more molecules and for data on states out of balance.
arxiv-2505-22976:
Kewei Lian and three co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on a test for world models that must keep space straight. A world model fakes how a scene shifts as an agent moves. If it forgets where things are, plans built on it fail. Past test sets stress looks, not long range space sense. Their set, LoopNav, is built on loops.

Agents walk loops in the game Minecraft and come back to the start. The set holds a vast span of video with the moves logged. A new score checks if the model's inner scene graph stays in line on the loop. It shrugs off pixel level noise. Data, tests, and code are open for later work.
arxiv-2505-24876:
Ashraf and co-authors present Agent-X, a 2025 benchmark for testing AI agents on hard visual tasks that take many steps. Older benchmarks lean on made-up, single-turn questions and judge only the final answer. Agent-X holds 828 tasks with real images, image sets, videos, and written instructions. The tasks span six settings, among them web browsing, driving, sports, security, and math.

A scoring framework grades each step of the agent's work, not just the outcome. It checks whether each step was right, whether the chain of steps made sense, and whether tools were used well. Even the best current model families solved fewer than half of the tasks end to end. The authors point to weak multi-step reasoning and tool use as the main bottlenecks.
arxiv-2506-01076:
Sergey Goncharov, Pouya Partow, and Stelios Tsampas give a general proof that two styles of program meaning agree, in a 2025 paper. Programming languages are defined by operational rules. Small-step rules describe one move at a time. Big-step rules jump straight to the final result. Both styles are used everywhere in practice. Their agreement is usually proven case by case, from scratch. A shared abstract argument was missing.

The authors work inside a higher-order mathematical framework. They define an abstract notion of big-step semantics there. It complements an existing abstract small-step notion. A general construction derives the big-step version from the small-step one. An abstract equivalence theorem follows. The result is proven once, for all languages fitting the frame. The paper is aimed at semantics researchers. It promises to retire repetitive proof work. Language designers gain a reusable guarantee.
arxiv-2506-01176:
Adyan Dordzhiev proves a finite form, in a 2025 preprint, of a deformed version of de Finetti's theorem. The classic theorem says an endlessly exchangeable random sequence is a blend of independent, identical draws. A q-analogue replaces plain symmetry with a deformed one, tuned by a parameter q between zero and one. Dordzhiev states an asymptotic version of that analogue. The proof leans on the convex shape of the set of q-exchangeable probability measures.

The main payoff is a sharp speed limit. The gap between a finite q-exchangeable law and its limiting blend shrinks at a rate of exact order q to the n. No better rate is possible in general. Results of this kind matter wherever symmetry arguments justify simple models for complex data. The finite rate tells users how much data the idealization needs before it can be trusted.
arxiv-2506-01476:
Fei Guo and co-authors gauge, in a 2025 study, how long a light-struck electron takes to leave a solid, and how that span ties to the solid's symmetry. Time at the quantum scale is still poorly understood. The team use a method based on spin- and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy to clock the delay, down to attoseconds, spans far below a trillionth of a second.

They test solids of different dimensionality: flat layered crystals, a near one-dimensional crystal, and plain copper with full three-dimensional depth. The flat crystals took about 150 attoseconds. The line-like crystal took over 200. Pure copper took just 26. The split maps cleanly onto the dimensionality, or symmetry, of the solid. The authors say symmetry may be a key dial for quantum time scales.
arxiv-2506-02276:
Saurabh Singh and Dmitry Lagun move a generative modeling technique into latent space in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Stochastic interpolants bend one probability distribution into the next in a free way, powering today's generative models. To use them in jointly trained latent variable models was unexplored. The method needs straight access to samples from both distributions. Latent Stochastic Interpolants solves this, learning the encoder, decoder, and the latent interpolant as one, end to end.

The training goal is an evidence lower bound set out straight in continuous time. Joint tuning lets the model learn latent forms that are of use. The interpolant turns a free prior into the encoder's aggregated posterior. This dodges the tight simple priors of normal diffusion models. It dodges the heavy cost of working in high-dimensional data space too. Tests on the large-scale ImageNet generation test show the way works at scale.
arxiv-2506-02976:
Rachid Zeghlache and a large group of co-authors sum up, in a 2025 preprint, a contest on using AI to track an eye disease. The disease is age-related macular degeneration, a leading cause of vision loss. Doctors track it with layered eye scans. The MARIO challenge, held at a 2024 medical imaging conference, asked teams to automate that tracking. Data came mainly from a clinic in Brest, France, with an extra set from Algeria.

Thirty-five teams took part, and the top twelve presented their methods. One task asked whether disease activity changed between two scans. The other asked teams to forecast the disease three months ahead for patients on drug therapy. On the first task, AI matched doctor-level skill. On the forecast task, no team did well yet. The paper lays out the data, rules, and winning methods as a benchmark for the field.
arxiv-2506-03476:
Chuyuan Li, Raymond Li, Thalia Field, and Giuseppe Carenini use language models to spot Alzheimer's disease in patient writing in a 2025 paper. Early help matters, and odd patterns in speech and text can warn of the disease. Their approach teaches the model by example: a few sample cases are placed in the prompt, a method called in-context learning.

Picking those samples by likeness worked poorly for this task. Their method, Delta-KNN, scores each training case by how much it lifts results, then picks stand-ins close to the new case. On two data sets and three open models it beat standard choices. With one model it even topped systems trained the full supervised way.
arxiv-2506-05476:
D Langis and co-authors compile a catalog of tidal disruption events, where a star is torn apart by a black hole, in work from two thousand twenty-five. Such events let astronomers study quiet black holes, but few had been seen. The catalog lists over a hundred confirmed events found through the end of two thousand twenty-four.

Light records span X-ray, ultraviolet, visible, and heat bands, with spectra shared in public. Most events fell in one spectral class tied to stars like the Sun. Three new cases may repeat, with second flares shaped much like the first. Heat and X-ray output seemed linked, which the team explores.
arxiv-2506-07976:
Junhong Shen and co-authors argue for a new way to make computer agents better in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Most gains now come from longer chains of thought before acting. But an agent that only thinks cannot learn new facts from the world or change its plan as it goes.

The team proposes scaling the length of contact with the task itself, so one run can include exploring, backtracking, and fresh planning. Simple prompting with longer contact already raised success on web tasks. Their training method then adjusts run length as the agent learns. The trained web agent set a new best among open models on two web benchmarks, and it balanced exploring and settling in a flexible way.
arxiv-2506-08576: The BESIII Collaboration reports a measurement tied to how a short-lived particle called the eta changes form. The measurement uses a decay of its heavier cousin into two charged pions and an eta. The work appeared as a particle physics paper in twenty twenty-five. The record's evidence is limited to the title and the collaboration's long author list. The methods, data, and results therefore cannot be described from what is given here.
arxiv-2506-09076:
Haley Stone and co-authors gave a probabilistic method to fill missing genetic distances in pathogen models in two thousand twenty-five. Genome data help map how disease spreads in space and time, but many cases are never sequenced. Gaps limit what spatial models can learn.

Their method estimates how far an unsequenced case sits, genetically, from known sequences in a transmission chain. It uses collection dates and observed divergence patterns, with no need for sequence alignment or known chains. They applied it to highly pathogenic bird flu in wild birds in the United States. The approach adds biologically plausible data with stated uncertainty, at a scale suited to larger studies.
arxiv-2506-09176:
Haoyuan Cai, Zhenghao Peng, and Bolei Zhou let the robot itself ask for help while learning from a human teacher. Their paper from twenty twenty-five works in interactive imitation learning. A supervisor watches and steps in to show the right move. Constant watching taxes the human, though. Their AIM method learns when a demo is worth requesting.

A proxy value function mimics the teacher's rule for stepping in. It scores states high when the agent strays from expert conduct. As the agent improves, those scores fall on its own. Requests thus cluster on states where help counts most, including safety-critical ones. Tests in continuous and discrete control show less takeover cost than an uncertainty-based rival. Learning ran faster too, with fewer demos and fewer world steps. Code and a demo video are public.
arxiv-2506-11076:
Minyu Chen, Guoqiang Li, Ling-I Wu, and Ruibang Liu sic language models on dead code, in a 2025 paper. Dead code, instructions that never run or results never used, bloats programs, misleads maintainers, and can hide malware tricks. Compilers catch simple cases, but sophisticated dead patterns slip through, and cleanup usually demands tedious manual work.

Their framework pairs a compact code model, which flags suspicious lines through attribution scoring, with large language models fine-tuned on a big annotated dataset. The large models judge each suspect, explain why it is dead, and write the patch. Scores for finding unused and unreachable code exceeded ninety-four percent, beating a leading general model by about thirty points. The system spans several languages and closes the loop from detection to correction automatically.
arxiv-2506-11176:
Anatoly Krasnovsky offers a light path into chaos engineering: discover the service graph, then simulate failures on it. The paper from twenty twenty-five notes that live fault injection is costly and risky to run often. Hand-built dependability models, the safer rival, rot fast and take scarce expert time. His claim is that a connectivity-only model suffices for availability estimates under fail-stop faults.

The discovered model is just the dependency graph plus replica counts. Traces, mesh telemetry, and config files feed an automatic discovery step that fits into delivery pipelines. A DeathStarBench social network case tests the idea. Graphs pulled from Jaeger traces track live injection results closely across failure rates. Replication cases land near zero median error. The pitch: triage chaos tests with cheap models first.
arxiv-2506-11676:
Sumedha Biswas, Peter Jonker, M. Coleman Miller, Andrew Levan, and Jonathan Quirola-Vásquez wrote a 2025 paper on fast X-ray flashes in space. These flashes last minutes to hours and their source is still unknown. One idea says they come from magnetars, young neutron stars with strong fields, born when two neutron stars merge.

The team compared how many flashes are seen with how often such births should happen. Mergers of two neutron stars look too rare to explain all the flashes, even if each one made a flash. So they checked other birth paths, such as the collapse of a white dwarf and mergers of white dwarfs. Counting these rates helps narrow which sources could plausibly power the flashes.
arxiv-2506-11876:
Christina Selby and co-authors set out ways to judge the sharpness of 3D maps built from satellite images, in a 2025 paper. Such maps serve scene modeling where ground surveys or aircraft scans cannot reach. Knowing their true resolution tells users what missions the data can support and whether new methods are really improving.

The team covers three data forms: point clouds, surface models, and mesh models. They describe tools and workflows that score each form against high-grade airborne laser scans used as reference truth. Their checks run largely on their own once set up. They then show results across datasets of mixed quality, showing how the scores separate sharp maps from coarse ones.
arxiv-2506-14176:
Renao Yan set out a steadier way in twenty twenty-five to search for neural network architectures. The search is for pathology image classification. Off-the-shelf vision models fit medical images poorly. Hand design has tight limits. Plain architecture search is shaky in its results. Yan gives an initialization strategy. It is guided by network similarity. It seeds the one-shot search so the search converges in a more reliable way.

Domain adaptation is woven into the search too. It deals with gaps in staining between pathology data sets. It deals with semantic scale variation as well. On the BRACS breast pathology benchmark, the method beat the approaches that exist in classification accuracy. It put a focus on clinically relevant features too. Pathologists need that trait in a model to trust it. The work aims at use in practice. It holds edge computing settings, where compute is scarce.
arxiv-2506-14276:
Jack Cole and Mohamed Osman argue for deep learning as the way to crack the ARC reasoning test, in this 2025 paper. The test asks AI to infer abstract rules from a few examples, and most systems score poorly. Deep learning, though, has trained skillful networks across vision and language. The authors bet that same strength can learn fresh abstractions.

Their method trains networks on the fly at test time, starting from a pretrained language model. Two tricks add gains: fine-tuning during the test itself, and a voting scheme over augmented views. Accuracy rose several-fold with each trick. An early version won a 2023 ARC contest, and the final one set the best private test score at the time. The paper names test-time training as a core ingredient for reasoning in new domains.
arxiv-2506-15876:
Nicolás Barnafi, Alberto Martín, and Ricardo Ruiz-Baier propose an adaptive finite element method for deformable image registration. Registration warps one image onto another, a core task in medical imaging. Fixed meshes waste effort where images are smooth and under-resolve where they are not.

The authors pair the method with a residual-based error estimator whose efficiency and reliability they establish theoretically. The estimator guides adaptive mesh refinement and coarsening, concentrating computation where the registration is hardest. The nonlinear equations behind the method are solved with a pseudo time-stepping fixed-point scheme, accelerated by Anderson acceleration. An efficient data structure based on forests of octrees with space-filling curves supports the implementation. Numerical results on application-oriented problems illustrate the performance gains. The work gives imaging scientists a registration solver that spends its budget where the anatomy demands it.
arxiv-2506-16276:
Ming-Qiang Ren and co-authors report a 2025 finding of clean superconductivity at the border between two materials. They grew a single layer of a barium arsenide compound on top of films of an iron-based superconductor. Borders between unlike materials often breed new behavior, and here the pair produced a full superconducting gap, with no leftover normal electrons at low temperature.

The gap held up to a top temperature of twenty-six kelvin in their spectra. It stayed strong even when the film below was thinned to a single layer, unlike the bare film, whose transition fades fast when thin. The authors credit the near-perfect crystal quality of the stack, uniform in both shape and electronic behavior. The result shows how a well-made border can protect and even host superconductivity.
arxiv-2506-16376:
Kristof Cools wrote a 2025 paper on a faster equation for modeling waves that scatter off mixed material bodies. The base equation handles bodies made of chunks, each with its own traits. Where three or more chunks meet along a line, past fixes either fail or double the work.

Such systems are solved step by step, and the step count hinges on how the matrix values spread. Cools builds a single trace form of the equation that stays local in spirit. Its step count grows only slowly as the mesh gets finer. He works out the discrete form in full. Broad tests back the method's accuracy, settling, and speed. The equation also shows no false inner echoes.
arxiv-2506-17276:
Alexandre Le Nepvou puts forth a new modal logic built on layers of becoming, not on whole possible worlds. In the old Kripke view, each world in the set is fully formed and fixed. That view, he says, misses how things come to be, step by step and place by place, in an uneven way.

His Stratified Actualization Logic tags its signs with levels of how stable a thing is, and he calls these levels admissibility regimes. Each level works on a layer of what could be, and shifts link one layer to the next. The work sets out the syntax and the rules for what signs mean, states the axioms, and proves the system is sound and complete. He sketches uses for time and becoming, for quantum decoherence, and for modal metaphysics.
arxiv-2506-17776:
Dyuman Aditya, Colton Payne, Mario Leiva, and Paulo Shakarian wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It wires machine learning models into a logic engine, so that what the models see can drive clear, stated decisions in work flows.

The engine, PyReason, uses a form of logic that holds real-valued scores as truth ranges. Model outputs such as probabilities thus turn into logical facts. The system polls the models, refreshes the facts, and reworks the least model at once, so calls can be made in real time. Time sense, knowledge graph ties, and full trace of the reasoning are built in. The fit suits plants, clinics, and office flows where steps must be both fast and open to audit.
arxiv-2506-19576:
Martina Amongero and Pierpaolo De Blasi work on finding groups inside networks in a 2025 paper. In many networks, points in the same group link to each other more often than to outsiders. A common model captures that pattern but leaves open how many groups there are.

Their approach uses flexible Bayesian methods that let the group count stay unknown. The new twist is forcing the model to respect the within-group linking pattern from the start. They study when that extra rule actually helps compared with the standard model. A broad set of simulated tests shows the cases where the gain appears, giving network analysts clearer guidance on when to use it.
arxiv-2506-23276:
David Guzman Piedrahita and co-authors test how language models behave in public goods games, where cooperation must survive free-riding. Models are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents, so how they balance self-interest against the group matters. The team adapted a game with institutional choice from behavioral economics. Models repeatedly decided whether to pay a cost to reward cooperation or punish defection.

Four behavior patterns emerged. Some models built and held high cooperation. Others swung between engagement and withdrawal. A third group slid downhill over time, and a fourth stuck to fixed strategies whatever happened. The surprise was that strong reasoning models, such as the o1 series, cooperated badly. Some plain models cooperated consistently well. The authors warn that sharpening a model's reasoning does not by itself make it a better team player. Their code is public for others to test deployment risks.
arxiv-2506-23476:
Yi-bo Shen and co-authors used correlation functions to probe what two exotic particles are really made of. Over twenty years, experiments have found many hadron states that do not fit the simple quark model. A leading idea is that some are loose molecules of two ordinary hadrons. The team focused on the Ds0*(2317), testing four possible recipes for its makeup, each built around a bound pair of a D meson and a kaon.

Each recipe predicts a slightly different fingerprint in the correlation between a D meson and a kaon produced together. The fingerprints separate cleanly when a bare compact state is mixed in. The same approach applied to the famous X(3872) particle also distinguished its internal mixtures. Future collision measurements can read these fingerprints and settle the recipes.
arxiv-2507-00276:
Hidetoshi Nishimori, Masayuki Ohzeki, and Manaka Okuyama proved a link in twenty twenty-five between two odd effects in spin glasses. Spin glasses are magnetic alloys with frozen, disordered spins. In temperature chaos, a tiny temperature shift completely rearranges the spin state. In the reentrant transition, cooling drives the system from an ordered phase back into a less ordered one.

Working in the finite-dimensional Edwards-Anderson model, the authors add correlations among the disorder variables. Assuming a spin glass phase exists at finite temperature, they show temperature chaos follows logically from reentrance. The two effects, long treated as unrelated curiosities, turn out to be two faces of one structure. The result offers a new view of spin glass physics beyond the standard mean-field picture.
arxiv-2507-00376:
Manohar and Mallikarjunaiah studied adaptive simulations of cracking in strain-limiting solids in twenty twenty-five. Phase-field models smear a crack over a small zone, using a damage variable. This avoids direct tracking of crack surfaces. The AT1 variant is popular for quasi-static brittle fracture. But proving that adaptive mesh refinement converges is hard.

The authors study an AT1 model inside elasticity theories with algebraically nonlinear stress-strain laws. They propose two refinement algorithms driven by local error indicators. Minimizer sequences from the first converge to a set tolerance. Sequences from the second are proven inherently convergent, needing no stopping rule. Simulations of an edge crack under anti-plane shear loading checked bulk, surface, and total energies. They showed both algorithms outperform standard approaches.
arxiv-2507-01076:
Vanja Stojanović and Bor Pangeršič give the mutual-visibility problem its first empirical workout in a two thousand twenty-five algorithms paper. The problem asks for the largest set of graph vertices that can pairwise see each other along paths avoiding other chosen vertices.

The problem is NP-complete, and theory had outrun practice. The authors implement three methods: a direct random heuristic, a hypergraph-based approximation, and a genetic algorithm. On smaller graphs all three match known theoretical values. On larger instances, solutions diverge from theoretical limits and loose bounds make quality hard to judge. On graphs with known optima, the genetic algorithm and heuristics performed best.
arxiv-2507-01276:
Some decays are banned in the Standard Model, so seeing one would point to new physics. The four authors study tau lepton decays into an electron plus a pair of mesons within a supersymmetric model that adds a local B-L gauge symmetry. The three channels are tau to electron with two pions, with a pion and a kaon, and with two kaons. They ask how the predicted rates for these flavor-violating decays respond to the model's parameters.

Using the latest experimental data, the authors trace which parameters move the branching ratios most. The numerical work shows the main drivers are the non-diagonal elements that link the starting and ending leptons. The paper offers the analysis as groundwork for experiments hunting these decays, since a future detection would signal physics beyond the Standard Model.
arxiv-2507-01976:
