Sivaroopan and colleagues survey in twenty twenty-five how researchers fake network traffic for testing and training. Real traffic data is scarce, private, and sometimes impure, so generated copies that keep its character are valuable. The survey maps the field from classic statistical models through modern deep learning generators, including commercial tools.

It compares approaches side by side on data types and model families, and ships an AI tool that applies the comparison to any new paper. The authors then list open problems, from realism checks to privacy risks. They close with future directions, aiming the survey at both researchers and practitioners who need a structured map of the area.
arxiv-2507-03676:
Peter Allen, Julia Böttcher, Yoshiharu Kohayakawa, and Mihir Neve prove a hardier version of a classic graph embedding theorem, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The Sauer-Spencer theorem says a dense enough host graph swallows any guest graph of bounded degree. The new result asks whether a randomly thinned host, keeping each edge with some small chance, still contains the guest.

Above a probability threshold their answer is yes, and the threshold is best possible apart from a log factor. They also soften the host's degree demand to a new boundary value, which they bound and guess exactly, tying it to a famous open conjecture. A sharpened blow-up lemma, proved along the way, may serve other problems, the authors note.
arxiv-2507-05576:
Mehdi Elahi, Mohamed Elshamy, Abdel-Hameed Badawy, and Ahmad Patooghy wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It studies a sly chip attack, the intermittent thermal Trojan, which twists a processor's heat data at random times to stay hid.

Multi-core chips lean on heat reads to stay safe and fast. A Trojan that fires in bursts slips past threshold checks with ease, the team shows. They map how start time and burst length change the harm. Their guard is a set of tiny learned classifiers that watch for odd heat signs at run time. Catch rates jump by wide margins over past methods. Any twist past a tight band is caught every time.
arxiv-2507-06576:
Sina Kalantarzadeh and Nikhil Kumar improved lower bounds in twenty twenty-five on the gap between multiflows and multicuts in planar networks. Given many source-sink pairs, a multiflow routes goods for all of them at once, while a multicut removes edges to disconnect every pair. The cut always costs at least the flow; their ratio is the gap.

For a single pair the gap is one, but in general it can grow without bound. For planar graphs, the best lower bound had stood at two for decades. The authors raise it to sixteen sevenths. More importantly, they develop fresh techniques for proving such bounds, which they expect to transfer to other network problems. The work sharpens knowledge of how far flow and cut can diverge on flat networks.
arxiv-2507-07976: Zehua Lai and Lek-Heng Lim prove the Pierce-Birkhoff claim for splines, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Splines are smooth piecewise polynomials laid over a flat-cut split of space. The claim says each can be written as a finite lattice blend of plain polynomials. A pure existence proof comes first, then a deeper pass that yields workable bounds.
arxiv-2507-08976:
Matthew Evans imports the idea of nilpotence into BCK-algebras, an algebraic setting far from the groups where nilpotence is classical. He begins with the derived subalgebra and builds a derived ideal from it. That construction quickly pays off in category theory.

Commutative BCK-algebras turn out to form a reflective subcategory of all BCK-algebras. Evans then defines central series and nilpotence, and proves basic properties. Within any variety, the nilpotent members form a sub-pseudovariety but usually not a variety. Algebras of nilpotence class at most c form a variety only when c equals one. A closing result says every finite BCK-algebra is nilpotent.
arxiv-2507-09276:
George Andrews and Mohamed El Bachraoui study a family of q-series, infinite sums built from a variable q, that depend on two whole numbers, k and m. For the first few choices of those numbers every term of the series is positive, but for larger choices nobody knows whether positivity still holds. The question matters because these sums also count certain two-color partitions.

A partition splits a whole number into parts, and here the parts come in two colors, with each arrangement weighted by a sign that depends on how many even parts it has. If the generating sums stay positive, that fact turns into inequalities comparing counts of these partitions. The paper works out that link and draws the inequalities from it, while leaving the general positivity question open.
arxiv-2507-10376:
Mohammadhossein Talebi and four co-authors build Raci-Net, a learning tool that tracks a self-driving car's own move in bad weather. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Cars lean on cameras, laser scans, and motion sensors to sense the world and gauge their move. Sight-based sensors sit open to harsh weather and faults. Past tools cope with faults such as a turned mount or a lost link, but fade in snow, rain, and poor light. Raci-Net joins sight, motion, and radar data. It leans on each sensor's strength, and shifts each one's weight as the state of the world changes. The aim is a move gauge that stays true when the sky turns bad.
arxiv-2507-12076:
Khatua, Krishnamoorthi, Koo, and a large team study a magnet built on a chiral trillium lattice. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. In such a lattice, magnetic ions sit on a three-way web of shared triangles that twists in space. Webs of this kind are a hot test bed for odd quantum states.

They probe one iron-based compound with heat, resonance, and muon tools. Two stages of magnetic link growth show as the sample cools. A weak order sets in at very low heat, and a small field can wipe it out. Muon tests show the spins keep moving, with no freeze. Weak order and liquid-like motion thus live side by side.
arxiv-2507-13576:
Hunter Monroe's 2025 paper in logic and computer science asks when one formal theory can stand in for another as a proof system. The yardstick is p-simulation, which says one system can turn any proof from the other into a short proof of its own. Monroe proposes a way to pin down when this happens between two theories.

The proposal rests on how well one theory can interpret the other inside its own language. Monroe shows the link runs both ways for a theory extended by one extra claim. The paper also states stronger conjectures that would imply open results, such as Feige's hypothesis and the existence of one-way functions.
arxiv-2507-15176:
Jason Gaitonde and Elchanan Mossel study how badly an attacker can warp a Markov chain's long-run behavior, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Markov chains wander between states by fixed odds, settling into a stationary pattern. Corruption here rewrites the exits from a small share of states, chosen adversarially.

For chains with a spectral gap, PageRank-style variants prove robust. The corrupted chain's settled pattern stays close to the original, within a polynomial of the corrupted share. The bounds need no dimension terms and scale gracefully. PageRank thus acts as a simple regularizer against broad, realistic tampering, they argue.
arxiv-2507-15876:
Eric Benhamou and five co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on trend following funds, known as CTAs. These funds ride price trends, from slow breakouts to fast momentum bursts. Which horizon pays best, and how the two mix, stays in dispute. The team splits fund returns into short trend, long trend, and broad market parts.

Their split uses a Bayesian graphical model that updates over time. It shows how each part drives the funds' gains and risk. The mix of horizons shapes the risk adjusted score in clear ways. The work gives allocators a fresh lens on an old debate in managed futures.
arxiv-2507-16576:
Ahmed Lekssays, Husrev Taha Sencar, and Ting Yu present a security tool named AZERG in two thousand twenty-five. Analysts write threat reports in plain text, but sharing threat data in the standard STIX format still takes much hand work by experts. AZERG aims to turn report text into structured STIX data on its own.

The tool splits the task into four steps: find entities, name their types, find linked pairs, and name each link type. The team fine-tuned language models for each step. They also built a data set from one hundred forty-one reports, with thousands of marked entities and links. Their scores beat other models they tested, by two to twenty-five percent across tasks.
arxiv-2507-17776:
Jie Fan builds a formal logic for a layered kind of not-knowing made famous by a public remark about unknown unknowns. The paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. In logic terms, Rumsfeld ignorance means not knowing, and not knowing that you do not know. A recent paper by Kit Fine drew striking results about such states.

Fan notes a snag: in Fine's setup, Rumsfeld ignorance can be defined from plain ignorance, which makes some results too easy. The fix is to let the two hidden knowledge links differ, with one a subset of the other. That change keeps most of Fine's valid claims while blocking the shortcut. Fan then gives full rule sets for the logic over several classes of frames. The framework is used to recheck Fine's results one by one.
arxiv-2507-17876:
Rıza Özçelik, Sarah de Ruiter, and Francesca Grisoni flipped molecule design on its head in 2025. Chemists want new molecules with good traits, but examples of good molecules are scarce, while poor examples abound. Training only on rare winners wastes most available data.

Their trick trains a generator on the plentiful poor examples to learn which way in model space means worse. Then they steer the model the opposite way to create good designs, with no winner examples needed. Across dozens of design tests with small molecules and proteins, the reversed models made more varied and more successful candidates than winner-trained ones. The method also handled two goals at once and few-shot jobs well.
arxiv-2507-17976:
Maria Vlachou studies how to spot, in advance, when a chat-based image search will fail to find what the user wants. Her paper appeared in twenty twenty-five. In this task, a user views a shown image, gives word feedback, and hopes the next turn brings the right item. If the item is not in stock, more turns just waste time and raise stress.

Vlachou builds tools that read the top shown items turn by turn and flag likely fails. Tests used shoe and dress data sets, with two fail types split apart. Flags worked well when the system itself was at fault. Flags worked less well when the item was simply not in stock.
arxiv-2507-18376:
Farms generate too few labeled photos to train good vision models, and diffusion models, the generators behind modern image AI, may fill the gap. Xing Hu and co-authors review their use across smart farming in this 2025 paper.

The survey covers disease and pest spotting, sharpening satellite views, forecasting crop growth, and managing resources. Diffusion models beat the older generator style on stability and image quality, and they shine at making training data where little exists. Heavy computing needs and shaky transfer between regions remain the main brakes. The authors see steady real-world gains as the tools mature.
arxiv-2507-19576:
Byungmin Kang and Patrick Lee propose a resonance test for a quantum spin liquid. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, targets kagome antiferromagnets, magnets on a corner-shared triangle lattice. Spin liquids hide fraction-like excitations called spinons, which carry no charge. Normal resonance couples to charge, so spinons seem out of reach.

Two paths let an outside field still stir the spinons. One works through the emergent fields that spinons do feel. The team computes the absorption for Dirac-type spinons in Landau levels. Per layer the signal is small, but no skin depth limits the stack. A named new material could give a signal on par with graphene.
arxiv-2507-21176:
Farzana Islam Adiba and Rahmatollah Beheshti present a method for revealing subtle biases in medical language models, in a paper from 2025. Models used in care can carry unfair patterns that harm decisions. Those patterns are often hidden and hard to trigger with plain test questions.

Their framework pairs knowledge graphs with helper models that act as agents. Adversarial prompts are crafted to provoke biased answers, in the style of red teaming. The graph structure lets the tests trace multi-step links between concepts, so complex bias patterns surface. Trials covered three datasets, six models, and five bias types. The method revealed more of the hidden bias, and at larger scale, than common approaches. The aim is to find flaws before clinical use.
arxiv-2507-21676:
Mohsen Abedi and three co-authors work out how many access points a high-speed wireless site needs, and where to put them, so each user keeps a clear line of sight. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

New bands give huge speed, more users, and sharp place sense. But their signals fade fast when the line of sight is blocked, and stray paths are weak. The site here is one where blocks sit at chance places and can move. The team casts the place as a graph, whose nodes are small cells of ground. On that base they seek the least count of points, in the best spots, that keeps the line of sight sure.
arxiv-2507-21876:
Raeed Mundow and Adi Nusser compare a neural network with a classic statistical method for weighing galaxy clusters, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Cluster mass is a key cosmic quantity, yet the galaxies around a cluster mix members with stray passers-by that fool simple counts.

The network, an autoencoder with convolutional layers, learned from mock galaxy catalogs. The classic method assumes clusters of like mass share one galaxy pattern. Tested on simulated clusters, the network's mass guesses scattered about a third less than the classic method's when using galaxy positions. It also won with velocity-based inputs, despite a bias that distorts distant samples. The authors present machine learning as the sharper scale for clusters.
arxiv-2507-21976:
Tanvir Khan, Aranya Saha, Ismam Swapnil, and Mohammad Haque wrote this machine learning paper, published in 2025. It tests ways to shrink large multimodal language models, which read both images and text, so they can run on modest hardware in medical settings.

Big models are costly to run, a real barrier in clinics. The team fine-tuned a vision-language model for medical use, then pruned parts of it and rounded its numbers down with care for which parts matter most. They also add a new way to pick which layers to prune. The squeezed seven-billion-parameter model fits in four gigabytes of graphics memory, a seventy percent saving. It also scored slightly higher than models shrunk by older methods at the same size. The paper maps the trade-offs of a prune, fine-tune, then quantize pipeline.
arxiv-2507-22176:
Avrachenkov and Freidovich estimate slopes from coarse, uneven, noisy samples with a likelihood and spline method, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Many sensors report rarely and at irregular times, with noise on each read. Finding the rate of change from such data is hard. Classic observers struggle when sampling is coarse and noise is high.

Their estimator caps the size of a higher slope to keep fits stable. The solution takes the form of a smooth spline curve. A fresh parameterization yields fast online updates as data arrive. Two variants trade smoothness against computing speed. Simulations beat high-gain observers and twisting methods under coarse, noisy sampling. The gain helps systems that cannot sample faster.
arxiv-2507-22776:
Tim Flühmann and co-authors tackle how to judge a medical AI's accuracy when no labeled answers exist for new data, in this 2025 paper. Hospitals need to watch model performance after deployment, yet fresh scans rarely come with truth labels. Older tricks infer accuracy from the model's own confidence scores. The team extends those tricks to estimate the full confusion matrix, not just one score.

They test the methods on chest X-rays under real site shifts and under simulated shifts in scan style and disease rates. The matrix estimates tracked clinically relevant counts well on real shifts. Simulated shifts exposed failure modes in current techniques. The authors warn that monitoring tools must be matched to the true deployment setting before use in safety oversight.
arxiv-2508-00076:
Sarah Barbosa and co-authors train a neural network to read the air of distant Earth-like planets from their reflected light, preparing for a future flagship telescope. Their paper appeared in 2025. They generated nearly one hundred ten thousand synthetic spectra for planets with atmospheres like Earth's three great eras: early, middle, and modern. The network learned to recover gas amounts under two telescope designs, with noise and model variation separated.

Oxygen recovery faltered for the middle era's thin air, and methane read reliably only when plentiful. One ultraviolet band pinned modern ozone almost perfectly. The network leaned mostly on visible light, with the ultraviolet decisive for ozone and the infrared for methane and carbon dioxide. Skill faded past about 1.7 micrometers, a design hint for the telescope.
arxiv-2508-01576:
Jeanelle Dao and Jadelynn Dao present a smartwatch, in a 2025 preprint, that alerts deaf and hard-of-hearing wearers when their name is spoken. Hundreds of millions of people live with serious hearing loss. Catching a spoken name in a busy room is a daily problem for them. Their device, Lumename, listens on the watch itself and answers with vibration plus a visual signal. The model must be tiny and quick on cheap hardware.

Training data was the bottleneck, since one user's voice samples are few. The authors reshaped those samples with audio tricks to mimic other ages and voices. A search over model settings found a compact design with low power use. The finished watch ran on an Arduino-based board. Its name detection stayed above ninety percent accurate. The paper frames the device as a low-cost aid that works without a phone or cloud link.
arxiv-2508-02176:
Andrew Tropin, in a solo paper from twenty twenty-five, built a test library for live coding setups. Such setups let a coder grow a program without pause, with fast checks of guesses. But tests are oft run apart, by command line, cut off from live tools like debuggers and value views. Coarse runs and lost context slow the loop and break focus.

Tropin's library gives tests a runtime form inside the live setup. On failure, the coder gets the full tool kit at the fail point at once. Workflows built on it rerun tests in less than a second. Readers who build code tools learn how to keep test speed inside the flow state that live coding sells.
arxiv-2508-02276:
Xiangru Tang and a large team build CellForge, a crew of smart agents that design models of how single cells react to change. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Told how a cell will act when its genes or drugs shift is a core task in disease work. It needs skill from many fields at once. CellForge takes a data set and a task, reads the past work, parses the data, and finds past models to beat. Its agents, each with a bent for data, cell life, or deep learning, then shape a model plan through talks checked by a critic. The aim is a plan that can be run and tested, not just a claim on paper.
arxiv-2508-02376:
Matus Krajcovic, Peter Demcak, and Eduard Kuric test, in a 2025 preprint, whether a lifelike virtual person can run an online survey better than a chatbot. Text surveys suffer from careless, skimpy answers, since no one feels present. The authors built a tool that puts a photorealistic avatar into a survey. It speaks, listens by speech recognition, and converses through a language model. Eighty British participants took psychometric surveys one of two ways: talking with the avatar or typing to a chatbot.

Over two thousand responses were collected. Avatar interviews drew more informative, detailed answers than the chatbot. Engagement ran higher yet took less time. Satisfaction, though, did not clearly improve. Interviews blamed taste, pauses in turn-taking, and unease at near-human faces. The authors read the results as a promise: survey talk with embodied agents feels closer to a real interview, if the rough edges are smoothed.
arxiv-2508-02776:
Low-mass dark matter haloes are a sharp test of what dark matter is, and strongly lensed arcs can reveal them through tiny bends in the light. Earlier work reported such haloes in ALMA observations of SDP.81, a lensed dusty star-forming galaxy. The authors reanalyze those data to check how sturdy the claims are. They find the data do support extra angular structure in the lens mass beyond a smooth elliptical profile.

But they find no evidence for the two previously reported sub-halo detections. Mock data show they would have caught a reported halo of about a billion solar masses if it were real. Testing systematics, they conclude the earlier claim was likely spurious, caused by a smooth model that fit the multipole structure poorly. They urge future searches to include multipoles up to fourth order and to demand a well-fitting smooth model first.
arxiv-2508-02976:
Hanwen Ren, Ruiqi Ni, and Ahmed H. Qureshi presented a method in twenty twenty-five that helps robots move objects to a target pose in cluttered rooms. Robots in warehouses and hospitals need this skill, but older methods are slow, need expert demos, or learn by trial and error. The team's method uses a neural network shaped by physics rules.

The network learns to solve the Eikonal equation, which gives the fastest path time through a space. No expert data is needed. While moving an object, the robot can also change its grip on the fly when the plan calls for it. Tests in simulation and on a real robot beat leading rivals on planning time, path length, and success rate across many objects.
arxiv-2508-03276:
Terra Blevins, Susanne Schmalwieser, and Benjamin Roth ask if language models bend their style toward the user they talk with. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. In human talk, people tend to match each other's words and tone. Whether models do the same, and by the same means, was not well tested.

They set model replies to real dialogues next to the true human replies, across many models and three dialogue sets. Models match the talk style strongly, in fact more than humans do. The match shifts by trait. Tuned and larger models bend less than raw and smaller ones. The authors doubt the same inner drive lies behind human and model acts.
arxiv-2508-03376:
Jun Wu and colleagues introduced a quantum computing method in 2025 called CutVQA. Today's quantum machines have too few qubits for many useful tasks. One workaround cuts a large circuit into small parts that fit, but stitching the parts back together can demand a huge number of repeat runs.

CutVQA searches for good circuit designs with the cuts already in mind, then tunes each small part on its own. On two standard test tasks it matched the accuracy of full circuits. At the same time it cut the repeat-run cost by a very large factor and at least halved training time. The work shows design and cutting work best together.
arxiv-2508-04376:
Eva Gallardo-Gutiérrez and Javier González-Doña wrote this math paper in two thousand twenty-five. It studies local spectral traits of operators built by subordinating a semigroup, a flow of operators over time, against a measure.

The authors show such an operator lacks the single valued extension property, and that its local spectral subspaces are dense, while the adjoint has the Dunford property and trivial subspaces. They then apply this to the classic Cesàro operator on Hardy spaces, where the local spectrum at any non-zero function matches the full spectrum. A last part treats semigroups of composition operators, where the traits hinge on the shape of the linked Koenigs domain.
arxiv-2508-04976:
Sakib, Hu, and Abdelzaher extend a way to fit sharp object finding into the tight time and compute bounds of small edge machines. Their paper, from two thousand twenty-five, is called CSRAP.

The past way gathers the parts of a frame that count into a small canvas, which can be worked at the needed rate. The new way lets the canvas change size, and lets its rate part from the rate of the source frames. The team runs a known finder on a small board, over road video from a known set. The new freedoms give a better trade of quality for cost at each point. That means a higher mean quality for the same spend.
arxiv-2508-05476:
Chaohui Gong, Zhiying Wu, and four peers make CT-like scans from MR scans by joining two kinds of MR views. The work came out in 2025. Fake CT scans spare sick folks the rays of a real CT scan. They also dodge some blur from moves. That makes them of use when staff plan care.

Most past ways worked from one MR view at a time. This way, MM2CT, joins T1-weighted and T2-weighted scans. Those two views light up not-quite-the-same flesh. Its core is a Mamba build, picked since it tracks wide links at low cost. That cost is less than big shift-based builds need. A small shift step adds fine grain work. The parts join traits from both views while they keep place links whole. The aim is a fake CT true enough for real care work.
arxiv-2508-07776: Paweł Duch, Martin Hairer, Jaeyun Yi, and Wenhao Zhao wrote a paper from 2025 on the long-run behavior of a classic quantum field model in three dimensions, over all of space. They show the dynamics are well posed for all time. At high temperature, any two solutions driven by the same noise draw together at an exponential rate. That pull lets them name a single steady distribution for the system, which meets the standard axioms of a healthy field theory.
arxiv-2508-08376:
Qi Zhang and Wen-Tao Xu prove that two distinct quantum phases can melt into each other continuously, settling a long-standing question. Their paper appeared in 2025. The phases are the toric code and the double semion, both carrying the same basic topological order yet genuinely different. Earlier work found only abrupt transitions or a phase in between. Both phases can be born from a richer parent order, so the team perturbed that parent model.

They confirm a direct continuous transition of the XY-star type, by mapping it to two coupled Ising models. At the transition, exotic parent-order particles become free, revealed by order parameters and loop measurements. The authors say the result opens a theory of phase changes beyond the standard condensation story.
arxiv-2508-09076:
Timothee Benard, Weikun He, and Han Zhang wrote this mathematics paper, published in two thousand twenty-five. It asks how well numbers can be approximated by rationals when the numbers are drawn from a fractal measure. Classic results by Khintchine and Schmidt settle the question for ordinary volume. This work moves it to self-similar measures in any dimension.

The bridge is a random walk on a space of lattices. The team shows the walk spreads out evenly in a strong, effective sense. New tools include a bootstrap scheme that pushes the walk past algebraic roadblocks. They also refine Dani's classic link between approximation and dynamics. Along the way they prove that self-similar measures do not clump near algebraic surfaces. The outcome extends both the yes-or-no law of Khintchine and the counting estimates of Schmidt to fractal settings.
arxiv-2508-10176:
Shihang Liu and six co-authors use a faint radio signal from the young cosmos to bound a soft form of dark matter. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

The signal comes from the dawn of stars and the age when their light lit gas anew. Its strength across scales holds facts on how mass clumped, which dark matter rules. The team runs full models of that age with the soft form's traits built in. They find the soft form cuts small clumps, which delays the key ages and makes them shorter than in the cold form. Early on, the signal's shift is ruled by the soft form's smooth spread.
arxiv-2508-11676:
Maksym Shamrai and Vladyslav Hamolia build a map of the world's languages from the inner weights of large language models, in work from 2025. Older maps rely on features chosen by hand by linguists. The pair instead let the model itself supply the features.

They score which weights matter most for each language, using a pruning method adapted for the task. Those scores form a vector for each language, and distances between vectors place languages in a shared space. The study covers 106 languages and several multilingual models. The map matches known language families well. It also shows surprise links that may hint at past contact between peoples or shared paths of change. Code, vectors, and a viewing tool are public.
arxiv-2508-11776:
Arpan Das and Arpan Kanrar settle an open case in brace theory in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Braces are algebraic structures tied to set-theoretic solutions of a famous equation. Recent work classified braces for several families of groups with a large cyclic subgroup; the count settled down as groups grew.

The modular maximal-cyclic family was the leftover case. The authors show these braces allow only one non-cyclic way to add elements. Unlike the earlier families, their number keeps growing with the group's order instead of stabilizing. That contrast makes the family a genuine exception. The paper closes a classification thread opened by a conjecture of Guarnieri and Vendramin.
arxiv-2508-12476:
Haojie Chen and Yang Yang introduce a new kind of eigenvalue in their 2025 paper on Hermitian tensors. A tensor is a grid of numbers with many indices, a step beyond a matrix. Eigenvalues are the special scale factors that reveal a tensor's core behavior, and this new type, written with a hat over the H, fits tensors with complex entries.

The authors give easy-to-check sets that must contain these values. From them, they derive tests for when a Hermitian tensor counts as positive in the math sense. They then apply the tools to a curvature question in complex geometry. Their method re-proves the algebra behind recent results by two other teams, which supports the new definitions.
arxiv-2508-12776:
Rajabinasab and co-authors propose a forest-based method for spotting outliers without labels in this 2025 paper. Their approach grows from randomized principal component analysis, a fast approximate method. A related forest structure had already sped up nearest-neighbor search.

The new method builds a forest of these randomized projections. It derives an outlier score from the forest's own structure, with no training labels. Across several benchmark datasets, the method beat classical and recent rivals on some and matched them on the rest. The authors also stress-test its robustness and speed. They present it as an efficient, dependable choice for unsupervised outlier detection in practice.
arxiv-2508-13076:
Isaiah Andrews, Jiafeng Chen, and Otavio Tecchio rethink estimation in economics in twenty twenty-five. In over-identified models, the model is usually wrong in some way. Misspecification is the norm, not the exception. Then different estimators stop being rival routes to one target. Each estimator defines its own estimand, its own answer.

The authors review recent use of generalized method of moments in a top journal. Formal specification testing is rare there, they find. Estimators that would be inefficient under a correct model are widely used, including hand-picked moments. They synthesize recent theory into guidelines for transparent, robust work. A new result shows Hansen's J-statistic measures the range of estimates reachable at a given precision. Readers get a clearer contract between method and meaning.
arxiv-2508-14976:
Chandra and three co-authors build a bot test that shifts with the user in this twenty twenty-five paper. Word tests for bots grow weak as solver tools learn their set forms. A test that breeds fresh trials can stay a step past those solvers.

Inside, a breed net makes fresh sight trials while a sound twin runs in sync. A learn agent sets the trial's grade from how the user acts in real time. Rule and net checks then split man from bot in the end call. Tests show more true folks pass and more stock bots fail than past tests. Big new aid bots can still crack it, the team says in plain words.
arxiv-2508-15376:
Cong Wang and colleagues rebuilt dynamic driving scenes with neural Gaussians in a 2025 paper. Simulators and autonomy stacks need faithful three-dimensional reconstructions of real streets, but driving scenes mix static backgrounds spanning huge depth ranges with cars and pedestrians moving in complex, sometimes non-rigid ways. Earlier Gaussian splatting methods worked at small or object scale. DriveSplat handles the whole scene in one Gaussian representation, splitting the treatment: backgrounds get a learnable level-of-detail scheme that allocates Gaussians adaptively across near, middle, and far depth ranges.

Moving actors are modeled object by object, with rigid global motion plus a two-stage deformation that first shifts anchors, then updates the Gaussians, capturing bending and articulation. Extra regularization steadies the optimization. The unified design aims at city-scale, dynamic reconstruction rather than curated clips.
arxiv-2508-16176:
Ryan Niu, Shoichi Koyama, and Tomohiko Nakamura personalize spatial audio from body measurements in this 2025 paper. Head related transfer functions describe how ears and head color sound by direction. Measuring them per person is costly, so datasets stay small. Recordings differ in source positions across datasets, which blocks pooling.

Their method first learns a latent code for the sound magnitude pattern. An autoencoder conditioned on source position makes codes comparable across datasets. Body measurements then predict the code for a new listener. Merging datasets makes neural training feasible at last. Tests beat current network methods on estimation accuracy. Personal spatial audio could reach headphones without a lab visit.
arxiv-2508-16576:
Anyu Ying and nine co-authors benchmark how to train speech recognizers for children, whose voices differ sharply from adults and whose labeled data are scarce. Fine-tuning adult models is the common shortcut, but training from a flat start on child speech had never been compared systematically. The team ran the comparison inside the open ESPnet toolkit.

Self-supervised speech representations, they found, lean toward adult speech, and flat-start training on child data reduced that bias. Scaling the model helped steadily up to a billion parameters, then flattened. Age-by-age analysis of recognition and speaker verification exposed weaknesses in proprietary systems like Whisper. The public benchmark aims to make child speech research more reliable and open.
arxiv-2508-16676:
Jiacheng Li and a large team of co-authors rescale network weights mid-training to steer large language models onto better paths. Their paper from twenty twenty-five presents WISCA. Most training gains come from architecture or optimizer tweaks. Weight patterns, the spread and relative size of the weights themselves, get less systematic care. WISCA rescales weights while keeping model outputs unchanged at the swap.

The output-preserving trick bends the training trajectory without a restart. Gains show in loss and in zero-shot validation across several builds. Grouped query attention models profit most clearly. LoRA fine-tuning runs gain as well. The method is light: no structure change, no new data. The authors frame weight hygiene as a free lever that training pipelines have left idle.
arxiv-2508-16976:
Bin Pan and four colleagues present Joint Parameter Selection, a fine-tuning method that protects domain generalization, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Domain generalization means doing well on new target domains after training on few source domains. Large pretrained vision models are the usual starting point. Full fine-tuning, though, can damage the generalization built into them.

Some methods tune only a subset of parameters. That balances fitting the task against keeping generalization. Joint Parameter Selection limits updates to a small, sparse subset. The authors prove a generalization error bound that reflects update sparsity in a direct way. A selection mechanism with dual operators picks parameters. It looks for gradients that are steady and strong across source domains. Tests on benchmarks showed scores above leading domain generalization methods. The results back selective fine-tuning as both efficient and effective.
arxiv-2508-17376:
Jiali Cui, Yan-Ying Chen, Yanxia Zhang, and Matthew Klenk present ShaLa, a 2025 generative framework for learning one shared latent space across data types like images, text, and audio. Many multimodal methods record every combination of details, which can bury the high-level concepts the modalities share. Classic multimodal autoencoders aim at that shared core but often infer it weakly and synthesize poorly.

ShaLa pairs a new inference architecture with a second-stage diffusion prior over the shared code. Across benchmarks, it beat leading multimodal autoencoders on coherence and synthesis quality. It also scaled to more modalities, where earlier designs faltered as the shared space grew complex. The authors pitch clean shared codes as the route to cross-modal generation and inference that actually hang together.
arxiv-2508-19876:
Sepideh Shafiei and Shapour Hakam present an open data set for the computer study of Iranian classical music, in a 2025 paper. At its center is the radif, a fixed body of melodic units that students learn and performers draw on. Such material had lacked a structured digital corpus.

The data set pairs audio with symbolic MIDI files, aligned phrase by phrase, plus written transcriptions and comparison tables drawn from many performers and scholars. Sections cover one master's full radif, material from a second, and samples of a florid vocal ornament sung by noted twentieth-century singers. Each unit carries a code for easy reference. Parts are openly licensed, while some recordings are cited so users can find the originals. The authors invite wider collaboration.
arxiv-2508-21576:
Zhijie Zhang and ten co-authors use detailed simulations to trace where the hot gas halo around Milky Way-like galaxies comes from. Their paper came out in 2025. Such halos glow faintly in X-rays, and their origin tests theories of how galaxies form.

In every version of their simulation with star feedback, the total X-ray brightness matched observations of the Milky Way and similar galaxies. But the simulated glow faded too fast with distance from the center, falling well short of the extended emission recent observations show. Star feedback, from winds, radiation, and supernovae, shaped only the inner halo. The authors conclude that extra heating is needed, perhaps from gravity, from the central black hole, or from cosmic rays.
arxiv-2509-00176:
Muhammad Ali and Salman Khan present Waste-Bench in 2025, a benchmark for vision-language models in cluttered waste scenes. Such models join sight and text and shine on standard photos. Waste in the real world is messier: piles are cluttered and objects are deformed, which strains visual understanding.

Their data set targets waste classification under those hard conditions. A deep evaluation method then probes the robustness and accuracy of current models on it. Results expose a clear need for stronger robustness before such models can sort waste reliably. The set and study give builders a hard, realistic test for the next round of model gains.
arxiv-2509-00276:
Yuxiang Liu leads a team of nine authors who present RITE in 2025, a text embedding method that builds reasoning into search. Embeddings turn text into vectors for dense retrieval, which finds documents by meaning. Encoder models do this well for surface matches, but complex queries need reasoning past word overlap, where they fall short.

Large language models reason strongly, yet prior embedding uses of them stress context over reasoning. RITE first generates intermediate reasoning text in token space, then computes the embedding from that enriched input. The simple change lets the model's logic shape what gets retrieved. Zero-shot tests, with no task training, are the target setting for the gains.
arxiv-2509-00476:
Omar Khalid Ali Mohamed, writing alone, builds a malware detector meant to work across data sources, not just one dataset. Malware is harmful software, and detectors trained on a single source often fail on new kinds while also costing much compute.

Mohamed trains separate LightGBM classifiers, fast decision-tree models, on three datasets that cover fixed file traits, call behavior, and memory patterns linked to hidden code. He keeps only top features, then blends the models' probability scores with weights found by grid search, a scan of options. The blend reaches a macro F1 score, a balanced accuracy measure, of 0.823 on cross-domain checks, beating single models with low overhead.
arxiv-2509-01476:
Language models with retrieval can look facts up, yet they still sometimes answer when they should admit ignorance. Youchao Zhou, with seven co-authors, asks whether retrieval-augmented models know when they do not know. Such models should refuse questions their knowledge, internal or retrieved, cannot support, but that refusal skill had not been studied closely.

The team tests calibration across different states of internal and retrieved knowledge. Against expectations, when all retrieved documents were irrelevant, the models still tended to refuse some questions they could have answered correctly on their own. That over-refusal pattern raises a second question about how refusal behavior aligns with calibration quality. Zhou and the co-authors present the study as a probe of a blind spot in hallucination research, where retrieval and refusal have mostly been judged apart.
arxiv-2509-01776:
David R Burt, Renato Berlinghieri, and Tamara Broderick give trustworthy error bars for spatial links with yes-no or count data. Health teams often ask how disease presence shifts with heat or pollution across places. Past methods may assume the model is right or that places were sampled at random. Both assumptions fail in much real spatial work.

The authors give the first intervals with guaranteed long run coverage for such links with discrete outcomes. Their proof handles noise that varies by place and sampling that is not random. Standard methods can miss coverage badly and even flip the sign of a link in tests. Their method holds the promised coverage in those same checks.
arxiv-2509-01876:
Naoki Isobe leads five co-authors on using the PRIMA mission to probe particle acceleration in jets from active galaxies. Jets are narrow beams launched by giant black holes at galaxy centers. Their hot spots, where jets slam to a halt, likely speed particles at strong shocks. To judge that speeding, the field strength at the hot spot must be known.

A bend in the synchrotron spectrum, called the cooling break, can reveal that strength. Its frequency balances two cooling routes for fast electrons. For typical hot spots, the break should sit near the far infrared band PRIMA covers. The authors map a feasible observing plan for near, well studied hot spots. The same trick may extend to the broad lobes of radio galaxies.
arxiv-2509-01976:
Geoffrey R Hosack leads nine co-authors in a Bayesian model for ranked vegetation cover tracked over space and time. Their data are foliage scores for four invasive weed species under active management. Scores follow a standard field scale and count as ordinal data, meaning ordered grades rather than exact amounts. Records are sparse, with few high cover sightings.

A sequential ordinal form turns the likelihood into a binary model given hidden effects. That form dodges ordering constraints on category cut points that burden cumulative models. A separable space-time structure keeps parameters readable despite sparse grades. Fast approximate Bayesian fitting yields maps of each species response. The weeds differ by habitat, control effort, and access, yet share short spatial ranges and strong time persistence.
arxiv-2509-02276:
Susana Nunes, Samy Badreddine, and Catia Pesquita pitch REx, a way that pays for clear grounds in drug reuse hunts on knowledge graphs. Knowledge graphs map multi link bio data and back new hunches for drug use. Forecast ways need strong grounds in plain terms to win trust, not just high scores. Their way makes grounds from link forecast paths found in the graph.

A learn by reward agent hunts ground paths led by pay for good ground traits. Field term sets pad those paths so grounds rest on firm bio facts. Three known graph tests host the drug reuse case in their work. Grounds check forecasts next to bio facts in their tests with good fit. Scores beat top past ways too, which pairs clear grounds with truth.
arxiv-2509-02376:
Jesse Hemerik wrote a 2025 solo statistics paper extending a popular resampling test called maxT, built to control the familywise error rate, the chance of any false claim. The new version targets a looser goal called false discovery exceedance control.

That goal keeps the share of false finds among all claims below a set level with high probability. Hemerik's method is also simultaneous: one threshold is reported, yet stricter thresholds keep the same guarantee at the same time. For small sets, the bound even forces zero false finds. Power stays close to the strongest rival method, under the same assumptions. The paper also allows confidence envelopes with data-driven shapes, fixing a known limit of earlier simultaneous methods.
arxiv-2509-02476:
Haichen Hu and David Simchi-Levi wrote a 2025 statistical learning paper on judging how well a trained model will perform, without assuming a simple model class. Their setting covers penalised risk minimisation with Bregman losses, a flexible family of error measures.

The method, called wild refitting, perturbs outputs in derivative space with random signs, then retrains a second predictor on the altered data. The gap between the two fits, called wild optimism, upper-bounds the true excess risk with high probability. Only a single dataset is required, plus access to the training procedure as a black box. That model-free flavour suits deep networks and generative models, whose complexity defeats classical theory. The authors tune the noise scale to keep the bound valid.
arxiv-2509-02576:
Sujoy Majumder, Nabadwip Sarkar, and Debabrata Pramanik wrote a 2025 complex analysis paper revisiting the Brück conjecture, a statement about entire functions that share values with their derivatives. Their route runs through first-order partial differential equations, using the solutions of such systems in several complex variables.

Working in higher-dimensional complex space, the authors show the conjecture holds under certain extra conditions. Along the way they prove a Borel-Caratheodory theorem in that setting, a result bounding a function by its real part. Several basic facts about order and hyper-order, measures of how fast entire functions grow, are also established for several variables. The paper extends a one-variable uniqueness theory into higher dimensions.
arxiv-2509-02676:
Jeff Steinhauer, Kyriakos Destounis, and Richard Brito wrote a 2025 general relativity paper on waves inside a Schwarzschild black hole, the simplest black hole type. Textbooks say everything inside falls to the singularity, and light-like waves do follow that path in the geometric optics limit.

Beyond that limit, axial gravitational ripples can form quasibound states that decay before ever reaching the singularity. These modes are overdamped, meaning they fade without oscillating. Working in coordinates that avoid ambiguities at the horizon, the authors map the mode shapes. The relevant master function stays nonzero at the future horizon yet dies away inside. Observers falling along timed paths could in principle register the modes. The result softens a common assumption about the black hole interior.
arxiv-2509-03176:
Serra Aksoy evaluated ways of judging explanation methods for neural networks in a 2025 study. Attribution methods assign credit to input features, showing which pixels pushed a medical image model toward its answer. Judging those methods usually means cutting their maps at one threshold, turning shades of credit into black and white.

Aksoy shows that single cutoffs can flip method rankings wildly, even by hundreds of percentage points. Her fix scores methods across every threshold at once using an area-under-curve measure of overlap. On skin imaging, one method beat two familiar rivals by wide margins under that fairer scoring. Performance also swung strongly with lesion size. The standards proposed aim to make explanation choices evidence-based in medicine and beyond.
arxiv-2509-03376:
Hui Chen and 3 co-authors built a 2025 method for unmixing hyperspectral images, which record many narrow color bands per pixel. Each pixel usually mixes several pure materials, called endmembers, in proportions the analyst wants to recover. Deep methods often fail to capture both wide spatial dependencies and fine local boundaries at once.

Their framework, T-CAGU, pairs a transformer, which models long-range links, with a content-adaptive graph network that strengthens local relationships. Multiple propagation orders let it learn the graph structure dynamically, adding robustness against noise. A residual mechanism preserves global information and steadies training. Experiments showed superiority over leading earlier methods. The code is publicly available for reuse.
arxiv-2509-03576:
Marco Berton and three co-authors wrote a 2025 review comparing narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies with the type 1 active galactic nuclei now seen in the early universe. Narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies are nearby systems with small black holes feeding at high rates. The James Webb Space Telescope has revealed similar highly accreting black holes at very high redshift.

Across many wavelengths, the distant objects resemble their local cousins in several physical properties, including the puzzling little red dots. Differences remain, likely tied to different environments and evolutionary paths. The review gathers what is known about the local class into a handbook for researchers studying early objects. It also gives local-universe specialists an entry point into early active nucleus evolution, arguing the comparison can sharpen understanding of extreme accretion.
arxiv-2509-04076:
Lennart Clasmeier and four co-authors teach a robot to plan its own movements in a 2025 research paper. Classic planning software checks many paths and stays reliable, but it can be slow. The team trained a learning model on paths those planners produced for the NICOL robot, a human-like research machine. Their model works from keypoints, a sparse set of joint positions, and builds motion step by step in a diffusion process.

Cleaning hidden biases out of the training data mattered more than feeding in detailed scene scans. Even without those scans, the model found collision-free paths in up to ninety percent of test cases. It also finished about ten times faster than the classic planners.
arxiv-2509-04276:
Jianning Deng and two co-authors reconstruct movable objects from just a handful of unposed photos in a 2025 research paper. Articulated objects, like laptops or pliers, change shape as their parts move. Earlier methods demanded many views plus exact camera positions shared across poses. Their system, PAOLI, works with as few as four photos per pose and no known camera positions. Each pose is first rebuilt on its own, which creates a matching problem across poses.

A dense deformation field, a map of how points shift, aligns the separate rebuilds and links corresponding points. Robust fitting then separates still parts from moving ones and recovers the joint settings. Self-guided fine-tuning polishes shape, appearance, and motion together. Benchmarks and real objects confirm accurate results.
arxiv-2509-04376:
Hao Ju and two co-authors build a search system that finds people behaving abnormally from a written description in a 2025 research paper. Security teams may need to locate someone who fell, collided, or was struck, using only words. Large multimodal models understand images and text deeply, but their generative knowledge does not naturally serve precise retrieval. Their framework, AnomalyLMM, works from coarse to fine, narrowing candidates before checking subtle behavioral cues.

A training-free cookbook adapts the big model without new teaching data. Masked prompts, saliency guesses about what stands out, and knowledge-aware re-ranking focus attention on anomaly signs. On the PAB benchmark, the only public set for this task, accuracy edged past the strongest baseline, with readable alignments between words and behavior.
arxiv-2509-04476:
Seojin Kim and three co-authors change how molecule generators chop molecules into pieces in a 2025 research paper. Text-to-molecule models turn written descriptions into molecular structures, promising help for drug discovery. Molecules are usually tokenized atom by atom, which captures local connections but misses global structure like ring systems. Their model, CAMT5, tokenizes at the substructure level instead, treating meaningful chunks as units. An importance-based training strategy emphasizes the key substructures.

Experiments across generation tasks showed CAMT5 beating previous state-of-the-art methods while using only a small fraction of the training tokens. A simple ensemble that aggregates several models' outputs boosted results further. Code is public. Better tokenization, rather than bigger data, drove the gains.
arxiv-2509-04576:
Ce Zheng and one co-author, Tingting Yang, cut the communication cost of splitting language model work between a gadget and a base station in a 2025 research paper. Speculative decoding lets a small draft model guess several tokens that a big model then verifies, speeding generation. In AI-native radio networks, the device drafts and the base station verifies, but sending the full vocabulary probability list uplink devours bandwidth. Their scheme transmits only the top candidate tokens with their raw scores and indices.

Bandwidth falls sharply while inference quality holds. A formula for the optimal draft length maximizes throughput, and theory bounds the achievable speedup. Experiments confirm both efficiency and effectiveness, making collaborative inference over wireless links more practical.
arxiv-2509-04876:
Expert language model agents often work in parallel without truly coordinating what they know. Jusheng Zhang, lead author with four co-authors, present OSC, a framework for deeper collaboration, in a 2025 paper. The framework sits between agent selection and result aggregation, where linguistic interaction becomes a bottleneck.

Each agent builds a model of its collaborators' knowledge and cognitive state. Real-time gap analysis then lets agents adjust content focus, detail level, and expression style. Experiments on complex reasoning and problem-solving benchmarks show better task performance and communication efficiency. The authors frame the result as turning parallel workers into a collaborative team.
arxiv-2509-05376:
Eye tracking in learning games can reveal who a student is, Abdul Rehman and three co-authors warn in a 2025 paper on privacy in interactive learning. Gaze data help detect developmental disorders, but the same signals can be traced back to a child's identity.

The authors first show how student identities and diagnoses can be predicted from game-based eye data in several scenarios. They then present a two-stage framework using real-time anonymisation, dummy identities with administrator-only access, and federated learning across clients, where training stays on local devices. Their tests report high diagnostic accuracy while blocking identity backtracking. Rules such as the GDPR and trust through transparency frame the design.
arxiv-2509-05476:
Predicting a patient's survival odds as new measurements arrive can improve by training only on similar patients, Minzee Kim and Joel A. Dubin propose in a 2025 biostatistics paper. Joint models link a biomarker measured over time with the timing of an event like death.

Standard dynamic prediction refits as fresh longitudinal data arrive, but uses the whole dataset each time. Their similarity-based approach trains on a targeted subset chosen to resemble the patient at hand. In thorough simulations and an application to intensive care data, the targeted training improved prediction accuracy. The idea is simple and practical: neighbours in data space may forecast a patient better than the crowd.
arxiv-2509-05676:
Life insurance tied to a green investment fund needs both a sound fund and a hedge, Katia Colaneri and three co-authors address in a 2025 mathematical finance paper. Unit-linked policies pay benefits that follow fund performance, and adding environmental criteria complicates both construction and risk control.

Their fund rule selects assets by firms' carbon intensity directly, avoiding ad hoc screening on commercial ESG scores, and it is tested on real market data. For the insurer, market, carbon, and mortality risks are hedged with a quadratic method that minimises the variance of hedging costs, since markets are incomplete. A numerical study with an efficient simulation scheme checks the hedge's performance.
arxiv-2509-05776:
Rebuilding a full three-dimensional shape from a partial medical scan is the problem addressed in a 2025 paper by Jonathan Aellen and three co-authors. Their tool is the point distribution model, a statistical summary of how a body part's outline varies. The paper focuses on pose, meaning the alignment between training shapes and the partial target shape.

Misaligned pose, the authors show, biases the rebuilt shape and its stated uncertainty, especially when only a small part is visible. Their fix adjusts an existing model to one target before use, without needing the original training data. The adjustment is exact for shifts and close for small rotations. Because it runs as a quick preprocessing step, clinics can drop it into current pipelines and gain accuracy while keeping the speed of linear models.
arxiv-2509-05976:
The spin of the second black hole born in a merging pair is modeled in a 2025 paper led by Zi-Yuan Wang with five co-authors. Gravitational wave catalogs show a link between mass ratio and effective spin that weakened in the newest data, prompting a search for its physical origin. The authors test a recent, weaker prescription for winds from helium stars.

Detailed stellar models in the MESA code, with tidal interaction and internal rotation, show the second-born spin barely cares about the helium star's stage or companion mass. Wind loss dominates instead: heavier progenitors yield slower-spinning black holes. A fitting formula captures the result, and population synthesis with COMPAS finds no mass-ratio-spin correlation in either formation channel studied, a puzzle the authors leave for alternative physics.
arxiv-2509-06176:
Training people who can govern artificial intelligence is the design problem of a 2025 paper led by Raphaël Weuts with six co-authors. Teaching on AI ethics is scattered across fields and cut off from practice, while failures in the field keep recurring. The authors pull the literature and new rules together into a modular cross-field course.

Their term plan weaves the technical basics together with ethics, law, and policy, drawing on European, Chinese, and international frameworks. Failures in practice, such as bias, wrongly set goals, and breakdowns of oversight, are linked to specific teaching strategies. Input from affected groups and hands-on learning run throughout. The course aims at graduates who can diagnose risks, handle the rules, and work with many groups.
arxiv-2509-06476:
Winds blown out by a feeding black hole take center stage in a 2025 astronomy paper led by Jacob Tutterow, with nine co-authors. The team studies NGC 3516, a nearby Seyfert galaxy whose outflowing gas is hard to separate from ordinary rotation. Long-slit spectra from Hubble and a ground-based instrument supply the data.

Fitting several Gaussian curves to key emission lines lets the authors split rotation from outflow. A two-cone wind model then matches the moving gas well. The glowing oxygen pattern, they argue, comes from dusty spiral arms lit by the cone, which Earth sees along one edge. Cloud speeds also turn over as radiation pushes outward and gravity pulls back, and the clouds seem to start in the inner dusty spirals.
arxiv-2509-06576:
Messy hospital codes from many institutions are organized into clean hierarchies by Yinjie Wang and four co-authors in a 2025 health informatics paper. Electronic health records mix diagnoses, medicines, and lab results, but each site uses its own codes and terms. That mess blocks large studies that combine records across hospitals.

Their framework, MASH, works automatically. Neural optimal transport aligns codes between institutions, and learned embeddings in hyperbolic space, a geometry suited to trees, build the hierarchy. Training draws on pretrained language models, patterns of codes appearing together, written descriptions, and known labels. Applied to real records, MASH produced readable hierarchies for diagnosis, medication, and lab codes. Notably, it built the first automatic hierarchies for local lab codes that previously had no standard structure at all.
arxiv-2509-06676:
How fast a widely used optimization method settles down is pinned down exactly by Hadi Abbaszadehpeivasti and one co-author in a 2025 optimization paper. The Douglas-Rachford splitting algorithm finds a point where two maximally monotone operators sum to zero, a task behind many feasibility and optimization problems. Precise rates, rather than rough bounds, were missing.

The authors obtain an exact convergence rate for the method and show it cannot be improved, at least for convex feasibility problems. They also give conditions that are both necessary and sufficient for the faster linear form of convergence. Composite optimization problems, where a cost splits into simpler pieces, get their own analysis of the method's behavior. The paper ends with several conjectures about that setting, marking where the theory of this workhorse algorithm remains unfinished.
arxiv-2509-07076:
Seth Koren, Yuhsin Tsai, and Runqing Wang set limits on first-order phase transitions during dark energy domination, in a 2025 paper. Late in cosmic history, once vacuum energy took over the energy budget, such a transition could still have happened. Some stored heat would turn into other forms, such as radiation we cannot see.

Particle physics models with very many possible vacua give this broad idea a concrete push. The simplest limit comes from how fast the universe expands, measured through the Hubble rate. But that test only senses transitions that involve a large share of the dark energy. The authors find much sharper limits once the uneven effects of transition fluctuations on cosmic microwave background photons are counted. For a range of transition rates, today's data allow only a small fraction of the vacuum energy to have been released.
arxiv-2509-07276:
Pierre Briaud and 5 co-authors propose a new way in 2025 to demonstrate quantum advantage, the point where a quantum computer beats classical machines on a useful test. Their test is solving systems of multivariate polynomial equations, sets of equations in many unknowns, over the field with two elements. The systems are drawn at random from a set distribution, with fewer equations than unknowns.

A quantum algorithm based on a 2022 breakthrough framework is shown to solve such systems in expected polynomial time. Classical hardness is not proven but conjectured, after a review of known classical attacks, for equations of degree above two. If the conjecture holds, degree-three equations suffice to instantiate a random oracle and gain a strong form of quantum advantage. A verifiable, non-interactive test would give the field a clean public benchmark.
arxiv-2509-07376:
People who lose speech after a stroke still have a face, and a face carries clues about voice. Yejin Jeon and 4 co-authors work on face-to-speech synthesis in a 2025 research paper. Their system generates a voice from a facial image, aiming to sound like that person. Earlier methods used pre-trained visual encoders that discarded fine details such as gender or ethnicity.

The new method splits the face into small segments and merges them step by step into a rich representation. It learns speaker attributes in both the visual and acoustic domains at once. Training pairs several views of a speaker, under varied angles and lighting, with the same recordings. Subjective and objective tests show better face-voice match and more stable synthesis. Such tools could give non-speaking people a voice that feels like their own.
arxiv-2509-07476:
Evgeny Feigin, writing alone in 2025, defines global forms of positroid varieties in algebraic geometry. Positroid varieties are special solution sets inside Grassmannians. A Grassmannian is the space of all flat subspaces of a fixed size. These varieties arise as images of Richardson varieties from flag varieties under a natural map. They link geometry with combinatorics and with the theory of group actions on vector spaces.

Feigin embeds positroid varieties into quiver Grassmannians for cyclic quivers. He then varies the quiver data to build global positroid varieties inside a type A global affine Grassmannian. The general member of the family matches the classical positroid variety. The special member sits inside a juggling variety. He shows the families are flat and describes their scheme structures and special fibers. The work unifies objects that once lived in separate settings.
arxiv-2509-07576:
Mathis Brichet and 2 co-authors optimize inbound transportation planning for a global carmaker in a 2025 operations study. The shipper-side problem, motivated by Renault's supply chain, decides how parts flow from suppliers to plants across a worldwide network. Their formal problem integrates flow consolidation with explicit bin-packing, time-expanded routing, and regularity constraints that keep operations predictable week to week.

An iterated local search method, mixing large-neighborhood search with optimization-based perturbations, solves the problem at industrial scale. On real data with over 700,000 commodities and 1.2 million arcs, the method lands within about 7.9 percent of the best known lower bound. Against legacy planning it shows a 23.2 percent cost-reduction potential. The framework now runs in production at Renault, supporting weekly strategic decisions, with internal estimates near 20 million euros saved per year.
arxiv-2509-07776:
Tatiana M. Nikiforova, writing alone in 2025, proves a homeomorphism theorem for sums of translates on the real line. Sums of translates build a function by adding shifted copies of kernel functions to a background field, generalizing logarithms of weighted algebraic polynomials. The kernels are concave on each side of a singularity at zero, and the translate positions can be chosen freely along the line.

For each placement, local maxima of the sum are taken over the intervals between consecutive translates and the two outer rays. The differences between successive local maxima form a vector-valued function of the placement. Under monotonicity assumptions on the kernels, Nikiforova proves that this difference map is a homeomorphism, a continuous bijection with continuous inverse, onto its range. Such rigidity results underpin equilibrium and approximation problems where translate positions must be solved from prescribed peak data.
arxiv-2509-07876:
Stacey Jeffery and 1 co-author place a newer proof tool within the known family of quantum lower-bound methods, in a 2025 theoretical computer science paper. Proving that a quantum algorithm needs many queries is hard, and the compressed oracle technique had recently scored many successes in quantum cryptanalysis. Older methods, such as the polynomial and adversary methods, had well-understood relative strengths.

The authors show the compressed oracle is actually a special case of the multiplicative adversary method. That placement matters because it lets researchers import classical intuition with confidence and compare techniques on common ground. A unified picture of proof methods helps cryptographers certify that quantum attacks on real systems cannot run faster than claimed.
arxiv-2509-07976:
Purnendu Karmakar and 1 co-author ask whether recent cosmic data point to changing dark energy or to modified gravity, in a 2025 cosmology paper. New baryon acoustic oscillation results from DESI and a fresh supernova compilation hint that dark energy may evolve over time. The authors instead test a gravity theory based on non-metricity, called f(Q) gravity, using a model-independent reconstruction.

Rebuilt dark energy density is extended to perturbation-level quantities: the effective strength of gravity and a damping parameter that alters how gravitational waves travel across the universe. Gravitational wave propagation then becomes a discriminator. Future detectors could tell a universe with evolving dark energy from one where gravity itself departs from Einstein's rules.
arxiv-2509-08076:
Planet-hunting Doppler measurements are polluted by the host star's own restless surface, and Justin Harrell with 1 co-author test ways to clean the signal in a 2025 astronomy paper. Magnetic activity cycles on a star can mask a planet's tug or imitate one. Flexible Gaussian process models describe the activity well, yet they can be too flexible and swallow real planetary signals.

A curvature-penalising objective keeps the activity model from overfitting long-term cycles, and the techniques are applied to the 55 Cancri system, a well-studied multi-planet system around a nearby star. High-pass filtering plays a complementary role. Cleaner activity removal decides whether small, close-in planets, the kind most like home, show up in radial velocity data at all.
arxiv-2509-08376:
Video is split into what moves and what stays, by a self-supervised method from Xiao Li and 5 co-authors in a 2025 computer vision paper. Earlier disentangling methods leaned on strong assumptions about the data. Their transformer pipeline instead generates flexible implicit features for frame-by-frame motion and whole-clip content at the same time.

A low-bitrate quantisation bottleneck forces the motion code to stay compact and discrete, which promotes clean separation and a meaningful motion vocabulary. The separated codes then condition a diffusion model that reconstructs the video. Editors and animators want exactly this split: swap the motion, keep the scene, or restyle the content while the action plays on unchanged.
arxiv-2509-08476:
Naming which deepfake method forged an audio clip, not just crying fake, is the new task set by Li Wang and 5 co-authors in a 2025 audio forensics paper. Binary real-or-fake judgements no longer meet practical needs, and older source tracing only worked inside a closed set of known generators. Their verification task targets open-set tracing, where the forging method may be unfamiliar.

A dual-branch architecture, Audity, extracts evidence from audio structure and from generation artefacts separately. Experiments show the combined branches trace sources effectively. Investigators and platforms need attribution, not suspicion alone: knowing the tool behind a fake voice recording shapes takedowns, prosecutions, and defences against the next generation method.
arxiv-2509-08776:
Maryam Ansarifard and 5 co-authors propose an end-to-end method to compress channel data for massive MIMO in a 2025 paper. MIMO uses many antennas, and feedback about the channel grows with antenna count. Most learning methods ignore quantization and entropy coding, which limit real use.

An attention step guided by spatial correlation learns compact codes that are also cheap to store. Quantization and entropy aware training are built into the whole system. Tests beat prior end-to-end schemes by clear margins indoors and outdoors. The rate and distortion trade-off improves. The authors present the method as ready for practical feedback systems.
arxiv-2509-08976:
Ya-Ting Yang and 1 co-author outline a multi-echelon theory of cyber warfare in a 2025 paper. Cyber conflict spans policy down to technical tactics, yet prior work often studies isolated tools or tactics. A holistic view is needed for resource choices and risk control.

Game theory models attacker and defender choices and supports equilibrium and risk analysis. Combined with AI, it can guide strategy across policy, operations, and technical levels. A synthetic conflict called RedCyber illustrates how levels depend on each other. The authors note more resources do not always mean more advantage. Future work on resilience and cross level planning is proposed.
arxiv-2509-09376:
Lumeng Liu and 5 co-authors use flow fluctuations to probe nuclear deformation in a 2025 paper. Nuclei can take an octupole, pear like shape, but if that shape is fixed or just vibrates is still open. High energy nuclear collisions give a fresh probe through triangular flow.

Multi-particle cumulants of triangular flow are studied in uranium on uranium collisions. A cumulant size and a ratio each scale in a straight line with the fourth moment of the deformation. With a known link to the second moment, both the mean and the spread of shape swings can be pulled out. That can at last split fixed from dynamic origins. Early state models for quark gluon plasma also gain.
arxiv-2509-09476:
Rajesh Dutta and 1 co-author extend a diagram method for modelling two-dimensional infrared spectroscopy in a 2025 chemical physics paper. Classical response functions are promising for such simulations, yet a tidy diagram picture, of the kind quantum treatments enjoy, was missing once a system touches its surroundings. A version for isolated systems left the long-time response unstable.

Working under a weak-anharmonicity approximation, Dutta and his co-author add system-bath coupling and find conditions where the bath settles the response. Their formula stays simple and matches the quantum counterpart when Planck's constant tends to zero. Stability turns out to hinge on the bath's spectral balance, and an amide band application shows the method in action.
arxiv-2509-09576:
Matthew D. A. Orkney and 1 co-author trace how the Milky Way's disc formed and survived in a 2025 study built on cosmological simulations. They run a statistical suite of galaxies with Milky Way-like mass and ask whether star motions today faithfully reveal when the disc first spun up. Big radial mergers, they find, often scramble that record beyond recovery.

At low metal content, the early proto-disc and stars kicked upward by mergers blur together, and kicked-up stars stay a minority even after major events. Real survey data, though, show very old metal-rich-in-alpha populations still rotating strongly. That fact favours gentler last mergers, below a one-to-four mass ratio, and dates the main interaction to roughly eleven billion years ago.
arxiv-2509-09976:
Jianping Fu and 4 co-authors test how crystal disorder changes superconductivity in iron selenide in a 2025 paper. Five single crystals held graded amounts of disorder. Each was checked for structure. Each was checked for how charge flows. Each was checked by its heat response. Disorder dragged two key numbers down. One is the transition point. The other is the upper critical field.

Heat tests confirmed two energy gaps side by side. One gap is larger and round. The other is smaller and varies with direction. Added disorder ironed the smaller gap toward roundness. Iron selenide sits between two regimes of pairing. Disorder slides that balance toward the classic BCS end. The ratio of gap to Fermi energy fell by more than half across the set.
arxiv-2509-10076:
Apostolos A. Tegos and 4 co-authors study an indoor wireless scheme where antennas can slide along a waveguide to wherever they help most in a 2025 communications paper. Pinching antenna systems light up points along a room-length guide, shrinking the air gap between transmitter and receiver and building strong line-of-sight links. The setup pairs two users with two pinching antennas on the uplink, the road from devices back to the network.

Instead of the usual non-orthogonal access, the transmitters split each message into parts, a rate-splitting design meant to harden the link against interference. The authors derive closed formulas for the outage probability, the chance a link fails outright. Computer checks confirm the formulas, and the rate-splitting version plainly beats its non-orthogonal rival on the same pinching hardware.
arxiv-2509-10176:
Ghitha Nadhira Azka Rahiemy and 2 co-authors re-derive a quantity that quietly controls how stiff neutron star matter can be in a 2025 nuclear physics paper. Inside quantum hadrodynamics, the effective nucleon mass links the meson forces between single particles to the bulk behaviour of dense matter. The authors work through the scalar density integral behind that mass in full detail, then check the algebra numerically with Gaussian quadrature until the two answers agree to high precision.

With the machinery trusted, they vary the model's parameter sets and watch the effective mass move. Those shifts flow straight into saturation behaviour, compressibility, and the pressure curve that decides a neutron star's size. The model family leans stiff overall, and the mass calculation becomes a clear window between microphysics and star-scale outcomes.
arxiv-2509-10376:
Luca Henrichs, Anton J. Heckens, and Thomas Guhr study ultrafast extreme events, the sudden price crashes and spikes that hit stock markets in fractions of a second, in this 2025 empirical finance paper. Algorithmic and high-frequency trading are prime suspects in these events, and their speed leaves regulators almost no time to intervene.

Comparing event characteristics across years of United States market data, the authors find liquidity playing the dominant role in triggering such events, with a general pattern in how they unfold. They also track how markets recover afterward. Recovery patterns repeat across years, while the recovery rate itself shifts with market sentiment. Despite those shifts, the authors read their results as pointing toward a degree of universal behavior in these extreme episodes.
arxiv-2509-10576:
Chengyuan Zhang and Suzhe Xu study what happens when young people make art with generative AI, in this 2025 paper. They surveyed 112 young learners and art students about working alongside an image-generating system. The questions covered how creators see their own role, what happens to originality, how the working process changes, and how taste and judgment form during co-creation.
