Most respondents treated the AI as a partner that sparks ideas and widens options, not a mere tool. At the same time they worried about styles flattening out and authorship blurring. Students shifted between roles, directing, conversing, and discovering, in a loop of intent, generation, choice, and refinement. The authors argue teaching should shift toward critical judgment.
arxiv-2509-10676:
Margaret Voetberg and four co-authors add explanation tools to a neutrino-hunting network in this 2025 paper. The network is NuGraph2. It is a graph neural network that tags neutrino interactions in particle detectors. AI is spreading through science. Users increasingly demand to know why a network reached its answer. They want that before trusting a result in print.

The add-ons probe the network from several sides. They examine the output classifications. They examine the edge connections between graph nodes. They probe the geometry of the network's internal latent space. General-purpose tools, built for this purpose, do the probing. No single method proves the network understands anything, the authors stress. Together, though, the views reveal how the classification is put together. The techniques transfer to other networks beyond this one. The code is public.
arxiv-2509-10876:
Anna Ritz-Zwilling and four co-authors present this 2025 mathematical physics paper on the Kitaev quantum double model, a lattice system used to study exotic particle-like excitations called anyons. Their goal is to count how many quantum states share each energy level in the model.

Working with any discrete group and any closed surface shape, the team derives the level counts from the fusion rules of the model's vertex and plaquette excitations. From those counts they obtain an exact formula for the model's partition function at any temperature and any system size. Exact results like this give researchers a firm benchmark for a model that sits at the heart of topological quantum computing research.
arxiv-2509-10976:
Waquar Ahmed and 4 co-authors explore a route to a magnetic Hall effect with no magnets in this 2025 paper. Their setting is a single kagome layer. A kagome layer is a lattice of corner-sharing triangles. It is filled with d-electron atoms. A canted order, where spins tilt out of the plane, can bend electron paths. The bend comes from the material's own Berry curvature.

When the tilt gives a spin pattern with a twist, the summed curvature can lock the Hall response to whole-number steps. That is the quantum anomalous Hall effect. It needs no outside field and no strong spin-orbit coupling. In the best case the step number could reach five. Real materials, with uneven hopping, give smaller steps. Flipping the tilt could flip the sign, a feature the authors note for quantum devices.
arxiv-2509-11576:
Kunpeng Li and 8 co-authors rebuild high-grade plasma turbulence on coarse grids in a 2025 study of the Hasegawa-Wakatani model, a reduced system that captures drift-wave turbulence. Physically sound closure models, which sum up unresolved small scales, remain a long-standing challenge in plasma work.

Guided by a theory called direct interaction approximation, the authors set a six-term closure structure mixing diffusion and hyper-diffusion. Neural networks informed by physics then learn the transport coefficients from data. Some learned coefficients turned negative in certain regimes, a sign of inverse transport that standard closures miss. The extended model matched spectra and fluxes of high-resolution runs while using far coarser grids, for about a tenfold speedup.
arxiv-2509-11676:
Saketh Vishnubhatla and 7 co-authors build a disaster assessment tool that answers what-if questions in a 2025 paper. Standard tools predict severity from current conditions using past data. They are not built for intervention, where a user changes inputs to test counterfactual scenarios.

Their tool works in real time, drawing on satellite imagery, news, and social media. Beyond gauging severity for a chosen region, it explains the causal weight of varied factors behind the estimate. It also gives actionable recourses, concrete steps that could ease the situation and aid mitigation planning. The source code is public. The authors frame the system as a complement to standard predictive disaster work rather than a replacement for it.
arxiv-2509-11776:
Helmut H. Pitters finds a hidden Poisson structure inside a classic random quantity in this 2025 probability paper, authored alone. For a Lévy process, a random motion with independent stationary increments, he studies the positive sojourn time: how much of the elapsed time the process spends above zero.

Stopped at an independent exponential time, that sojourn time equals in distribution a sum over the points of a Poisson process whose intensity is written explicitly through the process's positivity probabilities. The representation ties the quantity to the celebrated Poisson-Dirichlet distribution. Pitters also characterizes the sojourn time through its double Laplace transform. As corollaries, the Poisson picture yields fresh derivations and extensions of the classical arcsine laws of Lévy, Kac, and Getoor and Sharpe, plus the full distribution for a half-stable subordinator with drift.
arxiv-2509-12176:
Collin Guo and Yi Qian study editing faces with AI when no matched before-and-after pictures exist, in a 2025 paper. Realistic face changes that preserve a person's identity are in demand for entertainment and other uses. Autoencoders, a simpler method, can capture rough identity but often lose fine detail.

The authors build a guided CycleGAN, a system that learns to translate between two sets of unpaired images. They add spectral normalization for stable training, losses that protect identity and overall look, and landmark-weighted rules that keep facial geometry steady across pose and lighting. In experiments, their method beat autoencoders on realism, perceptual quality, and identity preservation. It approached a paired-data method on curated sets while needing no paired examples.
arxiv-2509-12476:
Small reasoning models are cheap to run. But they are hard to train when nobody has time to grade their homework. Sumanta Bhattacharyya and two co-authors propose R2tA in 2025. The recipe lets a big model audit the reasoning traces of a base model. It repairs those traces. Then the small model trains on the repaired traces.

Training runs in two stages. Supervised fine-tuning comes first. Preference optimization follows. The final answer is thus conditioned on cleaned-up reasoning. The test bed is grading database design diagrams. Prompt-only systems miss errors there, or invent them. A curated set of six hundred diagram variants carries the test. Planted mistakes span eleven categories.
arxiv-2509-12576:
Algebra asks whether good properties survive standard constructions, and a short 2025 note by Haydee Lindo and two co-authors answers one such question in the negative. The property is reflexivity of modules, and the construction is the trace, a tool recently used to test how close a ring is to being well-behaved.

A question raised by Dao, Maitra, and Sridhar asked whether reflexivity is preserved when passing to trace ideals. The note supplies a counterexample, so the answer is no in general. It then maps territory where the answer turns positive, in the setting of one-dimensional, analytically unramified Cohen-Macaulay local rings.
arxiv-2509-12676:
Fully homomorphic encryption lets a cloud compute on data it cannot read, but the binary version of the scheme is slow and its multi-bit extension cramps number sizes. Jiaao Ma and two co-authors present Taurus in 2025, a hardware accelerator that widens multi-bit Torus-FHE to ciphertexts of up to ten bits.

Novel transform units and key-reuse tricks feed the memory bandwidth the scheme craves, and a compiler removes duplicate operations. Measured speedups are dramatic: thousands of times faster than a processor, over a thousand times faster than a graphics card, and several times faster than the best prior accelerator. It even runs private inference on a GPT-2 scale model.
arxiv-2509-12776:
Renjie Wang and 4 co-authors combine trajectory optimization with reinforcement learning for quadrupedal jumping in a 2025 paper. Jumping needs dynamic take-off and adaptive landing, an needed part of four-legged robots' locomotion. Earlier studies mostly assumed a flat landing ground, which is impractical in many real-world settings.

Their system generates a reference motion with trajectory optimization, and a reinforcement learning agent learns to track that motion on rough terrain. A reward relaxation method encourages exploration during the landing recovery period, helping the robot learn compliant landing skills. Broad tests validated accurate tracking and safe landing across various scenarios. Terrain-adaptive landing extends quadruped jumping beyond the laboratory settings assumed by earlier work.
arxiv-2509-12976:
Taher Yacoub and 27 co-authors report a 2025 contest on finding proteins by the shape of their surface. In this task, a user gives one protein surface and asks for others like it. This year the contest added a new clue: the electric charge pattern spread over the surface, a trait that helps set what a protein does.

Nine teams sent in fifteen methods in all. Each was tested on a large set of more than eleven thousand protein surfaces with known charge patterns. Scores tracked how often the right matches came back, and how clean those matches were. The best methods used the charge pattern as well as shape. That held true even for classes with few cases, which shows the worth of the extra clue.
arxiv-2509-13276:
Fabrice Baudoin proves in 2025 comparison theorems for horizontal Laplacians on foliations with minimal leaves. Riemannian foliations layer a space by submanifolds. Minimal leaves keep volume steady, a clean setting for sub-Riemannian tools and heat flow.

Distance-based comparisons generalize past work in one frame. Carnot groups of any step fall inside the scope. Consequences include a Bonnet-Myers bound on size. Stochastic completeness and Lipschitz smoothing for the semigroup follow too. The unified frame replaces scattered proofs with one route for layered spaces. Analysts gain a single check for curvature-style bounds.
arxiv-2509-13476:
Md Masud Rana, Farjana Tasnim Mukta, and Duc D. Nguyen present DeepGGL in a 2025 paper on predicting how strongly a drug binds its target. When drugs are designed from structure, one question sits at the centre. How tightly will a candidate molecule hold onto its protein receptor? Deep learning now beats the older empirical and physics-based tools at this task.

DeepGGL learns from the geometry of the pair. It is a deep convolutional neural network, built with residual connections and an attention mechanism, inside a framework that learns from geometric graphs. Special subgraphs do the fine work. They are bipartite, weighted, and coloured, and they operate at many scales at once. The team tested DeepGGL against well-known models on the CASF-2013 and CASF-2016 data sets. It came out on top, with clear gains across a range of measures.
arxiv-2509-13576:
Haodong Li and 7 co-authors give a new way to rebuild CT scans from few views in a 2025 paper. Taking fewer X-ray views cuts the dose a patient gets and speeds the scan. But it also leaves flaws in the image, and scanners, protocols, or body types that differ from the training data can make the flaws worse.

Their method weds a diffusion prior, what a strong image model has learned about how scans should look, with a classic step-by-step rebuild. The prior is trained across many data sets in a way that lets it learn both traits tied to one source and traits shared by all. In use, that mix helps the rebuild stay true when the case at hand is unlike the training cases. The aim is scans that hold up in real clinic use.
arxiv-2509-13676:
Xiaobo Yang and Xiaojin Gong rethink how multimodal language models see images in a 2025 computer vision paper. The task is referring image segmentation: picking out the region a phrase describes. Pairing a big language model with the Segment Anything Model works well. But it costs heavily, largely because images become very long lists of visual tokens.

Inspired by text tokenizers, the pair use SAM's own semantic superpixels as visual words. A superpixel is one coherent image region. Compressing each superpixel into one token shortens the sequence. The length adapts to scene complexity. A positional embedding records each region's shape and place. An aggregator guards fine detail. Token counts fell by over ninety percent with no performance loss, speeding both training and inference.
arxiv-2509-14476:
Jiasen Lu and seven co-authors present AToken in 2025, a unified visual tokenizer that turns images, videos and 3D assets into shared tokens. Tokenizers usually specialise: one for faithful rebuilding, one for meaning, each for a single medium. A shared code would simplify multimodal models.

AToken encodes all three media into a shared four dimensional latent space, serving reconstruction and understanding together. A pure transformer design with four dimensional position encoding handles varied resolutions and durations. Training avoids adversarial losses, using perceptual and Gram matrix losses instead for stable, high quality rebuilding. A staged curriculum expands from still images toward harder media. State of the art reconstruction is claimed within one tokenizer for many visual forms.
arxiv-2509-14676:
Yaogan Mensah, writing alone in 2025, defines spectral Barron spaces inside quantum harmonic analysis, a framework that blends classical signal analysis with quantum ideas. Barron spaces collect functions whose frequency content obeys a weighted summability rule. Their spectral version needed a careful foundation.

Mensah studies the fundamental properties of the new spaces. Completeness, whether limits of well behaved sequences stay inside the space, is established. Continuous embedding results show how the spaces sit inside neighbouring function spaces. As an application, existence and uniqueness are proved for a solution of a Schrödinger type equation in this setting. Function space foundations decide which learning and physics models can be analysed with guaranteed solutions.
arxiv-2509-14876:
Zihan Wang and Vladimir Shikhman add the Allee effect to the Ramsey model of economic growth in a 2025 economics paper. The Ramsey model chooses saving and consumption over time to do as well as possible. The Allee effect describes populations that shrink to zero below a threshold size but level off above it, a pattern known from ecology.

With that population rule in place, consumption per person settles at two different long-run levels depending on which side of the threshold the population starts. The striking main result is that long-run consumption per person ends higher when the population dies out than when it saturates. The authors connect this to their earlier findings on capital per person in the Solow-Swan model. One comparison, between consumption-to-capital ratios, depends on the curvature of the production function.
arxiv-2509-14976:
Alessandro Arduino and four co-authors model how metal objects move inside MRI rooms under the Lenz effect in a 2025 medical physics paper. When a conductive object moves through a magnetic field, induced currents push back against the motion. Near a scanner, that braking can surprise staff handling equipment.

Their model writes the motion as an ordinary differential equation and approximates the Lenz effect by neglecting the skin effect, the tendency of currents to hug the surface. That simplification separates how the force depends on position and velocity, giving a simple numerical procedure for objects of any shape. Validation used a filmed aluminium plate rotating as it fell inside a scanner. A second study pushed a plate toward the bore through the fringe field. Predictions matched the measured motion well.
arxiv-2509-15176:
Hendrik Müller weighs the future of the CLEAN method for radio sky imaging in a solo 2025 review. CLEAN has built radio images for decades. It is fast, tough, and woven into calibration work. Next-wave telescopes will swamp it with far more data and far wider brightness ranges than it was made for.

CLEAN treats the sky as a set of point sources. That view limits how well it can recover broad, faint glow, and it resists full automation. Müller surveys the options: multiscale CLEAN forms, compressive sensing, likelihood methods, Bayesian tools, and AI-based methods. Forward models buy image quality and honest error bars at higher cost. Hybrid forms keep CLEAN's workflow but add modern math.
arxiv-2509-15276:
The BESIII group reports the first sighting of transverse spin alignment of lambda hyperons in one key decay, in a 2025 paper. The data come from a vast set of events of a charmonium state logged by the BESIII detector at the BEPCII collider in China. In the decay chain, lambda and anti-lambda hyperons form as a pair and then break into proton-pion pairs.

The alignment shows as a pattern in those decay paths. The group gauges the phase gap between the electric and magnetic form factors that rule the process. The key angular value is now known far more sharply than in past work. A phase gap between the pair's two wave parts is also seen, and an effectual reach is drawn out. The results sharpen the picture of the strong force inside hyperons.
arxiv-2509-15476:
Zhu Li leads a team that tests how well AI models spot sarcasm in speech. Sarcasm often hides in tone, not words, so a model may need sound, text, and video at once. The team test both language only models and models that take many input types. They use two data sets, one in English and one in Chinese, and try two ways of grading.

In one grading style, sound alone works best on both data sets. Adding other inputs helps on one set and hurts on the other. In direct grading, one model leads before training, and fine tuning lifts scores a lot. Their error study shows extra inputs can fix some misses and cause others. Careful choice of inputs is the lesson.
arxiv-2509-15576:
Haru Momozu leads a large team that sharpens A/B tests on websites. Such tests compare two versions on live visitors to gauge a change. A classic trick splits visitors into like groups first, then samples from each group. That split cuts noise, but only if the right traits are chosen for it. The team tackle choosing those traits.

Their method picks traits one by one, mocking up the sampling process at each step to judge the gain. They also estimate the cost of their picking method. On fake and real data sets, the method beats other noise cutting tricks. The gain grows when several traits track the outcome. Better picks mean more sensitive tests.
arxiv-2509-15776:
Kangcheng Li and Yunwen Lei analyze a training booster called Lookahead. Lookahead keeps two sets of weights for a model and blends them on a cycle. It has been shown to lift the base optimizer it wraps, such as stochastic gradient descent. Most past theory covered training fit, not how well the result travels to new data.

The pair study stability: how much the trained model shifts when the data shift slightly. From that they derive bounds on the gap to new data, for both plain and strongly curved losses. Their bounds drop a strict smoothness demand that older work needed. In the plain case they show a linear speedup with batch size. The work ties tuning and generalization together.
arxiv-2509-15976:
A. Fraser-McKelvie leads a large team that reads the life story of a barred galaxy from its parts. Overlapping parts of a galaxy are hard to pull apart, since their light blends. Their survey, GECKOS, studies edge on galaxies. This pilot work takes one barred galaxy and splits its light into five parts using an infrared image.

Three parts dominate in turn across the galaxy: a main disc, a boxy bulge, and a nuclear disc. Mapped onto spectra data, the three parts sit in distinct spots in motion space. Their stars' ages and metal mixes then tell a story. The main disc formed over a long, steady phase, fed in part by low metal gas. The method shows how parts can be read apart.
arxiv-2509-16276:
Block-based coding platforms are common in schools, but they lack the AI help many teachers now want. Bahare Riahi and Veronica Catete interviewed eight K-12 teachers about their classroom needs, half from science and tech fields and half from other subjects. They asked about grading, course building, resource growth, and watching student progress.

Both groups wanted honesty checks, adaptable AI, custom rubrics, and rich feedback for grading. Non-science teachers stressed creative tasks and judgment-based grading more. Both groups also wanted daily tracking and tools to curb distraction. The findings list concrete features that future school platforms should add.
arxiv-2509-16476:
Vision-language models waste most of their compute on image patches no one is looking at. Qinyu Chen and Jiawen Qi let the human eye decide where the work goes. Their GazeVLM frame takes gaze points as a guide. It keeps sharp detail there and adds only a coarse view of the rest. No training or model surgery is needed.

On a question-answering test with real gaze data, visual tokens fell by over ninety percent. Total compute halved as well. Answer quality still beat the full-image baseline under blind judging. The fovea-like trick suits glasses and headsets, where gaze is already tracked and power is scarce.
arxiv-2509-16676:
Nauman Ali Murad and Safia Baloch survey a shift in computing in a 2025 paper. New AI agents can act on their own, set sub-goals, and adapt as they learn. Such agents could reshape how systems are built, run, and governed. The pair map what that change could mean across cloud, edge, and local setups.

Their survey weighs new designs for systems that host roaming agents. It also weighs new rules for who controls them and who answers for their acts. Daily operations would need an overhaul as agents take on more tasks. The authors argue that wise placement of agent autonomy is key. The paper gives planners a map of choices ahead.
arxiv-2509-16776:
Hassaan Hashmi, Spyridon Pougkakiotis, and Dionysis Kalogerias boost wireless links with smart walls in a 2025 paper. A reflective surface can bounce signals toward users. Tuning it jointly with the sender is a two-stage problem under random channels. Later steps are often solved only roughly. The team design a learning method built for that roughness.

Their method uses gradient guesses that need no exact formulas. They prove it settles near a good answer under mild terms. Tests confirm it works across rough settings. Passive surfaces could then aid real networks without costly active parts. The work fits future high-speed wireless design.
arxiv-2509-16876:
Jiun-Ting Li, Bi-Cheng Yan, Yi-Cheng Wang, and Berlin Chen grade pronunciation for language learners in a 2025 paper. Automatic assessment gives feedback at the level of sounds, words, and full phrases. Past systems leaned on sound-level inputs alone. The team add multi-task pre-training and hand-built features for fluency and stress.

Those features come from human-designed formulas, such as speech rate and pause length. They help the model give scores that a learner can act on. Tests on a public speech set improved scoring and matched human proficiency ratings better. Clear, targeted feedback could help learners fix stress and rhythm, not just single sounds.
arxiv-2509-17376:
Shunichiro Orikasa, writing alone, links two themes in geometry in a 2025 arXiv paper. One theme is systolic geometry, which studies the shortest loops a shape cannot shrink away. The other is positive scalar curvature, a sign that a space bends outward in an averaged sense. Whether the two themes constrain each other in high dimensions is not clear.

Orikasa's main theorem bounds the two-dimensional stable systole from above on certain high-dimensional manifolds. The manifolds carry positive scalar curvature and meet a stated stretch-scale condition. The proof blends geometric measure theory, in the line of Gromov's systolic inequality, with curvature estimates from the Gromov-Lawson relative index theorem. Spinorial methods run through the argument. The author offers the mix as a fresh frame for studying how curvature metrics and systolic size interact.
arxiv-2509-17476:
Mallikarjun B. R. and six co-authors animate a still portrait from a driving video. Their 2025 arXiv paper targets portrait animation: one source photo must take on the pose and expression of a person in a clip. Old methods built on morphable face models or warping often lacked expression range, flickered over time, or failed on new faces and big head turns.

Their diffusion framework uses masked regions of the driving video, namely the eyes, nose, and mouth, as firm motion cues. Training uses cross-identity supervision, so the look of the driver cannot leak into the output. The design adds few new parameters on top of a trained diffusion model, which speeds convergence and aids generalization. Spatial and temporal attention lets frames inform each other, catching subtle motion and cutting flicker. Past frames also guide each new one for a steadier result.
arxiv-2509-17576:
Aksel Tacettin and five co-authors plan how a quantum network should grow entangled states on demand. Their 2025 arXiv paper starts from a hard fact: protocols need several entangled states at once, each above a floor fidelity. States waiting in memory decay, and once one drops below the floor it is useless, while generation itself is a matter of chance.

The team models the system as a Markov decision process. At each step a policy picks the generation settings, trading success odds against the fidelity of the state produced. Dynamic programming then yields policies that minimize the expected wait until enough good states are on hand. Sequential attempts are the trap the policy avoids, since early states rot while later ones are still being made. The work speaks to the control layer of future quantum networks.
arxiv-2509-17776:
Cristina Stratan, Claudio Mandrioli, and Domenico Bianculli want more than a yes or no when code breaks a rule. Their 2025 paper works with checks that run while a program runs. A plain fail mark does not say which lines of code caused the fault.

Their tool traces data flow back from the failed check. It then marks the runs with extra facts and picks out the lines at fault. On more than a hundred rules in ten projects, it found the right lines in most cases. It also cut the lines a user must scan by at least nine tenths.
arxiv-2509-17876:
Eric Stopfer and Friedrich Wagner run a broad test of quantum methods for picking a stock mix. Their 2025 bench study deals with portfolio choice, where a mix must balance gain and risk. Fans of quantum gear have pitched this task as a good early use case.

The set holds hundreds of cases built from real stock data, with up to a thousand assets. Classic solvers found proven best answers in seconds on all cases. A tuned classic shortcut also beat quantum runs on quality for the same time. The authors close that room for a quantum edge here looks very small.
arxiv-2509-17976:
Oleksiy O Vakhnenko and Vyacheslav O Vakhnenko build a twelve-part wave system on a near-one-dim lattice. Their 2025 paper aims at physics uses for multi-part models that can be solved in full. The work sits in a known semi-discrete scheme for such wave systems.

From a base system, the pair derive both a twelve-part and a six-part form. A set of local saved quantities, found by a direct step method, drives that cut-down. They set out which symmetry types each system allows. Charge flow in the big system turns out to ride on just four of its six sub-parts.
arxiv-2509-18176:
Wendong Yao and 4 co-authors forecast ground sinking and rising from sparse radar points. Their 2025 paper deals with InSAR data, which tracks ground shift from space but at scattered points. Such forecasts back city safety and hazard plans, yet sparse input has blocked top vision tools.

Their frame turns the scattered points into a dense space-time block. A hybrid net then learns space patterns and time trends at once from that block. On radar data from eastern Ireland, it beat strong baselines by a clear margin. Checks show the baselines fell back on a plain stay-same guess.
arxiv-2509-18376:
Graph neural networks sort nodes in networks, but their choices are hard to explain. Burouj Armgaan and four co-authors present GnnXemplar, a tool that explains a whole class of choices at once. Their 2025 paper draws on exemplar theory from the study of how minds sort things. Instead of tiny repeated patterns, the tool picks standout example nodes.

The tool finds nodes that stand for many others in the network's learned space, framed as a coverage problem with a fast greedy fix. It then turns the areas around those nodes into plain-language rules with help from large language models. The rules refine themselves through repeat prompts. On varied test sets, the method beat older explainers on faithfulness, scale, and human clarity. A study with sixty people backed the clarity claim. The aim is trust in systems that sort people and things.
arxiv-2509-18476:
Spintronics seeks electric currents whose spins point one way, for low-power devices. Lv Zhiheng, Cai Jiangtao, Ma Dengpan, Xing Yan, and Liu Zhifeng report a locking effect in altermagnets in this 2025 paper. They call it spin-axis dynamic locking. A field along one crystal axis drives a current of mostly spin-up electrons.

Along the cross axis, the same setup yields an equal spin-down current, enforced by symmetry. A diagonal field then gives a pure spin current across the flow, with ideal full conversion of charge to spin. The effect traces to a tent-shaped band structure with separated Fermi lines that resist backscattering. A broad computer screening found the effect in many materials. Two named cases, a layered crystal and a synthesized bulk compound, come close to the ideal limit. The authors see a route to devices steered by field direction alone.
arxiv-2509-18876:
Matter inside a neutron star is a soup of neutrons, protons, and electrons under crushing density. Aziz Rabhi, Olfa Boukari, Sidney S. Avancini, and Constança Providência study its collective vibrations under strong magnetic fields in this 2025 paper. They use a covariant Vlasov approach, a relativistic kinetic frame. Several mean-field nuclear models supply the forces.

They derive the dispersion relations for waves running along the field. Two families appear: isovector modes, where neutrons and protons move against each other, and isoscalar ones, where they move together. A strong field births low-lying isovector modes absent without the field. Neutron-like modes barely notice the field. Proton-like modes split into new branches tied to Landau levels, the quantized orbits a field imposes. Those branches can run even at high density. The results map how magnetized star matter rings.
arxiv-2509-18976:
Matthew R. Buck, writing alone, classifies ball-like surfaces inside a family of four-dimensional symplectic spaces. The spaces are Milnor fibres of cyclic quotient T-singularities, a mouthful that means spaces built near a certain kind of singular point. Inside them sit Lagrangian spheres, surfaces with a special balance property. Buck asks how many truly distinct such spheres exist, up to smooth deformation.

He proves a finitely generated group of symmetries sweeps one fixed sphere through every class. Earlier classifications lived in simpler spaces, either monotone or simply connected, and this family is neither. The proof builds fibrations whose spheres match cycles in a simpler picture, reducing the count to a mapping class group computation. The tools include pseudoholomorphic curves and symplectic field theory. The results also support a guess about what generates the full symmetry group.
arxiv-2509-19176:
Sourav Chatterjee and Oren Yakir prove that a lattice model of interacting gauge and Higgs fields forgets its past exponentially fast in one regime. The model places a U(1) gauge field and a Higgs field on a grid, with two knobs: the inverse gauge coupling and the Higgs length. In the regime where symmetry is fully broken down, they show correlations decay exponentially whenever the Higgs mass term is positive and the coupling is weak enough. An older result from 1978 needed the mass large as well.

The theorem confirms a phase diagram sketched by Fradkin and Shenker in 1979. The proof expands around a massive Gaussian field using a cluster expansion in the tradition of Glimm, Jaffe, and Spencer, following work by Balaban and co-authors. Removing the large-mass requirement closes a long-standing gap between the physics prediction and rigorous mathematics.
arxiv-2509-19276:
Reconstructing an image from blurred or partial measurements needs a strong prior, a good guess about what images look like. Tim Y. J. Wang and O. Deniz Akyildiz borrow that prior from pre-trained latent diffusion models, the engines behind image generators. Their approach needs no new training. They frame the sampling of plausible solutions as a gradient flow in the model's latent space, following the geometry of probability distributions known as Wasserstein flow.

A divergence term keeps the flow close to the diffusion prior while the data term enforces agreement with the measurements. The balance yields samples from the posterior, the full set of images consistent with both. Tests on standard inverse-problem benchmarks use the public Stable Diffusion model as the prior. The authors report the method performs well there, offering a training-free route to principled image restoration.
arxiv-2509-19376:
Matthew Grofsky, writing alone, separates two problems that search systems using retrieval often blur together: finding fresh information, and tracking how a topic evolves. His testbed is cybersecurity data, including hard cases from the national vulnerability database. For freshness, he adds a lightweight recency layer with a half-life prior, which favors newer items. A similarity-only baseline scored zero at surfacing the newest relevant item, while the prior did far better on the standard test.

On the hard test, where the newest item is not the closest match in meaning, the method stayed partial and sensitive to settings. For topic evolution, his heuristic tracker scored poorly, but the blame sat with its labeling rule, not its clustering. Fixing the rule alone lifted the score sharply. Grofsky contributes the decoupling itself, with a reference implementation and an honest account of scope.
arxiv-2509-19476:
Merging the weights of two trained language models can blend their skills, such as math and code. Yutaro Sigrist and Andreas Waldis ask whether merged models should be judged by more than their task scores. They built a test pipeline that checks both outward behavior and the language facts stored inside the model. Their test case merges chat-tuned, math-tuned, and code-tuned models from one model family.

Merged models usually scored between their two parents on tasks. Yet their stored sense of word forms and sentence shape could beat both parents. Task scores and inner scores also ranked the merges in near-unrelated orders. The authors argue that score-only checks can hide real gains and losses. Their pipeline gives builders a fuller way to judge a merge before use.
arxiv-2509-19576:
The early universe expanded at a furious pace in the era called inflation, then settled down. Ramon Herrera and Carlos Rios ask which energy landscapes could drive that burst inside Rastall gravity, a variant where matter and curvature trade energy. Their method works backward: they fix how the spectrum of early ripples should look, then solve for the landscape that yields it. The ripple pattern is written as a function of how much expansion remains.

They treat two cases: a fixed Rastall strength, and one that drifts in a straight line as expansion proceeds. Both landscapes are checked against the latest Planck satellite data. The fits limit the free settings of each model. Reconstruction studies like this one map the range of early-universe stories that altered gravity still permits. Future sky surveys can then narrow the field.
arxiv-2509-20776:
Sparse matrix work sits at the heart of many science codes, and moving rows and columns around is a core task. Elaheh Hassani, Md Taufique Hussain, and Ariful Azad present new methods for that work in a 2025 paper. The methods run on machines that split memory across many nodes.

Their plan has three steps. Each process first finds the nonzero entries it holds. Next, the processes swap the data they need. Then each one builds its local piece from what arrived. This cuts the data traffic that older multiplication-based methods need. Threads that never wait on each other speed the local work further. The team tested the code on two campus clusters and the Perlmutter supercomputer, reporting much faster runs than known libraries such as CombBLAS and PETSc.
arxiv-2509-20876:
Attosecond light pulses, lasting billionths of a billionth of a second, are made when intense lasers strike gases. Feng Wang and eight co-authors show how to steer that process with squeezed light in a 2025 physics paper. The process is high-order harmonic generation, a tabletop source of such pulses.

Electrons in the gas can take a short path or a long path before releasing harmonic light. The authors find that phase-squeezed light suppresses the long path, while amplitude-squeezed light suppresses the short one. Time-frequency analysis traces the effect to quantum fluctuations in the squeezed field, which shift the phase matching. The result gives attosecond science a new quantum knob for shaping its fastest flashes.
arxiv-2509-20976:
Image clustering groups pictures without labels, and semi-supervised learning could help, but it usually needs a running start. Yue Duan and three co-authors build an adaptor that removes that requirement in a 2025 paper accepted by IEEE Transactions on Image Processing. Their adaptor is called ASD.

Existing integrations demand pretraining, clustering stages, or an already trained model before semi-supervised methods can join. ASD instead samples pseudo-labeled data at random from the unlabeled pool. An instance-level classifier learns those samples with semantically aligned labels. By tracking how predictions on unlabeled data move between classes, the system extracts clustering structure. The result is out-of-the-box deep image clustering, where semi-supervised learners start cold and still contribute.
arxiv-2509-21076:
A droplet hitting a surface spreads, splashes, or slides depending on how its edge moves. Yifan Han, Gerd Mutschke, and Kerstin Eckert simulate that wetting dynamics in three dimensions in a 2025 fluids paper. Their framework uses the volume of fluid method in the Basilisk solver.

The key piece is a geometric interpolation scheme that reads the contact line velocity accurately from the simulation grid. A dynamic contact angle model, including hysteresis between advancing and receding angles, feeds that velocity into realistic motion. The authors validate against experiments on spreading, splashing, and sliding droplets, reporting quantitative agreement. They also compare dynamic and static contact angle models. The work serves applications from coating and printing to cooling sprays.
arxiv-2509-21476:
Two competing constructions of Nori motivic sheaves turn out to be the same theory. Emil Jacobsen and Luca Terenzi prove that equivalence in a 2025 paper. One theory came from Ivorra and Morel, the other from Ayoub. Motivic sheaves are a universal cohomology framework in algebraic geometry. A canonical equivalence removes doubt about which construction to use.

The proof exploits the six functor formalism systematically. Tannakian theory of motivic local systems supplies the backbone. As a consequence, realization functors from Voevodsky motivic sheaves into Nori motivic sheaves are obtained. Those functors are compatible with all six operations. Tubach had built such functors by different methods earlier. The comparison unifies the foundations of the subject.
arxiv-2509-21576:
Long horizon planning defeats vision language models that must emit action sequences directly. Muyu He and 9 co-authors test a different role for those models in a 2025 paper. In text settings, language models translate problems into a formal planning language for a solver. That formalizer role improved long horizon results. Multimodal versions remain scarce and often rely on gross simplifications.

Five pipelines for vision language model formalization are presented. They tackle one shot, open vocabulary, multimodal formalization into PDDL, the Planning Domain Definition Language. Past work used predefined object vocabularies or overly similar examples. Evaluation runs on an existing benchmark. The suite tests whether models that cannot plan can still formalize problems for verifiable solvers.
arxiv-2509-21676:
Expressive synthetic speech fools anti spoofing systems that ignore prosody, the rhythm and melody of speech. Aurosweta Mahapatra and 2 co-authors build a prosody aware detector in a 2025 paper. Humans use pitch patterns and voiced structure to sense fakes instinctively. Their framework, HuLA, learns in two stages with multiple tasks. A self supervised backbone anchors the design.

In stage one, the backbone trains on real speech with pitch prediction and voiced classification as auxiliary tasks. That mirrors human perceptual learning of natural prosodic variation. In stage two, spoof detection and prosody tasks train jointly on real and synthetic data. Prosodic mismatches between natural and expressive synthetic speech become the detection cue. Experiments show gains for expressive and emotional fakes.
arxiv-2509-21876: Temurboy E. Rajabov and Sergey V. Sudoplatov study model theory, the branch of logic that links formal sentences to the structures they describe. Their 2025 paper asks when a property stays true as one passes between structures. It asks how two views of that question connect: the semantic view, about truth, and the syntactic view, about form. They give characterizations for several settings, including subalgebras, congruence relations, the Henkin construction, and the Tarski-Vaught test. A last part studies traces for types and related objects.
arxiv-2509-22076:
Jannik Breitkopf and Stefan Ulbrich develop a calculus for steering shock waves by adjusting a system's starting state. Their 2025 paper works with hyperbolic conservation laws, equations whose solutions form shocks, and with the generalized Riemann problem: an initial state that is smooth on each side of one jump. The control consists of those smooth parts plus the jump's position. Because shock positions move when the control changes, the analysis first transforms everything into a fixed reference layout.

In that reference space, the authors prove the solution between shocks depends on the control in a smooth, differentiable way. Back in physical coordinates, the shock curves and the states between them inherit the same smooth dependence. A direct consequence is that tracking-type objective functions, the kind optimal control minimizes, are differentiable too.
arxiv-2509-22176:
Hot water can sometimes freeze faster than cold, a puzzle known as the Mpemba effect. Sreemayee Aditya, Alessandro Summer, Piotr Sierant, and Xhek Turkeshi ask whether the same trick appears inside quantum complexity itself. Their 2025 paper studies four resources that quantum resource theories use to measure quantumness: coherence, imaginarity, non-Gaussianity, and magic. They track how each resource fades as random quantum circuits evolve.

Starting the system in resource-rich product states, coherence and imaginarity showed a true Mpemba effect: the richer start relaxed faster. Non-Gaussianity and magic did not. All four resources, though, showed a related twist the authors call the Pontus-Mpemba effect. A brief initial heating stage sped up the later relaxation, compared with cooling directly. The authors read the results as evidence that Mpemba-style physics reaches beyond heat and asymmetry. It emerges inside the very measures that define how complex a quantum state is.
arxiv-2509-22676:
Ethan Kahn models how electric fields steer charged droplets inside an airflow, to guide spray control design. Electrospray can bend droplet paths, with uses in fuel-air mixing and flow control. His framework couples a steady airflow simulation over a NACA 1912 airfoil channel with a reduced particle model. Droplets feel viscous drag and electrostatic force as they travel.

Uniform-flow tests confirmed that steering weakens as the free stream speeds up and inertia grows. In the airfoil field, an opposing field lengthened droplet residence and even reversed flow in slow pockets. From these runs he derives a criterion for the minimum field that causes reversal. A control authority map marks where modest fields give strong response.
arxiv-2509-22776:
Claire E. Williams and 9 co-authors simulate the first star clusters under the universe's early streaming motion. After the Big Bang, baryons streamed supersonically past dark matter, which shaped gas in the smallest halos. Observations hint that early clusters reached extreme stellar densities, where feedback could barely halt collapse. Their AREPO simulations form first clusters with no feedback, testing how dense Lambda CDM halos can get.

Clusters reached high densities even in regions of strong streaming, as long as feedback stayed weak. The brightest, most massive objects could be within JWST's reach. Single clusters below a certain mass remain hard to detect, though gravitational lensing could reveal rare cases. The team also explores cluster clustering as a probe of the streaming speed.
arxiv-2509-22876:
Emotional cues can steer a language model out of stuck, wrong lines of thought. Gabriela Pinto and 8 co-authors build HEART, a test-time method that needs no new training. It swaps between a sharp, critical tone and a warm, supportive tone. The critical tone helps the model spot errors, and the warm tone helps it try fresh ideas.

The team tested HEART on seven hard benchmarks, among them Humanity's Last Exam and GPQA Diamond. It also faced LiveCodeBench, a coding test. Across varied models, HEART beat plain, emotion-free baselines on accuracy. The authors argue that guiding feelings may be a next step for machine reasoning.
arxiv-2509-23076:
Finding one point that solves an equilibrium problem and many fixed point problems at once is the goal here. Peter U Nwokoro and 3 co-authors design a hybrid algorithm for that search. The setting is a uniformly smooth, uniformly convex Banach space. The maps involved are a broad class of generalized non-expansive maps. The equilibrium problem is a generalized mixed one.

Their algorithm hunts a common element of both solution sets. The authors then apply the result to an optimization problem. They state that the findings extend and generalize several known results. The article is theorem driven, in the style of fixed point theory.
arxiv-2509-23476:
High-pressure hydrides can hide crystal forms that slow searches never reach. Lewis J. Conway and Chris J. Pickard speed the hunt with cheap learned potentials called EDDPs. Their searches pair random structure sampling with these potentials in place of costly density functional theory. Training data grow as the search runs, so no prior knowledge of hydrides is assumed at the start.

At a pressure of one hundred gigapascals, the wider searches covered more mixes, bigger cells, and far more candidate structures. They recovered many known forms and found new ones, including hydrogen-rich phases of several compounds. The authors also report that big pre-trained universal potentials did worse here, due to instability or slow inference.
arxiv-2509-23676:
A reasoning model writes a long chain of thought before answering, but does the answer really use that chain? Jue Zhang and 3 co-authors probe three distilled DeepSeek R1 models in three stages. Plain tests first show that including the reasoning text improves answer quality across domains. Attention analysis then finds answer tokens leaning hard on reasoning tokens, with certain mid-layer heads tracking the reasoning path, even its self-correcting turns.

Finally, activation patching perturbs key reasoning tokens and watches the answer change. The edits reliably steer the final answer, proving a real flow of influence from reasoning to output. The team releases its data and code.
arxiv-2509-23776:
Materials scientists need process records that machines can read, yet the ontologies for them are heavy and hard to reuse. Ebrahim Norouzi and 3 co-authors survey workflow and process ontologies to mine their hidden design patterns. Ontology design patterns are small, reusable modeling solutions, but they are rarely published in a form domain experts can find. The team checks how well the surveyed ontologies meet the needs of process representation in materials science.

They also propose a baseline method that extracts design patterns automatically. It is scored against curated ground-truth patterns. All extracted patterns and the workflow are released openly on GitHub.
arxiv-2509-23976:
Turning a financial contract's specification into blockchain code that is correct and cheap to run is a translation few can do by hand. Maruf Ahmed Mridul and Oshani Seneviratne train a reinforcement learning agent to do it. The agent, trained with proximal policy optimization, picks code snippets from a fixed library to build Solidity contracts from Common Domain Model specifications. A two-phase curriculum teaches correctness first, then shifts the reward toward saving gas.

On unseen test contracts, the agent cut gas costs by up to about thirty-six percent against unoptimized baselines. The authors present the method as a viable bridge from financial agreements to efficient on-chain code.
arxiv-2509-24476:
Heavy quarks are born in pairs through several distinct mechanisms, and each leaves its own fingerprint in how the pair moves together. Jiaxing Zhao and 5 co-authors use the EPOS4 event generator to study those patterns in proton-proton collisions. Their focus is quarkonium, the bound state a heavy quark and antiquark can form.

The patterns between heavy mesons directly mirror the production mechanism at work, the simulations show. Those same patterns also shape the momentum spectra of the quarkonia produced. Reading them thus gives a handle on which mechanism dominated. The work ties production theory to measurable spectra in high-energy collisions.
arxiv-2509-25276:
Henrique Gomes rebuilds gauge theory starting from matter geometry rather than symmetry. His twenty twenty-five physics paper argues that fibre bundles come first. Gauge groups then arise as symmetries of a few basic fibres. Every matter field is a section built from those fibres.

That starting rule forces electric charges onto a whole-number lattice. It works even when the symmetry group is not compact. A symmetry-first theory on the real line would allow irrational charge ratios. The standard model satisfies the geometric constraint, Gomes shows. Both mass-giving mechanisms then follow from fibre shapes. The Higgs effect and Yukawa couplings emerge without symmetry breaking language.
arxiv-2509-25976:
Emil Leeb-Lundberg, a solo author, applies localization methods to a twisted supersymmetric theory in a 2025 physics paper. Localization is a technique that reduces hard quantum field calculations to exact formulas. The author studies theories with vector and matter fields placed on a sphere, after a topological twist.

A new exact formula is derived for certain observables, written as a distribution integrated along the real line. The formula is checked on a classic gauge model, where it reproduces the known selection rule for correlators. Using hyperfunctions, the author then shows the distribution form matches the standard contour integral form. The result agrees with a known residue prescription from geometry.
arxiv-2509-26576:
Li and six colleagues train neural operators to read the hidden causes of aortic aneurysms in twenty twenty-five. A thoracic aortic aneurysm is a bulge in the chest aorta that can tear or burst. Many distinct insults to the wall can start one. The team simulated hundreds of bulges from varied fiber damage and sensing faults.

Maps of wall stretch and springiness fed networks that had to name the starting insult. One network design, UNet, won across all data formats. Stretch maps alone gave far worse reads than stretch plus springiness. The team urges full field measures of both in patient checks. Such maps could guide care tailored to each case.
arxiv-2510-00076:
Xin Lyu wrote this 2025 theory paper on learning under a strict privacy rule. The setting is Littlestone classes, a standard family of tasks for online learning theory. The learner must keep each person's data private while still making few mistakes. Earlier private learners for this task paid a very high cost in extra errors.

Lyu gives a private online learner whose mistake bound improves on the old one doubly exponentially. The gain comes from a cleaner reading of a trick called irreducibility, plus careful use of a sparse selection method. The same ideas also improve the batch version of the learner, with the best possible dependence on target accuracy. The result comes close to the known lower bound for private learning here. It narrows a long-standing gap between private and ordinary online learning.
arxiv-2510-00176:
Alicia Middleton and fourteen colleagues published this 2025 instrumentation paper for the Simons Observatory in Chile. The observatory maps the cosmic microwave background with tens of thousands of superconducting detectors. Each detector module needs a routing wafer that carries bias lines and tiny shunt resistors. The team tested every wafer, more than seventy in all, before assembly.

Wafers were screened warm in the lab and again at a tenth of a degree above absolute zero. The average shunt resistance landed close to the design value of four hundred micro-ohms. Spread across all wafers was only about four percent of that value. Resistance dipped slightly toward each wafer's edge, a trend smaller than wafer-to-wafer differences. Warm factory data predicted the cold results well, which closed out screening for the observatory and its upgrade.
arxiv-2510-00476:
Arushi Sharma and three colleagues published this 2025 paper on opening the black box of language models trained on code. Such models power tools that demand trust, yet their internal concepts stay hidden. The team proposes Code Concept Analysis, which clusters token embeddings into human-readable concept groups. Static analysis tools and prompted language models jointly label the clusters at scale.

The framework tracks how concepts distribute across layers and shift under fine-tuning. Discovered concepts stayed stable when code was rewritten in meaning-preserving ways. Fine-tuning reshaped them predictably, sharpening syntax or spreading semantics across languages. A user study on programming-language classification showed concept-based explanations beat token-level attribution scores. Human judges found the token roles far clearer, with explainability up by thirty-seven percentage points. The authors release a labeled concept resource to ground future interpretability work.
arxiv-2510-00676:
Martinez and Zelazo present a formation control method for groups of moving agents in this 2025 arXiv paper. Such groups, from drone swarms to satellite fleets, must settle into a planned shape while each agent only talks to a few neighbors. Most methods fix distances or bearings between agents. Their approach instead uses only rotation symmetry constraints between neighbors.

A potential function built from those symmetries defines the control law that steers the agents. The authors prove that a spanning tree with just n minus one links, the fewest that keep a group connected, is enough to run the scheme. They then extend the design so the whole formation can travel, rotate, and scale along a planned path. Simulations, including a cube formation in three dimensions, confirm the method works as claimed.
arxiv-2510-01176:
Lee and seven co-authors at Meta present a real-time, audio-driven facial animation system at SIGGRAPH Asia 2025. Photorealistic 3D avatars could make virtual reality meetings feel face to face, but driving them from speech alone usually means slow offline processing. Their system encodes audio into latent facial expression sequences as the sound arrives, then decodes them into a photorealistic avatar. Generative diffusion modelling supplies the rich range of expressions that natural conversation needs.

Two design choices keep latency under fifteen milliseconds of GPU time per frame. An online transformer never waits for future audio, and a distillation pipeline compresses iterative denoising into a single step. The framework also accepts emotion conditions and gaze data from headset eye cameras. In experiments it beat offline state-of-the-art baselines on animation accuracy while running one hundred to one thousand times faster, and live VR demos confirmed the pipeline.
arxiv-2510-01376:
Pathrikar listens to how a quantum-corrected black hole rings and radiates, compared with its classical counterpart. The Frolov black hole replaces the crushing singularity with a regular core, courtesy of quantum gravity ideas. Perturbing it with light and matter waves produces characteristic quasinormal tones.

Standard approximation methods extract the dominant tone and its first overtone, plus the filtering factors for escaping radiation. Deviations from the classical charged black hole quantify the quantum corrections' fingerprints. An associated temperature estimate completes the emission picture. Ringing, in short, can audition candidate quantum black holes. Grey-body factors describe how the hole's gravity filters escaping waves. Sixth-order approximations, cross-checked higher, secure the numbers. Padé averaging steadies the approximation where plain series wobble. Electromagnetic and Dirac probes ring at different tones. Regular black holes are testable in principle, not just prettier.
arxiv-2510-01676:
Nasr and colleagues at Google and Google DeepMind wrote this 2025 security study of a live production system. The system is Gmail's malware detection pipeline, which scans files attached to mail. One model in the pipeline, Magika, identifies each file type and routes the file to a specialist checker. The authors ask whether fooling that one model can break the whole pipeline.

By changing just 13 bytes in a malware sample, the team fooled Magika in most test cases. Misrouted files then reached the wrong detector, which raised the chance of slipping through. The attack worked in nine out of ten cases they tried. The authors also built a defense and deployed it with Google engineers. Against the defended model, even a well-funded attacker needed 50 changed bytes for a far lower success rate.
arxiv-2510-01776:
Zayyani and three co-authors raise the data rate of noise-based communication in this 2025 letter. Noise modulation sends information inside random thermal noise, using almost no transmit power. A generalized quadratic modulator encodes bits in the mean and variance of that noise. The authors simply add the outputs of two such modulators together.

The combined signal forms a 16-ary modulator, much like quadrature amplitude modulation in classical radio. Bits now ride on four different means and four different variances at once. The authors give conditions that keep the sixteen states distinguishable at the receiver. With parameters chosen to meet those conditions, simulations beat both the single quadratic modulator and a Kirchhoff-law Johnson noise scheme. The gain is a smaller bit error probability, paid for with more complex hardware. Adding still more modulators could push the scheme to even higher orders.
arxiv-2510-01976:
Dobrinoiu and four co-authors ask whether annotation habits reveal how a person reads values in this 2025 paper. Value concepts mean different things to different people, shaped by culture and experience. AI systems that miss that subjectivity tilt toward majority viewpoints. The authors test whether a language model can predict one person's value interpretation from examples of their other judgments.

The examples cover four subjective dimensions: sentiment, emotion, argument, and topic annotations, shortened to SEAT. Across zero-shot and few-shot settings, giving the model all four dimensions at once worked best. Single dimensions helped less, and a no-information baseline trailed them all. Annotators also varied widely in how predictable they were. The study is small and controlled, but the authors say it is the first to use annotation behavior, rather than demographics, as the lens. It lays groundwork for larger validation of personalized value prediction.
arxiv-2510-02076:
He, Shuryak, Wu, and Zahed build light pentaquark states on the light front in this 2025 particle physics paper. Pentaquarks hide five quarks inside one hadron, and their spectra test how confinement really works. Light-front dynamics suits partonic questions, but constructing clean states there is tricky. The authors place the states on a regular four-simplex geometry.

Their explicit basis diagonalizes the Hamiltonian for light pentaquarks with confinement built in. The resulting eigenstates are free of center-of-mass motion and satisfy exact boundary conditions. Hyperfine interactions, in color-spin or flavor-spin form, lift the degeneracy among the sixteen states. The split spectrum compares fairly with some empirical excited nucleon states. The authors also discuss the quark probability distributions inside these states. A tidy basis like this turns pentaquark spectroscopy into systematic computation. It connects the constituent quark picture with the partonic language experiments actually probe.
arxiv-2510-02176:
Williams, Cleeves, Gross, and Baker chase the missing sulfur in planet-forming disks in this 2025 astrochemistry paper. Sulfur is essential to life, yet gas in protoplanetary disks shows strikingly little of it. The element must hide in forms that telescopes barely register. The team updated a two-dimensional, time-dependent disk chemistry model with new sulfur species and hundreds of new reactions.

They varied the volatile sulfur supply, the carbon-to-oxygen ratio, the starting molecular form, and the cosmic-ray rate. The most abundant sulfur carriers included CS, SO, and the ices of sulfur dioxide and carbonyl sulfide. Gas-phase sulfur abundances swung strongly with the carbon-to-oxygen ratio. Model columns were checked against values derived from disk observations. Much of the sulfur evidently locks into ices and less visible reservoirs. Knowing its hiding places matters for tracing sulfur from clouds into planets, and eventually into biology.
arxiv-2510-02276:
Li and co-authors present BioX-Bridge, a cheaper way to move knowledge between body signal types. Their 2025 health machine learning paper starts from a simple fact. Signals like heart and brain traces reflect one connected body. A model trained on one signal type often cannot help with another. Labeled data for the new type is scarce. Classic transfer runs a big teacher model beside the student. That pairing costs heavy compute and memory. BioX-Bridge instead learns a small bridge between two frozen models.

The bridge uses prototypes to link the two representation spaces. A two-stage search picks the best layers to connect. Tests spanned several biosignal datasets and tasks. Performance matched or beat leading transfer methods. The bridge needed far fewer trainable parameters to do it. Clinics with modest hardware could adapt models this way. Scarce labels stop being a hard wall.
arxiv-2510-02476:
Li and co-authors pick ensemble members by trusting a model own uncertainty estimates. Their 2025 paper studies biomolecule efficacy prediction with tabular foundation models. The test task predicts how well siRNA molecules silence their targets. TabPFN, an in-context learner, beat specialized predictors on the task. It used only straightforward sequence based features. Performance, though, swings with the context examples provided. Ensembling models trained on different subsets can stabilize results. The question is which members deserve a seat. Their method, OligoICP, reads each model predicted spread. Models with the lowest mean uncertainty join the ensemble.

Uncertainty and true error correlated negatively in their tests. Confident models really did err less on this task. The chosen ensemble beat naive averaging clearly. It also beat one model trained on all data. Labels are unavailable when tuning real deployments. A label free selection rule is therefore valuable.
arxiv-2510-02876:
Hassan and co-authors grade eggs without cracking them open. Egg grade and freshness shape food safety and price. Checking them the usual way means breaking eggs for lab tests. That wastes product and slows packing lines. The team's framework, ELMF4EggQ, judges eggs from the outside only. It uses a photo plus the egg's shape and weight. The study also built a small public data set for the task.

The set holds 186 brown-shelled eggs. Experts labeled each egg by lab measures like yolk index and Haugh unit. Deep networks pulled features from the photos. Classic classifiers then voted as an ensemble on the fused features. The combined approach beat photo-only and table-only models by clear margins. Grade calls reached a strong accuracy level, while freshness proved harder. The authors still see real promise for packing plants. The method is cheap, fast, and gentle on the product.
arxiv-2510-02976:
Paz and co-authors control a heavy skid-steered platform in real time. Such machines turn by skidding their wheels against the ground. Precise path tracking, though, is hard under shifting loads and terrain. The team built a nonlinear predictive controller for the job. It looks ahead along the path and plans each move. A multiple-shooting method shapes that planning step.

Careful buffer handling keeps the solver from wasting cycles. Warm starts and a capped step count bound the run time. Each control update thus lands within a fixed, known window. The controller matched the pace of its fastest sensor. Tests on three path shapes showed sharp gains. Position and speed errors fell far below prior published results. Those gains came on a full-size, heavy-duty machine, not a toy. Safe, exact motion matters most where such platforms work near people.
arxiv-2510-03376:
Ghosh, writing from Siemens in Germany, presents a 2025 arXiv paper on checking object detection inside industrial plant diagrams. Piping and instrumentation diagrams guide how plants are built, run, and repaired. Turning them into digital twins starts with spotting every symbol and tag correctly. Detection software has grown strong, yet few tools grade its output without slow human review. The paper uses a visual language model as an automated judge instead.

The judge scans detector output for missing symbols and clashing labels. It also checks tag text tied to symbols and judges how well boxes hug their targets. Local close up passes then hunt for objects the first pass missed. Automating these checks cuts the review load on engineers sharply. It also enables workflows that adapt when diagrams arrive in varied styles. Plants gain a faster path from paper drawings to living digital models.
arxiv-2510-03476:
Bakić, Horawa, Li-Huerta, and Sweeting present a 2025 arXiv paper that proves a twenty five year old number theory conjecture in its first cases. Gross proposed in 2000 that certain coefficients of quaternionic modular forms hide special values of L-functions for cubic twists. The forms live on the exceptional group G2 and echo a classic pattern found by Waldspurger for quadratic twists. That older pattern even fed into progress on the congruent number problem. Until now, no cases of the cubic version were known.

The team proves the conjecture when the underlying modular forms are dihedral. Their proof gives the first examples where the predicted link between coefficients and L-values holds in full. The result opens a door: methods that settle the dihedral case may extend to wider families. Arithmetic geometers gain a new bridge between automorphic forms and the values that govern deep questions about numbers and curves.
arxiv-2510-03776:
Almeida and colleagues wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on how robots predict where nearby people and machines will move. The team studies agents with different roles and motion patterns, such as pedestrians, cyclists, and workers. Their question is whether using class labels for each agent makes forecasts more accurate. They focus on small and uneven datasets, a common problem for a robot in a new place.

The authors compare pattern-based methods with deep learning methods on two datasets, one from robotics and one filmed outdoors by drone. Class labels improved accuracy in most settings for every method they tested. Deep learning worked best when training data was balanced and plentiful. Pattern-based methods did better when data was scarce or some classes were rare. The results help builders choose a prediction method that fits the data they actually have.
arxiv-2510-03976:
Onah and Gutiérrez-Vega wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on equilateral triangular waveguides. A waveguide channels electromagnetic waves along a hollow tube, and the triangle is a rare shape with exactly buildable wave patterns. Instead of solving Maxwell's equations head-on, solutions come from superposing plane waves that obey the boundary conditions. Earlier masters, including Lamé and Schwinger, used that trick for this shape.

The authors push further into two practical properties: attenuation, meaning how fast signals weaken, and the quality factor of each mode. They derive fully analytic, closed-form expressions for both, which the literature previously lacked for this waveguide. Number theory, through the Eisenstein integers, gives them a rigorous ordering of the allowed eigenvalues. Their attenuation curves match known results and show sharp turning points unlike those of elliptic waveguides. The work completes a classical problem with exact formulas engineers can use.
arxiv-2510-04076:
Vahidi-Moghaddam and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv survey on making data-driven control policies fast enough for real machines. Model predictive control is safe and but needs an accurate model, which complex systems rarely provide. Data-driven alternatives learn from interaction or raw input-output data, and language model agents now draft control formulations from instructions. These methods share a weakness: heavy computation and memory that strain onboard hardware.

The paper organizes the landscape across model predictive control, its learning-based variants, reinforcement learning, and data-enabled predictive control. It then details eight efficiency strategies, including reduced-order modeling, function approximators, and convex approximations. For data-enabled control, combining singular value reductions with a neural approach looked especially promising. The authors sketch hybrid designs that balance data-driven adaptability against model-based reliability. The survey gives practitioners a roadmap for deploying optimal control under real-time limits.
arxiv-2510-04376:
Abdulrahman Tamim wrote this 2025 paper on a new way to think about how neural networks learn. Most accounts treat training as a walk downhill on a loss surface, guided by gradients. Tamim instead treats learning as a map between network settings and learned features. He uses category theory, a branch of math on structure and maps. The key question is whether two training paths can be bent into each other smoothly.

Tests on image tasks gave a clear pattern. Networks trained along paths that bend into each other scored within half a percent of each other. Networks on paths that do not bend together differed by more than three percent. A shape tool also picked out stable spots that predicted good test scores. The paper argues that these shared structures explain why very different training runs can end up working the same way. It also offers tools for transfer learning.
arxiv-2510-04476:
Tomas Figliolia and four coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on making attention in large models cheaper. Attention lets each token in a sequence look at every other token, which is powerful but costly. Its memory cache also grows with sequence length, so long contexts get expensive fast. Earlier fixes shrank the cache but left the main compute cost mostly untouched. The team moved the whole attention step into a smaller shared space.

Their method, called compressed convolutional attention, projects queries, keys, and values down before the attention math runs. A grouped variant adds head sharing on top for even tighter savings. In tests, the grouped version beat rival methods at equal cache size on dense and mixture models. It reached eightfold cache compression with no quality drop against standard attention. Training and first pass generation also ran much faster on modern graphics hardware.
arxiv-2510-04676:
Qiyu Wei, Haowei Wang, Richard Allmendinger, and Mauricio Álvarez wrote this 2025 paper on finding optima faster when tests are expensive. Bayesian optimization steers costly experiments with a statistical stand in model. Versions treat every past trial as equally useful for the search. The authors argue that some trials matter far more than others. Their method scores each past sample by counterfactual credit. The score asks how the search would have gone without that sample.

That credit feeds into the rule that picks the next trial point. Budget then flows toward regions where good trials proved the optimum likely hides. The team proved the method keeps a sublinear regret guarantee over time. On synthetic and real benchmarks, it reached the global optimum sooner than rivals. Simple regret, the gap to the best value, also fell faster. The idea suits tuning and design tasks where each run costs real time or money.
arxiv-2510-04776:
Ebenezer Awotoro and nine coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on a platform that unifies data on membrane proteins. Membrane proteins stud cell surfaces and are targets of over half of modern drugs. Their structures fill several databases that disagree, drop fields, and block computing. The team built MetaMP, a web framework that merges those sources into one place. Machine learning inside the platform enriches and checks the metadata.

Eight interactive views let users explore structures without wrestling files. Built in tools classify structures and flag outliers for review. The authors demonstrate three uses of AI on the platform. It predicts which segments cross the membrane. It reconciles legacy databases against each other. And it classifies structures with explanations a human can inspect. In validation, MetaMP settled seventy seven percent of data conflicts. It named the class of new proteins correctly ninety eight percent of the time, beating expert curation.
arxiv-2510-04976:
A. Koujok and six co-authors demonstrate a new kind of signal filter in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their device mixes two technologies that process waves instead of electric charge. One part, a nano-oscillator, produces a broad and messy microwave signal. The other part is a magnonic circuit that carries spin waves.

The team feeds the messy signal into the magnonic circuit. By adjusting only a magnetic field on that circuit, they pick out one narrow frequency band. The output is a clean spin-wave signal with a far narrower linewidth. Turning the field retunes the chosen frequency at will. The result points toward compact, low-energy filters for future wave-based computing.
arxiv-2510-05076:
Praise Adeyemo, Dominic Bunnett, and Fabián Levicán study how to embed weighted projective spaces in this 2025 arXiv paper. A projective variety can be placed inside ordinary projective space using powers of an ample line bundle. Small powers may fail to give a clean embedding. Geometers ask for the smallest power that works and also yields projective normality.

Weighted projective spaces correspond to simple polytopes called rectangular simplices. The authors give several criteria, based on arithmetic properties of the weights, for bounding the needed power. Their bounds are sharp in many cases. They also build combinatorial tools that construct families showing extreme behavior. The results extend earlier work by Payne, Hering, and Bruns and Gubeladze.
arxiv-2510-05476:
Wang and colleagues rethink how supercomputer programs talk across machines. The standard tool, MPI, lets programs on separate nodes exchange data through network links. Those links rely on complex software stacks built for Ethernet and similar hardware. Their 2025 paper, cMPI, routes the same exchanges through shared memory instead.

The shared memory uses CXL, a newer link that lets processors treat pooled memory like their own. Both one-sided and two-sided MPI exchanges run through the shared memory pool. The team built cMPI on a real CXL platform and solved problems with data layout and cache consistency. The study was presented at the SC25 supercomputing conference. For small messages, the new route cut latency sharply compared with network paths. Gains reached dozens of times on some latency and bandwidth tests. The work opens a path for CXL inside high-performance computing systems.
arxiv-2510-05576:
Daryanoosh adapts a quantum optimization algorithm to systems with many states per site. Qubit hardware speaks binary, but bosons and other systems live in larger local spaces. Mapping those spaces onto qubits leaves an infeasible region that pollutes calculations. His 2025 paper removes the pollution by design rather than by penalty.

The trick is choosing mixing Hamiltonians that never leave the feasible subspace. He compares binary, symmetric, and unary encodings under this lens. For symmetric mapping, the standard bit-flip mixer proves optimal by gate count. The other encodings pay a cost that grows with the number of QAOA layers. Penalty terms remain the common alternative, but they waste search effort as dimensions grow. He then finds ground states of the repulsive Bose-Hubbard model. The method works in both strong and weak interaction regimes. The framework also covers quantum approximate thermalization tasks.
arxiv-2510-05676:
Vandervorst and colleagues bring gradient boosting to graph data for fraud detection. Boosted trees dominate tabular learning, while neural networks own graph learning. Fraud, though, lives in relationships between people, claims, and accounts. Their 2025 G-GBM method grows trees that read graph neighborhoods directly.

The method concatenates feature vectors along simple paths inside each node's egonet. A case-weight adaptation lets the boosting machinery use those graph features soundly.
