The authors use a randomized feasibility method that samples a few constraints at each step and moves using Polyak steps.

They pair those feasibility steps with gradient steps on the objective. Two cases are covered: a smooth, strongly convex objective, and a convex objective that may be nonsmooth. Step sizes adapt as the method runs. The work gives theory for optimization problems where the constraint set is known only through many separate pieces.
arxiv-2601-20376:
Alessandro Cerioni tackles zero-order diffraction, a bright unwanted spot that plagues computer-generated holography. In phase-only holograms shown across the full field of view, this stray light sits in the middle of the image. Cerioni introduces an interferometric method that cancels it with a suppression beam.

The beam is arranged to interfere destructively with the zero-order light, in a plane matched to the spatial light modulator that shows the hologram. A camera in the loop guides the setup. Cleaner holograms matter for holographic displays and imaging, where the central artifact now limits quality.
arxiv-2601-20476:
Evanfiya Logacheva and five colleagues test whether giving examples in context improves AI-generated diagrams for teaching. Generative AI is now widespread in computing education, yet the quality of its materials worries teachers and students. The authors build a method for diagram code generation that uses in-context examples shaped by rhetorical structure theory.

The method aims to align model output with user expectations. Their title flags the catch: one hallucinated example can spoil the whole set. The study speaks to any teacher using AI to draft figures, code, or exercises. One bad example, as the title warns, can spoil the whole bunch.
arxiv-2601-20576:
B.-H. Yue and six colleagues probe the link between halo mass and radio jet activity in quasars. Quasars that look very similar can show a wide range of radio jet powers, and the reason is not understood. The large-scale environment is thought to play an important role.

A quasar's halo, the dark matter structure hosting it, sets much of that environment. If halo mass tracks jet power, environment would explain part of the spread. The answer would connect the small-scale physics of black hole feeding to the cosmic structures galaxies live in.
arxiv-2601-20676:
Zhuo Chen and six co-authors build a smarter agent for answering questions about images. Their 2026 paper tackles visual question answering, or VQA. A VQA system must join what it sees with what it reads. Only then can it answer well. The team adds a planning step to guide that work.

One known boost for VQA is retrieval-augmented generation. The system fetches extra image and text evidence before it answers. But the standard recipe chains many stages, and each stage waits on the last. The authors propose a planning agent to run this process with less waste. The paper speaks to the push for AI that answers hard, knowledge-heavy questions about pictures.
arxiv-2601-21076:
Abhijith Shaji and five co-authors fill in missing brain scans with a generative model. Their 2026 paper concerns Alzheimer's disease classification from magnetic resonance imaging. Deep learning predicts such disorders well from MRI. Combining multiple scan types can raise diagnostic performance. T1-weighted and diffusion-weighted scans each carry distinct information. Complete multimodal datasets, however, are not always available. Missing scans can block a patient from the best model.

The authors use a conditional diffusion model to impute the missing scans. It generates diffusion-weighted images from T1 scans. The filled-in data then feed the classifier. This multi-modal imputation keeps patients in the pipeline despite gaps. The approach serves clinics where scan time and cost vary. It is a practical step toward robust medical AI.
arxiv-2601-21276:
Haoming Huang and five co-authors study what happens to code quality when AI agents write pull requests. These agents now help with coding tasks and can produce changes fast. Speed, though, may come with costs that only show up later in review and upkeep.

The authors compare AI-written changes with human ones and track how reviewers react. Their title sums up the worry: more code, but less of it reused. Large fresh blocks can be harder to review and maintain than small edits that build on what exists. The study gives teams data on how agent output lands in real projects.
arxiv-2601-21676:
Dongsu Bak and Jae-Weon Lee ask how the seeds of supermassive black holes formed inside halos of ultralight dark matter. The early universe shows giant black holes surprisingly soon after the Big Bang. Their seeds must have grown from something, and light dark matter halos offer a setting.

The authors focus on the halo's Jeans scale and its dense central core, called a soliton. Gas trapped by that core can collapse directly into a heavy seed. The team identifies the conditions for that monolithic collapse. The picture connects the odd bright objects dubbed little red dots to a concrete seed story.
arxiv-2601-21776:
Chiara Ribaldone and Jacques Kontak Desmarais work on a basic task in the study of solids: computing the electrostatic potential inside a crystal. Because a crystal repeats forever, the sums behind that potential converge slowly, and Ewald-type techniques exist to speed them up.

Their 2026 preprint introduces a model charge density designed to cancel the multipole moments of the crystal's charge distribution, up to any chosen order. With those moments removed, the Ewald sums converge faster. Faster and more accurate potentials matter for simulating materials. Since electric forces shape almost everything a solid does, from its structure to how it carries charge and heat.
arxiv-2601-22176:
Isabel Tardón and Pablo Martín-Santamaría turn a French composer's craft into math. Jean Barraqué wrote stark, fierce music in the last age. He built his works from rows of notes that grow and spread, called proliferating series. In the old serial craft, the gaps from note to note stay fixed as a row is worked.

Barraqué kept a new thing fixed. What stays the same is the swap of notes that takes place from one step of the growth to the next. The pair sort and rank these rows with math. Their work lets us test scores and notes with care. It shows how this dense music was planned from the inside, note by note.
arxiv-2601-22276:
Mingyu Lu, Soham Gadgil, Chris Lin, Chanwoo Kim, and Su-In Lee value the people whose work trains image models. Their 2026 preprint, SurrogateSHAP, needs no fresh training runs to do the job. Text-to-image models now sit inside daily creative work, so fair pay for data is a live issue.

The method scores a whole set of a person's data at once, not one item at a time. Fair scores can back fair pay and a sound market for data. The team frame their tool as a base for that market. It gives a clear path from use to credit.
arxiv-2601-22376:
Run Wang and a large team build road maps for self-driving cars from whatever cameras a car happens to have. High-grade maps mark lanes and road parts in fine detail. Their 2026 preprint, FlexMap, notes that most builders demand a fixed, tuned camera rig. A dead camera or a new fleet layout can break them.

FlexMap aims to work from loose, varied camera setups. It turns flat views into a top-down road map in a way that bends with the rig. Safer maps from any rig would help fleets grow. The work targets a real weak point in road AI.
arxiv-2601-22476:
Ruizhe Zhong, Xingbo Du, and Junchi Yan built one learner that plans chip layouts under many design rules at once. Floorplanning sets the place and shape of each block on a chip. Their 2026 preprint, RulePlanner, notes that 3D stacks of layers make the rules far harder to obey.

Their reinforcement learner aims to meet the full rule set in one pass, not rule by rule. A unified planner could cut design time for dense chips. It could also find layouts human teams miss. The work targets a key step in chip design. It treats rules as the core problem.
arxiv-2601-22676:
Jinrui Sun, Tong Jia, Minghua He, and Ying Li built VarParser, a log parser that leans on the variables inside log lines. Logs are the first place engineers look when a big service fails. Their 2026 preprint notes that parsing — turning raw lines into clean events — is the first step for fault hunts.

Past parsers lean on the fixed text and slight the variable parts. VarParser flips that focus, and finds the variables carry rich signal. Better parses mean faster, truer fault diagnosis. The work serves the teams that keep online services alive. It is a small shift with wide reach.
arxiv-2601-23076:
Jayadev Joy and Sundeep Rangan recover signals in crowded, noisy radio bands planned for 6G. Receivers in the upper mid-band must work over wide bandwidths near strong neighboring signals. Under ideal hardware, linear receivers could suppress those neighbors.

Real hardware saturates and quantizes coarsely, so interference leaks across the spectrum in nonlinear ways. Their learning-based recovery is built for that messy reality. Cleaner reception in shared bands is key to faster, more reliable future wireless networks. Front-end nonlinearities are the practical villain: saturation and coarse quantization leak strong interference into the wanted band. The setting is upper mid-band spectrum planned for sixth-generation networks, where wide bandwidths meet dense neighboring signals.
arxiv-2601-23176:
Christian Robles and Suvrath Mahadevan test a new chip of tiny mirrors for solar spectroscopy. The device, a high-efficiency digital micromirror unit, works as a reconfigurable light modulator. It can reshape the field of view in real time during observations.

That flexibility allows targeted spectra of magnetically active solar regions, plus full-disk scans. The authors report the motivation and early tests for the instrument. Agile targeting could help solar physicists catch fast-changing regions as they flare and evolve. Early tests are the paper's scope, checking that the micromirror device performs as the spectroscopy design requires.
arxiv-2601-23276:
Shuhong Liu and eight co-authors model CCD noise from physics to clean deep-sky images. Sky imaging stays noise-limited under real observing conditions. Standard pipelines remove structured flaws, but random noise in the sensor is mostly left unresolved.

Learning-based cleaning is promising, yet paired training data are scarce and science needs interpretable models. Their physics-based making framework generates realistic CCD noise for training. Faithful noise models let cleaners learn the sensor's true behavior instead of generic blur. Physically interpretable, reproducible noise models are a stated requirement, since scientific imaging cannot rest on black-box flaws.
arxiv-2602-00176: Feng Tian and coauthors propose a posterior continuation frame for diffusion inverse problems such as image repair tasks. Full band guidance can mislead at high noise, where clean estimates carry score errors and high frequency directions are weakly identified. Their method exposes measurement bands in line with the current noise level. It builds middle steps that stress currently reliable bands and return gradually to full band consistency. A sampler joins a diffusion predictor with band limited fixes and a Haar domain rule.
arxiv-2602-00276: Aditya Kumar and William W. Cohen fix LLM planners that break domain rules. Language models reason well on math and code, yet often fail symbolic planning tasks. Their plans routinely violate stated constraints, such as walking through walls. The authors propose Localized In-Context Learning, which spots the first violation in a trace. It then injects a minimal example showing correct behavior for that failing step, beating explicit instructions and full trajectory examples.
arxiv-2602-00376: Delia McGrath and team introduce MATRIX, a multimodal benchmark and post training framework for materials science. Existing benchmarks make it hard to assess whether visual data during training improves explanation beyond text guidance. MATRIX evaluates basic theory, research work, and interpretation of real lab artifacts across several types. As a controlled diagnostic, it isolates visual grounding by comparing training on text alone with paired images. Despite small amounts of mixed data, visual guidance improves lab reading by 10 to 25 percent, with 5 to 16 percent gains on text work.
arxiv-2602-00576: Tushaar Gangavarapu and colleagues ask whether changing training data mix can steer optimisers toward better generalisation in large language models. Comparing gradient descent with sharpness-aware minimisation, they show the latter induces a lower simplicity bias, a key factor in its better generalisation. Upsampling or augmenting late-learned examples cuts simplicity bias the same way and lifts generalisation. Tests across several language models show relative accuracy gains of up to 18% on reasoning tasks with AdamW and Muon fine-tuning.
arxiv-2602-00776: Bartosz Bieganowski and colleagues document stable patterns in crypto order-book microstructure across assets of very different size. The same engineered book and trade data show similar predictive weight and SHAP shapes for assets from BTC to small tokens. A unified CatBoost pipeline with a direction-aware goal and time-series cross checks finds feature rankings and partial effects stable despite varied liquidity and volatility. A flash-crash test, where taker and maker results diverge, validates classic adverse-selection theory and flags systemic algorithmic trading risks.
arxiv-2602-00876: Samuel Moor-Smith and colleagues test whether multiple opinion dynamics models, stylized and realistic alike, hold up against empirical data. Standardized comparison against data is still lacking. Such models inform issues like climate change and vaccination and guide policy design. Their data-science-like validation first calibrates free parameters on an initial year range, then predicts the next wave from the prior wave. They trial the procedure on simulated data, then on European Social Survey topics, with toy models and real models alike.
arxiv-2602-00976: Philip Choi and colleagues study knots whose SL2(C) character varieties exceed dimension one, called X-large. One build uses split link diagrams with rational tangle swaps, giving an account for most X-large knots in tables. A second build uses braids and flips, driven by study of the Turk's head knot Th. It extends to Turk's head knots where p and q are odd, so the authors guess all of these knots are X-large. They also give a non-orientable analogue of Thurston's theorem.
arxiv-2602-01076: E. Ya. Paryev asks whether light made on nuclei can unmask the inner build of two charged bottomonium-like states, Zb(10610) and Zb(10650). His crash model, built on the nuclear spectral map, weighs four inner builds for each state: tight four-quark packs, loose meson pairs, and two blends of both. He works out rates and ratios on carbon and tungsten targets at set beam energies and angles. The readouts react in distinct ways to each inner build, so near-future high-grade tests could tell them apart.
arxiv-2602-01176: Yunus Laitinen Imanov and co-authors ask when cheap physics truly saves costly high-grade runs for partial differential equations. High-grade runs cost much, while cheap coarse or plain-physics runs skew results, and past mixed plans fail in silence when cheap runs mislead. Their sharp sample bound shows learning the gap from cheap runs cuts high-grade runs by a set factor tied to gap size. Their gated GaMF-PINN learns where to trust cheap runs, falls back to pure physics elsewhere, and adds honest doubt bands.
arxiv-2602-01376: Mark Higgins uses the Double Heston model freshly, letting spot-volatility correlation wander for exotic pricing. The two Heston sub-variances share volatility-of-volatility and mean-reversion but differ in spot-volatility correlation, widening classic Heston to stochastic correlation. As an affine model, it prices European options fast in closed form. Its key trait, a positive link between skew moves and spot moves, matters for barrier deals. Adding stochastic correlation lifts out-of-the-money knockout and one-touch prices and swap fair strikes.
arxiv-2602-01476: Stefan Clarke and Bartolomeo Stellato use conformal prediction to stop mixed-integer solvers early. Solvers often find the best solution early yet spend most time proving it optimal. Their method learns, across similar cases, when to terminate a solver. A neural network reads the true optimality gap from solver state, and conformal prediction calibrates a stopping threshold with rigorous probabilistic quality guarantees. On five families from the distributional MIPLIB library, it cuts solve time by over 60% while keeping solutions within 0.1% of optimal with 95% probability.
arxiv-2602-01576: Woosung Koh and colleagues model a mobile screen not as pixels but as runnable web code, letting one vision language model predict what an interface shows next. Text based models lose visual detail, while visual models struggle to render words and lean on slow pipelines of tools. Their code based route keeps language skill for exact text, and the team builds gWorld, open weight models at two sizes, with a framework synthesizing code training data. Across six benchmarks the models set a new accuracy versus size frontier.
arxiv-2602-02476:
Enise Kartal and 5 co-authors show that a special drive mode steadies a graphene resonator's frequency, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Graphene resonators suit sensing and timekeeping, but their tiny size and softness make them strongly nonlinear, which harms frequency stability. The usual Duffing regime, where stiffness depends on amplitude, converts amplitude noise into frequency noise.

Running the resonators in a phase-locked loop, the team set parametric oscillations beyond the bifurcation point against Duffing oscillations at the same amplitudes. The parametric mode reached a lower Allan deviation, the standard stability measure, at fast averaging times. Strong nonlinear damping built into the parametric regime cuts the amplitude-to-frequency noise conversion. A small model matched the phase spread and pointed to that damping as the main cause. The findings suggest nonlinear damping losses can push fine sensing past standard limits. The effect held at the same drive strength in both modes.
arxiv-2602-02576:
Rita Rani and 4 co-authors construct a universe that bounces instead of beginning in a singularity, inside a modified gravity theory, in a 2026 arXiv paper. The framework is Weyl-type f(Q) gravity, where gravity is encoded in non-metricity, the failure of lengths to stay fixed under transport. A power-law form of that quantity drives the model.

The cosmos contracts, reaches a minimum size near time zero, and re-expands without ever hitting a singular point. Near the bounce the null energy condition is violated, and the equation-of-state parameter crosses the phantom divide, behavior called quintom-like. Accelerated expansion follows the bounce, resembling inflation. The authors check the Hubble and deceleration parameters, the adiabatic stability index, and scalar field behavior. Instability appears right at the bounce while dark energy dominates the energy conditions. The model is offered as a viable nonsingular alternative for early-universe dynamics.
arxiv-2602-02776:
Scagnetto Arjuna tests whether a heartbeat can serve as an ID card at genuinely large scale, in a 2026 study of electrocardiogram biometrics. The literature lacked large-scale evaluations with operational metrics and standardized protocols, making studies hard to compare. Identity information turns out to live even in simple tabular features extracted from the signal.

A small neural embedding network on those features already performs non-trivially. Embedding models trained with a face-recognition-style loss then jump in performance when moving from tabular features to raw waveforms, and improve further with more training data and consistent normalization. On the large test set, verification reaches high true-accept rates at strict false-accept thresholds, with an equal error rate near two and a half percent. Closed-set identification and an open-set two-stage pipeline also perform strongly. ECG carries a measurable individual signature.
arxiv-2602-03476:
Feeling a virtual object's shape through a fingertip is still crude in most virtual reality systems. Yihao Dong and 4 co-authors propose TactDeform in a 2026 paper, inspired by how a real finger pad deforms when it touches surfaces. Their finger-worn electro-tactile interface renders patterns that change with the interaction, whether the user is approaching, touching, or sliding.

The rendered patterns also follow the geometry, distinguishing features and textures of the virtual object. In a study with 24 participants, users discriminated textures and identified geometric features far better than with a baseline approach. A free exploration phase added design lessons for future tactile interfaces. The work points toward touch displays that encode shape, not just vibration.
arxiv-2602-03576:
Why some superconductors reach unusually high transition temperatures remains one of condensed matter's open puzzles. Yu-Cheng Zhu and 2 co-authors argue in a 2026 paper that the lattice itself, treated quantum mechanically, holds part of the answer. Standard phonon theory ignores nuclear quantum many-body effects, which the authors say distorts phase diagrams.

Adding those effects to first-principles calculations, they find a lattice quantum disordered phase in two superconductors, H3S and a lanthanum nickel oxide. The phase fills a triangular region of the pressure-temperature diagram, and its boundary tracks the superconducting dome's left edge. The phase's peak temperature matches the maximum transition temperature, suggesting it both seeds superconductivity there and feeds its pairing mechanism.
arxiv-2602-03776:
A limit order book records the standing bids and offers behind every trade, and simulating what might have happened would help stress-test trading plans. Zhuohan Wang and Carmine Ventre propose DiffLOB in a 2026 paper, a diffusion model that generates order book trajectories conditioned on future market regimes. Existing generators either replay typical dynamics or need a live interacting agent.

DiffLOB conditions on trend, volatility, liquidity, and order-flow imbalance, so it can answer what-if questions: how would the book evolve under a different regime? The authors build a three-part evaluation for such counterfactual generation. It checks controllable realism, whether intervening on a regime changes the dynamics consistently, and whether the synthetic trajectories improve downstream regime prediction.
arxiv-2602-03876:
Ranking can teach a language model more than raw scores, argue Kyuseong Choi and 4 co-authors. Their 2026 paper presents GOPO, a training method for tasks like summarization and chat where no answer is simply right or wrong. GOPO keeps only the order of candidate rewards and discards their sizes.

Compared with the standard GRPO method, GOPO reaches higher reward scores during training. Independent judge models rate its outputs better at most checkpoints. It also matches GRPO quality in far fewer training steps. Results hold across several tasks and model sizes.
arxiv-2602-03976:
B. Thomasson and 5 co-authors ask whether star clusters and stellar multiples share one origin story. Their 2026 paper links the initial mass function, which counts stars by birth mass, to how gas cores fragment into multiple systems. The starting point is the heavy core mass function seen in a massive star-forming region.

A scale-free hierarchical fragmentation model breaks cores into ever smaller pieces. At least four levels of fragmentation are needed to reproduce the observed turnover in stellar masses. The same process sets how many massive stars end up in multiple systems. Mass distributions and multiplicity, the model suggests, are two outputs of one cascade.
arxiv-2602-04176:
Middleweight black holes may grow by repeated mergers at galactic centers. Amanda Newton and 4 co-authors model that growth in nuclear star clusters around a supermassive black hole. Their 2026 semi-analytic study includes direct collisions between black holes and stars plus gravitational-wave captures between black holes.

Starting mass assumptions decide everything. The upper-limit population grew intermediate-mass black holes of several hundred solar masses; the lower-limit one grew none. Most heavy products eventually sink and merge with the central supermassive black hole. Some black holes in the starting population were themselves merger products, seeding faster growth.
arxiv-2602-04376:
Two black holes bound by a cosmic string make an exotic lens. Clémentine Dassy and 1 co-author compute light deflection in the gravimagnetic dipole spacetime in a 2026 paper. The spacetime describes equal-mass black holes with opposite NUT charges, connected by a Misner string whose tension can vanish at a chosen separation.

That tuning gives a stable pair of counter-rotating black holes held at a set distance. Numerical simulations trace massless particles past the system, revealing gravitational lensing patterns for sources at infinity in the equatorial plane and along the axis. The work catalogs observable signatures of a solution long treated as a mathematical curiosity.
arxiv-2602-04476:
Byungwoo Jeon and 4 co-authors present a 2026 method to help multimodal language models keep sight of images during long reasoning. As these models generate long chains of thought, visual details can fade, and later steps may drift away from what was actually shown.

Their framework, VaLR, creates special internal tokens aligned with vision before each reasoning step. Training ties those tokens to output from vision encoders, the parts that process images. Across benchmarks needing long context or precise perception, VaLR beat earlier approaches. One visual spatial test improved by about twenty percentage points. The method also showed scaling behavior at test time that earlier models lacked.
arxiv-2602-04576:
Saikat Panja, Ayon Roy, and Anupam Singh ask when a solution found in a simpler number system can be lifted to a richer one, in a 2026 algebra paper. They work with polynomial equations whose unknowns are matrices that must commute with each other.

The setting involves a complete local ring and its residue field, a simpler system obtained by reducing values. A solution over the field is given first. The question is whether matching matrices over the ring exist. When the reduced target matrix is cyclic, the authors show lifting always works under conditions modeled on Hensel's lemma, a classic lifting tool. The result clarifies a structured corner of matrix equation theory.
arxiv-2602-04676:
Baptiste Anselme Martin and Thomas Ayral use classical tensor networks to warm-start quantum circuits in a 2026 paper on the variational quantum eigensolver. That algorithm prepares ground states, the lowest-energy states of a system, but its training can stall on barren plateaus where gradients nearly vanish.

The authors pre-optimize circuits with differentiable two-dimensional tensor networks for a standard magnet model. The prepared states reached high energy accuracy, even for larger systems beyond one dimension. Pre-optimization opened gradient zones that did not shrink exponentially with size. They also measured the classical cost of evaluating energies at these starting points. That analysis identifies where quantum hardware could scale better than classical simulation.
arxiv-2602-04776:
Hungarian conversational speech is the testbed for Máté Gedeon and Péter Mihajlik in a 2026 study of speech recognition. Conversation data with many speakers is scarce for lower-resource languages, so the authors simulate dialogues from single-speaker recordings.

Their speaker-aware simulation stitches recordings into realistic multi-speaker exchanges. A variant also models pauses based on utterance length, capturing how timing works in real talk. Fake Hungarian dialogues were made from a large speech corpus and mixed with real conversation for training. Across many settings, speaker-aware data beat naive concatenation. The pause variant gave modest, systematic gains, strongest when the source conversation statistics matched the target domain.
arxiv-2602-04976:
Andrew S Gavin and 12 co-authors describe detector electronics in this 2026 instrumentation paper. The TRISTAN detector upgrades the KATRIN experiment, which studies neutrinos by measuring tritium decay with extreme precision. TRISTAN adds over a thousand silicon drift detector pixels to hunt for heavy sterile neutrinos, each pixel facing very high electron rates.

Ordinary readout designs cannot keep up, so the team built a data acquisition system around remote analog-to-digital conversion, placing the conversion close to the detector. The paper lays out the design concept and the system as actually built. Flexible signal processing logic and data management are tuned for high-rate, high-precision running. The work shows how the electronics meet the demands of the sterile neutrino search.
arxiv-2602-05176:
When several language models work as a team, through routing, debate, or merging, one bad member can poison the whole system. Ziyuan Yang and 3 co-authors quantify that risk in this 2026 paper, whose title nods to a popular traitor-hunting game. They engineered four categories of malicious models and slipped them into four kinds of collaboration systems.

Across ten datasets, the damage was severe, with reasoning performance down about seven points on average and safety performance down about eight. Domains that depend on careful multi-step thought suffered most. As a defense, the authors add external supervisors that watch the collaboration and disable or mute members that misbehave. Supervision recovered about 95 percent of the lost performance on average. Making collaboration fully resistant, they conclude, remains an open problem.
arxiv-2602-05476:
Clustering points into a few balls with small total radius is a classic task, and modern versions add fairness rules and allow some points to be left out as outliers. Ameet Gadekar studies the fair sum of radii problem, where the chosen centers must represent each group fairly. He gives an algorithm with a provable error bound that runs in fixed-parameter tractable time, so the hard cost depends mainly on the number of clusters.

The method also works when the goal is any monotone symmetric norm of the radii, not just their sum. Its error bound is shown to be tight under a standard complexity assumption. One run produces a short list of answers, one of which is near-best for every such norm. The method rests on step-by-step ball finding and a three-way split in the best clustering.
arxiv-2602-05776:
A robot policy trained in one world often falters in another whose dynamics differ, and offline data from the source world could help if the mismatch can be repaired. Mengbei Yan and 7 co-authors study cross domain offline reinforcement learning, where a source data set is available beside a smaller target one. Simply merging the two can hurt, since source transitions obey the wrong physics.

Their algorithm, Selective Transition Correction, rewrites source data into target data instead of filtering it away. An inverse policy model and a reward model correct the actions and rewards of source transitions to align with target dynamics. A forward dynamics model then keeps only corrected samples that match the target better than the originals did. Experiments across environments with dynamics shifts show the method beating existing baselines. The authors argue correction exploits source data more fully than filtering.
arxiv-2602-05976:
A barycenter is a kind of average point for a spread of points or measures. Most work uses positive weights, but signed problems allow negative weights too, which show up in statistics and in solvers for gradient flows. Matt Jacobs and Bohan Zhou study these signed Wasserstein barycenter problems across transport costs, asking when the answer is unique.

Negative weights break the convexity that makes the unsigned problem tame, so the signed case is far harder. With only one positive weight, the authors extend a 2025 uniqueness result to any cost with a certain convexity trait. For arbitrary weights, they set up the dual problem through Kantorovich potentials and give a condition under which a steady dual answer yields an optimal signed barycenter. The paper maps where signed averages can be trusted to be one of a kind.
arxiv-2602-06176:
Large language models can solve hard reasoning problems, yet they still fail at surprisingly simple ones. Peiyang Song and 2 co-authors present a survey devoted entirely to these reasoning failures. They sort reasoning into embodied kinds, tied to the physical world, and non-embodied kinds, split into intuitive and formal logic.

Failures get a second sorting: deep flaws built into model design, limits that show up only in certain fields, and brittleness under small changes to a problem. For each failure type, the survey gives a definition, reviews known studies, weighs causes, and lists fixes people have tried. The authors also maintain a public collection of the research they cover.
arxiv-2602-06276:
Online ads face a privacy problem: browsers no longer say exactly which click caused a purchase. Lorne Applebaum and 5 co-authors study learning from attribution sets, where each conversion is linked only to a set of candidate clicks. Privacy-preserving browser tools report data in exactly this coarse form.

Working against an adversary that builds the sets from a prior guess, the team constructs an unbiased estimate of the true loss from these blurred signals. Standard risk minimization on that estimate comes with guarantees that grow stronger as the prior gets more informative, and stay robust when the prior is off. Simple tests on standard data beat the heuristics industry commonly uses, especially when sets are large or overlapping.
arxiv-2602-06476:
Teams of learning agents often share one network to save resources, but sharing can make every agent behave the same. Kyungbeom Kim and 2 co-authors present Prism, a sharing scheme that keeps diversity. Their trick works in the spectral domain: shared networks are decomposed by singular value decomposition, the standard factorization into directions and strengths.

All agents share the same singular directions, while each agent learns its own mask over the singular values. That split encourages distinct behaviors without giving up scalability. Rival diversity tricks cluster, prune, or mask weights and pay more for it. Across homogeneous and heterogeneous benchmarks, from grid food tasks to robot control suites, Prism stayed competitive while using resources more efficiently.
arxiv-2602-06976:
Chen Shen and five co-authors ask how language models can code in a programming language they have never seen. Coding skill in models usually mirrors pretraining data, and collapses on unfamiliar tongues. Rather than costly fine-tuning, the team studies inference-time language acquisition, where a model masters a new tongue by interacting with limited outside resources during the task itself.

Their framework, ILA-agent, gives models learning moves that mimic human learning: exploring docs, applying knowledge, and verifying results by running code. To test it fully they built Cangjie-bench, a multi-task benchmark for the novel statically typed language Cangjie. Across code making, translation, and repair, ILA-agent clearly beat retrieval-augmented rivals, and a look at agent paths reveals new behavior patterns alongside lasting gaps.
arxiv-2602-07276:
Steering a language model with activation vectors is cheap, but one fixed direction per task cannot handle tasks that mix several capabilities.  Pengrui Han and fourteen co-authors present Steer2Adapt, which composes steering vectors instead of learning each one from scratch.

Tasks are assumed to share a small set of underlying concept dimensions, captured as a reusable low-dimensional subspace. A new task is handled by finding a combination of basis vectors from only a handful of cases.  Experiments across nine tasks and three models in thinking and safety show the approach working.  Users get fast adaptation that reuses structure instead of relearning it each time.
arxiv-2602-07376:
Safety judgments vary across cultures and demographics, yet match data sets draw annotators from narrow pools.  Usman Naseem and five co-authors build Demo-SafetyBench to model demographic pluralism at the prompt level, separating value framing from responses.

First, prompts from an current dataset are reclassified into fourteen safety domains, retaining demographic metadata and expanding thin domains, yielding 43,050 samples.  Then several language models rate pluralistic sensitivity under zero-shot inference, with balanced thresholds reaching high reliability.  Alignment teams get a benchmark that asks whose safety values a model reflects, not just whether it refuses.
arxiv-2602-07676:
Spinning Q-vortex solitons are localized, rotating field shapes, and proving they exist on finite domains needs variational tools. Caroline Brumelot and one co-author show that they exist for a complex scalar field with a sextic potential, reduced to a nonlinear boundary value problem.

Two distinct kinds are proved: a ground state from minimization under a constraint and an excited saddle-point state from the mountain pass theorem. Bounds on frequency, amplitude, and domain size, plus exponential decay estimates, are derived. A spectral-Galerkin computation shows shapes, size saturation, and how spin rate depends on norm and winding number. Mathematical experts get proof, bounds, and numerics for them in one package.
arxiv-2602-08076:
Searches for breaks of Lorentz sameness in ghost particles usually assume empty space, but high-energy ghost particles travel through Earth itself. Simon Hilding-Nørkjær and three co-authors study uneven Lorentz-breaking effects in matter, where the planet's field changes the picture.

They review vacuum patterns, including way-tied daily shifts, then show that when the energy-tied breaking Energy rule grows like to Earth's matter field, strong overlap appears. The results include way-tied ringing boosts, a large-scale breakdown of ghost particle-anti-ghost balance for certain tools, and further marks absent in vacuum. Ghost particle physics teams gain new readings for testing whether space-time balance holds exactly.
arxiv-2602-08276:
Research on language-model agents is fragmented, with conceptual methods tangled in implementation details and superficially distinct ideas proliferating. Haoyu Jia and two co-authors argue the root cause is the absence of an analyzable, self-consistent formal model, and propose the Shape Context Model for characterizing agents through context structure.

On that foundation they build a declarative implementation method and a sustainable engineering workflow called Semantic Dynamics Analysis, spanning the full lifecycle of agent research and development. The workflow yields sound insights into agent mechanisms and supports rapid, systematic comparison. Agent teams gain a shared language for saying what an agent design actually is, independent of the code that implements it.
arxiv-2602-08376:
Shrinking a language model after training usually degrades it, especially at very low bit counts. Xinyu Wang and four co-authors introduce OJBKQ, a layer-wise quantization method that treats rounding as a joint optimization over activations and weights. Their arXiv paper frames each layer's problem as a constrained integer least-squares task with many right-hand sides.

That task is hard in general, so the authors adapt two classical nearest-plane methods, Babai and Klein, to find low-residual solutions column by column. Tests on large models show lower perplexity at three and four bits than existing post-training methods, at similar compute cost. Readers get a principled rounding scheme that squeezes models harder without retraining.
arxiv-2602-08576:
Multiple sclerosis often shifts from a relapsing-remitting course to a progressive one, and one hypothesis treats that shift as a sudden threshold crossing. Nikola Mirkov and two co-authors survey the evidence for a percolation-style phase transition in MS progression. Their arXiv paper centers on whether the relapsing-remitting balance can break abruptly, like a network crossing a percolation point.

The survey gathers theoretical models invoking critical thresholds, network studies of percolation robustness, clinical markers showing thresholds or early warnings, and counter-evidence favoring gradual change. Readers get a balanced map of a contested idea: threshold-like signals exist, but the case for a true abrupt transition remains open.
arxiv-2602-08776:
Teleoperation logs for contact-rich robot tasks hide a design choice: demonstrations may record the robot's execution, the leader's command, or both, and those signals are not interchangeable. Cuijie Xu and nine co-authors propose Dual-State Conditioning, which conditions on both signals while predicting future commands. Their arXiv paper targets visuomotor policy learning where contact matters.

Execution-only data discards command offsets that generate contact, while command-only data omits the robot's response. Conditioning on both exposes mismatch between command and execution as a signal for contact, delay, load, and operator correction. On a low-cost setup without force or tactile inputs, the method beats execution-only and strong command-only baselines across real contact-rich tasks. Readers get a practical default input-output setting for imitation learning.
arxiv-2602-08876:
What happens when two dense stars spiral past each other if gravity works slightly differently than Einstein described? Gabriel Luz Almeida and three co-authors study binary motion in a theory that adds a massless scalar field tied to the Gauss-Bonnet invariant. Using effective field theory, they strip away the mediating fields to get the pair's motion.

They derive formulas for the scattering kick and the deflection angle through third order in the post-Minkowskian expansion, which tracks effects by powers of gravity's strength. Where earlier post-Newtonian and post-Minkowskian results overlap, the new formulas agree. The work sharpens tests of gravity beyond general relativity.
arxiv-2602-08976:
Machine learning models often stumble when the world shifts away from training data. Jiaqi Wen and one co-author strengthen distributionally robust optimization by building ambiguity sets from generative models. A good ambiguity set must stay faithful to the nominal distribution while covering enough alternative scenarios, and it must keep the optimization tractable.

Their GAS-DRO algorithm solves the inner worst-case search over a parameterized generative space, with proven stationary convergence. Implemented with a diffusion model, it beats rivals on out-of-distribution generalization in machine-learning tasks. The work offers a practical recipe for robustness that reaches beyond the support of the observed data.
arxiv-2602-09076:
Robots weaving through crowds usually treat each person as a moving dot, discarding posture cues. Nhat Le and two co-authors test whether skeletal features improve trajectory forecasts. They systematically compare two- and three-dimensional keypoints plus derived biomechanical signals on the JRDB data set and a new 360-degree panoramic social-navigation collection.

Lower-body 3D keypoints alone cut average displacement error by 13 percent, and adding biomechanical cues gains another 1 to 4 percent. The advantage survives with 2D keypoints from monocular panoramic images, showing surround vision captures useful motion cues. The message for robot design is simple: watch the legs.
arxiv-2602-09176:
Squeezing data with loss, at finite block lengths, is ruled by two numbers: the rate-loss function and the spread. Eyyup Tasci and one co-author extend spread theory to sources whose parts are separate but not the same, a form that covers Gaussian sources with memory. Under a loss budget that may be passed with chance at most epsilon, they prove a result. The minimum rate equals the finite-blocklength rate-loss term plus a spread fix scaling as one over the square root of block length.

The key tool is a point-mass product proxy measure. It widens sample-based spreads beyond same parts while keeping the add-up rule, allowing typical-set cases for sums of unlike terms. For Gaussian self-linked sources, they also gauge how fast the finite-blocklength numbers near their limits via covariance values.
arxiv-2602-09376:
Masahiro Kaminaga's single-author 2026 paper studies Schrödinger operators with finitely many concentric spherical shell interactions in three dimensions. Each shell is defined through a quadratic form, with continuity across the shell and a jump in the radial derivative. A boundary-integral approach built on the free Green kernel yields an explicit resolvent formula for any number of shells with bounded couplings.

That formula includes a Krein-type expression and a boundary operator whose failure to invert marks the discrete spectrum, and it respects reduction by partial waves under rotation symmetry. The two-shell case with constant couplings gets a full treatment: the ground state, when it exists, sits in the s-wave sector, and bound states obey an explicit secular equation. Widely separated shells nearly recover single-shell levels, while tuned coincidences split levels by tunneling. Core-shell quantum-dot scales calibrate the two configurations.
arxiv-2602-09676:
Michel Mandjes and two co-authors study the workload spread of a finite-size queue driven by a band one-sided Markov added process. Their 2026 paper gives the Laplace-Stieltjes transform of the workload at a fast spread time, thereby alone pinning its transient spread. The approach joins several splits with known swing-theory results for band one-sided Lévy flows.

For the special case of Markov-tuned compound Poisson input, the authors also derive results for idle time and the total amount of lost work. A series of number tests closes the paper, showing the exact transient work. Finite-size queues with Markov added input thus gain a full transient account grounded in swing theory.
arxiv-2602-09876:
Eigenvalues link the shape of a space to the spectra of problems posed on it. Rodolphe Abou Assali introduces a new biharmonic Steklov problem on forms with Dirichlet-type boundary conditions in his 2026 paper, and shows that it is elliptic. The work gives variational accounts of its eigenvalues and proves that its spectrum is discrete.

The paper then establishes Kuttler-Sigillito bounds, which connect the eigenvalues of different problems on forms with curvature quantities on the space. These bounds let readers compare spectra across problems through the shape of the space. The result ties a new boundary problem to a classical family of bounds, giving geometers a fresh tool for reading spectral information from curvature.
arxiv-2602-09976:
A corrigendum is a short note that repairs a published result, and this 2026 note by Pedro Macias Marques, Chris McDaniel, and Alexandra Seceleanu does exactly that. It addresses their 2025 paper on higher Lorentzian polynomials and Hodge-Riemann relations. A gap in the main result needed closing, and the note supplies the missing step.

The argument starts from a homogeneous bivariate form, which defines a Toeplitz matrix at each size. Using Hodge theory and Schur polynomials, the authors prove that total nonnegativity of a larger Toeplitz matrix implies it for the smaller one. That implication seals the gap and restores the original paper's main claim.
arxiv-2602-10076:
Altermagnets, with their distinctive patterns, are natural fits for piezomagnetism, where strain induces magnetization. A 2026 paper by Beryl Bell and Jörn W. F. Venderbos studies the orbital version of that effect in simple lattice models of pure, insulating altermagnet systems in two dimensions. Earlier work had focused mainly on spin response under strain.

The authors derive general small-scale rules for orbital magnetization under strain and for orbital piezomagnetic polarizability, the defining response of pure altermagnets. Applied to three four-sided models, two d-wave and one g-wave, the results split: d-wave cases show linear polarizability, the g-wave case a nonlinear effect. Berry curvature of the occupied bands sets the polarizabilities.
arxiv-2602-10376:
Graph ideals link combinatorics to algebra. A 2026 paper led by Jennifer Biermann, with six co-authors, gives a new description of the h-polynomial for cover ideals of finite simple graphs. The same form covers Alexander duals of squarefree monomial ideals. Both edge-ideal and cover-ideal h-polynomial degrees are then expressed through the graph's independence polynomial. The key quantity is how often minus one occurs as a root of that polynomial.

For edge ideals, the degree is the independence number minus that count. For cover ideals, it equals the vertex count minus two minus that count. The count is also the additive inverse of both quotients' a-invariants. Recursions and closed formulas for the count cover broad graph families. They analyze which regularity-degree pairs arise for cover ideals in chordal classes, with extremal examples. They close with a conjectural bound on the gap.
arxiv-2602-10576:
Boxiao Wang and six co-authors turn language models into adaptive equation hunters in a 2026 paper. Symbolic fitting distills rules from data, and language models bring strong scientific priors to hypothesis making. But current systems treat the model as a static generator steered only by prompts, so search feedback never updates its internal models.

Their system, PiT-PO, trains the model with reward-based learning under a dual-constraint process. One constraint enforces layered real validity; the other regularizes tokens at fine grain to curb redundancy. The model thus evolves into an adaptive generator whose proposals stay physically consistent and mathematically lean. The paper places this as a step from prompt-guided guessing toward learned scientific discovery.
arxiv-2602-10776:
Max Haas and three co-authors speed up variational quantum eigensolvers for electronic ground states in a 2026 paper. Combining the ExcitationSolve optimizer with established rule selection methods like energy sorting, they build an approximate ground state. A unitary coupled cluster ansatz needs only a single sweep over the rule pool.

Fast older preprocessing selects most relevant rules, cutting the hardness of older variational tuning. The paper further shows that second-order perturbation theory emerges as the first-order Taylor expansion of the protocol. That expansion, in a link measure, clarifies why the method works. The result is a computationally lean route to molecular ground states on near-term quantum hardware, where every tuning step costs dearly.
arxiv-2602-10876:
Mohamed Camil Belhadjoudja extends backstepping control to higher-sized domains in a 2026 paper. Backstepping for straight-line partial rules is well built, but higher sizes lag: most methods exploit symmetries or restrict to box-shaped domains. The one symmetry-free approach for general regions, domain stretch, needs running an auxiliary rule at every instant to copy the control.

The paper takes on domains with graph-steady edges, a class beyond boxes that still admits tractable design. The work was sent as a long abstract to a 2026 networks and systems meeting. It moves backstepping closer to real shapes where controls must handle rough shapes without symmetry crutches.
arxiv-2602-11076:
Sixth-making mobile networks must honour strict slice promises, yet latency spikes resist quick diagnosis. Kavan Fatehi and six co-authors propose AE-MAPPO, a multi-agent method that weaves six focus mechanisms into slice control and surfaces them as free, faithful accounts. It works in three phases: predictive, reactive, and inter-slice tuning.

In an ultra-reliable low-latency case study, the method resolves a spike in milliseconds. It restores latency near one millisecond with near-perfect trust, and cuts troubleshooting time sharply while keeping other slices running. The paper argues that clarity need not trade against speed, a key claim for trustworthy real-time network automation.
arxiv-2602-11576:
Quantum processors built from superconducting circuits need a way to switch the link between two qubits fully off and back on again. Hui Wang and seven co-authors test a coupler made from two resonators, tracking how the effective qubit-qubit link changes in both frequency and time as qubit frequencies are tuned against the coupler. Shifting a qubit frequency by only about 50 megahertz moves the link from its off point to a working two-qubit gate point.

The double-resonator design also brings practical wins: simpler fabrication, less flux noise, and fewer cables crowded into the dilution refrigerator. Those traits matter because wiring and noise grow painful as processors scale up. The authors present the circuit as a promising building block for much larger superconducting quantum machines.
arxiv-2602-12576:
The Atiyah-Patodi-Singer index of Dirac operators is a deep invariant linking analysis, geometry, and topology, and capturing it on a lattice is a subtle task. Shoto Aoki led this work with six co-authors, constructing a lattice gauge theory formulation of that index for domains with compact boundaries in a flat torus. The key idea exploits equality to the spectral flow of domain-wall fermion Dirac operators, generalised here to cases without product structure near the boundary.

For sufficiently small lattice spacings, the formulation correctly captures the continuum Atiyah-Patodi-Singer index, as the team proves. Readers get a rigorous lattice route to a continuum invariant, extending domain-wall fermion spectral flow beyond product-structure boundaries. That extension matters for lattice gauge theory on realistic domains, where boundaries need not factorise neatly.
arxiv-2602-12676:
A key challenge for the projection method applied to the Landau-Lifshitz equation is the lack of rigorous theory backing for stability of its projection step. Changjian Xie works alone here, giving a semi-implicit numerical scheme built on the first-order Backward Differentiation Formula mixed with one-sided extrapolation and a Crank-Nicolson-type norm-preserving step.

The scheme shows three key traits: structure preservation, numerical stability, and first-order accuracy in time. In practice, the scheme not only preserves the unit-length rule of magnetisation, but also achieves stable long-time simulation with larger time steps than explicit methods. Readers get a rigorously backed, structure-preserving solver for the Landau-Lifshitz equation with proven stability and accuracy.
arxiv-2602-12976:
Streaming data arrive unlabelled and ever-changing, so anomaly detectors must cope with concept drift that erodes scores over time. Jin Li and three co-authors present VAE++ESDD, a method combining incremental learning with two-level ensembling: an ensemble of varying autoencoders predicts anomalies, while an ensemble of number-based drift detectors watches for change. Each detector uses a number-based workings to flag drift.

Tests on real and mock datasets with severely or extremely low anomaly rates and varied drift patterns show the method beating strong plain rivals. It also beats state-of-the-art rivals by a significant margin. For operators monitoring streams where anomalies are rare and conduct shifts, the two-level design offers a practical answer: detect drift explicitly, adapt incrementally, and let ensembles stabilise both tasks at once.
arxiv-2602-13176:
Measuring how far a person can reach matters clinically, but marker-based motion capture is costly and complex. Seth Donahue and nine co-authors validate a single-camera, AI-driven markerless approach for quantifying upper extremity reachable workspace. Nine unimpaired adults performed a standardised reaching task toward targets on a virtual sphere around the torso, shown in a VR headset, while marker-based systems and eight FLIR cameras recorded simultaneously.

Monocular analysis of two camera views compared frontal and offset configurations. The frontal view agreed strongly with the marker-based reference, with minimal mean bias of 0.61 plus or minus 0.12 percent reachspace per octant. The offset view underestimated workspace reached by 5.66 plus or minus 0.45 percent. The findings support frontal single-camera assessment, especially for anterior workspace, as the first validation of monocular markerless capture for this task, promising broader clinical use.
arxiv-2602-13376:
This manuscript has been withdrawn by its authors, who state it was made public by mistake before internal review was complete. It should therefore be read as a withdrawn draft, not as a published or endorsed result. In its draft form, it proposed an online, reference-free way to judge flowchart image-to-code generation in production, where no ground-truth code exists to check against.

The draft framework used two automated checks: OCR-based recall to gauge content coverage from text pulled out of the input image, and visual entailment precision to catch hallucinated elements. Their harmonic mean formed a single quality score, and validation on FlowVQA showed strong agreement with ground-truth metrics. Giang Son Nguyen leads the withdrawn draft with four co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13576:
Judges built from language models are now central to evaluation and alignment, guided by natural-language rubrics and checked on benchmarks. This paper exposes a vulnerability in that workflow called Rubric-Induced Preference Drift: edits to a rubric that pass benchmark validation can still shift a judge's preferences systematically on target domains. Because rubrics act as a high-level decision interface, even natural, criterion-preserving edits can induce drift that aggregate metrics and spot checks miss.

Worse, the flaw can be exploited: benchmark-compliant rubric edits steered judgments away from a trusted reference, cutting target-domain accuracy up to 9.5 percent on helpfulness and 27.9 percent on harmlessness. When those judgments train downstream models, the bias propagates and hardens into policy. Ruomeng Ding leads the work with five co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13776:
Fractionalization, shown by spin-charge separation in the one-dimensional Hubbard model and fractional charges in the fractional quantum Hall effect, marks strongly linked quantum systems. Yet probing excitations' anomalous dimensions is hard. This paper proposes an off-diagonal dissipative response test, using dissipative response theory, to detect spin-charge separation. By dissipating spin-down particles and measuring spin-up response, it uncovers a time signature. The off-diagonal response crosses from cubic-in-time growth at short times to linear-in-time decay at long times.

The short- and long-time coefficients encode the anomalous dimensions and velocities of spinons and holons, providing clear evidence of fractionalization. The signal vanishes without spin-charge separation. Predictions verified via tDMRG, with tiny-scale values linked to Luttinger values by Bethe ansatz, establish the test as a probe of fractionalization in quantum matter. Liang Tong leads the work with two co-authors.
arxiv-2602-14176: Mehrdad Kalantar and one co-author study a trait of group inclusions called conjugacy co-amenability, close kin to co-amenability. It seeks a state, not compactly backed, that stays fixed under the conjugation act of a group on the von Neumann algebra built from conjugates of a subgroup. The note proves settings and cases where the trait holds, and notes a tie to proper proximality that spurred the idea.
arxiv-2602-14276:
A. Said Gurbuz and four co-authors offer a 2026 arXiv data set for machine-use agents that must grasp screens. Agents need a structured view of a screen: what parts are seen, where they sit, and what text they hold. Yet most grounding data sets label only a small, task-tied subset per screen, capping reach and carry-over.

ScreenParse offers dense notes of all seen UI parts, with boxes, 55-class types, and text, across 771,000 web shots and 21 million parts. It was built by Webshot, an auto line that renders varied URLs, pulls notes, and applies vision-model relabeling and quality sifting. From it, the team trained ScreenVLM, a compact 316-million-weight model that decodes a ScreenTag markup with a form-aware loss.
arxiv-2602-14376:
Yuliang Wu and five co-authors propose a 2026 arXiv method for measuring surface deformation from event cameras. Visual deformation measurement recovers dense deformation fields by tracking surface motion, but classic image methods need tiny inter-frame motion, limiting dynamic scenes or demanding high-speed cameras with heavy storage costs. The paper fuses events and frames instead.

Events supply temporally dense motion cues, while frames supply spatially dense precise estimates. Revisiting solid elastic modeling, the authors build an Affine Invariant Simplicial framework that splits the field into linearized low-parameter sub-regions, easing ambiguities from sparse, noisy events. A neighborhood-greedy optimization lets well-converged sub-regions guide poorly converged neighbors, curbing local error buildup in long dense tracking.
arxiv-2602-14576:
Sebastian Gloor and six co-authors present a 2026 arXiv terahertz quantum cascade laser built for high-temperature operation. The two-well device uses the InGaAs/AlInAs material system, whose lighter effective mass and higher energy barriers boost gain above 150 Kelvin. Processed in copper-based double-metal waveguides, devices lased up to a maximum operating temperature of 188 Kelvin, with maximum current density 1.4 kiloamps per square centimeter.

Thin active zones and modest bias keep Joule heat low, so the devices run at a 10 percent duty cycle up to 170 Kelvin. The result pushes terahertz quantum cascade lasers toward more practical temperatures, narrowing the gap between laboratory devices and applications that need compact terahertz sources without deep cryogenic cooling.
arxiv-2602-14876:
Amar Deo Chandra explores the magnetic field of NGC 4631 X-8, an ultraluminous X-ray pulsar with a spin period near 9.7 seconds, discovered in XMM-Newton observations in 2025. The pulsar shows one of the largest spin-up rates among its class, near minus 9.6 times ten to the minus eight seconds per second.

Different models place its surface field roughly between three-tenths and seven times ten to the fourteenth gauss. Long-term evolution under steady accretion suggests it will likely become a millisecond pulsar with a decayed field near ten to the ninth gauss in about a million years. A young, extreme pulsar gains a magnetic biography, from monster field to quiet spinner.
arxiv-2602-14976:
Santos and colleagues study Godel-like solutions in Galilean gravity. This is a geometric form of gravitation for slow-moving matter, set on a five-dimensional manifold. In this setting, matter fields gain a covariant account, while plain Newtonian dynamics returns through an immersion into usual spacetime. The team adopts a Godel-like metric ansatz and couples gravity to a Galilean fluid drawn from a variational principle.

The result is a set of highly nonlinear, coupled field equations. Exact solutions follow from fixing the matter sector in line with those equations. The resulting setups describe rotating slow-motion universes. As a consequence, the linked Killing vector stays spacelike everywhere, and no closed timelike curves arise.
arxiv-2602-15076:
Liu and colleagues study sample complexity for online constrained Markov decision processes, the safety-aware form of reinforcement learning used in driving, robotics, and healthcare. Current methods often break safety rules or demand many samples to reach near-optimal policies. The team treats two settings: relaxed feasibility, where small violations are allowed, and strict feasibility, where none are allowed.

Their model-based primal-dual algorithm balances regret against bounded violations, drawing on online reinforcement learning and constrained optimization. Under relaxed feasibility it returns a near-optimal policy with bounded violation and high probability, using a sample count that matches the lower bound for unconstrained problems. Under strict feasibility it returns a near-optimal policy with zero violation, with sample needs governed by the Slater constant that sizes the feasible region. Learning constrained problems online, they conclude, is no harder than learning unconstrained ones when small violations are allowed.
arxiv-2602-15176:
Wegele and colleagues track through-thickness liquid transport in partly saturated needle-punched nonwovens with X-ray radiography. Nonwoven fibre networks underpin filtration, insulation, and geotextiles, where liquid uptake and release govern performance. In needle-punched felts, barbed needles entangle fibres and partly reorient them toward the thickness direction, forming pillars and heterogeneity.

Dynamic thickness-direction transport in partly saturated networks stays hard to access, due to opacity and fast timescales. The team pairs micro-CT of dry structure with X-ray radiography as droplets land. Transport is quantified against saturation and needling intensity with a Washburn-type descriptor. Transport depends exponentially on saturation, matching prior in-plane permeability models. Stronger needling reorients fibres toward the thickness direction, forming flow pathways that enhance transport even as single-phase permeability falls. Needle-punch thus emerges as a key tuning parameter for liquid transport.
arxiv-2602-15376:
Prasad and Chawla systematically compare learning-based likeness tools for virus finding. Code hashes such as MD5 and SHA-256 give a true name, but any single-bit change gives a new code. That is great for trust checks but caps use in attack chasing, virus study, and online sleuthing, where foes add tweaks.

Likeness tools fix this flaw by allowing rough pairing, letting linked strings give prints. Labs have offered likeness hashes and place-sensitive codes such as ssdeep, sdhash, and TLSH, plus machine-learning tools making vectors from traits. These tools have been tested alone, using varied sets and rules. Each tool is tested under a setup with trade scores. This is the study testing likeness tools side by side. Findings show no method does well across all sides; each shows swaps, hinting systems must join partner sorting and likeness tools rather than lean on one method.
arxiv-2602-15476:
Scalco and colleagues ask when talk about a topic runs dry online, and what fills the gap. They treat supply and demand for news as two linked forces, and they use the loop between them to spot stretches when little sound news is on hand. Their case is the COVID-19 vaccine rollout in six European states, tracked through Facebook, Google, Twitter, Wikipedia, and news sites.

The team finds that such dry spells line up with a drop in high-grade news in circulation, and with more low-grade posts taking hold. They also measure the reverse state, a flood of news, which they link to current ideas of an infodemic. Readers who follow health news will find a clear way to name these risky gaps, and why they leave people more open to being misled.
arxiv-2602-15576:
Krüger and colleagues report dust counts from Nozomi, Japan first Mars mission, launched in July 1998. Its Mars Dust Counter, an impact ionisation detector, logged 96 particle impacts. Those came while the craft sat in Earth orbit and later in interplanetary space, before a board failure ended operations in April 2002. The team sets those counts beside dust data from the Ulysses spacecraft detector in the same region of space.

Impact speeds and masses line up broadly with Ulysses, and Earth-orbit speeds show no sign of Earth-bound natural dust or of space debris. The interplanetary impact rate varies by about a factor of two, matching an engineering model of interplanetary dust. Impact directions cluster near the ecliptic plane, as expected for interplanetary grains. No cometary trail impacts were firmly identified, but the data stand as a reference for future missions such as MMX and DESTINY-plus.
arxiv-2602-15676:
Kucukahmetler and colleagues ask how neural forecasters picture the systems they predict. Networks can forecast complex dynamics well, yet their inner picture of latent geometry stays poorly known. The team studies forecasters through alignment, using anchor-based relative embeddings that strip away rotation and scaling ambiguity in latent spaces.

Across seven classic dynamic systems, from periodic to chaotic, family patterns emerge. MLPs match other MLPs, RNNs match RNNs, while transformers and echo-state networks forecast strongly despite a weaker match. That match mostly tracks accuracy, yet high accuracy can coexist with a weak match. Relative geometry thus gives a simple, steady basis to compare how model groups encode dynamic structure, and where their inner pictures part ways.
arxiv-2602-15776:
Yang and colleagues address partial sight in multi-agent systems, a critical barrier to teamwork and choices. Belief-based methods look mainly at past events without fully using global information. Talk-based methods often lack a robust model for using the extra information they provide. Their Global State Diffusion Algorithm, or GlobeDiff, infers the global state from local views. It frames state guessing as a multi-modal diffusion process.

That framing overcomes doubts in state guessing while inferring the global state with closeness. The authors prove that guessing error under both single-mode and multi-mode shapes can be bounded. Many tests show the method reaching better scores and guessing the global state well. It offers multi-agent systems a sound way to see the whole board from partial views.
arxiv-2602-15976:
Foster and colleagues report early results from a survey of jellyfish galaxies in the Coma cluster, galaxies trailing gas opposite their direction of travel. These tails show ram pressure stripping at its most extreme, as cluster gas peels material from galaxies plunging through it. The full survey will cover twenty nine such galaxies picked from radio tails.

From five galaxies observed with the WEAVE Large Integral Field Unit, the team finds tail light dominated not by star formation but by diffuse gas excited by shocks. Three clues point that way: LINER like line ratios, boosted oxygen to hydrogen ratios in tails versus disks, and elevated gas speeds and dispersions in the tails. The picture emerging is one where ram pressure shocks, not newborn stars, light up jellyfish tails.
arxiv-2602-16676:
Luis Zapata and Luis Rodríguez present high-resolution VLA and ALMA views of Orion South, taken more than fifteen years apart. The goal was to hunt for orbital motion in three close binary systems in the region. No shifts in position angle appear, but in two cases the sky-plane separation changes markedly.

Those shifts let the authors gauge total binary masses in the range of one to two solar masses. Disk masses are also gauged from millimeter emission. Dust-to-star mass ratios fall between four and eighteen hundredths, values fitting very early Class 0 protostars. Star formation researchers get fresh orbital clues for young binaries still wrapped in their birth disks.
arxiv-2602-16776:
Joheen Chakraborty and co-authors report the first direct measure of the period derivative in a quasi-periodic eruption. They find a smoothly rising period in the source ZTF19acnskyy, nicknamed Ansky. Most eruption models invoke repeat encounters of a small companion orbiting a huge black hole in an extreme mass-ratio inspiral. A rising period is surprising in those models, though not impossible.

Several accounts are explored. Stable mass transfer driven by impulsive loss events is one. Velocity kicks at closest approach from tidal pulls is another. Apparent shifts from relativistic precession or light travel-time delays in a binary black hole hierarchy is a third. Mass-transfer change in a disk instability model is a fourth. None fully explains the data, so more work on rising eruption periods is urged.
arxiv-2602-17476:
Jun Nian, writing alone, examines the cosmological constant problem through Schwarzian theory. Sky surveys point to a small, positive constant that now rules the energy budget of the universe. Yet quantum estimates miss its measured value by about one hundred twenty orders of magnitude. Building on earlier work by Gibbons, Nian sets the puzzle inside a quantum gravity frame built on Schwarzian theory and ensemble averaging.

From that frame he works out the observed dark energy density and its equation of state. In his account, the constant comes from averaging over time reparametrization modes. That link ties a long-standing cosmic puzzle to the statistics of those modes. It offers a quantum gravity route to the measured density, rather than leaving the value as an unexplained input.
arxiv-2602-17576:
Konstantin Bliokh asks how fast localized packets of light move in free space. He treats the case with field theory, scalar wavepacket math and quantum formalism side by side. A packet that stays confined in space turns out to carry two speeds at once.

The group velocity, tied to energy flow, runs below the speed of light. The phase velocity, tied to momentum, runs above it. The two multiply to the square of the speed of light. Gaussian and higher-order beams make the claim concrete. The paper also flags fine points in the quantum account built on the photon wavefunction. Both speeds can thus coexist with no clash with relativity.
arxiv-2602-17676:
Xingcheng Xu and team argue that familiar AI misalignments are not mere training glitches but rational outcomes of flawed inner models. Sycophancy, hallucination and strategic deception resist fixes via reinforcement learning, and current safety frames lack a unified theory for why they persist. The paper adapts Berk-Nash Rationalizability from economics to AI.

In that frame, an agent optimizes against a flawed subjective world model. Unsafe conduct then emerges as a stable misaligned equilibrium or as cycles of swing, depending on reward design, while deception locks in through equilibrium or epistemic indeterminacy. Tests on six leading model families map phase edges of safe conduct with care. Safety appears as a discrete phase set by epistemic priors, not a smooth function of reward size. That points to subjective model design as a must for robust alignment.
arxiv-2602-17876:
Nived Rajaraman and Yanjun Han study interactive learning of single-index models via stochastic gradient descent. Stochastic gradient descent is a cornerstone method for high-dimensional optimization, famed for empirical success. Recent theory explains how it enables feature learning in high-dimensional nonlinear models, above all the single-index model with independent, identically distributed data.

The sequential learning task examined here concerns single-index models, a setting likewise called generalized linear bandits or ridge bandits. There, stochastic gradient descent is simple and natural, yet its learning motion stays largely unexplored. Like the optimal interactive learner, it passes through a distinct burn-in phase before entering the learning phase. When the learning rate schedule is picked suitably, one procedure alone delivers sample complexity and regret guarantees close to optimal in both phases, across a broad class of link functions. It thus stays highly competitive under adaptive data.
arxiv-2602-18176:
Kaisen Yang and four co-authors improve how masked diffusion models pick their next words. These models can fill in blanks in any order, but current samplers act greedily, taking the surest token now without weighing what it costs later. That narrow view can pile up doubt and yield weaker text.

Their answer is the Info-Gain Sampler, a training-free decoder that uses the model's two-way view to weigh present doubt against what a choice reveals about still-hidden spots. Across reasoning, coding, creative writing, and image tasks it beat older masked-diffusion samplers, lifting reasoning scores by roughly three to twelve points and winning about sixty-three percent of creative writing comparisons. The code is public, so other teams can test it directly.
arxiv-2602-18276:
Michelle Mora and eight co-authors design antennas and foreground checks for the CANTAR global 21-centimeter experiment. Their 2026 paper faces a hard detection: the faint cosmic dawn signal hides behind bright foregrounds and instrument quirks. The team builds a simulation frame to test antenna color response, tune designs, and judge site quality.

Beam models and Haslam sky maps yield dynamic spectra covering the EDGES blade dipole and new dipole and monopole designs tuned by particle swarm optimization. The new designs run smoother in color, notably between seventy and one hundred twenty megahertz, and mid-latitude sites between minus forty and plus five degrees look best for foreground suppression. Bayesian checks of public EDGES data find foreground and ionosphere models consistent only when no absorption feature is included. The validated foreground ensemble supports a two-phase CANTAR plan: Antarctic calibration first, mid-latitude science later.
arxiv-2602-18776:
Reading a number aloud in Arabic is not one skill but many, spanning numerals, addresses, dates, quantities, and prices, in two numeral systems. Anas Alhumud, with two co-authors, presents ArabicNumBench in 2026, a benchmark that tests large language models on Arabic number reading across 210 tasks and tens of thousands of test cases.

Seventy-one models from ten providers were run under four prompting strategies, and accuracy ranged from very low to near perfect. Few-shot chain-of-thought prompting more than doubled zero-shot accuracy on average, yet the most accurate models often produced unstructured output, lacking Arabic reasoning markers. Only a handful of models generated structured output consistently, showing that getting the number right and following the format are distinct abilities.
arxiv-2602-18876:
When a superfluid flows past an obstacle, vortices can nucleate and change the flow entirely. Thomas Frisch, with two co-authors, studies in 2026 a two-dimensional superflow governed by the Gross-Pitaevskii equation, passing over finite rectangular blocks. The focus is on sharp corners, extending earlier work on smooth obstacles.

Local speed boost near sharp corners crucially controls the key speed for vortex birth. For both wall and well setups, key speeds are identified as functions of block width and height or depth. Theory and code runs agree well. The result gives a simple guide for how stable superflow stays past blocks with sharp features. It applies directly to atomic Bose-Einstein cold gases and related superfluid systems. Corners matter more than smooth curves here. Sharp edges set the limit.
