arxiv-2602-19076:
Judging an altermagnet effect by how much it needs spin-orbit coupling may miss the biggest prize. Xukun Feng, with five co-authors, challenges that habit in 2026 by uncovering a magnetic orbital Hall effect that is nonperturbative in SOC strength. Its symmetry properties come first in the paper's argument.

The effect is strictly barred in conventional collinear antiferromagnets, yet open across the ten spin-Laue classes for collinear altermagnets. Though it needs coupling to appear, it grows to giant size, matching or passing the nonrelativistic spin Hall effect. The same symmetry permits collinear-polarized orbital currents that are unusual, and those currents allow perpendicular magnetization to be steered with no applied field. First-principles calculations point to strong room-temperature responses in CrSb and FeSb2, a sign that altermagnetic orbitronics may matter far more for high-performance magnetic memory than had been assumed.
arxiv-2602-19176: Debattam Das, with two co-authors, studies inert and ambiguous conjugacy classes in the modular group from a purely combinatorial viewpoint in 2026. Word length in the free-product form of the group drives the analysis. Exact counting formulas and asymptotic growth rates follow for both class types. The inert-class formulas are the first obtained without analytic trace methods. A combinatorial framework for ambiguous classes is established alongside.
arxiv-2602-19376:
Hanabusa Senga and eight co-authors study superconducting and mechanical traits of several body-centered cubic alloys, including HfNbTiVZr, NbTiZr, HfNbTi, HfNbZr, and HfNbTa. They measure critical temperature, Debye temperature, electronic heat coefficient, and Vickers hardness, then compile a matching data set for other equiatomic five-metal alloys. The goal is testing an idea about the high-entropy effect in such superconductors.

The idea links a negative link between electron-phonon coupling and Debye temperature to shorter phonon lives in highly jumbled alloys. Ternary alloys with less jumbling show no sharp change in that link, giving the idea only limited support. Yet across binary through senary alloys, a common negative link appears. The authors also propose hardness as another way to gauge Debye temperature, aiding alloy design.
arxiv-2602-19676:
Short gas puffs into ADITYA-U tokamak plasmas calm gradient-driven microturbulence, lifting core temperature and energy confinement time. Jaya Kumar Alageshan and ten co-authors run global electrostatic gyrokinetic simulations to trace the effect. Gas injection flattens the radial density profile near mid-radius, and that flattening damps the trapped electron mode (TEM) already present.

With TEM-driven turbulence down, turbulence-driven heat transport falls and core temperature climbs. Repeating the puffs on a schedule repeats the suppression events, improving overall confinement time. Readers get an active control story: timed gas puffs as a lever on microturbulence in ADITYA-U.
arxiv-2602-19776:
Monoidal theories give a graphical, diagram-based algebra for reasoning about information flow in systems from circuits to quantum processes. A 2026 arXiv paper by Leo Lobski and Fabio Zanasi develops layered monoidal theories, which generalize that idea to descriptions at several levels of abstraction at once.

A layered theory lets several monoidal theories, plus maps between them, live inside one string diagram with no loss of rigour or meaning. The paper builds the foundations of this layered setup and shows it at work in probability and in cases from circuits, quantum processes, chemical reactions, and concurrent processes. Readers gain a single diagrammatic language for mixing levels of description.
arxiv-2602-20176:
D-peptide binders targeting L-proteins hold therapeutic promise. Generating them with machine learning remains largely unexplored, even as target-conditioned peptide design advances rapidly. A 2026 arXiv paper by Ziyi Yang and nine co-authors shows cross-chirality generalization is feasible. Injecting axial features into equivariant polar vector features lets models trained on homo-chiral data design hetero-chiral binders.

Implemented within a latent diffusion model, the method designs D-peptide binders that beat existing tools in computational benchmarks and show efficacy in wet-lab validation. To the authors' knowledge, theirs is the first generative AI for de novo D-peptide binder design validated in the wet lab. It offers fresh views on handling chirality in protein design, showing training data from one chirality can generalize to the mirror-image task.
arxiv-2602-20276:
A large team led by Daniel L. Walker presents the data processing behind a major survey of the Milky Way center. The ALMA Central Molecular Zone Exploration Survey, called ACES, mapped the galaxy's inner central zone in millimetre-wave light using three ALMA array setups. This third survey paper describes the molecular-line processing and first data release, showcasing two molecular tracers, HNCO and HCO+.

The showcased maps trace gas motion at fine spectral resolution and were checked against earlier single-dish surveys and targeted ALMA views of central clouds. One striking result is the wide presence of parsec-scale, line-shaped absorption features seen in HCO+, whose origin remains unknown. The release includes data cubes for every survey field plus combined mosaics and derived maps of intensity, noise, and gas velocity. Together, they give researchers a detailed, lasting view of dense central gas.
arxiv-2602-20376:
Ria Stevens and five co-authors study how low-rank structure simplifies discrete quadratic optimization. They maximize a complex-valued quadratic form over the Kth roots of unity. When the objective matrix has rank r, the global maximizer belongs to a candidate set whose size grows slowly with rank and dimension. The set can be built deterministically by enumerating vertices of a hyperplane arrangement. The algorithm runs in parallel across processors.

For nearly low-rank settings, the matrix is a noisy version of a rank-r matrix. Applying the method to a spectral cutoff gives a stated approximation guarantee tied to noise size and the eigengap. A random sampling variant needs a sample size free of dimension, cutting runtime sharply. Experiments on synthetic tests and graphs for Max-3-Cut match or beat semi-definite programming quality on such cases, while scaling to problems with at least a million variables.
arxiv-2602-20776:
M. C. Gandikota and four co-authors simulate a dense pack of soft, athermal particles that never stop pushing in one direction. In two dimensions they map the jammed state and ask how much active force it takes before the pack yields and starts to flow.

The yield force grows with pressure to the power 1.17, tracing a clear yield line. Redistributing the active forces through a contact network gives a robust scaling law that holds across the whole jammed phase, not just near yielding. Inside that phase the pack shows elastic, plastic, and yielding events, and its force patterns depart from passive systems at small forces.
arxiv-2602-21276:
Neural network training explores rugged loss landscapes, and the optimizer chosen shapes where it lands. Jianneng Yu and Alexandre Morozov compare stochastic gradient descent with a quasi-Newton method in this 2026 arXiv paper. Stochastic descent uses only gradients, while the quasi-Newton method uses curvature for direction and golden-section search for step size.

Kernel principal component analysis plus a new path-finding algorithm, FourierPathFinder, maps the solutions each method finds. Stochastic solutions sit separated by lower barriers, while quasi-Newton solutions, when fit extensively, reach deeper, more isolated minima that generalize worse. The lesson is that landscape exploration strategy, not just final loss, determines how robust and transferable a trained network becomes.
arxiv-2602-21476:
Chun-wei Ho and three co-authors propose a knowledge-driven, model-based approach to audio segmentation and source separation. Here knowledge means facts tied to the data, such as music scores. A model means a tool for segmentation and recognition, such as a hidden Markov model.

Unlike standard learning, the framework needs no pre-segmented training data with given categories and boundaries. It learns straight from the input audio plus its related knowledge sources, building all needed models on its own. Tests on simulated data show score-guided learning gives very good music segmentation and separation. On movie tracks, using sound-category knowledge beats data-driven methods that lack such information.
arxiv-2602-21876:
A kidney transplant can extend life and life quality in end-stage renal failure. More people gain if fewer donor kidneys were thrown away. Machine learning can flag high-risk organs early, so rescue allocation can boost organ use. Yet results are hard to compare across data sets.

Peer Schliephacke and seven co-authors tested donor kidney discard models. They trained five models plus an ensemble on 4,080 deceased donors in Germany: Deep Learning, Random Forest, Logistic Regression, Gradient Boosting, and Decision Tree. They used one frame with standard feature work and Bayesian tuning, scoring separation, fit, clarity. The ensemble scored best on separation. Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and Deep Learning scored alike and beat Decision Trees. Platt scaling improved fit for tree-based and neural models. SHAP put donor age and renal markers first across models. Steady prep, feature choice, and testing matter more than algorithm choice.
arxiv-2602-21976:
Ocean waves and ocean currents push each other around, yet most models treat one side of that exchange as fixed. Jacques Vanneste and William R. Young build a model in which waves and currents shape each other in both directions. Wave energy travels through a space of places and wave directions, while the currents follow a standard wave-current system, linked by shifts in wave speed and by wave momentum.

The key demand is consistency: the weight used to average current speeds must match the structure of wave momentum, so that total momentum and energy stay conserved. The authors trace this consistency back to a deeper variational structure drawn from the rotating equations for water with a free surface. The result is a tidy, energy-safe model for seas where waves and currents interact strongly.
arxiv-2602-22276:
Literature reviews in software and requirements engineering multiply as publications explode, and AI-generated reviews add speed at the cost of rigor, transparency, and shared data. Oliver Karras and four co-authors present EmpiRE-Compass, a neuro-symbolic dashboard that lowers the barriers to accessing, replicating, and reusing review data. Its goal is to make secondary studies sustainable.

The dashboard semantically structures review data in research knowledge graphs and uses language models for easy, dynamic access and reuse. Built and tested on two requirements-engineering use cases with a modular design, it shows how reviews can share their underlying artifacts. Researchers gain reviews they can check, rerun, and build on, not just read.
arxiv-2602-22476:
Eta Carinae is a supermassive binary shedding mass through stellar winds at a rate unmatched elsewhere in the Galaxy. The XRISM Collaboration reports high-resolution X-ray spectra of the system, observed in 2023 and 2024 as emission rose toward periastron passage in 2025. The colliding winds continuously produce shock-heated, X-ray-bright plasma, captured here in the iron K band by the Resolve microcalorimeter.

Hydrogen-like and helium-like lines reveal three velocity parts. Two broad ones move at thousands of kilometers per second, likely from the shocked companion wind. One narrow part moves at a few hundred kilometers per second. Iron fluorescent lines show a modest blueshift matching the primary wind, and the spectra confirm a Compton shoulder on the helium-like line complex for the first time. Both glowing and scattered profiles suggest the binary is viewed from the companion side.
arxiv-2602-22776:
Simone Gasperini and four co-authors recast a high-energy physics chore as a tuning task. Unfolding means getting back the true spread of a physics amount from sensor data blurred by chance noise and steady error. Starting from a smoothed quadratic tuning form, they build a setup spanning standard and quantum-ready methods.

A quadratic binary tuning form of the goal runs straight on quantum annealers and hybrid solvers. Their open-source package, QUnfold, mixes standard mixed-integer solvers with a D-Wave hybrid solver. Benchmarks against standard RooUnfold methods, including matrix flip, repeat Bayesian unfolding, and SVD, show strong scores with smoothing built into the goal.
arxiv-2602-23076:
Anthony Palmieri and three co-authors analyze step counts for Frank-Wolfe methods in constrained bilevel tuning. They study Frank-Wolfe methods for limited bilevel problems when the lower-level problem is solved only roughly, yielding biased and inexact hyper-slopes. Inexact forms of plain Frank-Wolfe, plus away-step and paired Frank-Wolfe, are studied.

Landing rates in the nonconvex setting under slope errors join with new bounds on hyper-slope errors from repeat and rough hidden slope math, giving overall step-count guarantees for bilevel Frank-Wolfe. Tests on two real-world uses confirm the theory and show usable strength.
arxiv-2602-23176:
Alberto Mayorgas and three co-authors study excited-state quantum phase transitions in a three-level Lipkin model. A larger state space and several separatrices create rich spectral patterns shaped by chaos. Such transitions are well mapped in two-level models. They are much harder to pin down when regular and chaotic motion mix.

The team charts the distinct dynamical zones with Poincaré sections and Peres lattices. They then pair chaos-sensitive measures with standard transition diagnostics for a static analysis. The degree of chaos and the Kullback-Leibler divergence prove highly effective. They complement the mean-field limit and the participation ratio. Together these tools form a standard framework for chaotic three-level systems, setting up future work on their dynamics.
arxiv-2602-23676:
Ao Li and eight co-authors address prior-compare false recalls in scan report writing, where vision-language models invent old findings unbacked by current studies. They propose Semantically Decoupled Latent Steering, a training-free, use-time method.

Unlike signal steering, which often suffers meaning tangles, their method builds a meaning-free nudge vector via LLM-driven meaning breakdown and a QR right-angle step. That right-angle step is key: shape constraints filter out medical meanings tangled in standard main part analysis, making sure steering targets only the old-compare axis. Tests on BiomedGPT show the method beats the false-recall-cutting versus medical-scores trade-off. Tests on MIMIC-CXR, with zero-shot transfer to CheXpert Plus and IU-Xray, show toughness. On MIMIC-CXR, old false recall odds fall, with FilBERT score dropping from zero point two three seven three to zero point one eight eight nine.
arxiv-2602-23876:
Ning Gao and five co-authors present RF-Agent, a system that automates the design of reward functions for low-level control tasks. The 2026 paper notes that language models can draft dense rewards from task descriptions, but greedy or evolutionary refinement wastes past feedback and searches inefficiently, limiting gains on complex tasks.

RF-Agent treats reward design as sequential decision-making by a language agent, and steers the search with Monte Carlo tree search. That structure reuses historical feedback across stages and uses the model's multi-stage reasoning to judge promising reward candidates. Tests on many diverse low-level control tasks show clear improvements over prior reward-design methods. The framework offers a more systematic way to turn task descriptions into effective rewards without heavy expert handcrafting.
arxiv-2602-23976:
Alejandro Gomez Cadavid and twelve co-authors present a pipeline that covers large-scale portfolio selection from start to finish, with limits on how many assets may be held. Tests run on trapped-ion quantum hardware. The 2026 paper starts by denoising a correlation matrix and finding groups of correlated assets. It then splits those groups so each piece fits the available qubit budget.

Each piece becomes a hardware-ready optimization subproblem. It is solved with a non-variational method, so no classical parameter-training loops are needed. Low-energy candidates are recombined into global portfolios, and a two-stage repair routine enforces feasibility while preserving the asset count. Benchmarks on a large Standard and Poor's 500 universe, run on a barium system, show that larger executable subproblems cut decomposition error. They improve objective values and risk-return trade-offs over randomized baselines.
arxiv-2602-24076:
Aleksandar Borković and two co-authors present a computational model for short-range van der Waals interactions between beams and shells, such as fibers and membranes. The 2026 paper targets a costly six-dimensional integral over the volumes of a beam and a shell. The integral is split here into a five-dimensional analytic pre-integration over the beam cross-section and a surrogate plate. Only a one-dimensional numerical integration along the beam axis remains.

The resulting inverse-power interaction potential joins the potential energies of Bernoulli-Euler beams and Kirchhoff-Love shells. The total energy is discretized with isogeometric finite elements, and the nonlinear equilibrium equations are solved by continuation. Error estimates, convergence analysis, and two numerical examples support the method. In short, a hard sum is cut into a cheap part and a thin part. The thin part runs along the beam alone.
arxiv-2603-00076: Basu tests how clinical large language models react to plain patient value words, the core of shared choice-making. From vignettes built on 98,759 de-identified Medicaid visit notes, he runs four model groups across 13 value settings in two clinical fields, for 104 trials in all. Default leanings differ by group, and advice shifts stay small even though each model notes patient values in non-control trials. Decision-matrix and self-report aids each raise directional concordance by 0.125 across a 78-trial second phase.
arxiv-2603-00176: Tan, Yan and Yang present AMPLIFY, a language-model-augmented framework for rebalancing shared e-scooters and bikes. A baseline module handles normal rebalancing, while a language-model module adjusts strategies live when demand surges, vehicles fail or rules intervene. The adaptation module reads system context, demand forecasts and baseline plans, refining its moves through self-reflection. Tests on real Chicago e-scooter data show better demand satisfaction and system revenue than baseline policies.
arxiv-2603-00476: Jiang and three colleagues expose a timing flaw in browser use agents, where pages change between planning and action so agents act on stale assumptions. They frame this check to use gap as a TOCTOU security flaw and test ten popular open agents across synthetic and real sites, finding the flaw widespread. Dynamic or hostile page content can exploit the gap to trigger unintended actions. A light fix that watches page changes during planning and rechecks state just before acting cuts insecure execution and side effects.
arxiv-2603-00676: Wu and nine colleagues build K2-Agent for layered mobile device control, separating knowing what from knowing how and letting both evolve together. A high level planner starts from one demo per task and runs a summarise reflect locate revise loop to distil know what by self evolution. A low level doer trains with curriculum guided group relative policy optimisation, balancing samples with split rewards and feeding demos to guide successful runs. On AndroidWorld the agent reaches 76.1 percent success from raw screenshots and open source backbones alone.
arxiv-2603-00876: Liu and three colleagues build BioProAgent to make language-model plans safe for real wet-lab work, where a hallucinated step can wreck equipment or ruin an experiment. A deterministic state machine enforces a design, verify, and fix cycle before any hardware moves, while symbolic grounding shrinks device detail to cut token use roughly sixfold. On an extended bench test it reached 95.6 percent physical compliance, far above the 21 percent of a baseline method.
arxiv-2603-00976: Wang and seven colleagues speed video generation with PreciseCache, a plug-in cache that skips only genuinely redundant computation instead of degrading quality. One part compares low-frequency differences between steps to spot skippable steps, while a second part finds redundant blocks inside steps that still run. On several backbones it averages 2.6 times faster on Wan2.1-14B with no noticeable quality loss, fixing the usual cache trade-off.
arxiv-2603-01176: Shaji and four colleagues estimate states for hybrid systems that touch their world at times, like docking craft and planet robots. Contact makes doubt jump in steps, so their optimal-control-based particle filter uses saltation matrices to map doubt through contact events. A path-integral plan using the smoothing-control duality makes the method robust to outliers and non-Gaussian noise. It was tested against strong rivals on a bouncing ball and a spring-loaded upside-down pendulum.
arxiv-2603-01276: Montagud-Camps, Grappin, and Verdini test whether MHD turbulent simulations can reproduce the slow 1/R fall of solar wind proton temperature between two-tenths and 1 au. Using expanding box model equations that add mean radial wind expansion to 3D MHD equations, they track slow solar wind plasma with quasi-2D spectral anisotropy. Varying Mach number, expansion parameter, plasma beta, and spectrum range and slope, they start turbulence at the inner edge with Mach number one and a mostly perpendicular spectrum. They find radial temperature curves near 1/R on average.
arxiv-2603-01376: Makni, Meng, and Mazumder present a 2026 paper on shrinking large language models by splitting each weight matrix into a sparse part plus a low-rank part. Their method, 3BASiL-TM, tunes the split layer by layer, then refines all layers together so compressed outputs stay close to the original. Tests report the WikiText2 perplexity gap for a compressed LLaMA-8B model cut by over 30 percent.
arxiv-2603-01576:
Earth models that map the planet from space have had little fair testing on ice and snow regions. Saurabh Kaushik, Lalit Maurya, and Beth Tellman fill that gap with a new test set in this 2026 work. Their Cryo-Bench covers glaciers with debris, glacial lakes, sea ice, and glacier fronts across many regions and sensors.

The team scores fourteen large Earth models against two standard image baselines. With frozen cores, a classic baseline still leads on mean overlap score, while top Earth models sit close behind. With just a tenth of the training data, Earth models pull ahead, which suits sparse polar labels. Full tuning gives mixed gains unless learning rates are tuned too, a practical tip the authors stress for users.
arxiv-2603-01976:
Luu Le, Hoang-Loc Cao, Ha-Hieu Pham, and colleagues classify white blood cells under messy real-world conditions. Their 2026 work serves hematology tasks like infection checks, leukemia screening, and treatment monitoring. Stain and scanner differences shift cell appearance a lot between labs and data sets.

Rare but vital cell types also drown in a sea of common ones, a severe imbalance problem. Their framework first normalizes stain, then splits training into two decoupled stages. Stage one learns transferable features with instance-balanced sampling across all cells. Stage two rebalances the classifier with class-aware sampling and a hybrid loss that weights rare classes. At test time, ensembles of backbones plus augmentation steady the final calls, and the system topped a named 2026 challenge leaderboard.
arxiv-2603-02076:
David Almog, Lucas Lippman, and Daniel Martin test how workers react when AI, not a human, will judge their work. Their 2026 online experiment assigns a real work task under known evaluator types. Firms and schools increasingly weigh AI assessment for reviews, hiring, and grading.

Workers told an AI would judge them produce a higher quantity of output. Controlling for quantity, their output quality runs lower by both human and AI grades. They also reach for external tools, including language models, more often under AI judgment. That extra tool use does not explain the quantity or quality gaps between groups. The hidden cost is a shift in effort allocation, not merely cheating, which evaluators should weigh before adopting AI judges.
arxiv-2603-02176:
Hao Li, Chunjiang Mu, Jianhao Chen, and colleagues tackle skill overload for AI agents in this 2026 paper. Agent skills are small add-on tools that agents can call to do tasks. Thousands now exist, so picking and chaining the right ones is hard. Their framework, AgentSkillOS, sorts skills and then runs them as linked plans.

First, skills are filed into a tree of skills by what each one can do. Next, a task is split into a chart of steps, each matched to skills. The team built thirty rich tasks to test how well agents pick skills. Tree search came close to perfect picking, even as skill counts grew huge. Planned chaining also beat plain calling with the same skill set.
arxiv-2603-02276:
Ahmad Al-Badawi, Faizuddin Ahmed, and colleagues build a black hole model with extra matter in this 2026 paper. The model is a charged Hayward black hole in anti-de Sitter space. A Hayward core replaces the central singularity with a smooth de Sitter center. Two added ingredients are a cloud of strings and a perfect fluid form of dark matter.

Treating the cosmic constant as pressure, the team derives the hole's heat traits. They confirm a classic relation and find a small-large phase switch like a gas-liquid one. Free energy shows the swallowtail shape expected below the critical pressure. Expansion cooling reaches far lower relative values than a standard charged hole. A holographic engine cycle runs at fair efficiency, helped by strings and hurt by the dark fluid.
arxiv-2603-02376:
Bodun Hu, Yoga Sri Varshan V, Saurabh Agarwal, and Aditya Akella automate GPU kernel writing in this 2026 paper. Kernels are the small programs that run the math on graphics chips. In large model training, kernels must move data between chips as well as compute. Hand-writing kernels that do both well is slow and error-prone.

Their framework, CUCo, uses AI agents and needs no training of its own. Agents generate kernels that orchestrate compute and communication together. That joint view opens gains that compute-only tuning cannot reach. Prior tools focused almost only on computation, leaving communication largely untouched. CUCo beat leading baselines and cut end-to-end latency by up to about one and a half times. The work targets large-scale training and inference alike.
arxiv-2603-02476:
Favreau Jean-Marie, Gerard Yan, Lafourcade Pascal, and Robert Léo solve a tiling puzzle in polynomial time in this 2026 paper. The Calisson puzzle fills a hexagon of triangles with lozenge tiles. Some edges are prescribed as tile boundaries, and neighbors across them must tilt differently. No fast algorithm was known for this recent game.

Their advancing surface algorithm runs in cubic time in the hexagon's side length. It can even be run by hand with pencil and eraser. The method reframes classic height function ideas from Conway and Thurston. Tilings lift to stepped surfaces, and heights solve a system of difference constraints. A graph layer makes the hidden algorithmic structure explicit. A region is tilable exactly when its weighted graph has no negative cycle.
arxiv-2603-02576:
Zhaoyu Zhu, Shuhan Zhang, Rui Gao, and Shuang Li rework a core learning method for agents that choose smooth, continuous actions. Their 2026 paper starts from the geometry of Wasserstein distance, a way to measure how far one spread of choices is from another. From a stepwise update in that geometry, they derive a new policy gradient method.

The method, called WPPG, swaps between a transport step and a smoothing step done by blurring with a bell curve. It never needs the policy's log density, so it suits flexible policies defined as push-forward maps. The authors prove steady linear convergence, even with rough value estimates. Tests on standard control tasks gave results on par with leading methods.
arxiv-2603-02676:
Wicaksono Leksono Muhamad, Joanito Agili Lopo, Tack Hwa Wong, and colleagues entered a shared logic task with a parsing-first method. Their 2026 system paper addresses content effects, where the topic of a logic problem sways a model's judgment. The effect grows worse across languages.

Their method rewrites each syllogism, a short two-premise argument, into a standard logical form. A strict parser then decides validity by rule, not by feel. On the SemEval-2026 Task 11 multilingual benchmark, the system placed in the top five on every subtask. It also cut content effects sharply. The result offers a lean rival to heavy fine-tuning or fixes inside the model's activations.
arxiv-2603-02876:
Eliseo Bao, Anxo Pérez, Xi Wang, and Javier Parapar build a scorecard for AI personas that imitate people in conversation. Simulated personas now stand in for users in modeling, social reasoning, and behavior studies. Most current grading leans on another model acting as judge, giving one opaque number with little grounding in real human talk.

Their framework, Eval4Sim, grades along three axes. Adherence checks whether the persona's background quietly shows in its lines, consistency checks whether the identity stays distinct across chats, and naturalness checks whether the flow feels human. Scores compare against a real human corpus and penalize drifting too far in either direction. The method works with any dialogue dataset that labels its speakers.
arxiv-2603-03076:
Jakob Hofstad pins down the largest tree that hides inside a random graph. Each edge of the graph shows up with a set chance, picked on its own. The biggest tree that fits, using only edges that show up, tends to land on one of two next-door values.

Past work proved this tight result for fixed chances, and for chances that fade slowly. Hofstad extends it to all fading chances above a stated floor. Below that range, the picture flips. For chances in a lower band, the biggest tree provably does not settle at the value plain averages predict. The two results draw a sharp line where simple averages stop describing random graphs.
arxiv-2603-03276:
Shengbang Tong, David Fan, John Nguyen, and a large team train multimodal models from scratch to learn what actually makes them work. Native models that mix language and vision are usually adapted from language-first systems, muddying every design lesson. Their 2026 study runs controlled pretraining experiments with no language pretraining in the way.

Four findings stand out. One visual representation excelled at both understanding and generation. Vision and language data proved complementary, each boosting the other. World modeling emerged naturally from unified training rather than special design. Mixture-of-experts scaling worked efficiently and induced modality specialization on its own. Scaling analysis also shows vision is far more data-hungry than language, an asymmetry the expert architecture helps balance.
arxiv-2603-03476:
Anat Dahan and Samah Ghazawi read brainwaves as strings of symbols, borrowing tools from string algorithms. Their 2026 framework searches EEG recordings for recurring temporal motifs, short patterns that repeat, using order-preserving and Cartesian tree matching. Those matchers care about relative ups and downs and hierarchical shape, not absolute size, so patterns survive amplitude rescaling. The result complements the usual spectral and complexity analyses.

As a proof of concept, the framework was applied to a public dataset of people with attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder and matched controls. The ADHD group showed far more frequent motifs, meaning more repetitive neural activity. Their motifs were shorter, with larger jumps between samples, and their pattern trees were shallower, with fewer hierarchical levels. The authors propose the method as a step toward objective markers for tracking neurodevelopmental disorders.
arxiv-2603-03576:
Alex Fischer and seven colleagues design a near-deterministic factory for multi-photon quantum states. Photonic quantum computing needs many single photons on demand, but pair sources fire probabilistically. Their 2026 scheme multiplexes in frequency and time, aiming to gather single photons, each in its own frequency bin, into one shared place and moment, ready to use together.

Optical quantum memories reshape each heralded photon's timing, while an array of fiber Bragg grating reflectors steers frequency and time jointly. The calculation folds in realistic losses and assumes only commercially available hardware. With a single free-space switchable delay loop as the memory, the design could feasibly produce eight-photon states about a thousand times per second. The authors frame the rates as realistically achievable, not laboratory best cases.
arxiv-2603-03976: Xiang Yu and colleagues study the Omega(2012) resonance with QCD sum rules, assuming an S-wave molecular pentaquark state. The negative-parity contribution is isolated through parity-projected sum rules, and two-body strong decays are studied via three-point correlation functions. Analysis yields a mass and a total two-body decay width for the molecular state, with a ratio of two-body decay branching fractions also obtained. Results match experiment within uncertainties and support the molecular pentaquark interpretation.
arxiv-2603-04476: Xu and colleagues adapt language models to physical design Tcl scripting. Modern EDA flows depend on Tcl, yet general models fail amid scarce data and strict reliability needs. The team adapts Qwen3-8B for Innovus Tcl generation, with a benchmark across five task types and three levels. A synthesis pipeline extracts commands, lints, back-infers requirements, and builds reasoning chains into a 10,000 tuple set. Two stage training plus syntax and functional checks yield higher pass rates than leading models.
arxiv-2603-04676: Li decodes the pulse of reasoning VLMs in multi-image understanding tasks. Multi-image reasoning stays hard. During chain-of-thought generation, text-to-image attention shows diffuse pulses missing task-relevant images. A positional bias in attention across images also appears. PulseFocus, a training-free method, structures reasoning into interleaved plan and focus blocks with soft attention gating. Forcing explicit planning of which image to examine, then gating attention to the referenced image, sharpens focus. Gains reach 3.7 percent on the BLINK benchmark, with a smaller gain on MuirBench.
arxiv-2603-05276: Samandar Samandarov and the rest of the team present Whisperer, visual prompting learning diffusion preprocessors adapting inputs in pixel space for frozen EasyOCR. Frozen models are stable and lean but lag on mismatched spreads, which Whisperer handles with input boosts. Training clones by-chance found gain policies. A four-stage course grows lucky gains from chance search of a partly trained model. On worn synthetic text images it cuts character error rate a lot, beating hand-made older models like CLAHE, without reinforcement learning pitfalls.
arxiv-2603-05376: Juan Guillermo Garrido and Emilio Vilches study prox-regular sweeping processes. They present an integral formulation for bounded-change paths, a global inequality against allowed paths, compared with differential-measure formulation. In the not-convex method, the rule includes a quadratic fix showing hypomonotonicity. Under mild smoothness, including time lower smoothness and picking-growth giving rich paths, the two forms prove the same. This yields a unified answer notion. A Brézis-Ekeland-Nayroles-type characterization via a prox-regular residual follows, nonpositive along admissible paths, with answers at zero.
arxiv-2603-05476: Cunha and Lehum study ultra-Planckian 2 to 2 scattering where an Abelian gauge theory meets agravity, the scale-free, renormalizable version of quadratic gravity. They give analytic results for unpolarized squared matrix elements across many tree-level channels, including photon-photon, fermion-fermion, and annihilation ones. They keep photon-graviton interference and check gauge-fixing independence. The amplitudes show forward and backward enhancements from small momentum transfer, boosted by the 1/p4 graviton propagator, while every channel's differential cross section scales in the same way as 1/s.
arxiv-2603-05576: Bahar and team address spreading robot skill policies to novel conditions, where copy learning stays stuck in the training region. Transfer learning offers path making robust to setting and task changes but remains data-hungry and weak at zero-shot spread. Their joint learning approach builds a common form of forward and inverse tasks, using extra forward demos from new setups to execute inverse tasks without direct guidance. Tests in mock and real-world environments with hard handling skills show the framework beating diffusion-based and multi-mode VAE rivals.
arxiv-2603-05776: Fodeh and colleagues build a benchmark and a fine-tuned language model for pulling structured patient voice from patient-written text. Patient accounts carry lived experience, social context, and care engagement that shape adherence, coordination, and equity, yet such signals seldom arrive in structured form. Their system, PVminerLLM, beats prompt-based baselines across several datasets and model sizes, reaching up to 83.82 percent F1 on code prediction. Strong results persist even with smaller models, showing that dependable extraction need not demand extreme scale, with code and models slated for public release.
arxiv-2603-06076: Maslyuchenko, Morawiec, and Zürcher examine a linear rule tied to a working rule that comes from fixed measures under multi-D changes. Working through the rule's repeats, they get a plain formula solving that rule within a chosen class of functions. Their central result proves that a fully smooth fixed measure exists for a multi-D transformation stretching old p-adic maps into higher sizes.
arxiv-2603-06276: Shetty and colleagues investigate large language models for story point estimation, the unitless project specific effort estimates helping scrum teams forecast sprints. Machine learning models, especially deep neural networks, predict points from titles and descriptions but need ample same project training data with human annotated ground truth. The authors test language models predicting points with no training data or only a few examples. With four models on 16 projects, zero shot prompting outperforms supervised deep learning trained on 80 percent of the data, and few shot prompting improves predictions.
arxiv-2603-06476: Bhakta and colleagues report the first millisecond pulsar found in the massive globular cluster NGC 6316, expected to host tens of such pulsars. Using the Green Bank Telescope and Parkes, they present a timing solution for PSR J1716-2808A, a millisecond rotator in a binary with a low-mass companion. The pulsar sits within half a core radius, with a negative period derivative implying a far-side location and acceleration toward us. Its negative period derivative also caps cluster acceleration and bounds the magnetic field, while external acceleration supports cluster membership.
arxiv-2603-06676: Joseph and team present a hybrid few-shot model with explainable AI to spot and stage maize, rice, and wheat leaf diseases under limited labelled data. Siamese and Proto Networks in a round-based setup learn telling disease features from few examples. Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping shows key decision regions in leaf images for clarity. On custom few-shot datasets, the model hits high accuracy, precision, and recall, with F1-scores often past 92% across stages. The tool offers a promising solution for data-tight farm disease monitoring.
arxiv-2603-06976: Shaukat and colleagues present the first large-scale evaluation of document chunking for dense retrieval across domains. Their study benchmarks dozens of segmentation methods across six knowledge domains using five embedding models, spanning fixed-size, semantic, and LLM-assisted approaches. LLM evaluator scores judge retrieval, using Normalised DCG at five as the main metric, plus Hit at five and MRR. Content-aware chunking beats naive fixed-length splitting. The top strategy, Paragraph Group Chunking, led scores and top-rank hit rates, while simple fixed-size character chunking fared poorly.
arxiv-2603-07176: Eriksson and colleagues learn good starting branching orders for SAT solvers before solving begins. Finding such orders is hard, yet a good first order can speed conflict-driven clause learning solvers a lot. The team offers three labeling methods to find usable orders in a tractable way, then trains a graph neural network to predict them. Tests show the learned order speeds random 3-CNF and pseudo-industrial benchmarks and generalizes to much larger instances, though it fails to speed the hardest cases.
arxiv-2603-07276: Mammadov and colleagues reframe conditional image generation with flow maps around learning the right starting noise. A noise adapter is trained alongside the flow map so that one pass from noise lands on samples matching both the given observation and the data prior. The shift matters because flow maps lack the step-by-step path that diffusion models use to fold in constraints. Tests on inverse problems show well-calibrated samples in a single pass, with large speedups on ImageNet.
arxiv-2603-07376: Avsar and colleagues use two observed collisions in the Fomalhaut belt to constrain its unseen planetesimals. A model tuned to the collision rate, system age and dust mass yields a massive belt. Its transition from evolved to pristine bodies sits at over a hundred kilometres in radius. The fit also implies further crashes are likely. Keeping watch on Fomalhaut and nearby debris disks is therefore worthwhile.
arxiv-2603-07576: Nashed and Eid study black holes in symmetric teleparallel f(Q) gravity in two-plus-one dimensions. With a power-law form for f(Q) they derive exact charged and neutral answers, then probe their heat and geometric traits. Central blowups run stronger than in general relativity, and horizon counts shift with charge, non-metricity coefficient and cosmological constant. By charge, geodesics may or may not reach the singularity, and heat stability holds, with a shape check based on the Euler characteristic rounding out the study.
arxiv-2603-07776: Meleti and Huang discuss a style transfer method that represents images in the brushstroke domain instead of the RGB domain. Computer vision style transfer has long modified image pixels to incorporate artistic style. Real artistic work consists of brushstrokes of different colors on canvas, making pixel-based approaches unnatural for such images. Their brushstroke-domain method offers better visual improvement over pixel-based methods.
arxiv-2603-08076: Rakotoniaina and colleagues study subtree counts in conditioned Galton-Watson trees, a classic model of random branching. Take such a tree with offspring mean 1 and condition it to have exactly n nodes. Under a mild moment condition, the count of a fixed rooted plane tree as a general subtree is asymptotically normal as n grows. Both mean and variance grow linearly in n. The limiting distribution stays nondegenerate except in special cases where variance stays bounded. These results confirm a conjecture of Janson on subtree counts.
arxiv-2603-08176: Obster presents fat Lie theory, a new view of representation theory for Lie groupoids and algebroids. The work introduces the category of fat extensions alongside the category of abstract 2-term representations up to homotopy, known as ruths, which are the intrinsic objects behind usual split 2-term ruths. He obtains a one-to-one correspondence between these categories and relates it to the known equivalence between 2-term ruths and VB-groupoids and algebroids. Fat extensions of groupoids, he shows, correspond to general linear PB-groupoids.
arxiv-2603-08276: Huang and colleagues develop population density estimators for right-censored distance sampling. The point-centred quarter method is widely used for density counts. But current methods for cut-off data from cut search radii rest mainly on a Poisson model with complete randomness, leaving a gap for clustered groups. The authors build a unified likelihood- and moment-based framework for cut-off point-centred quarter sampling under Poisson and negative binomial models. Their NBD-based ones account for spatial aggregation and censoring.
arxiv-2603-08476: Rodriguez and colleagues tackle robot imitation learning on mixed-dynamics tasks, where policies blur modes in demonstrations. Their LAR-MoE splits learning in two. Pre-training learns a latent code for observations and future actions through student-teacher training. Post-training steers routing by that latent structure, avoiding expert collapse with few parameters. On LIBERO it claims a 95.2% success rate with 150M weights. On a surgical bowel grasping and retraction task it matches a supervised mixture-of-experts baseline without phase labels, moving zero-shot to ex vivo porcine tissue.
arxiv-2603-09076: Bowen Yi and colleagues study when parameter-based watchers exist for nonlinear systems. The PEBO approach turns state guessing into online parameter finding, tackling many open guessing challenges. Success rests on transformability, a one-to-one answer to a fitting partial differential equation, and identifiability, a single parameterization from the final nonlinear fit model. The paper gives enough rules for both.
arxiv-2603-09176: Li-Tong Deng and Yong-Xiong Li work out Iwasawa invariants for even K-groups of rings of integers in the cyclotomic Z2-extension over real quadratic fields. By tracking how Dirichlet L-series values split under 2-adic tests for negative integer arguments, they derive a formula for the size of the 2-primary part at large layers. The formula fixes the lambda and mu invariants and comes with a bound on where it starts to hold. Applications cover tame kernels and explicit invariants for wide families of fields.
arxiv-2603-09276: Shion Takeno and Shogo Iwazaki fill gaps in the regret theory of Gaussian process Thompson sampling for Bayesian optimization. Most past work bounded only expected regret, unlike the richer results for the upper confidence bound method. They prove a lower bound showing polynomial dependence on the failure odds. They also bound the second moment of cumulative regret, plus lenient and cumulative regret over the horizon. Several lemmas along the way relax conditions used in recent analyses.
arxiv-2603-09376: Shubham Thwal and Suman Majumder simulate how cylindrical confinement changes the collapse of a polymer when solvent quality suddenly turns poor. Molecular dynamics reveals two stages: local clusters form and grow like a pearl necklace into one sausage-like cluster, then that cluster rounds into a spherical globule by surface-energy minimization. A shape parameter separates the stages and yields their relaxation times. The pearl-stage time ignores cylinder radius, while the sausage-stage time varies with radius before saturating.
arxiv-2603-09776: Magdalena Vilaxa-Campos, Nathan Leigh and Taeho Ryu model what happens when one star in a binary pours mass straight onto its partner. Their analytic model splits the stream into parcels, each on its own orbit under the gaining star alone. Direct hits add spin weakly, so the star can gain much mass without spinning to its limit. Tight orbits and fast donor spin keep the most mass.
arxiv-2603-09876: James A. Barron, Gregg A. Wade and Colin P. Folsom report five years of magnetic monitoring of Polaris, the famous Cepheid star. Spectra from the ESPaDOnS instrument at the Canada France Hawaii Telescope show a surface field that barely changes over time. Its slow periodic swing gives the first direct rotation period for a classical Cepheid. Combined size and spin data point to a star tilted toward our view.
arxiv-2603-09976: Dohyeong Kim and coauthors measure black hole traits for Type-1 active galactic nuclei in the North Ecliptic Pole Wide field. The sample joins optical and mid infrared detections, with spectral fits giving continuum brightness and line widths for several key lines. Using mid infrared light softens dust effects, yielding masses and Eddington ratios for hundreds of objects across wide redshift. About a third prove dust obscured, with brightness much understated otherwise.
arxiv-2603-10176: Giovanni Mazzolari and coauthors test whether radio selection can uncover heavily obscured active galactic nuclei in the J1030 field. That field pairs deep radio data with some of the deepest X-ray coverage available. Defining radio excess against the star formation rate from spectral fitting, they select sources inside the Chandra footprint with no X-ray detection. Deep limits and stacking point to very high obscuration, supporting a Compton thick population.
arxiv-2603-10376: Ting-Wei Chang and co-authors study the algebra structure of multiple Eisenstein series in positive characteristic, building on series of arbitrary rank introduced earlier. They prove a class of linear independence results for these series. The q-shuffle algebra of multiple zeta values, they show, embeds into an inverse limit of the Eisenstein series spaces over rank. The related algebra E matches that zeta algebra tensored with itself. As a payoff, E is an associative algebra, settling a conjecture from the earlier work.
arxiv-2603-10476: Panatchakorn Anantaprayoon and co-authors teach language models to negotiate their way to shared values, rather than aligning a lone agent. Two self-play instances take opposing personas and talk through synthetic moral dilemmas, hunting for fixes both sides can accept. Training uses AI feedback, scored by Collective Agency, an aim of ever wider agency. The result matched a single-agent baseline on that aim, while resolving conflicts far better and keeping general language skill intact. The authors frame negotiation training as a practical path for collective choices.
arxiv-2603-10576: Ki-Seng Tan introduces a p-adic L-function for each ordinary elliptic curve over a global function field, paired with a large p-power extension of the base field. The function is pinned down by matching special values of the twisted Hasse-Weil L-functions. It satisfies a functional equation, plus specialization and restriction formulas tied to the dual Selmer group. The Iwasawa main conjecture, with this function as its analytic side, is proved in several cases, and in high rank reduces to intermediate extensions on an open set.
arxiv-2603-10676: Kosti Koistinen and co-authors propose an attention graph neural network, with space and time built in, for explainable anomaly detection in industrial control systems. Such systems face growing cyber-physical threats, while machine learning detectors suffer from poor explainability, false alarms, and drift. Their model treats sensors, controllers, and network entities as nodes in a learned graph, so attention can highlight the links behind an alert. It fuses SCADA, network flow, and payload data in one analysis. A conformal prediction layer controls false alarm rates and watches for drift.
arxiv-2603-10876: Jennifer D'Souza and coauthors release a bilingual corpus meant to make subject indexing in libraries easier to sustain across languages and at large scale. The dataset pairs English and German catalog records with terms from the Integrated Authority File, together with a machine-actionable version of that taxonomy. They profile the corpus and analyze errors from three systems, inviting evaluation of usefulness and transparency as well as raw accuracy.
arxiv-2603-11276: Tong Li and coauthors find exploration for contextual bandits hiding inside ordinary model training. This removes the need to bolt Thompson sampling or upper-confidence methods onto black-box reward models. Their observation is that the randomness of cross-validation-based regularization naturally induces Thompson-like exploration. This happens when actions are chosen greedily. They prove the equivalence exactly for two-armed bandits. They show empirically that the resulting greedy strategy explores reliably in large-scale business settings. It beats epsilon-greedy and other strong benchmarks.
arxiv-2603-11576: Sorrentino, Zhang, and Zhu study how Mather measures change under small C1 perturbations of a Tonelli Lagrangian. They focus on a case where the unperturbed measure sits on a quasi-periodic torus. The torus frequency is Diophantine, which keeps it clear of resonances. The team proves the perturbed measure moves in a Hölder continuous way as the perturbation grows. How rough that motion can be is set by the frequency's Diophantine index. They also discuss a route to Lipschitz regularity via KAM theory.
arxiv-2603-12176: Ke, Li, Pradhan, Markowitz, and Wu read animal behavior with vision-language models and no task finetuning. Pose tracking and behavior reading both lean on heavy human labels in current practice. BehaviorVLM guides pretrained models through explicit steps that a user can verify. For pose, multi-stage reasoning across time, space, and views flags weak labels through geometric checks. For behavior, clustering finds candidate segments, a vision model captions each clip, and a language model merges and names them. The pipeline scales to multi-animal data with little labeling.
arxiv-2603-12576: Keru Wang and co-authors revisit how the distributional Bellman operator acts under the Cramér metric. Distributional methods track full return distributions, not just mean values. At the level of cumulative distribution functions, the update acts in an affine way. Its contraction then bounds how gaps between distributions can change. The team builds spectral Hilbert representations that match this geometry by exact conjugation. Their setup clarifies the operator structure behind such updates for later work.
arxiv-2603-13176: Dingcheng Huang and co-authors schedule perception modules by relevance for multimodal streaming in human-robot teamwork. Running every module on every frame piles up latency and hurts live performance. Robot events are sparse in information, so many modules waste work most frames. Their light scheduler uses past outputs to guess which modules the current scene needs. Tests cut latency against parallel pipelines and raised pose activation recall. Keyframe accuracy stayed high across the runs.
arxiv-2603-13276: Daniel Bretsko and co-authors introduce FastODT, a tree-based framework for efficient continual learning. Models in energy, weather, and sensing work face shifting data and tight compute budgets. Their oblivious tree model uses a Hoeffding bound to control its growth. Rapid learning and inference sit alongside efficient memory use and robust knowledge retention. Tests on energy and environmental time-series benchmarks matched or beat online and batch rivals. The authors present it as a scalable base for non-stationary settings with limited resources.
arxiv-2603-13576: Pinki Chahal and co-authors introduce a generalized K-space coherent averaging method for spin-orbit beam lattices. Spin-orbit beams couple orbital angular momentum to a two-level system like polarization or spin. Their method engineers two-dimensional lattices of such beams by coherent averaging in k-space. Programming the angle, amplitude, and polarization of input beams gives precise control over lattice geometry and period. It also controls orbital and radial degrees of freedom inside each unit cell. They demonstrate a micron-scale optical hexagonal lattice experimentally.
arxiv-2603-14176: Pham and co-authors present BluRef, an unsupervised method that sharpens blurred images without paired training data. Paired blur and sharp photos are hard to collect, so the method mines unpaired shots of like scenes. A dense matching model lines up a blurry image with sharp reference shots to make pseudo ground truth. No stored pairs or pre-trained nets are needed, so the method fits many settings and small devices. The authors report state-of-the-art results for deblurring.
arxiv-2603-14876: Maqsood and co-authors fuse AI prediction with a rule base for diagnosis support from lab results. Lab values carry quantifiable clues that can point to likely diseases. Their system pairs data-driven predictors with a clinically checked rule base. Data from 593,055 patients at 547 US primary care centers ground the build. Rules cover 59 conditions and can assign ICD-10 codes directly. A likely-diagnosis model spans 37 codes in 11 lab-based groups. Suggested follow-up tests help doctors confirm each lead.
arxiv-2603-15176: Bui-Xuan and co-authors study a network creation game where edges exist only at set time instants. Players add or drop time-labeled edges to cut their own costs. Costs mix edge upkeep with the sum of temporal distances to all other players. For strict temporal shortest paths, the price of anarchy stays constant when the upkeep factor is below two. At high upkeep, some equilibria cost far more than the optimum. The authors also exhibit a best-response cycle, so play may never settle at an equilibrium.
arxiv-2603-15276: Sourget and co-authors study how dataset diversity metrics behave and whether they predict classifier performance. Diversity is often praised but rarely defined the same way twice. They test metrics for images, text, and metadata on MorphoMNIST and the PadChest chest X-ray set. Reference-free image and metadata metrics linked weakly to AUC. FID and semantic diversity metrics linked much more strongly. A clinical expert named scanners as the main real-world diversity source, yet adding a scanner triggered shortcut learning in the model.
arxiv-2603-15376: Michels and Kachkachi study how spin disorder changes the heat a nanomagnet sheds under an alternating field, its specific loss power. Weak spin tilt from surface effects adds a quartic term to the anisotropy energy, scaled by a ratio they call zeta. Their semi-analytic formula mixes the balance susceptibility with a Langer-style relaxation rate. In slow-relaxation systems, tilt raises the loss power by lowering the energy barrier. Near the superparamagnetic edge, the trend can flip. Shape, sphere versus cube, also shapes the effect.
arxiv-2603-15576: Tran and Nguyen-Trung develop variance-reduced versions of the forward-reflected-backward splitting method for stochastic composite inclusions. Biased estimators had never been used for this problem class, due to a core technical hurdle. Their framework builds variance-reduced estimates of the forward-reflected direction and handles both fair and biased versions. Unbiased cases gain a one-over-k convergence rate and near-sure convergence to a solution. Biased cases, covering SARAH and hybrid methods, keep matching rates with stated oracle costs. Tests cover AUC optimization and policy evaluation.
arxiv-2603-15776: Dimopoulos and co-authors unite early inflation and late dark energy in one model. Metric-affine gravity with a Holst coupling can flatten a scalar potential. A quasi-pole shape then mimics Starobinsky inflation at early times. The same flattening can drive today's slow cosmic acceleration. Wave overproduction bounds and nucleosynthesis limits narrow the model hard. The scalar spectral index lands in a tight window near 0.966 to 0.967. That narrow range makes the model easy to test and falsify.
arxiv-2603-15876: Trybus, Rożko, and Skura find interpolants through refutation instead of proof. Refutation systems list which formulas a logic must reject. That mirror view can serve goals far past refutation itself. Their method grows from a refutation calculus for classical logic. Its core is a non-binary form of resolution. Many interpolant methods already exist in the field. The non-binary base marks this one as new. Theory and practice both enter the account.
arxiv-2603-15976: Zhang and co-authors grade AI-written scientific code the way library experts would. Pass or fail scores miss solver choice, memory care, and parallel sense. Their PETSCAgent-Bench judges code on five broad categories. A 14-evaluator pipeline mixes hard checks with model-based scoring. The harness compiles, runs, and measures each submission. Agent protocols let outside coding agents face the bench. Frontier models write clean, readable code on PETSc tasks. Hard correctness and library conventions still trip them often. Compiling code can still misuse the library, they show.
arxiv-2603-16276: Kamenshchik, Marrani, and Muscolino describe Carroll particles inside two-time physics. Carroll particles carry energy yet stay at rest. Two-time physics adds one time and one space dimension. A gauge symmetry there swaps positions with momenta, unifying many one-time systems. The team builds classical and quantum accounts of the Carroll case. They also link the extended phase space to Freudenthal triple systems. Those systems rest on a cubic Jordan algebra.
arxiv-2603-16776: Takeuchi studies how the motion of the observer distorts pair statistics in cosmology. Motion couples source selection, clustering, and how estimators are normalized. He builds a general framework that allows marked pair kernels and pair inclusion that does not factorize. In a simple limit, the leftover effect becomes a covariance between the selection score and pair excess. He shows that two galaxy populations can share a count dipole yet respond to a boost in opposite ways. He also derives contact terms and self-pair fixes for discrete harmonic estimators.
arxiv-2603-16876: Baba, Kishikawa, and Kodera present MARL-Rad, a multi agent learning system that writes radiology reports. Most agentic setups bolt fixed models into hand designed workflows, with no training for their roles. MARL-Rad splits chest X-ray reading among region agents plus one global agent that merges their work. All agents train jointly with clinically checkable rewards. On MIMIC-CXR and IU X-ray data, the authors report top scores on clinical metrics such as RadGraph and CheXbert. Blinded clinicians rated its reports as comparable to ground truth.
arxiv-2603-17076: Agarwal studies why the breakloose friction peak fades in large contacts. Breakloose is the force peak at the onset of sliding, strong at nanoscale but weak in macroscopic systems. He tests three minimal friction models with distinct loading geometries. In multi particle Prandtl-Tomlinson systems, size or heat promotes dephasing of depinning events. In end driven Frenkel-Kontorova chains, elasticity spreads stress and delays sliding. In uniformly driven chains, spring stiffness sets how slip events synchronize. He concludes that one peak shape can hide several mechanisms.
arxiv-2603-17476: Lee and co-authors introduce UniSAFE, a benchmark for the safety of unified multimodal models. Older safety tests split across tasks and formats, missing system-level flaws. UniSAFE spans seven input-output modality mixes with 6,802 curated cases. A shared-target design lets users compare failures across setups fairly. Tests of 15 leading models found more violations in multi-image and multi-turn cases, they report. Image-output tasks proved weakest overall.
arxiv-2603-17776: Namiq computes Betti numbers for chordal clique complexes and their Alexander duals. Chordal graphs order their maximal cliques in a leaf sequence. He finds graded Betti numbers for every skeleton of these complexes in closed form. Regularity, depth, and Cohen-Macaulay traits follow from the same formulas. For the dual side, an explicit minimal resolution sets the shifts. The Betti table even recovers the clique size data, up to one shift.
arxiv-2603-18176: Hosseinabadi and co-authors develop a theory of two-qubit T2 spectroscopy for quantum many-body systems. Set pulse sequences let a two-qubit sensor extract response and noise separately. Correlated dephasing then tracks how correlations spread in space and time. Low-energy excitation dispersion appears as light-cone-like profiles in the signal. Driving can add fringes outside the cone, and the method also separates ballistic from diffusive transport.
arxiv-2603-18276: Park, Hoshino, and Tanimura study how heavy water and light water differ in two-dimensional infrared spectra. They model the bond modes of H2O and D2O and how those modes trade energy. The 2D spectra show how drive, decay, and phase loss play out in each liquid. A full bath treatment, with memory and strong coupling, is key to match the spectral shapes. The H2O and D2O match-up lays bare the paths of energy and phase loss.
arxiv-2603-18376: Saha and co-authors present weak lensing shape catalogs for 30 merging galaxy clusters from SuperBIT. The balloon-borne telescope imaged the clusters over a 45-night flight in 2023, above most of the atmosphere. Metacalibration yields calibrated galaxy shapes for targets and calibration fields. Diagnostics check point-spread function residuals and shape correlations across the pipeline. Simulations with real flight conditions give a multiplicative shear bias of 1.1 plus or minus 7.8 percent.
arxiv-2603-18676: Jahshan, Ishay, and Yavits propose MANAR, an attention layer shaped by Global Workspace Theory. Standard attention lets all tokens talk at once, with no bottleneck. MANAR routes global context through a small trainable memory of abstract concepts. Retrieved concepts merge into one shared state, which then guides each token. Routing through that fixed-size state gives linear-time scaling. Weight copying from trained transformers eases adoption. Tests match or beat strong baselines on language, vision, and speech tasks, the authors report.
arxiv-2603-18776: Yu, Brendle, Johnson, and Starobinski design a market for sharing spectrum between passive and active users. Radiometers need quiet time-frequency tiles to keep retrieval error low. Their Vickrey-Clarke-Groves auction buys quiet tiles from active users. Payment follows each tile's marginal cut in error variance. The design secures efficient allocation and honest bidding. Exact auctions are too heavy on large grids, so a submodularity-based approximation steps in. Simulations with AMSR-2 data cut procurement costs by about 60 percent versus a fixed-band plan, while accuracy targets still hold.
arxiv-2603-19076: Li and co-authors present a real-time camera tracking system that works in moving, crowded scenes. Classic SLAM tools assume a still world and fail when objects move. Their system judges doubt for each pixel by checking how features clash across views. That doubt feeds an adjustable bundle step that can be trained end to end. The result tracks camera pose and scene shape in cluttered, dynamic settings. It runs at about ten frames per second. Code and data are shared in public, they note.
arxiv-2603-19176: Brunetto introduces FLAC, a method that builds the sound of a room from very few recordings. It learns a spread of likely room impulse responses, not just one fixed answer. A diffusion transformer shapes each response from cues on space, shape, and sound. FLAC can place sound at any point in a new room. With one recording, it beats prior eight-shot methods on two data sets. A new joint sound-and-shape score, AGREE, helps judge the results.
arxiv-2603-19576: Cheng and Yang study cusp formation in the shadows of black holes and other compact objects. Cusps come with three linked features: a topological charge shift, an equal-area law, and universal scaling. Because these traits stem from the shadow's global shape, they do not depend on metric details. The team checks this on a Kerr black hole with a running Newton coupling. The same behaviour holds for rotating traversable wormholes. The result gives a model-free way to read non-Kerr shadows.
arxiv-2603-19876: Sturm and co-authors set out a theory of x-ray scattering from excitons in atomically thin semiconductors. Excitons are bound pairs of electrons and holes, and light can pump them into the material. The team models how these excitons add new quasi-elastic features to the scattering spectrum. They also keep the usual scattering from electrons in the frame. By comparing pumped and unpumped spectra, the exciton charge pattern can be isolated. The method may reveal many-body effects in two-dimensional systems.
arxiv-2603-19976: Majumdar proves that a constrained matrix feasibility problem is complete for the existential theory of the reals. The problem asks if a partly specified symmetric matrix can be completed as a Gram matrix. The factors must be nonnegative and meet extra affine relations among entries. Hardness holds already at rank two, by a reduction from an arithmetic feasibility problem. Fixed anchor directions let inner products encode sums and products. The hardness extends to every fixed rank of two or more.
arxiv-2603-20176: Szymanowicz and co-authors present LagerNVS, a fully neural system for synthesizing new views of a scene. Recent work skips explicit 3D reconstruction for such tasks. The authors argue that 3D aware features still help the design. Their encoder starts from a network pretrained with explicit 3D supervision. A light decoder pairs with it, and photometric losses train the whole system. LagerNVS reached top feed forward scores, with 31.4 PSNR on the Re10k set. It renders in real time and works with or without known cameras.
arxiv-2603-20376: Kottmann and co-authors introduce flag decompositions for building quantum circuits with fewer wasted parameters. Their method carves a diagonal unitary out of a general one. The leftover flag circuit then needs only the optimal number of rotations. This yields parameter-optimal circuits for generic unitaries and matrix product states. Two compilation routes improve on prior art for key gate sets. Standard linear algebra routines keep the methods efficient at practical sizes. The approach should help compilers use each parameter wisely.
arxiv-2603-20576: Ma and co-authors build a benchmark for agents that answer questions over company data. Real data sits split across many systems, with copies that clash. Key facts often hide in plain text, not tables. Their Data Agent Benchmark holds 104 queries over 17 datasets. Four database systems are in play. The best agent scored just 57 percent on first try. They study how agents fail and draw lessons for future work.
arxiv-2603-20676: Trivedi and Joshi build a wider class of naked singularity spacetimes. The models extend the JMN family, which arise from gravitational collapse. Their version adds uneven density through a radial mass function. Tangential pressure does not vanish in these end states. Each model joins smoothly to a Schwarzschild exterior. When the photon sphere sits outside, the shadow matches a Schwarzschild black hole. Disk spectra show more high frequency light than Schwarzschild. Shifts from the base JMN model stay small.
arxiv-2603-20976: Musaffar and co-authors test whether language models can spot malicious intent inside human and AI teams. Support agents help with search, coding, and decisions, but attackers can poison data or inject prompts to mislead them. Past work cast such models as targets or attackers, not defenders. Using real team conversations over twenty five rounds, they frame detection as a task on interaction traces. The models flag malicious behavior in real time, without task specific detail. Simple heuristics miss the same behavior.
arxiv-2603-21076: Huang and co-authors report laser shock experiments on high entropy alloy films. High entropy alloys mix many main elements and are tuned for mechanical performance. Their behavior under shock loading was unexplored. They shocked two alloy films, each one micrometer thick, with a high intensity laser. An X-ray free electron laser probed the films during the shock. Diffraction showed a transient compressed phase. Surface speeds reached about five kilometers per second, showing these alloys can be measured under extreme shock.
arxiv-2603-21176: Zhu and co-authors present GIDE, a training-free image editing framework for diffusion large language models. These models tokenize images into discrete tokens, so standard noise inversion breaks and edits often damage structure. GIDE adds a discrete noise inversion step that captures latent noise in the token space. Editing then runs through grounding, inversion, and refinement stages. It accepts text, point, and box instructions while keeping the unedited background intact. On their new GIDE-Bench, it beats prior training-free methods by large margins.
arxiv-2603-21376: Pavlova and co-authors propose a transformer change that pushes models to reason out loud. They add an early-exit mechanism at intermediate layers. The model learns to exit at shallow layers when the next token needs little computation. After calibration, reinforcement learning rewards the earliest exit that keeps task performance. Early results on small reasoning models show adaptive computation per token. The idea aims to cut the excess internal computation that models could use for hidden planning. Hard tokens would keep the deep computation, while easy ones exit fast.
arxiv-2603-21576: Park and Park attack a memory bottleneck in long-context model inference. At each step, scanning the whole KV cache costs bandwidth that grows with context length. Their PRISM engine moves only the block choice step onto photonics. A query fans out optically to all blocks, and only the ranking matters, so low precision is fine. Built on thin-film lithium niobate, PRISM held perfect needle-in-a-haystack scores up to 64K tokens. They report a ten-thousandfold energy edge over GPU baselines.
arxiv-2603-21676: Chen studies depth-recurrent Transformers, which reuse one shared block to think deeper with no extra tokens. Fixed-depth models cannot change their reasoning effort, and chain-of-thought spends memory on long token streams. Looping a shared block adds steps at flat memory cost. Three tricks keep the loop stable past twenty steps: training on final outputs only, LayerScale starts, and an identity-biased gate. On graph reachability and nested logic, scores hit near-perfect once step counts matched task depth. The model also stretched past its training range.
arxiv-2603-21776: Lee and Kim study partisan warriors: commenters who cross into rival YouTube spaces mainly to attack. They analyze 1.85 million comments around the 2024 United States presidential debate, using language models to find attack targets. Cross-cutting commenters proved no more civil than those who stayed in their own camps. Conservative audiences tended to reward attacks on rival leaders, while liberal audiences sometimes punished them. Warriors were far more common in conservative-leaning channels. The pattern seems driven by channel culture more than by single video topics.
arxiv-2603-22276: Zelenin and Zhuravlyova make high-rank DoRA fine-tuning fit on a single GPU. DoRA splits weight magnitude from direction. Its forward pass needs row norms of a large dense product. Frameworks build that product in full, at about 512 MB per module. The authors factor the norm into base, cross, and Gram terms with small intermediates. They also fuse the DoRA steps into a single Triton kernel pass. On vision-language models, the fused code runs about twice as fast as the standard build.
arxiv-2603-22376: Wu and Hsieh present an AI Co-Scientist that runs search ranking research in a closed loop. Language model agents get direct cloud access, so ideas, code, GPU tests, and analysis cycle end to end. Simple agents handle routine work, while big choices go to a panel of three frontier models. On the live ranking task, the loop adds a further offline gain on top of a human transformer baseline. The best AI ideas were standard tricks from other fields that the ranking stack lacked.
arxiv-2603-22576: Bonás and co-authors introduce CAPITU, a benchmark for instruction-following in Brazilian Portuguese. Every task sits inside one of eight classic Brazilian novels, pairing checkable rules with cultural content. The set holds 59 instruction types in seven groups, all scored automatically with no human or model judges. Some rules test Portuguese word patterns that English benchmarks never touch. Eighteen leading models were tested in single-turn and multi-turn chats. Frontier reasoning models scored near perfect, while cheaper Portuguese-tuned models stayed competitive.
arxiv-2603-23076: Zhou and co-authors present MsFormer, a lightweight transformer for predictive maintenance of industrial devices. Sensor streams show patterns at many time scales, shaped by how machines work. Training data for failure prediction are often small. MsFormer samples the stream at multiple scales to catch those patterns. A tailored position encoding marks sequence order. Light attention with pooling replaces heavy self-attention, aiding small data. Tests on real datasets beat prior top methods. Gains hold across devices and operating conditions.
arxiv-2603-23876: Albert and Levandosky give tests that ensure key spectral facts for operators tied to solitary waves. They work with a class of semilinear elliptic equations. Wave stability work often assumes these spectral facts without proof. Their tests guarantee them. The checks need only the symbol of the linear operator, plus the sign and symmetry of the solution. So the tests can be run with no explicit formula for the solution itself.
arxiv-2603-24276: Liu rethinks how individual risk should be read from survival analysis. Hazard and survival functions are defined at population level, yet applied work often treats them as personal risk. Liu models event times as coming from hidden, person-specific hazard paths. Population curves are then averages over varied hidden paths. He shows those paths cannot be identified from survival data, even when population curves are fully known. Classic survival models can be sorted by how they handle this hidden spread. The framework sets clear limits for inference.
arxiv-2603-24976: Chakraborty and co-authors study how stacked bilayer graphene shifts between metal and insulator states. A sideways magnetic field plus a cross-sheet electric field can open or close a gap in the sheet. Past work needed fields above 100 tesla, far too strong to use. Adding skew links between layers changes the low-energy picture. A small electric field restores the gap. The team finds two field-driven shifts, near 1 tesla and near 10 to 25 tesla. The result hints at a sharp switch for spin-selective flow.
arxiv-2603-25076: Kawalec extends the prime zeta function to a wider strip of the complex plane. The extension holds under the Riemann hypothesis, with care for the branch cut. He gives a simple formula for the continued values wherever the real part tops one half. The prime zeta function sums over primes, so its reach past the known zone is a delicate matter.
