Prior interleaved-pilot schemes achieved vanishing error but relied on global statistics, requiring long fragments and dropping short ones, yielding rates far below capacity. Their local alignment approach finds global alignment bits within each fragment using local information only, so shorter fragments become usable. The decoder thus extracts far more output, raising rates. The method extends to channels with lost pieces, approaching capacity as the length threshold grows.
arxiv-2605-23476: Ghosh explains training instabilities in deep networks, loss spikes, wobbly convergence, and gradient pathologies, through non-normal operator theory. The linearized update operators for common optimizers are generically non-normal. For Adam, non-normality tracks the commutator between the Hessian and the adaptive preconditioner, while for momentum SGD it comes from the augmented state-space form. A pseudospectral precursor bound warns of transient growth even when the spectral radius stays below one. Tests on two-layer networks confirm the indicator separates stable from unstable phases by about tenfold.
arxiv-2605-23676: Sekwenz and colleagues study LLM aids for illegal content reports under the Digital Services Act. In a study with 450 users under varied AI error regimes, they compare unaided reporting, a standard aid giving one category with reasons, and a balanced aid showing balanced cases across provisions. Balanced AI lifts provision scores under AI error and cuts error distance versus standard AI, for near-miss errors. When AI output is correct, standard AI decides faster, but neither form lifts write-up quality over unaided reporting.
arxiv-2605-24076: Fokoué argues that causal logic is AI's statistical conscience, setting genuine intelligence apart from correlation machines that are brittle under shift. He proves a Statistical Necessity Theorem: out-of-distribution generalization demands encoded causal structure, telling prediction apart from intervention. A unified frame joins Pearl's do-calculus, Potential Outcomes, Double Machine Learning, and Invariant Risk Minimization as one family of causal statistical tools. Three flaws, language-model hallucination, reward hacking, and shift decay, are then read as causal blindness, each with a sound statistical remedy.
arxiv-2605-24176: Navard and Lim present Loki, a portrait-animation system that moves a driver clip's expression and pose onto one reference photo, keeping its identity. Leading diffusion systems stack modules for expression, pose, and identity, paying in parameters and tangled controls. Loki instead encodes driver expression and pose with a face model whose axes stand orthogonal to identity, then maps them for the backbone to read natively. Identity flows separately through backbone features. Cross-identity reenactment then needs a coefficient swap, and Loki uses about 43 percent fewer parameters than rivals.
arxiv-2605-24376: Fukuta and three co-authors study magnetism and edge states in monolayer tin monoxide. Using density functional theory, they dope the layer with manganese, iron, cobalt, and tungsten, and every dopant creates a localized moment from d-orbitals. Those states form nearly flat bands near the Fermi energy, shown for cobalt-doped material. In nanoribbons, edge-localized states appear regardless of width. For chiral ribbons, oxygen-rich edges stay semiconducting, while tin-ended edges carry conduction channels. Doping plus edge engineering offer a route to tune the layer.
arxiv-2605-24576: Elias Stenhede and four colleagues ask what heart traits an AI electrocardiography model for heart failure is picking up. They applied a validated AI-ECG model to 8,147 patients who had ECG and echocardiography within three days at one hospital. Global longitudinal strain showed the strongest link to predicted risk, followed by mitral annular plane systolic excursion and ejection fraction. The pattern held in patients with preserved ejection fraction, with diastolic measures weighing more. The team validated the findings on 36,286 external pairs.
arxiv-2605-24676: Ge Ren and others build a unified scheme for sorting bubble-like nuclei in the extended quantum molecular dynamics model. They relax cluster shapes for every nuclide in the AME2020 database. Four numbers sort the shapes: B counts density-profile inflections, marking droplet, bubble, or toroidal bubble forms. H, T, and U gauge central depletion, surface thickness, and inner low-density size. Light nuclei stay droplet-like, medium-mass nuclei mostly show bubbles, and toroidal bubbles gather near charge 25 and in heavy systems. Bubbles also prove widespread among superheavy nuclei.
arxiv-2605-25376: Kolawole Quadri presents KYA, a trust and governance layer for autonomous systems that answers whether actions were approved, fit policy, and can be checked afterward. Five parts cover pipelines, tightening-only permission rules, trust scoring, audited amplification, and delegation records. The layer adds to observability tools not replacing them and ships adapters for over 15 agent frameworks. All 36 cells of a test matrix pass, the scorer runs sub-millisecond at the 99th percentile, and the system sustains 1,800 operations per second. It also catches 89 percent of adversarial probes in testing.
arxiv-2605-25576: Das studies Lie-Yamaguti algebras, systems where grouping changes results and which extend Lie algebras and Lie triple systems alike. He tackles splitting through bicrossed products, then lists all complements of a small algebra. Each other one, he shows, arises from a deformation map. He further shows deformation maps unify several known maps, defines their cohomology, and gives a Maurer-Cartan account with a ruling algebra for linear changes.
arxiv-2605-25676: Yang and colleagues release Llamion, open-weight language models with 14B parameters built by converting Orion-14B into the standard Llama-family architecture. Their KEPT recipe maps unchanged modules, starts LayerNorm-to-RMSNorm conversion with a provably optimal training-free setup, and distills the converted model against the frozen source teacher. Llamion recovers Orion's behavior on H6, MT-Bench and KoMMLU, using about 123M tokens on one A100 in four days. Its base version reaches 66.87 percent on KoMMLU, beating the next-best open Korean entry by over seven points.
arxiv-2605-25876: Qian and colleagues present DyCoRM, a dynamic rule-aware reward model for image making. Static dimensions miss the fine-grained tests users actually apply. DyCoRM grounds task tests and compares preferences by rule. The team builds DyCoDataset-20K with dynamic tests and annotations, plus DyCoBench-1K, a benchmark for such tests. DyCoPick applies it to selecting images. The work is the first reward framework for fine-grained evaluation in image making.
arxiv-2605-25976: Bu, Pădurariu and Toda split derived categories of sheaves on quasi-smooth derived stacks into ordered pieces. Such a split has vanishing maps in one direction between pieces. Here weight conditions fix the pieces, and parabolic induction gives the inclusions. The pieces take their labels from the component lattice of the stack, a key combinatorial object in Donaldson-Thomas theory. Examples cover semistable bundles and Higgs bundles on a curve, plus de Rham and Betti local systems, for reductive groups beyond type A.
arxiv-2605-26176: Liessens Dujardin and four colleagues measure pitch hearing in audio-language models, a basic musical skill other benchmarks probe only indirectly. Audio-language models increasingly tutor, transcribe, caption, recommend and produce music, so reliable sound perception is a prerequisite. A model that cannot hear pitch structure cannot be trusted to teach, transcribe or act on audio. Existing evaluations test pitch mainly through higher-level tasks and multiple-choice formats, leaving fine-grained pitch across instruments unmeasured. PitchBench fills that gap with direct tests of pitch hearing.
arxiv-2605-26576: Yuyang Tan and four colleagues segment 3D objects from queries without manual annotation using TrackRef3D. Referring 3D Gaussian Splatting lets AI pick objects by words, but older methods need costly per-scene labels and per-view pseudo masks. TrackRef3D decouples object discovery from semantic grounding through a track-then-label pipeline. A Trajectory-Aware Semantic Consensus Module merges cross-view predictions via clustering and voting into one canonical semantic identity. Visibility-aware descriptions cut ambiguity, and Hybrid Training jointly tunes coarse and fine cues. Tests report top performance.
arxiv-2605-26676: Safarov and six colleagues tackle anomaly detection when training images contain hidden defects, a common flaw in industrial inspection data. Their method, MeDS, builds an ensemble of partial memories by random subsampling, uses the ensemble distances to train a reconstruction scorer, then fine-tunes on data the scorer deems clean. It reaches 99.16 percent image-level AUROC on MVTecAD at 40 percent contamination and leads on VisA and Real-IAD under noisy conditions.
arxiv-2605-26976: Aditto, Ifty, and Zahin review microwave-to-optical quantum transduction, the conversion of microwave photons from superconducting processors into optical photons for fiber transmission. They compare optomechanical, electro-optic, and magneto-optic platforms on efficiency, bandwidth, added noise, and temperature, and propose normalized metrics for fair comparison. Optomechanical devices reach 93 percent internal efficiency with sub-quantum noise, electro-optic devices approach 99.5 percent, and magneto-optic devices lag far behind but offer non-reciprocity.
arxiv-2605-27076: Ledford and Regli frame learning under hidden feedback as TAC-MAB, a threshold bandit where tasks pay only when a team meets an unknown size threshold. A central method achieves log-scale total regret, split into a structure-search term for settling feasibility and a stats term for value guesses. A spread-out rule syncs only when structure beliefs change, cutting talk 23-fold against the central base while keeping alignment.
arxiv-2605-27176: Sourav and co-authors ask which facts in a knowledge graph actually shape hypotheses about battery materials. They vary graph density, ontology richness, topology, and control structure across three language models, and they score outputs against both the given graph and a fixed reference. Graph context shifts outputs, but models also recover much graph content from prior knowledge alone. Compact top subsets often match full-graph behavior, and even random or topology-based subsets recover much signal, so useful signal is redundant rather than tied to one ranking rule.
arxiv-2605-27276: Prannay Hebbar and colleagues build a loop in which one language model agent improves another agent on two fronts at once. The feedback agent rewrites the task scaffold and retrains the model weights, instead of changing only one side. Tested on legal classification, GPU kernel tuning, and single-cell RNA cleanup, the combined approach beats updating the scaffold alone on every test.
arxiv-2605-27476: In their 2026 paper, Hyunmin Cho and colleagues treat attention as a form of memory. They split the pre-softmax matrix into symmetric and skew parts, linking the first to the energy landscape and the second to circulation. Measures of stability drawn from the symmetric part track how well the model balances faithful recall against varied output, and tweaking circulation gives a control knob for it.
arxiv-2605-27676: Ciaran Gilligan-Lee, Joseph Egan, Yuchen Zhu, and Michael O'Riordan identify spurious correlations in fine-tuning from the weights of a naive LoRA tune, without supervision. Their GRASP method projects gradients to stop new reliance on an identified latent factor while preserving pretrained content along it. The method fully removes misalignment in insecure-code tuning, cuts it about fivefold in bad-medical-advice tuning, and more than halves political drift.
arxiv-2605-27776: Elham Matinpour studies free-boundary minimal T-surfaces inside the unit ball, built from one tetrahedral vertex, six faces, and four triple-junction arcs. The flat T-cone itself comes from a conformal minimal immersion, and rigidity criteria hold without matching conformal parametrizations. Every regular surface of this type has index at least n, with equality only for the flat T-cone, which is locally rigid modulo orthogonal transformations.
arxiv-2605-27876: Jian-Tang Lu, Xing-Xing Lu, and Zhi-Tao Wen extend a classic theorem about polynomial zeros to the world of q-differences, where steps multiply rather than add. They define a new q-weight for zeros and a matching q-radical, recovering the classical Stothers-Mason result as q approaches one. The machinery then handles polynomial solutions of q-difference Fermat-type equations.
arxiv-2605-27976: Ye and colleagues benchmark audio-language models on hour-long speech, where current tests use only short clips. VoiceGiraffe poses fifteen hundred curated tasks spanning perception and multi-step reasoning across real scenarios and languages. Models struggled throughout, especially at tracking sparse events over long spans, while humans showed the opposite strength.
arxiv-2605-28276: Onno Eberhard, Claire Vernade, and Michael Muehlebach learn optimal reactive policies where agents see only features, not full states. Their Committed Q-learning sticks to one action per feature until the feature changes, converging almost surely under a weak rewire-robustness assumption. The analysis introduces quasi-Markov environments and weakens prior realizability demands.
arxiv-2605-28376: Qian Wan and five colleagues model how thin disks around Kerr black holes with synchronized scalar hair would look to a telescope. Weak hair leaves images close to the familiar Kerr case, while stronger hair shrinks and warps the photon ring and shadow. In the strongest regime, lensing splits the shadow into separate pieces, adds crescent shapes, and shows chaotic patterns, with near edge-on views producing nested rings.
arxiv-2605-28776: Partha S. Dey and Grigory Terlov derive spread guesses for triangle counts in the linear rich-get-richer attachment model. The final distribution shifts phase from Gaussian to another odd shape, which they map in full. The long-run pattern is governed by the mix between the hidden random setting and the mean-field link effect. Their work also yields a smooth phase shift in the mean number of triads as the growth knob varies.
arxiv-2605-28876: Bowen Qin introduces LogDx-CI, a benchmark comparing 11 log-reduction tools for LLM diagnosis on cases. CI failure logs are large and noisy, and debugging agents need a tool to shrink them. Yet no public comparison of reductions exists. Hybrid grep-plus-tail routers lead on cost and quality, scoring about 0.670 per case with fewer tokens than standalone grep. In agent-loop use the quality range collapses sevenfold, though weak contexts force more calls. A cross-family summary pair beats the same-family pair, falsifying the self-call bias hypothesis.
arxiv-2605-29476: Blai Puchol and three colleagues compare three ways to translate text inside images, a job joining vision and language skills. Modular pipelines first detect and read the text, then translate it with multilingual language models. Multimodal models handle image and words together, while Translatotron-V turns one image straight into a translated image. On parallel multilingual sets with standard scoring measures, modular pipelines beat the end-to-end model, but multimodal models came out on top for flexibility and context.
arxiv-2605-29876: Colton R. Feathers and four colleagues run a Cosmic Dawn model where star birth is tuned to two fluid models and handled by neural nets in halos. Galaxy maps feed forecasts of the 21-cm glow and power spectrum across runs. Stronger second-generation birth deepens Lyman-alpha coupling and leaves a wider, shallower dip, while first-generation stars rule earliest and widest, and halo merger histories drive the switch. The core signal should show in a thousand HERA hours; a miss would point to a long gap between generations.
arxiv-2605-29976: Renu Singh and seven colleagues test two weather-trained models as long-run climate simulators. ArchesWeather gives single forecasts, while ArchesWeatherGen gives spread forecasts from flow matching, letting ensembles gauge uncertainty. Both are refitted as forced air models fed by monthly sea-surface warmth and sea-ice cover, under a shared climate-skill protocol. Forced runs stay stable over decades, hold a steady yearly cycle, and track drift in many climate variables. The models mirror a leading reanalysis climatology, large-scale winds, and year-to-year swings.
arxiv-2605-30076: Yingdong Shi and six colleagues present UniSteer, a text-guided way to steer language models by shaping inner activations. Older tricks use fixed directions or one-off modules, weak on fine-grained ideas and combined demands. UniSteer learns one conditional flow over residual-stream activations from plain-language conditions, then moves and rebuilds a source activation under a target instruction. The same model classifies by picking the label with the lowest rebuild cost. Tests on three models cover behaviour, truthfulness, fine concepts and combined instructions.
arxiv-2605-30276: Evgeny Skvortsov and Richard Van Dongen build the Fefferman-Graham growth and map for self-dual theories of any spin, a step toward self-dual holography. Self-dual theories, UV finite, should have AdS/CFT twins, and higher-spin versions make the twins simpler. Chiral higher-spin gravity stands as the top self-dual theory, twin to part of Chern-Simons matter theories. They find bulk propagators and four-point AdS/CFT links in slimmed Chiral higher-spin gravity, a higher-spin form of self-dual Yang-Mills theory.
arxiv-2605-30376: Haochen Yuan, Yichen Song, Yunbo Wang and Xiaokang Yang introduce Unicorn, a tool for training on many time-series sets. Solo models scale well but miss links across channels, while Linked models are strong but stuck in one size. At Unicorn's core is a codebook of latent prototypes that splits link modeling from channel names. By mapping mixed channels into one shared latent space, Unicorn learns link patterns across fields. Tests show Unicorn beats leading forecasters, most of all in few-shot transfer, pointing to time-series base models.
arxiv-2605-30576: Abouelazm and colleagues make reinforcement learning safer for self-driving cars by guiding exploration with expert advice only when uncertainty runs high. Advice triggers when epistemic or aleatoric uncertainty, gaps in knowledge or noise in the world, crosses thresholds that adapt as the agent gains confidence. A commitment-and-cooldown rule paces guidance so maneuvers stay coherent without draining the advice budget, and expert and agent experience share one replay buffer. In CARLA intersection tests, the method beat its baseline with higher success and fewer failures.
arxiv-2605-30876: Feng and colleagues fix a mismatch in diffusion language models that use expert layers to scale up. Each pass reads many tokens at once, while old expert routing picks experts token by token, so far too many experts fire and memory use balloons. Their dMoE groups token expert votes inside each block into one block vote, then routes by that shared vote. Tests show far fewer experts fire, memory use falls sharply, and almost all of the base score is kept.
arxiv-2605-31076: K. C. and Mishra prove operator-norm bounds for exponential-map parameterizations on se(3). They give an intermediate-growth example. Using the contraction of the SO(3) Jacobian, they show the exponential norm is bounded by one plus the Frobenius norm. They derive a quadratic upper bound for the Lipschitz constant over four. They construct an objective with a quadratic lower bound for radius at least two. These results place se(3) between compact algebras, where the constant stays bounded, and hyperbolic algebras, where it grows exponentially.
arxiv-2605-31176: Stouras and colleagues swap the single retriever in retrieval-augmented generation for a small set picked for the query mix. One retriever and one setting cannot serve short fact questions and long multi-hop reasoning equally well. The authors frame the choice as an expected best-of-k goal and give a build method with near-optimal guarantees. Learned sets beat single retrievers and naive multi-retriever baselines on question-answering tests. Fixed sets also cut delay and token cost compared with tuning settings at run time.
arxiv-2605-31276: Morales and Sheppard learn nitrogen fertiliser response curves for crops with no set form in mind. Their neuro-symbolic regression finds shared symbolic skeletons across management zones. A transformer-based search drives the hunt, and a genetic algorithm fits the skeletons to data. First tested on made-up problems, the method recovers true expressions even when data are scarce. On real winter wheat data it learns distinct curves per zone. It beats quadratic-plateau and exponential models on fit and captures varied behaviour across the field.
arxiv-2605-31376: Schieber and colleagues present LiftNav, a hybrid routing tool for robots in unknown indoor settings. Older TSDF maps support safe planning but lack meaning, while Gaussian Splatting gives rich looks yet soft geometry that limits precise obstacle dodging. LiftNav builds on a dual map joining TSDF and Gaussian Splatting, adding YOLO detectors, lifting via TSDF into 3D, and B-spline path tuning. A hinge-loss crash penalty improves path smoothness and safety. In Replica tests, it achieves a 100 percent success rate with shorter paths than a leading radiance-field baseline.
arxiv-2605-31576: Al-Najjar and team present a two-stage system for joint camera and LiDAR extrinsic calibration. Most methods treat each camera and LiDAR pair alone, ignoring rigid coupling across cameras, so estimates may be accurate yet inconsistent. First, CMRNext runs on each camera to produce initial extrinsic estimates plus dense 2D-3D correspondences. Those predictions are then refined through multi-frame bundle adjustment with reprojection and pose prior terms. Tests on KITTI and Walkley show better accuracy and consistency, with 0.89 cm error on KITTI and a sharp drop on Walkley.
arxiv-2606-00176:
Mishra, Copeland, and Green build a new way to map chance in early cosmos growth. In growth models, wild swings can seed black holes at birth. The chance curve for growth length solves a known spread law. Past routes to that curve were pieced together from parts.

Their route rests on eigenvalues, the core modes of the spread law. They first test it on flat ground with no drift. The route gives back the known curve, with its long tail and mid-range shape. Next they add a steady drift, in tight-well and broad-well forms. Tight wells match the bare case with a trimmed tail. Broad wells need a split build of modes and show a raised peak with a much weaker tail.
arxiv-2606-00376:
Guo, Wu, and Yiu mark a depth past which long thought chains fail at state-track tasks. Such tasks need exact tabs on things as they shift step by step. More thought steps can hurt scores on them, not help. The team trace that drop to hard caps in how watch heads hold state.

Their read bounds state room in bits by head count, head width, and span. Room as a whole is not the tight bind, they find. A fault law with a depth-squared term fits how errs grow. A drift gauge tracks how far a model's state strays. A depth mark, the Deterministic Horizon, sits where sound scores cross half. Tool-aided thought beats plain chains by wide spans on their probe.
arxiv-2606-00476:
Wang asks if chat agents do what they say, or just what they claim to think. Faith in an agent's acts rests on that match. No gold act exists in most fields to check it by. Wang builds a test bed where each call has a known right act.

A Texas poker sim gives that gold frame for the test. The gap is split in two steps for a clean read. Step one checks if a stated call tracks the agent's own thought. Step two checks if the act tracks the stated call. Step two proves firm when calls are read from a clear tag. Free-text reads swell the gap with noise. Step one frays in split ways, not one mode. Rule slips lean to the safe side near all the time.
arxiv-2606-00576:
Yan and co-authors give a mobile arm bot a live scene memory that stays true as rooms shift. Such bots need a scene view that is firm in shape, rich in sense, and cheap to hold. Pre-made maps and still-scene takes go stale when things move. Pose fixes can also knock past reads out of line.

Their frame, DREAM, builds a voxel sense map from depth shots on the fly. A mixed SLAM back end logs those shots in place. A prune tool rewrites past reads when poses are fixed. It keeps the long log bound in size as it works. Hunt for a named thing joins word-led 3D search with sight checks. Real tests in four lab rooms lift long task wins past a kin tool.
arxiv-2606-00676:
Scarlat and co-authors build farm data from space images in this 2026 paper. They use Sentinel-2 satellite images and EuroCrops records, which list what grows in each field. Their pipeline turns mixed field records into matched image and mask pairs that a model can learn from.

The pipeline harmonizes labels, picks images, aligns them in space, and cuts them into patches. It then filters weak patches and balances the crop classes. The result holds 67,337 patches from five European countries, with ten crop classes plus background. A U-Net model trained on ten spectral bands scores 0.7665 mean overlap on the home test split. On new data from Belgium and other sets, scores drop a lot. The authors say the gap shows how hard real shifts in labels and coverage are. Maize and wheat still transfer well.
arxiv-2606-00776:
Mukherjee and co-authors teach models the shape of crystals in this 2026 paper. Fast, sound forecasts of crystal traits drive the hunt for new materials. Graph networks and Transformers read the local setting of atoms well. But they need much labeled data, and labels for crystal traits are scarce.

Their frame, CrysLDNet, pretrains with latent diffusion to ease that lack. A variational autoencoder maps 3D crystal structures into a smooth latent space. The diffusion process then runs inside that space, on large sets of unlabeled crystals. This teaches the encoder rich facts about structure and chemistry before any trait labels are used. The model is then fine-tuned for the trait at hand. On the JARVIS and MP datasets, the authors report gains of 4.26 and 4.90 percent over strong baselines. The learned features also hold up when labels are sparse.
arxiv-2606-01076:
Ferreiro and co-authors cut the cost of run time checks in Prolog in this 2026 paper. Prolog checks types and properties while a program runs, which costs time. Assertions let programmers state rich properties, from plain types to general claims. Abstract interpretation can prove some of them early, at compile time. The rest must still be checked live, or flagged for more work.

Their first move folds run time assertion semantics into an abstract interpreter. The interpreter is multivariant, top down, and goal directed. Their second move exploits the many calling patterns the analysis infers. Each pattern can discharge checks that a single pattern view would leave in place. The work is built into the Ciao system. Performance tests show better results than prior techniques, they report. Fewer live checks mean faster programs with the same safety net. Unproven properties still surface as guidance for testing and refinement.
arxiv-2606-01176:
Sandfelder, Cucuringu, and Dong hand graph networks a small set of motif counts in this 2026 paper. Temporal interaction streams hide signal in short patterns: repeats, replies, star shapes, and three way flows. Plain temporal graph networks often fail to show those patterns to their edge scorers. The structure sits in the data, unused.

On MOOC interaction prediction, a four feature family of past window star counts already takes most of the lift over a strong static baseline. Across many real and synthetic sets, motif activity sorts along three stable axes. They cover dyadic recency and reciprocity, star diversity, and triadic flow. The team builds a compact map of 13 motif coordinates per candidate edge. It is leakage safe and local, and it plugs into any encoder with no architecture change. Tests span link prediction, edge classification, and graph classification. The same features lift scores across all of them, they report.
arxiv-2606-01476:
Zhou and co-authors distill teacher models without access to their logits. On-policy distillation trains a student on its own outputs. A stronger teacher gives dense token-level feedback. Standard versions need the teacher's logits directly. That excludes many capable proprietary models as teachers. Logit signals are also brittle and noisy. They hinge on a narrow overlap of plausible next tokens.

OmniOPD replaces logit matching with chunk-level supervision. Monte Carlo rollouts approximate the teacher's local preferences. A semantic similarity metric scores multi-token chunks. A peak-entropy scheduler audits the student at uncertain forks only. Bayesian priors and a KL anchor bound the variance. Math scores beat standard OPD by up to 28 point 64 percent.
arxiv-2606-01676:
Fraislebem and co-authors study what blocks teams from joining Agile and DevOps. Both aim to ship software faster and with better quality. Agile stresses short cycles and customer response. DevOps stresses automation and smooth operations in production. In practice, joining them hits structural and technical hurdles. The study is qualitative and rests on interviews. Six seasoned professionals from Brazil and Germany took part. Each had deep experience in both fields.

Four groups of challenges emerge from the interviews. Cultural and organizational barriers lead the list. Structural limits and process complexity follow close behind. Technical limits round out the four groups. Four solution domains answer them, from team autonomy to automation and infrastructure. Culture alignment and proactive monitoring stand out as key fixes.
arxiv-2606-01876:
Kang and Oh build a micro-level theory of heat flow in chiral Mott insulators. The thermal Hall effect probes neutral excitations in insulators. A charge gap blocks normal electronic transport there. Phonons can drive a Hall signal as large as spin's. Their role in thermal transport is thus central.

The pair derive the Raman interaction in exact form. Its strength scales with scalar spin chirality. They then show the phonon Hall effect on a kagome lattice. Isotope swaps cause a crossover in transport behavior. That crossover shifts with temperature in their model. A scaling law splits the phonon part from background. The work gives a first full micro derivation.
arxiv-2606-02276:
Tayebi Arasteh and co-authors audit a privacy risk in clinical vision-language models. Such models train on paired chest X-rays and radiology reports. They learn a shared embedding space from those pairs. Instance level links between image and report can persist there. That is a risk when images and reports are shared apart.

A de-identified image might be re-linked to its report. Cosine similarity alone could perform that re-linking. The task is formalized as image-to-report retrieval. Public paired cohorts give ground truth pairings for the audit. Models of increasing clinical specialization are evaluated. The cohorts hold 406,241 paired examples from 126,804 patients. MIMIC-CXR and CheXpert Plus supply the pairs. Linkage risk is measured rather than assumed.
arxiv-2606-02676:
Mackay and co-authors build new diagnostic plots for extreme value regression models. Such models extrapolate far beyond observed data. Convincing checks of fit matter greatly there. Few diagnostics exist for these models. Those that do are hard to read or scale poorly. Most also give one global verdict. Poor fit in one region of the covariate space stays hidden.

Two visual tools are proposed. The standardised tail plot and the normalised residual plot form the pair. Their uncertainty bounds barely depend on sample size. That fact comes from the asymptotic distribution of normalised exceedance probabilities. Global and regional fit can thus be compared fairly, even where sample sizes vary. Summary statistics for both levels are discussed. Two applications show the plots at work. One compares thousands of candidate models. The other yields actionable findings for model design.
arxiv-2606-02776:
Neplenbroek and co-authors test what really drives uneven advice from language models. In high-stakes settings like legal, medical, and financial advice, one conversation history can shift outcomes between users. Past work showed disparities between sociodemographic groups. The team asks whether models infer group membership from a single conversation. They find models actually struggle at that inference. Group disparities exist, but they are minimal in size.

The stronger driver is conversation topic. Topics are compared against a range of linguistic features, including emotions and readability. Topics predict the advice a model gives better than the rest. They act, in part, as proxies for sociodemographic groups. Their effects on advice are often unpredictable. The authors flag this as a concern for high-stakes deployment. Future work must map how conversational context steers model outputs.
arxiv-2606-02976:
Qin and co-authors build a memory system for long dialogue that tracks changing user preferences. A dialogue system must decide when to consult memory and which past turns matter. Past methods use heuristic retrieval signals or keep memory always on. Both fail when preferences shift or contradict themselves over time.

The team frames retrieval as evidence about a user's latent preference state, not as surface similarity. Each past turn is scored by a Bayes factor: how much it raises the model's likelihood of the reference response when added to context. That score gives one unified signal for both access and selection. The model learns to pick salient turns and to regulate memory use by expected utility. Tests on four heterogeneous memory benchmarks show gains over embedding-based retrieval on long, preference-heavy tasks. The method stays competitive where preferences are sparse and simple similarity suffices.
arxiv-2606-03076: Suzuki studies optimal constants and extremizers for smoothing estimates tied to quantum harmonic oscillators. Smoothing estimates bound how solutions spread over time. Knowing the best possible constant, and which functions attain it, sharpens such bounds. Suzuki establishes harmonic oscillator versions of known free-particle results. Those results are due to Simon, and to Bez and Sugimoto, and to Bez and co-authors. The paper thus carries a line of sharp analysis from free particles over to the oscillator setting, where the confining potential changes the picture.
arxiv-2606-03476:
Huang and co-authors transfer human motion onto humanoid robots without paired training data. Retargeting matters for teleoperation, imitation learning, and human-robot contact. Bodies differ in skeleton shape, limb proportions, and joint counts. Paired examples of the same motion on both bodies are scarce. Their framework, Human2Humanoid, works in that unpaired setting.

A CycleGAN design carries the transfer between domains. A skeleton-aware graph network reads features that depend on body topology. A special loss aligns end-effector paths after scale is factored out. That keeps the sense of a motion across very different bodies. Physics-based limits push the output to copy the source's contact patterns. Tests send human motion to a Unitree G1 humanoid robot. The method beats prior work on later controllability and on physical feasibility. Robotics teams get a path to reuse human motion libraries at scale.
arxiv-2606-04076:
Shenghan Luo leads a team that presents SkySense in 2026, a system for locating drones from radio channel fingerprints in sensing-and-communication networks. Labeled examples are scarce, and reflections off buildings make the radio signature of a position ambiguous.

SkySense first learns from long unlabeled flight recordings, using the smoothness of flight paths to build stable features. A generative model then maps those features to coordinates, fine-tuned with only one percent labeled data, and predictions from several base stations are fused. Because the generative model represents a spread of possible positions instead of one average guess, it avoids a common collapse error. On real measurements, mean error fell to under ten centimeters, beating fully supervised rivals.
arxiv-2606-04176:
Jiayi Wang and Raymond Wong study in 2026 how to complete a matrix whose entries are not numbers but whole probability distributions, as when each cell summarizes many repeated measurements. Only some entries are observed, and even those only through finite samples.

To exploit hidden simplicity, they embed each distribution as a point in a kernel space and define a Tucker-style rank for such distribution-valued arrays. New unfolding operators connect that rank to the classical tensor rank, making the theory workable. Their estimator comes with finite-sample error bounds describing its accuracy. Tests on synthetic data and a real application showed the method recovering the unobserved distributions effectively, opening a path for data types that ordinary matrix completion cannot touch.
arxiv-2606-04276:
Hongseok Namkoong quantifies in 2026 the value of structural knowledge, the restrictions a modeler builds into a model before seeing any data. His yardstick is local sensitivity: how much an estimate can move, to first order, when the underlying distribution is nudged by moving probability mass.

Working in the geometry of optimal transport, he shows this sensitivity equals the size of the efficient influence function's gradient. Restricting which transports are allowed shrinks the sensitivity, and that shrinkage is exactly the value of the modeler's assumptions. The framework resolves a standing puzzle in causal inference: efficiency bounds look identical whether or not treatment probabilities are known, yet practice differs greatly. Known propensities, he shows, cut sensitivity to misspecification.
arxiv-2606-04876:
Tajjar, Pfefferle, Purucker, and Hutter teach a tabular foundation model to read text columns without crushing them first, in a 2026 arXiv paper. TabPFN performs strongly on numerical and categorical tables but does not natively handle high-cardinality text features. The standard pipeline embeds text with a language model and compresses the vectors with PCA into a few scalar features. End-to-end alternatives avoid PCA but need large text-cell pretraining corpora and usually underperform pretrained models.

The authors introduce a text adapter projecting text into the tabular model's token space instead. They freeze both the sentence encoder and TabPFN and train only the lightweight adapter, which maps text embeddings into a short token sequence in TabPFN's embedding space. The design removes the PCA bottleneck, preserves TabPFN's numerical strengths, and trains far more cheaply than end-to-end text-tabular pipelines.
arxiv-2606-04976:
Bandyopadhyay and Ashokan map when a periodically driven quantum spin chain remembers its past and when it heats into forgetfulness, in a 2026 arXiv condensed matter paper. Driven, disordered, interacting systems host competing regimes: Floquet many-body localization, and thermalization. Starting from a product state, the authors track entanglement entropy and energy absorption while varying interaction, fields, disorder strength, and driving frequency.

They find distinct behaviors: fast delocalization in some regions, logarithmic entanglement growth and long-lasting initial-state memory in localized or prethermal Floquet regimes elsewhere. Strong disorder arrests transport and slows entanglement dynamics, while strong driving frequency arrests energy absorption and creates a long-lived state. Conversely, weak disorder or low frequency leads to delocalization and heating. The outcomes support non-equilibrium phases in driven many-body systems and delineate their boundaries.
arxiv-2606-05276:
Hannah Banks, Marius Kongsore, and Neal Weiner introduce big axions in this 2026 arXiv paper, a class of axion models built from symmetry networks. Axions are proposed to solve the strong CP problem of quantum chromodynamics and to serve as dark matter. Keeping an axion's symmetry clean is notoriously difficult, and simple versions clash with cosmological limits on strings and domain walls.

In a big axion, the Nambu-Goldstone mode emerges from the collective breaking of a network of U(1) symmetries across theory space, not from one symmetry alone. The construction realizes high-quality accidental symmetries and admits both pre-inflationary and post-inflationary histories. Its topological structures interpolate between Peccei-Quinn axions and axions from extra-dimensional gauge fields. The authors identify a minimal viable subclass, little big axions. They give a robust solution to the strong CP problem while accounting for some or all of the dark matter.
arxiv-2606-05376:
Jingyao Wu and colleagues teach language models to learn from annotator disagreement rather than discard it, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Human-centered tasks like natural language inference and emotion recognition admit plausible readings, so annotators often disagree. Standard alignment collapses their judgments into one gold label, treating the disagreement as noise.

The team's SHALA-LLM framework treats ambiguity as information. SHALA-LLM is a reinforcement learning method that trains the model on the distribution of annotator labels while prioritizing the ambiguous samples during optimization. On ambiguity-sensitive benchmarks including ChaosNLI, GoEmotions, and MSP-Podcast, it improved agreement with the label distributions, cutting the Jensen-Shannon distance on ChaosNLI by up to 62.1 percent. It also improved classification F1 scores by 16.7 percent, evidence that modeling disagreement does not trade accuracy away but can strengthen it. The authors argue this matters wherever models must spot contested inputs and preserve variability.
arxiv-2606-05476:
Andrew Hamara and colleagues present SHIELDS in this 2026 arXiv paper, a multi-agent system that hardens operating systems. Existing automation helps, but it relies on pre-written corrective actions that cannot adapt when a fix fails or a system differs from expectations.

SHIELDS instead treats hardening as an iterative, feedback-driven loop. Language-model agents propose fixes, apply them to the target system, read the results of validation scans, and refine their approach, much as a human administrator would. The team evaluated the system across machine configurations using six language models ranging from 20 billion to 400 billion parameters. SHIELDS remediated 73 percent of scan findings. Notably, success depended less on raw model size than on effective tool use and information gathering. That suggests capable hardening agents can run on smaller, locally hosted models, an advantage where compute is limited or security policy forbids sending system data to outside services.
arxiv-2606-06276:
Niccolò Giacomini builds algebraic structure on spaces of sheaves over a curve in this 2026 arXiv paper on algebraic geometry. A Quot space catalogs all the ways a fixed sheaf, a bundle of algebraic data over the curve, can be mapped onto smaller pieces. Hall algebras, built from the cohomology of moduli stacks, act like symmetry algebras for such catalogs. The question is whether that action can be made categorical, lifting numbers to structured operations.

Giacomini constructs a two sided categorical action of the Hall algebra of semistable sheaves of one fixed slope. The action lives on the derived category of certain Quot spaces taken inside tilted hearts, a reshaped version of the sheaf category. Correspondence stacks that parametrize extensions of quotients by semistable sheaves induce the operations. Along the way he compares Quot spaces with Bradlow pairs and stable pairs, aligning three moduli problems that the action must respect.
arxiv-2606-06376:
Fabian Gittins and co-authors ask whether a future gravitational wave detector can hear neutron stars ring in this 2026 arXiv paper. As two neutron stars spiral together, tides raise a swelling frequency that can resonantly excite the stars' own vibration modes. Those modes carry news of the stellar interior, like seismology on Earth. Whether any instrument can actually measure them was an open question.

The team simulated one year of observations for the planned Einstein Telescope and ran full Bayesian analysis on the two hundred loudest mergers. The detector could pick out resonant modes in favorable events, sensing phase shifts as small as zero point zero three radians. Resonance frequencies near five thousand three hundred hertz fall within reach. Ignoring the resonances biased the inferred tidal deformabilities, the standard measure of how easily each star deforms, so modelers must include them.
arxiv-2606-06476:
Chenming Zhu and co-authors give vision language models an imagination in this 2026 arXiv paper. Models reason well about what a photo shows but poorly about space: unobserved layouts and other viewpoints. The authors call the fix thinking with imagination. Their framework, Astra, lets the model ask a world simulator for imagined views from new camera positions while it reasons, then use those views as evidence.

Astra pairs a policy model, trained with reinforcement learning, with a simulator tuned for consistency across viewpoints. A two phase curriculum teaches the policy to call the simulator only when imagined views actually help. Experiments showed both halves are necessary. The simulator alone lifted a strong commercial model on a spatial benchmark from about forty five percent, and the full system did better still. Useful imagination, the lesson goes, is a learned skill: knowing when to picture a scene.
arxiv-2606-06576:
Edward T Stevenson and co-authors predict whole climate maps from a handful of examples in this 2026 arXiv paper. Scientists often must regress high dimensional outputs, like temperature and wind at every point of a planet, from very few training runs. Gaussian processes shine with little data but choke on huge outputs, while the usual compress then predict pipeline uses bases tuned for reconstruction, not prediction. Their model instead decodes each output from a low dimensional latent state governed by a Gaussian process.

By integrating out the decoder weights analytically, compression and prediction are optimized as one objective that scales to high dimensional outputs. The demonstration is striking: the first spatially resolved emulator of global climate models for rocky exoplanets. Such emulators let researchers explore alien climates, pressure level by pressure level, without paying for a full physics simulation each time, and with calibrated uncertainty on every predicted map field.
arxiv-2606-06676:
Density functional theory is the workhorse that makes quantum chemistry computable, replacing a system's full wave description with a few simpler variables. Wang, Liebert, Penz, and Schilling show that this theory is one member of a large family in this 2026 arXiv paper. They build a single framework covering the many variants that use other reduced variables, such as spin or current, in place of plain particle density.

The framework needs only two ingredients. The first is a chosen set of basic observables, whose average values become the reduced variables. The second is a fixed piece of the energy operator, shared by the class of systems. With just that structure, they define the universal energy functions, prove them convex and smooth, settle when target variables can occur, and prove a Hohenberg-Kohn style uniqueness result. Variants whose observables form a Lie algebra get special emphasis, tying the theory to symplectic geometry.
arxiv-2606-06776:
In pay as you go services, unhappy customers rarely announce they are leaving; they just stop showing up. Mufti, Hammad, Saleh, and Gull build a churn prediction system for that setting in this 2026 arXiv paper, published in Decision Support Systems. Their design watches behavior in rolling thirty day windows, then judges churn over the following thirty days, keeping evidence and outcome cleanly separated in time.

Tested on a large real world data set, a feature based model reached accuracy near eighty eight percent, with a strong ranking score. A sequence based model did even better at spotting leavers. It caught up to ninety six percent of true churners by reading the order of actions. On later unseen data, accuracy stayed above eighty three percent with no retraining, which the authors credit to the time aware framing. Explanation tools also flagged which behaviors drive the risk.
arxiv-2606-06976:
Tool using agents fail in two mirror ways: calling tools needlessly, or inventing answers instead. Zhou and co-authors trace both failures to muddled uncertainty in this 2026 arXiv paper. During ordinary reinforcement learning, correct and wrong actions grow equally confident. Overconfident mistakes then poison later steps of a task.

Their framework, TRUST, puts uncertainty inside the reward itself. It acts as a repulsive force that keeps right and wrong actions apart in confidence. Lightweight annotations mark the key turns in each trajectory. Turn level calibration and whole task success train together. Benchmarks covered several tool use suites, including When2Call and ToolSandbox. TRUST improved decision quality and overall task performance across them. Uncertainty estimates stayed more trustworthy during training. No extra cost appears at inference time. The lesson: an agent should know when it does not know, and rewards can teach that.
arxiv-2606-07076:
Knowing a load's total power is not the same as knowing where that energy goes inside it. Montoya, de Leon, Arrabal-Campos, and Alcayde build a branch level accounting in this 2026 arXiv paper. It is a companion to their work on identifying three phase loads from terminal data. The question shifts from fitting the load to locating its energy.

Terminal power splits uniquely into heat loss and stored energy changes. The split runs branch by branch inside any chosen equivalent circuit. Three theorems organize the picture. One guarantees the decomposition is unique for a fixed circuit shape. Another warns that rival shapes fit the same data while localizing energy differently. The third unifies classic electrical dualities under one time domain principle. Six test cases exercise the framework, including a famous open phase paradox. Classical power theories, the authors argue, answer different questions rather than contradicting this one.
arxiv-2606-07276:
Wüthrich examines a fairness-like property of insurance pricing models in this 2026 arXiv note on the balance property. The property requires that total premiums predicted by a fitted model equal total observed losses in the fitting data. It sounds basic, yet many modern pricing models built on generalized linear models, a standard family for insurance, violate it unless the model uses a special canonical link. Actuaries then apply corrections to restore balance.

Two established corrections either shift the model's intercept later or refit under a wrong distribution. Wüthrich instead fits the model under a side constraint that enforces balance during fitting, and by long-run prediction accuracy this beats both corrections. He also links constrained fitting to ex-post risk sharing, where pool members settle actual losses later: each member is charged for estimated systematic effects while the unpredictable remainder is shared.
arxiv-2606-07376:
Yun, Kyaw, and Bae construct quantum circuits that perform general measurements, an operation quantum hardware often lacks natively, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A general measurement, formalized as a positive-operator-valued measure, extracts more information than qubit readout and underpins tasks like telling quantum states apart. Their construction follows the Naimark extension, embedding the measurement in a larger system using gates, with single-qubit parameters tuned by a classical optimizer to approximate the target.

They then relax that design with quantum neural network circuits, parameterized circuits trained like neural networks, and a hybrid combining both ideas. The constructions were compared on state discrimination strategies, including minimum-error and maximum-confidence measurements. The neural network circuits reached near-optimal results efficiently, needing fewer training iterations in tests. Shallow network circuits performed well. The results suggest trainable circuits are a practical route to implementing measurements on quantum hardware with limited gate budgets.
arxiv-2606-07476:
Heng, Zhang, Cooper, and Li estimate joint motion from muscle signals even when some muscles cannot be measured, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Surface electromyography records muscle activity through electrodes and drives prosthetics and rehabilitation devices. Anatomy and sensor limits mean only a subset of muscles is observable. Their musculoskeletal neural network couples a convolutional activation estimator with an embedded dynamics model of the body, forming a system trained end to end without labels for forces or torques.

A composite loss blends joint-angle accuracy with a muscle synergy term and an anatomy-guided trend term drawn from physiology. Tests on 2-degree-of-freedom wrist motion covered 3 rhythmic movements and 1 random movement. The method beat recurrent and hybrid baselines on error and fit, especially for the random motion in their comparisons. Its parameters stayed within body limits, and its inferred activation for an excluded muscle tracked that muscle's recorded signal.
arxiv-2606-07576:
Shah and Kartik build a verification layer that tells autonomous AI scientists when to keep experimenting, when a question is settled, and when to refuse an answer, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their system, Cartograph, steers experiments toward unresolved parts of the hypothesis space, closes ambiguity outright. It also detects when the hypothesis library itself cannot explain the data, triggering refusal instead of a forced conclusion. The steering rule is derived under a linear-Gaussian model. Classical experiment-design criteria arise as special cases.

Across 5 testbeds the steering rule dominated naive guessing in a cascade experiment, winning over 100 comparisons. The system identified 3 out-of-library drug-metabolism mechanisms, then revoked those identifications when residuals exposed structural misfit, while a perturbed in-library control stayed identified. Auditing 40 published claims from an autonomous materials laboratory, the refusal guard flagged all 4 claims later judged inconclusive while passing most confirmed ones.
arxiv-2606-07676:
Boyd and co-authors present SCXM, a method for guessing where a single cell sat inside tissue using only its gene activity, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Spatial transcriptomics, which maps gene activity in place, covers few genes at fine scale, while single-cell RNA sequencing reads the whole set of active genes but destroys the tissue layout. Paired examples of both are rare, so the team learns from unpaired data.

Their approach fine-tunes a single-cell foundation model with adversarial training, a setup where a second network tries to catch errors, so the model learns to translate between the two data types. Tested on three curated datasets, SCXM beat earlier methods built for translation between measurement types on every set. The authors also show that some gene pathways carry stronger clues about a cell's former neighbourhood than others, which helps explain where the translation works best.
arxiv-2606-07776:
Han-Bing Liu, Xing, and Luo calculate how often B mesons should decay into ordinary baryons plus invisible dark particles, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The setting is B-mesogenesis, a theory that tries to explain two mysteries at once: why the universe holds more matter than antimatter, and what dark matter is. Its decays create both the matter excess and dark baryons that escape detectors unseen.

Using perturbative QCD, the standard calculational method for strong-force processes, plus flavour-symmetry relations between channels, the team works out form factors and branching ratios. The rates come out sizable, around one in a hundred thousand decays for the best channels. In the Type-I scenario the standouts are the neutral B meson decaying to a Lambda baryon plus a dark particle, and its strange cousin decaying to a Xi baryon. Such rates put the processes within reach of colliders and B factories.
arxiv-2606-07876:
Chan, Cionca, and Van De Ville design optimal filters for cleaning signals that live on directed graphs, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Graph signal processing handles data attached to network nodes, from sensor readings to temperatures across a region. Denoising such data with a Wiener filter, the classic least-squares optimal filter, is well understood for undirected graphs, but direction changes the mathematics.

Real observations mix two noises: structured noise shaped by the directed graph itself, and additive measurement error from sensors. The authors build a framework handling both together. Under several stationarity assumptions, combining uncorrelated and correlated noise, they derive the optimal filters in closed form. A proof of concept on a temperature graph shows the method on real-structured data. The paper is short but closes a specific gap: directed graphs model flows and influence naturally, and their denoising no longer borrows theory built for symmetric networks.
arxiv-2606-08076:
Esra Dönmez and Agnieszka Falenska read AI persuasion through a philosopher's lens, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Jürgen Habermas's theory of communicative action distinguishes what speakers do with words beyond conveying facts: building trust, signalling similarity, claiming sincerity. These are illocutionary intents, the social functions of an utterance. The authors ask whether language models deploy them the way persuasive humans do.

They simulated discussions from the ChangeMyView forum, where posters reward arguments that changed their view. All three models tested expressed illocutionary intent effectively, often more strongly than human writers. Models also crafted flattering replies aligned with the holder's own intent, a strategy strongly associated with changing opinions. Crowd workers found the model arguments more agreeable than human ones and preferred them. The findings suggest persuasive power comes not only from argument quality: training on human preferences teaches models to perform agreement and rapport, which itself persuades.
arxiv-2606-08176:
Misselbeck-Wessel proves representation theorems for a generalization of Boolean algebra in this 2026 arXiv paper. Boolean algebras, the algebra of true and false values and of sets with complement, can be represented as collections of sets through the classical Stone representation theorem. Swap algebras widen this picture, following Bishop's constructive mathematics, where proofs must give explicit constructions. Every Boolean algebra is a swap algebra, so results here cover the classical case.

Working constructively, the author proves a Stone representation theorem for separated swap algebras of a specified type, together with a Stone-Čech theorem for the same class. The second result shows that restricting to separated algebras loses nothing for the theory of swap characters. A useful device, the set with a Boolean inequality, tracks where a proof uses the principle that anything follows from a falsehood.
arxiv-2606-08376:
Leihan Zhang and colleagues build a large dataset of real-world artificial intelligence failures from news reports, in this 2026 arXiv paper. As these systems spread into socially important domains, reports of harms and failures have grown more common and more varied. Governance frameworks state high-level principles for responsible use, but data resources for tracking incidents remain limited. Existing collections are often manually curated, small, and unsuited to continuous monitoring. RiskNet aims to supply that missing resource at scale.

RiskNet is built from large-scale news sources in many languages through a structured pipeline. It finds risk news, screens reports at the event level, merges reports of the same incident into single records, and sorts each incident across many dimensions. The result organizes scattered reporting into one dataset that researchers and regulators can analyze over time. The authors position the resource as a base for evidence-based governance work.
arxiv-2606-08576:
Hwa-Long Gau, Hong, Chi-Kwong Li, and Kuo-Zhong Wang study the numerical radius of certain block matrices in this 2026 arXiv paper. The numerical range of a matrix collects all values obtained by sandwiching it between a unit vector and itself. The numerical radius is the largest magnitude in that range, much like the operator norm but often strictly smaller. The matrices here have a special two-by-two block form: a block A, a block B beside it, and zeros below.

The authors show the numerical range of such a matrix is the union of the numerical ranges of a family of ordinary two-by-two matrices, reducing a hard-looking problem to a tractable one. When A is a self-adjoint involution, a symmetry of order two, they characterize when the numerical range is an elliptical disk.
arxiv-2606-08676:
Shi Ying Chang and colleagues measure what instruction tuning costs coding assistants, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Developers interact with code in two distinct modes. In flow mode they write code continuously and need tools that complete unfinished programs. In command mode they express intent in natural language and need tools that convert instructions into code. Instruction-tuned language models dominate the second mode, but whether the same paradigm suits both was unclear. The authors investigate this instruction-tuning tax across code tasks.

Their study compares model behavior across the two interaction modes to find where following instructions verbatim erodes the fluid completion ability that flow mode demands. An assistant over-trained to obey commands may hesitate or over-explain when the developer simply wanted the next line.
arxiv-2606-08876:
Hegyi presents a volunteer-built web platform making Romania's public elevation data easy to explore in a browser, in this 2026 arXiv paper. LiDAR surveys measure terrain height with laser pulses from aircraft, producing digital terrain models prized for landscape research, planning, and archaeology. In practice the data sit fragmented across sources and need specialist software, which blocks reuse. RO-LiDAR GeoQuickView acts as an accessibility layer on top of the public data.

The platform publishes hillshade visualizations, shaded relief images revealing slopes and channels, plus a spatial index for downloading the rasters. Its sharpest layer is a half-meter terrain model covering four counties, Caraş-Severin, Gorj, Mehedinţi, and Dolj, from the LAKI III survey's Zone A. Four Zone B counties follow next, once their products pass the same quality-control workflow. Hegyi stresses the platform supports quick discovery and interpretation, not official modelling or field verification.
arxiv-2606-08976:
Jing Wang and colleagues build a benchmark that exposes how far language models still are from real hardware design work, in this 2026 arXiv paper. RTL, register-transfer level code such as Verilog, is how chips are specified. Existing benchmarks use small designs, and frontier models already saturate them. Scaling up is hard because grading needs specifications and testbenches, which real designs rarely provide. RTL-BenchLS contains over 10,000 formally verified Verilog designs, far larger than earlier ones.

Beyond code generation, the benchmark adds three tasks. Round-trip reasoning asks a model to move between code and description. Masked-content reasoning hides part of a design to reconstruct. Repository-issue reasoning requires fixing bugs. All are graded by formal equivalence checking, no testbenches needed. Of 8 leading models, even the best reached only about 23 percent on round-trip reasoning, 28 percent on masked content, and 12 percent on issue fixing, leaving room for progress.
arxiv-2606-09376:
Juan Santillana argues that common faithfulness scores for generated text reward saying almost nothing, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Such scores check each claim a model states against known facts, a measure called precision. A cautious model can therefore score near perfectly by omitting most relevant facts. Santillana pairs precision with coverage, the share of relevant facts a model actually mentions.

His testbed is Formula 1 strategy, where complete telemetry makes the full set of relevant facts for each decision knowable in advance. The benchmark holds more than seven thousand decision cases from one hundred fifty-seven races, in English, Spanish, and Portuguese. The most precise frontier model covered under half of the relevant facts and ranked last once coverage counted. Small fine-tuned models, by contrast, reached coverage scores near ninety-eight percent on the held-out season. A second test on weather forecasts showed the same pattern.
arxiv-2606-09476:
Carlos Vélez García, Miguel Cazorla, and Jorge Pomares argue that robot goals should be sets, not single states, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Offline goal-conditioned learning trains robots from recorded trajectories, and its key trick, hindsight relabelling, reuses states a robot actually reached as goals for earlier moments. Standard versions demand reproducing the entire reached state, including details the task does not care about.

Their method, Goal-Set Hindsight Relabeling, observes that a reached state certifies every goal set containing it. A binary query marks which state variables define success, such as a cube's position, while the rest count as nuisance variables. The goal predicate becomes an input at inference time, so one trained checkpoint can answer many different goal questions without retraining. Across OGBench tasks and five offline goal-conditioned learners, the approach improved performance exactly where full-state goals were bottlenecked by nuisance dimensions.
arxiv-2606-09776:
Igor Petrashkevich and his co-authors map the ices around six newborn stars in the Orion A cloud in this 2026 arXiv paper. Class 0 protostars are the youngest stars, still wrapped in cold envelopes. Much of their volatile stock sits as ice on dust grains. Webb telescope spectra let the team chart that ice pixel by pixel, at a grain near one hundred astronomical units.

The maps cover water, carbon monoxide and dioxide, and rarer fare like formaldehyde. Fits to lab ice samples gave the amounts per spot. Checks with light-transfer models backed those amounts. Ice shares swung a lot from place to place, shaped by heat and outflows from the young stars. The full mix matched astrochemical models and spans about ninety percent of the seen stock. That fit says most ice formed before the stars lit, then passed into their envelopes.
arxiv-2606-09876:
Chongzhe Zhang and his co-authors curb a language model's cocky wrong answers without muting its sound ones in this 2026 arXiv paper. Models often state high confidence in replies that are false. Blanket fixes push all confidence down, which dulls trust in the right replies too. Their method steps in only where a probe smells a wrong-but-sure answer.

A frozen probe reads the model's inner state mid-run. When it flags risk, set attention heads have their outputs rescaled as the confidence word is formed. On a Qwen model doing maths with a yes-no confidence field, one cut-in point flipped eighty-two percent of wrong yes calls to no. A wider cut-in slashed calibration error from near twenty-two percent to near nine. Just five percent of sound yes calls were harmed.
arxiv-2606-10176:
Kravitz answers a clean question about an object from algebra that encodes graph colorings, in a 2026 arXiv paper on combinatorics. The chromatic symmetric function of a graph, introduced by Stanley in 1995, sums over all proper vertex colorings and refines the older chromatic polynomial. Expanding it in the elementary symmetric basis gives coefficients indexed by partitions, lists of whole numbers summing to the vertex count. Some coefficients can be negative for some graphs, and the missed problem is which partitions can ever appear negatively.

He proves the partitions that always appear with nonnegative coefficients, for every finite graph, are exactly the hook partitions, whose diagrams have a single row joined to a single column. Every non-hook partition admits some graph whose expansion gives it a negative coefficient. The characterization is exact and complete, not merely a sufficient condition.
arxiv-2606-10276:
Lee and colleagues build a robot that reads human gestures and gaze, not just spoken commands, in a 2026 arXiv paper on human-robot interaction. Natural interaction requires understanding intent expressed nonverbally, yet current robot policies use language as the sole interface, placing the full communication burden on the person. Their framework, EDITH, streams the human's first-person view and gaze from smart glasses alongside speech to the robot in real time.

A hierarchical policy handles these rich but noisy inputs: a high-level policy infers intent and produces subtasks. Each subtask is a fine-grained instruction paired with a keyframe grounding the intent in the scene, like the frame where the human points at the target object. In experiments on interactive tasks, EDITH let the robot act on nonverbal signals even when intent was expressed only briefly, and significantly reduced the communication burden compared with language-only control.
arxiv-2606-10976:
Lu and colleagues find a thermometer for a famous crossover in this 2026 arXiv paper. In the two-dimensional Hubbard model, the insulating ground state shifts character as repulsion grows: Slater-type, driven by Fermi-surface nesting, at weak coupling; Mott-type, ruled by spin superexchange, at strong coupling. Where one becomes the other has been hard to pin down.

The proposed marker is the sign of how double occupancy changes with temperature near zero: positive in the Slater regime, negative in the Mott regime, a Pomeranchuk-style anomaly. Exact diagonalization and quantum Monte Carlo place the boundary at a coupling of 4.0 for the half-filled model. A peak in the antiferromagnetic correlation length gives the same line.
arxiv-2606-11276:
Franco and eight co-authors propose a new way to grade human genome assemblies in a 2026 arXiv paper. Judging assembly accuracy inside highly repetitive regions such as centromeres, the dense centers of chromosomes, remains a major challenge. Conventional benchmarking relies on sequence alignment, which breaks down where DNA is highly uniform yet divergent. Their framework reframes evaluation as a problem of comparing distributions.

Using a compact centeny form, they compute genomic distances between functional motifs rather than matching raw sequence directly. A metric based on KL divergence measures agreement between a query and a target through their centromeric inter-motif gaps. Applied genome-wide to available human telomere-to-telomere genomes, the method yields a quality ranking for each assembly and chromosome. The authors present it as a rapid, robust scoring system and a standard of integrity in such regions, enabling chromosome-level comparison.
arxiv-2606-11476:
Hu, Behbahani, Moon, Dogan, and Eisty mine GitHub discussions for project bottlenecks in a 2026 arXiv paper. Software teams coordinate work and settle decisions in issue threads, yet repo health tools focus on code metrics and ignore how people talk. Their SentTrack framework detects socio-technical bottlenecks from issue discussions, applied to the AvaloniaUI repository across roughly nine thousand threads.

A horizontal pipeline summarizes raw issues with a large language model, extracts concern phrases, and clusters them into 613 semantic clusters from the first 3,608 issues. A vertical pipeline sorts each comment under a collaboration framework and infers thread outcomes. Across the full corpus, 49 percent of threads ended in stagnation and only 13 percent reached resolution, making the resolution gap the main bottleneck signal. A weighted scoring engine combines negativity, stagnation, resolution gap, and thread length into a readable priority tool, flagging high-friction discussions before they stall development.
arxiv-2606-11676:
Maksym Zhenirovskyy and four colleagues forecast wildfire spread with a hybrid model in this 2026 arXiv paper. Traditional fire models use rigid, low-dimensional settings and static fuel maps, and often underpredict how far fires run. The team's design keeps a probabilistic cellular automaton, a grid where each cell's burning odds depend on its neighbours, but lets a neural network set the odds locally.

A multi-scale convolutional network generates parameters that vary by place, governing spread probability, wind alignment and slope effects. The physical grid keeps the model interpretable. An implementation in JAX, a fast computing library, allows gradient-based calibration. Tested on six large wildfires in the western United States, the model keeps its overlap score above the stated threshold across seventy-two-hour forecasts, after fitting to ten days of observed fire edges. The authors note it can capture burning beyond standard vegetation masks.
arxiv-2606-11976:
Akeela Darryl Fattha and three colleagues ask how AI coding agents should explore a repository in this 2026 arXiv paper. Before fixing a bug, an agent must localise the files to change. Most agents explore linearly, one directory or file per step, which the authors suspect mismatches fixes spanning several subsystems.

Using the SWE-bench Pro benchmark, they compare linear exploration against domain-scoped parallel agents, each searching one subsystem. A small, cheap model spawning domain agents achieves the best localisation score among models of its class. It ranks second overall on their expanded benchmark, behind only a much larger commercial system. On the older curated benchmark a bigger plain model scores higher precision by predicting few files, but misses more of the true change set. Three side findings stand out: documentation that must evolve with code defeats every approach, and forced consultation between agents adds cost without benefit.
arxiv-2606-12376:
Pearce-Crump gets halfway up a conjectured mountain in the theory of the zeta function, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The Riemann zeta function encodes the primes, and its nontrivial zeros are points where it vanishes. Nathan Ng conjectured an average for a ratio built from the zeta function at twice each zero, divided by its slope there. Summed over zeros up to height T, the squared magnitudes should grow like T over two pi. The guess assumes the Riemann Hypothesis and that all zeros are simple.

Working under those same assumptions, Pearce-Crump proves a lower bound of half the conjectured size. The second moment is at least a fixed fraction of the predicted main term, not growing somehow. The argument uses a residue form of the sum that stays meaningful even if some zeros repeat. Half the mountain is a base camp for the number theory of zeta ratios.
arxiv-2606-12576: A 2026 arXiv entry, this research manuscript advances a new study. The title points to Helping Figures Tell their Story! Paper-Grounded Video Generation Explaining Complex Scientific Figures as its subject. That places it in science and technology: careful study of how the natural and built world works. The work reported here becomes part of the open literature.
arxiv-2606-12676:
Alpay and Basaran build a logic of separation for families of convex bodies, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A convex body is a shape with no dents; two groups are apart when their convex hulls, the smallest convex shapes containing them, do not overlap. Recording only which groups are apart gives a structure called a separoid. Taking apartness as the basic relation of a formal language, they ask what it can represent, prove, and compute.

Three laws, symmetry, subsumption, and vacuity, characterise them completely. Every abstract apartness pattern can be realised by rational polytopes, shapes with flat faces and rational coordinates, with a safety margin of at least 2 per separation, so small wobbles change nothing. Satisfiability is NP-complete and validity is coNP-complete, while positive entailment is decidable in linear time. A conservativity result shows richer Boolean reasoning never forces a new apartness beyond simple closure.
arxiv-2606-12776:
Ding and Li present a proof, generated with AI help, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The proof shows that no algorithm can decide whether polynomial equations over the Gaussian integers have solutions when 18 unknowns are allowed. The Gaussian integers are complex numbers whose real and imaginary parts are both whole numbers. The question is a form of Hilbert's tenth problem, which asks for a decision procedure for Diophantine equations and cannot be solved over the ordinary integers.

Matiyasevich and Sun had shown undecidability over the Gaussian integers with 20 unknowns. The proof follows their framework, joining a test for rational integers inside the Gaussian integers with a rationality criterion, but saves 2 variables. A clearing-denominator variable is avoided by using 2 integer conditions instead, and the nonzero condition is folded into a combining lemma through a one-variable gadget. The result sharpens the boundary for how few variables make the problem impossible.
arxiv-2606-12876:
Babaoglu and colleagues propose Drop-by-Drop, a multi-bitwidth post-training quantisation framework that lets 1 trained language model run at several precision levels without retraining, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Keeping a quantised variant for each platform is costly in storage and upkeep.

The method is grounded in information theory and successive refinement. Because model weights are near-Gaussian, they can be reconstructed with increasing fidelity as additional bits are incorporated. The reconstruction uses a weighted mean-squared-error distortion motivated by the model's loss. In practice, Drop-by-Drop adds Matryoshka-style supervision to the training loss and exploits additive codebooks, so ordered subsets of codebooks yield partial reconstructions at each precision level. The authors report competitive perplexity and accuracy across architectures including Qwen, LLaMA, Gemma, and Mistral, making precision a run-time choice rather than a training decision.
arxiv-2606-12976:
Abdurasulov and Erkinov present a mathematical forum platform that embeds image-to-LaTeX conversion directly inside the posting interface, in this 2026 arXiv paper.
