Arabic writers place it about sixty miles from the river's mouth. Its western part had a wall with four gates. The ruler, the ḥakam, lived there in the city's only brick building, a palace.

Most people in Atel lived in huts or felt tents. The eastern part, Khazaran, held merchants of many nations. Muslims, Christians, and Jews all lived in the city. The ḥakan and his court were Jews, and his suite numbered fully 4,000 persons. In 969 the Russians destroyed the city. The entry draws its picture chiefly from Arab writers such as Mas'udi and Ibn Ḥaukal.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-avila-samuel-be:
Samuel ben Moses ben Isaac de Avila was a rabbi and preacher. He served at Mequenez in Morocco, then at Salé. He was born at Mequenez in 1687 or 1688. His book "Ozen Shemuel" gathers his sermons. Five treat repentance, preached before the Day of Atonement. Ten treat the Sabbaths of the Lord, preached before Passover and the feasts. Sixteen are funeral speeches for men of his own time.

The sermon book was printed at Amsterdam in 1715, with approvals from three rabbis. Samuel also published "Keter Torah," The Crown of the Law, at Amsterdam in 1725. That work pleads for freeing scholars from taxes. It gathers older rules on the same point, sets out rules for conduct, and adds notes on Rashi and on the treatise Nazir.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baba-ben-buta-2:
Baba ben Buṭa was a teacher of the Law in the time of Herod. He may have belonged to the family called the Sons of Baba. That family resisted the surrender of Jerusalem to Herod in 37 B.C. and hid from his wrath for ten years. A Talmudic tradition tells a different survival. In it, Baba alone of the teachers was spared by Herod.

The tradition, which the entry prints at length, brings the blinded teacher and the king face to face. Herod, not naming himself, asks Baba to curse a wicked slave, meaning himself. Baba refuses at every turn, citing verses against cursing kings, the rich, and rulers. When Herod at last owns who he is, he asks how such a man can repair his wrong. Baba's answer points him to rebuilding the Temple, in atonement for his crimes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baja-2376:
Baja is a city on the Danube in Hungary, busy with trade by the end of the eighteenth century. Jewish families settled there toward the middle of that century. A fire on May 1, 1840, burned the synagogue, the school, and the community records, so its first years are dim. The oldest entries in the burial society book date to March 6, 1791.

The entry names the early rabbis in turn. Meïr Ash gave up the post in 1815 so his friend Götz Schwerin could have it, and the community grew under Schwerin. The 1840 fire left all but three members destitute and 2,000 houses in ruins. Schwerin raised funds far and wide, and a new synagogue was dedicated Sept. 26, 1845, with a modern order of service. Schools and charities close the account.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-barabas-2476:
Barabas is the chief figure in Christopher Marlowe's play "The Rich Jew of Malta." It was first staged at the Rose Theater, Bankside, London, in 1591. Edward Alleyn created the role. A revival at Drury Lane in 1818, with Edmund Kean, failed to please. The entry calls Barabas an inhuman fiend with rare lapses into humanity, marked by cunning, vengeance, and a lust for gold.

Stripped of his wealth by Malta's governor, Barabas sends his daughter Abigail, feigning conversion, into his old home to fetch his hidden hoard. Then the murders pile up: two lovers set to duel by a forged letter, the nuns poisoned, two friars killed or framed, and blackmailers poisoned by flowers. Taken and left for dead, he betrays the city to the Turks and is made governor. His last trap, a floor over boiling oil, catches him instead when the rope is cut.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baruch-jacob-25: Jacob Baruch was president ("Baumeister") of the Jewish congregation of Frankfort-on-the-Main at the beginning of the nineteenth century, and father of Ludwig Börne. His father had been financial agent of the elector of Cologne. Contemporaries called Jacob "a man of sense, a courtier, sometimes orthodox, sometimes modern." In October, 1814, the community chose him as its representative at the Congress of Vienna, carrying a memorial on the rights of Frankfort's Jews. The community offered him 8,000 gulden for his services, and he refused.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bausk-or-bauske:
Bausk is a district town in Courland, Russia, counted in the census of 1897 at 6,543 people. About three thousand of them were Jews. Their chief work was trade and crafts, with 295 Jewish artisans named in the count.

The entry notes schools, a Talmud Torah, and aid for about 150 poor families at Passover. It then lists six rabbis of the town across the nineteenth century. The last named, in office from 1895, is Abraham Isaac Kook. A famed cantor and a medal winning teacher close the account. Two schools under government control and three private schools served the town, beside private teachers at home.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-behrend-israel-:
Israel Behrend was a German physician and medical writer born at Wittenburg in 1804. He died at Rostock on March 13, 1867. He took his medical degree at Rostock in 1827 and practiced in that city for forty years, building a large practice there.

His chief works treat a remedy against cholera in 1831 and a settled fever in 1853. Essays on homeopathy and facial pain ran in leading journals. Behrend also wrote in 1843 on the Jews of Mecklenburg and their claim to equal civil rights. His cholera book still holds value for its picture of care in that early year, as the entry notes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-benjamin-michae: Michael Henry Benjamin, a South African politician, was born in London in 1822 and died on June 11, 1879. About 1849 he went to Cape Colony and spent ten years at Graaff-Reinet, where he promoted useful bodies. He then moved to Port Elizabeth and spoke for it in the Cape assembly from 1864. He pushed a courts bill, brought in a stamp act, and helped found a bank. Back in England from about 1869, he worked for many Jewish communal bodies in London.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-beryl-3176: Beryl is a stone that ranges from blue to pale yellow. The entry says it is found all over the world. It names three kinds of the stone. They are beryl, aquamarine, and emerald. In Exodus, beryl held a place on the high priest's breastplate. It stood first on the fourth row. The entry also lists later mentions. Ezekiel and Daniel both name it in vision passages.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bick-jacob-samu: Jacob Samuel Bick was an Austrian author. He died at Brody in 1831. He wrote satire with force and skill. He was a leading pioneer of the haskalah. That movement spread culture among Galician Jews. His essays pleaded for secular knowledge and industry. Like other Maskilim, he favored farm work for Jews. Cholera killed him in 1831. His manuscripts burned four years later. A great fire at Brody destroyed them. Contemporaries mourned that loss deeply.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-blindness-3376:
Blindness presents statistics on blindness among Jews. Rates run higher for Jews than neighbors. In Bavaria Jews showed 13.81 blind per 10,000. Protestants there showed only 7.84. Prussia in 1880 showed a similar gap. Congenital blindness also ran higher among Jews. The United States shows little Jewish blindness. Strict immigration bars explain that, the entry says.

Causes puzzle the entry's author. Newborn infection drives much blindness elsewhere. That cause is rarer among Jewish mothers. So lower Jewish rates might be expected. Consanguineous marriage was blamed by some writers. Careful investigators reject that explanation. Eye diseases and heredity carry the weight instead.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-boil-3476:
Boil renders the Hebrew word shehin, from a root meaning to warm. The entry says the word marks an inflamed spot. In the Bible it names two forms of disease, both with painful swelling and discharge.

One form is the simple boil, limited to one spot and not catching. The other is the eruption linked with elephantiasis, a form of leprosy. Job's sore boils are placed with the second form. Leviticus gives priests tests for hard cases. A white-haired, sunken scar meant leprosy, while no spread in seven days meant clean.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-born-gustav-jac:
Gustav Jacob Born was a German histologist and medical author born at Kempen on April 22, 1851. He studied at Breslau, Bonn, Strasburg, and Berlin. He took his medical degree at Breslau in 1876.

Born rose at Breslau from assistant prosector to professor in 1898. His chair joined histology with comparative anatomy. New methods in microscopy and embryology made his name known. One method rebuilt small body parts in enlarged plastic form. He wrote about fifty essays and works. His chief work, on grafting experiments with amphibian larvae, came out at Leipsic in 1897. That same year he received the Prussian Order of the Red Eagle of the fourth class.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-breier-eduard-3: Eduard Breier was an Austrian writer born at Warasdin in Croatia on Nov. 3, 1811. He died at Zaiwitz near Znaim on June 3, 1886. His first novel, written in eleven days on furlough as an artilleryman, appeared in 1840. Its success turned him to journalism and fiction for good. He edited the Prager Zeitung till it was suppressed in 1848. In Vienna he became a popular writer of Jewish and Austrian tales. Wien und Rom and Kaiser Joseph are named as his most characteristic works.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-brussels-french:
Brussels, capital of Belgium, has no record of when Jews first settled there. The entry supposes they came soon after the city's founding in the seventh century. Jews there shared the fortunes of Belgian Jews in general. Crusaders left bloody marks, yet under later rulers the community prospered in the thirteenth century.

Disaster came in 1370, when a stolen host charge led to burnings and banishment, remembered as the miracle of St. Gudule. No trace of Jews appears again until after the Peace of Utrecht in 1713. Banishment decrees in 1716 and later were not enforced. Free settlement came only after 1794 under French rule. The entry follows chief rabbis and lists the city's many Jewish charities, schools, and aid societies.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-byron-george-go:
George Gordon, Lord Byron, was an English poet born in London on Jan. 22, 1788. He died at Missolonghi, Greece, on April 19, 1824. The entry treats only one part of his work: the Hebrew Melodies. Those lyrics are the sole Byron work tied to Jewish topics. He wrote them in 1814 to please his friend Douglas Kinnaird.

The melodies were set to music by Isaac Nathan, drawn from airs sung in Jewish worship. The entry judges them uneven: some have little that is Hebrew at all. She Walks in Beauty came from a ball, not a Bible scene. Others, like Oh Weep for Those, strike it as truly Jewish in subject. Byron himself was never pleased with the set and joked about it to Moore.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cantarini-3976: Cantarini was a noted family of Italian Jews whose line the entry traces to one small child. Gherescion Cantarini, at one year old, was driven from his home town of Asolo. He was taken to Padua in 1547. There his descendants led the Jewish community for the next 300 years. The entry itself is only an introduction. It promises a sketch pedigree of the best known members and then stops. Separate entries in the encyclopedia carry the single lives.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-carregal-carega:
Raphael Ḥayyim Isaac Carregal, a traveling rabbi and preacher, was born in Hebron, Palestine, on Oct. 15, 1733. Ordained at seventeen, he set out in 1754 on long voyages. Stays included two years in Constantinople, two in Curaçao, two and a half in London, and a year in North America. He died at Barbados on May 5, 1777.

At Newport, Rhode Island, in 1773, Carregal formed a close friendship with Ezra Stiles, later president of Yale. They studied together, argued over Messianic passages, and wrote to each other, mostly in Hebrew. Stiles left a warm, detailed memoir of his friend in his diary. Carregal seems to have printed only two brochures, both sermons issued at Newport in 1773.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-chuetas-pork-ea:
Chuetas, a name meaning pork-eaters, was forced on the descendants of secret Jews in Majorca. To pass as good Christians they ate pork in public while staying loyal to Judaism in private. Neighbors shunned them. At church they sat apart, and even their dead lay apart in the cemetery, the entry says.

When the Inquisition reached Majorca in 1488 it first offered amnesty, taking back 680 people for a heavy fine. Burnings began in 1509. A failed escape by sea ended in 1691 with more than fifty people garroted and burned. Relief came only with a royal decree of Dec. 16, 1782. Their descendants, the entry closes, now hold respected places on the island.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cohen-henri-447:
Henri Cohen, a French composer and numismatist, was born at Amsterdam in 1805 and died at Bry-sur-Marne on May 17, 1880. His parents moved to France in 1811 and gave him fine music training. He studied harmony with Reicha and singing with Lois and Pellegrini. Stays at Rome in 1832 and 1838 produced two stage works.

Settled in Paris from 1839, he taught and sang at concerts with success. A directorship at the Lille Conservatoire ended in friction with the administration. Back in Paris he directed the Cabinet des Medailles at the Bibliotheque Nationale and published on coins and bibliography. His music includes the lyric poem Marguerite et Faust of 1847 and a harmony treatise praised by Fetis.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cross-4776:
Cross carries two senses in this entry. The first is the stake used by the Romans at crucifixion. Jews of New Testament times spoke often of men carrying their cross to execution. The second sense is the Christian symbol itself. Jews called it warp and woof, or simply an idol. Law on its use turns on worship. A cross worshiped by Christians counts as an idol and is barred.

A cross worn as a plain ornament, with no religious aim, may be used. Still, Jews have shunned the sign as a Christian emblem. Pious Jews refused badges that bore it. Liberal Jews wore the Iron Cross as soldiers. Jewish artists could embroider crosses on dresses for Christian ladies, one ruling holds.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-daniel-hayyata-: Daniel Ḥayyaṭa, the Tailor, was a Palestinian teacher. Only two of his readings of Scripture survive in the Midrash. One treats a verse in Genesis, on the herdsmen of Isaac. The other treats a verse in Ecclesiastes, on the tears of the oppressed. His time can only be guessed. The rabbis named around him belong to the third and fourth centuries. The teacher cited after him, who builds on his views, is of the fourth generation of amoraim. So Daniel can not be placed earlier than that generation.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-david-samuel-49:
Samuel David was a French musician born in Paris on November 12, 1836, and he died there on October 3, 1895. He studied at the Conservatoire under Bazin and Halévy. In 1858 he won the Grand Prix de Rome for his cantata "Jephtha." In 1872 he became musical director in the synagogues of Paris.

David composed a string of operas and operettas performed in Paris, among them "La Peau de l'Ours" and "La Fée des Bruyères." His ode-symphonie "Le Triomphe de la Paix," from 1878, was his most popular work. He also wrote four symphonies, choruses, songs, and several operas that were never performed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dembo-isaac-507:
Isaac Dembo was a Russian physician born at Poneviezh, in the government of Kovno, in 1846. He studied Hebrew and rabbinical books until age fourteen, then turned to secular study. He took his medical degree at St. Petersburg in 1870. He served in hospitals and in the army during the Russo-Turkish war, winning a medal.

Dembo became known for a study of ritual slaughter. Campaigns in Switzerland and Germany sought to ban the Jewish method as cruel. After comparing methods in Russia and abroad, Dembo concluded the Jewish method caused less pain than any other. Leading scientists agreed with him. He published his findings in two German books at Leipsic in 1894.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dick-isaac-maye:
Isaac Mayer Dick was a Russian Hebraist and novelist born in Wilna in 1808. His father, a cantor, gave him a Talmudic schooling, and a Catholic priest secretly taught him German. He also learned Russian and Polish. In 1841 he became Hebrew teacher in the new government school for Jewish boys in Wilna.

Dick helped found a reform-minded synagogue in Wilna and argued for lifting up Russia's Jews. In later years the Romm publishing house paid him a small weekly wage to write Yiddish stories. Those tales, of many sizes, are said to number nearly three hundred. He was famed as a wit far beyond Wilna. He died there on January 24, 1893.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-duty-hebr-mizwa:
Duty is what a person owes to God, to other people, and to himself. In Hebrew it is mizwah, commandment, and later hobah, obligation. The word itself is too abstract for the Bible, the entry says. Its idea runs through the Bible in other forms.

Micah sums duty up as doing justice, loving kindness, and walking humbly with God. Philo makes man's highest duty the imitation of God. Jewish tradition grounds every duty in the Law as God's fixed will. Thinkers split duties into acts of the body and duties of the heart. The entry warns that viewing each rite as a debt can harden into legalism.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eichenbaum-jaco:
Jacob Eichenbaum was a Russian educator, poet, and mathematician. He pioneered modern schooling among Russian Jews. He was born at Krasnopolie, Galicia, on Oct. 12, 1796. He died at Kiev on Dec. 27, 1861. His father helped him master mathematics early.

At Zamoscz Eichenbaum joined a circle of progressive young Jews. He read the Bible rationally and studied Hebrew, German, and philosophy. In 1819 he rendered Euclid's Elements into Hebrew for his own use. Years of tutoring in rich houses followed. In 1835 he opened a modern Jewish school at Odessa. His Hebrew poems, Kol Zimrah, appeared at Leipsic in 1836.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-elijah-of-york-: Elijah of York was a tosafist in England. Men suppose he died in the York massacre of 1190. Old glosses call him by a place name read as York. That town was Eboracum in Latin in his day. The word the Saint stands after his name in one gloss. That word marks a martyr in most cases, the entry notes. From it men infer he fell in the killings. He learned under Isaac ha-Zaken as a pupil. Samuel ben Solomon may have taught him as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-enoch-ben-judah: Enoch ben Judah Lob was a German Talmudist and rabbi. He served the town of Schnaittach as its rabbi. His time was the start of the eighteenth century. He studied with his father and with Abraham Broda. His own writings do not stand alone in print. They are bound in with works of his father and grandfather. Two books of responsa hold that shared matter. One of them came out in the year 1708. No life facts beyond his studies are given here.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-esthonia-5876: Esthonia was a government of Russia and one of its three Baltic provinces, the entry says in a very short notice. Its total population in 1897 was 404,709, of whom 1,468 were Jews. The province lay outside the Pale of Settlement. Jews began settling there only in the last quarter of the nineteenth century. Those who came were artisans and others with special privilege. The entry gives no towns, institutions, or named persons. Its whole content is the province's status, the 1897 counts, and that late start to settlement.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fadl-da-ud-abu-: Da'ud Abu al-Fadl was a Karaite physician born at Cairo in 1161 and dead there about 1242. He studied medicine under two Jewish doctors named in the entry. He became court physician to Sultan Al-Malik al-Adil, brother and heir of Saladin. He also served as chief teacher at Cairo's Al-Nasiri hospital. One pupil, the historian Ibn Abi Usaibi'ah, called him the most skillful doctor of the age, with near-miraculous cures. His one named work is an Arabic drug book in twelve chapters, chiefly on antidotes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fenyes-fischman: Adolf Fenyes, born Fischmann, was a Hungarian painter born at Kecskemet on April 28, 1867, son of the town's rabbi. He first drew notice as a caricaturist. He then studied law at Budapest for two years, dropped it, and turned to art. He trained at Budapest, Weimar, and Paris. His chief works, prize winners in Paris and Budapest, are named as Prattling, The Quarrel, The Life of the Poor Man, and The Old Man. The entry gives nothing more about his life or later work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-frangi-hayyim-s: Ḥayyim Frangi, surnamed Ḥayyim Menahem, was a Turkish rabbinical author born in 1833 at Constantinople. He died there in 1903. He published two Hebrew works of his own. The first holds responsa and sermons in two volumes, printed at Salonica in 1867-83. The second, printed at Constantinople in 1902, gathers his legal decisions. They cover the twenty-five years in which he presided over the rabbinical tribunal. He also edited a work of one of his teachers, Eliezer of Toledo. It came out in two volumes in 1853.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-friedlander-lud:
Ludwig Friedländer was a German scholar of the classics, born at Königsberg on July 16, 1824. He studied at Königsberg and Leipsic from 1841 to 1845. In 1847 he began to teach classical language study at Königsberg. He became assistant professor in 1856 and full professor in 1858. In 1892 he retired to Strasburg, where he is an honorary professor. His chief work shows Roman manners from Augustus to the last of the Antonines.

It filled three volumes between 1862 and 1871. The entry calls it one of the finest works of its kind in its century. It was turned into French, Italian, and Hungarian. He also edited Martial, the feast of Trimalchio, and Juvenal, with notes. He has embraced Christianity.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-galina-moses-be: Moses ben Elijah Galina, a Greek scholar and translator who lived at Candia in the fifteenth century, is best known for Toledot Adam, printed at Constantinople in 1515. That work treats palm reading and face reading. It draws chiefly on Ali ibn Abbas and on a book ascribed to Aristotle. A shorter form later came out with a Judeo-German version. Galina also put Arabic works on stars and on geomancy into Hebrew.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-goldziher-ignaz:
Ignaz Goldziher was a Hungarian Orientalist. He was born in Stuhlweissenburg on June 22, 1850. He studied at Budapest, Berlin, Leipsic, and Leyden. He took his doctorate in 1870. In 1873 the Hungarian government sent him through Syria, Palestine, and Egypt. He spent months at Cairo's Azhar mosque hearing its sheiks lecture. In 1894 Budapest made him full professor. He was the first Jew admitted to its faculty.

His fame rests on a critical history of Arabic traditions. His "Muhammedanische Studien" gave that field its base. He also set Islam's theological movements in their true light. Ancient Arabic poetry was another strength. For Jewish science he traced Hebrew myth in the Bible. He compared Jewish and Arabic folk-lore of the Middle Ages as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gregory-xiii-ug:
Gregory XIII, born Ugo Buoncompagni, was pope from 1572 to 1585. He was born at Bologna on Feb. 7, 1502. He died at Rome on April 10, 1585. The entry paints him as kindly by nature but warped by intolerance. He let Jews return to Venaissin after their 1569 banishment. In 1581 he gave Jews safe-conduct through Italy. He also lifted the ban on interest.

His hostile acts were many. In 1578 he made Rome's Jews pay 1,100 scudi for the converts' home. In 1581 he barred Jewish doctors from Christian patients. That year he ordered all Talmud copies surrendered to inquisitors. In 1584 he forced Jews to hear missionary sermons each Saturday in their own synagogues.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-habakkuk-book-o:
The Book of Habakkuk is one of the twelve minor prophetical books. It falls readily into two parts: chapters one and two, then chapter three. The first part is a massa, a condemning prophecy, cast as a dialogue. The second part is a psalm.

In the dialogue the prophet laments moral corruption, hears God announce judgment through the Chaldeans, and protests the enemy's pride and cruelty. God answers that evil will not triumph and lists five woes against the oppressor. Chapter three sings of God's warlike power over earth, rivers, sun, and moon. The entry stresses the book's striking images and its core question: why God tolerates tyranny and wrong.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-haidamacks-1457:
The Haidamacks were Russian brigand bands of the eighteenth century. In a disordered Poland, Greek Orthodox peasants and Cossacks formed bands of runaway serfs, Saporogians, and Cossacks from Russian Ukraine. Stirred by priests, they struck at their Catholic masters, the Polish nobles, and at the Jews. In 1734 and again in 1750 they sacked towns across Kiev, Volhynia, and Podolia, killing many Jews and nobles.

The worst blow fell in 1768. A forged decree in Catherine II's name, ordering the killing of Jews and Poles, was spread abroad. Under Zhelyeznyak the bands swept the Kiev region. At Uman, the Cossack Gonta betrayed the city's trust and joined the attackers. Jews and Poles fought side by side on the walls, then died together in the streets and the synagogue. About twenty thousand Jews and Poles were killed at Uman alone.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-halafta-of-kefa: Ḥalafta of Kefar Hananiah was a tanna of the second century, junior to R. Meïr. In Meïr's name he hands down a maxim about conditions: a condition stated before the duty it hangs on is valid, but a duty stated first voids the condition. The Mishnah, at Abot iii. 6, keeps his homily on how many persons make a quorum for study of the Law. In the prayer-book Abot he is named R. Ḥalafta b. Dosa of Kefar Hananiah, though some copies drop the father's name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hananeel-ben-am: Hananeel b. Amittai was the spiritual leader of the Jewish community of Oria, in Italy, in the ninth century. He is said to descend from a Jerusalem family carried to Italy by Titus. The Ahimaaz Chronicle credits him with great learning and piety. It also says he was deep in the secret knowledge of Cabala, through which he worked miracles. The same chronicle tells of a disputation he held with the Archbishop of Oria. The brief entry rests on Neubauer and Kaufmann and adds no works or dates for him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hart-hebr-ayyal:
Hart treats the deer named by the Hebrew word ayyal, listed in Deuteronomy among clean animals fit for food. Deer of this kind were served at Solomon's table. The entry admits that the exact species once common in Palestine cannot now be fixed. The fallow deer is offered as a likely match.

Much of the piece gathers Bible images built on the animal. The hart stands for speed, grace, and tender care of young. One psalm uses its thirst for water as a picture of longing. Talmudic notes add facts about antlers, hunting with nets, and skin used for parchment. A proverb about money placed on a hart's horn warns of a bad venture.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hayyim-ben-isra: Hayyim ben Israel was a Spanish philosopher and author who lived at Toledo about 1272 to 1277. He came from the Israeli family. He was kin to Isaac Israeli, who wrote a noted work on astronomy called "Yesod Olam." Hayyim's own known work is a treatise on paradise. It survives only in manuscript. The entry is very brief, just a few lines. It gives no birth or death dates and names no other writings by him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hefker-7476:
Hefker is ownerless property under Jewish law. Property becomes hefker in set ways. An owner may renounce it in front of three men. A court may declare it so. The goods of a convert who dies without Jewish heirs also fall in this class. Things found in seas, rivers, or deserts count as ownerless too.

The first person to take hold of such property gains it. A renunciation must be open to all, not limited to one class such as the poor. If no one claims the goods in three days, the old owner may take back the renunciation. The article sets out how taking works, and how hefker differs from land held by long use.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-henschel-elias-:
Elias H. Henschel, born at Breslau on April 4, 1755, began life as an errand-boy and a physician's valet. A professor named Morgenbesser helped him gain support for study. He began anatomy at twenty-five and took his medical degree at Halle in 1787.

Henschel focused on obstetrics and became public accoucheur at Breslau. He helped introduce vaccination in Silesia. He also gave much time to the hospital for the Jewish poor. In 1813 he cared for a lazaretto holding 228 beds. During cholera he published advice for the public in 1831. Other writings covered diseases of pregnant women and newborn care. He died in 1839.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hezir-7676: Hezir is a name the entry gives to two men, listed in numbered order. The first was a priest, chief of the seventeenth monthly course in the Temple service, appointed by David. The second was a layman, one of the heads of the people. He signed the covenant with Nehemiah. The entry rests only on verses from First Chronicles and Nehemiah. It gives no dates, family detail, deeds, or sayings for either man, and no comment beyond the two identifications and their sources.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hivites-7776:
Hivites were one of the Canaanite nations dispossessed by Israel, the entry states. Their name may mean the villager or the midlander, by two cited scholars. The Hivite is counted as sixth son of Canaan. Hamor, prince of Shechem, was a Hivite.

Shechemites appear in Genesis as peaceful traders and cattle raisers. Later, fearing battle with Joshua's Israelites, Hivites used a trick to win safety, much as Jacob's sons had tricked them. Their four cities are named. The Gibeonites were spared for Joshua's oath. Their main body lay under Mount Hermon toward Hamath, the entry adds.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-horowitz-isaiah:
Isaiah Horowitz was a German cabalist, rabbi, and author born at Prague about 1555. He died at Safed about 1630. He studied in Cracow and married into a wealthy Vienna family. Money let him give to charity and build a large library. He soon led Jewish communal affairs in Poland.

Horowitz held rabbinates at Dubno, Ostrog, Frankfort, and Prague. In 1621 he moved to Palestine and settled in Jerusalem. A pasha jailed him for ransom in 1625, and he ended his days at Safed. His best known book, Shene Luhot ha-Berit, called the Shelah, sums up Jewish religion, law, and mystic teaching. It stayed popular for centuries.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-illowy-bernhard:
Bernhard Illowy was an American rabbi born at Kolin in Bohemia in 1814. He died near Cincinnati on June 22, 1871. He came of a line of Talmudists and studied at Presburg under Moses Sofer. He took a doctorate at Budapest and studied further at Padua under Luzzatto. Teaching at home gave way to a search abroad for a pulpit.

Illowy crossed to the United States and served at Syracuse, New Orleans, and Cincinnati. He stood as one of Orthodoxy's ablest champions, with deep Talmudic learning and fine command of tongues. He helped call the Cleveland rabbinical conference of 1855, but its Reform leanings blunted his sway. His press pieces, above all in Hirsch's Jeschurun, picture American Judaism of his day.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-isaac-eisak-ben: Isaac Eisak ben Jacob Haber was rabbi at Tikotzyn and Suwalki, in Poland, in the first half of the nineteenth century. His ritual work "Bet Yitzhak" appeared at Sudzilkow in 1836. He also wrote "Seder Zemannim," on the precepts tied to set dates, printed at Warsaw in 1844. That same year brought his commentary on the Passover haggadah, with notes by his son Joseph. Another work, "Magen we-Zinnah," defended the Cabala against the attacks of Judah de Modena.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-israel-isser-be: Israel Isser ben Ze'eb Wolf was a Russian rabbi who lived at Vinnitsa, in Podolia, in the nineteenth century. He wrote "Sha'ar Mishpat," novellae on the Hoshen Mishpat part of the Shulhan Aruk, in two volumes printed at Königsberg in 1860. A second work, "Sha'ar De'ah," treats the laws of interest in the Yoreh De'ah. It was published as an appendix to the first work. The entry gives no dates or posts from his life beyond his town.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jaca-hebr-8376:
Jaca is a city of Aragon, in Spain, where Jews lived as early as the eleventh century. The city became the seat of a Jewish high school. Its Jews faced close rules: the king assigned them one city mill for their grain, at a set tax, on top of the usual imposts. In 1281 they had to help pay for mending the town walls, hurt in the French invasion. In 1289 they owed the king 6,000 sueldos toward an expedition against Sicily.

Violence came twice. In the Shepherds' outbreak of 1321, no fewer than 400 Jews of Jaca were killed on July 14. In 1391 Jews there were killed or baptized by force. By 1438 the shrunken community could pay only 200 sueldos in taxes. Two scholars of the late fourteenth century, Seraiah ben Daud and Samuel Almosnino, wrote from Jaca to Isaac ben Sheshet.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jacobs-joseph-k: Joseph Jacobs, known as Jacobs the Wizard, was an English conjurer born at Canterbury in 1813. He first appeared in London in 1835, when he presented the Chinese ring trick. At the Strand Theatre in 1841 he won great success with costly apparatus. In 1850 he invented a trick that produced bowls of water with goldfish from under a shawl. He performed in America in 1854 and in Australia and New Zealand in 1860, and died on Oct. 13, 1870.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jekuthiel-ibn-h: Jekuthiel ibn Hasan was a statesman and man of science in the eleventh century who lived in Saragossa. He may be the same man as an astronomer who served as a judge in Cordova and wrote on the stars. At Saragossa he held high office under the emir, and the poet Solomon ibn Gabirol praised his learning, modesty, and kindness as a patron and friend. In a revolt in 1039 the plotters beheaded King Mundhir and Jekuthiel with him. Gabirol mourned him in a poem of more than 200 verses.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jezelus-8676: Jezelus is a name that appears twice in the First Book of Esdras, in lists of men who came back from captivity with Ezra. In the first place he is the father of Sechenias, head of a returning family. In the second he is the father of Obadiah, also a chief on the return. The brief entry gives no life for Jezelus himself. It only matches his name across books: in Ezra the first man is called Jahaziel and the second Jehiel.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jonathan-ben-uz: Jonathan ben Uzziel was the most noted pupil of Hillel. No legal rulings of his survive, but one tale shows his selflessness. A man whose children had behaved badly left him all his wealth. Jonathan kept one third, gave one third to the sanctuary, and returned one third to the children. Tradition credits him with a version of the Prophets into Aramaic, though scholars doubt the surviving version is his. He is said to have wished to render the Writings too.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kalonymus-ben-s:
Kalonymus ben Shabbethai, also called Kalonymus of Rome, was a judge of Jewish law, a Bible scholar, and a poet. He was born at Rome about 1030. His father headed the Jewish community there. Questions of law reached Kalonymus from Worms, Arles, and many other places. His name as a Talmud judge spread far past Italy.

In 1070, after the death of Jacob bar Yaḳar, Kalonymus was called to lead the rabbinate of Worms. He held it until 1096. The entry thinks he fell in the Crusader attacks of that year. With Eleazar ben Judah he ran the rabbinical school of Worms. His Talmud and Bible notes are lost as books. Later writers, Rashi among them, still quote them often.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-key-10076:
The Hebrew word for a key means "the opener." In Bible times a key worked a door bolt, not a lock of the modern kind. The bolt had holes that caught iron points in the door post. The wooden key bore nails in the same pattern. Slid in from the side, it lifted the points and freed the bolt.

The entry reads the old tales by this light. Ehud could bolt Eglon's door from inside with no key. The king's servants needed the key to get in. To bear the key on the shoulder marks high office, as in Isaiah. Four Levites kept the key of the Temple. The Talmud adds a figure of speech. Three keys, it says, God keeps in His own hand: rain, childbirth, and the waking of the dead.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-korobka-meat-ta:
Korobka is the part of the Russian basket tax that fell on kosher meat and poultry. Jews first devised the tax themselves to fund poor relief, hospitals, and schools. Control sat with the ḳahal, then passed to town government. When the ḳahal bodies were abolished in 1844 the tax turned from voluntary to required.

Farming out the meat monopoly then made the burden worse. Other parts of the basket tax were loosely gathered while the meat tax was pressed hard. Kosher meat cost 2 to 3 cents per pound more than other meat in many places. The entry stresses that the poor paid most and ate worst for it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lachish-9576:
Lachish was a city in Judah first named when its king joined four others against Gibeon. Joshua beat the allies, then besieged and took the city. Rehoboam later rebuilt it among his strong towns. King Amaziah fled there from a plot and was killed there all the same.

The siege of 701 B.C. dominates the account. Sennacherib's army sat before Lachish while Hezekiah paid for safety and envoys went on to Jerusalem. Palace carvings at Kuyunjik show the siege and captives in fine detail. Digs at Tell al-Ḥasi found eight stacked cities, from about 1700 B.C. down to Greek pottery ages. The entry calls the mound a place of fierce battles over more than 1,200 years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-law-reading-fro:
Law, Reading from the, describes the custom of reading parts of the Pentateuch in synagogue on Sabbaths and holy days. Josephus and Philo trace the weekly reading to Moses. Ezra read the Law to the returned exiles over the eight days of Sukkot. The practice made the Torah the property of the whole people.

Cycles of reading ran seven years, then three, then one. Babylonia's one-year cycle split the Torah into 53 or 54 weekly sections. On Sabbath morning seven readers are called up; on the Day of Atonement six, on holy days five, on week-days three. Festival readings are listed day by day.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lerma-judah-ben:
Judah ben Samuel Lerma was a Spanish Talmudist of the mid-sixteenth century. He wrote "Lehem Yehudah," a commentary on Pirke Abot. He also wrote a treatise on the soul. Both came out together at Sabbionetta in 1554. In his preface he laments the burning of the Talmud in Italy that year.

Fire later destroyed most of Lerma's responsa. Thirty were saved by his pupil Simhah ben Gershon ha-Kohen. The pupil printed them at Venice in 1647 as "Peletat Bet Yehudah." The entry warns readers not to confuse him with a later Judah Lerma, a rabbi of Belgrade.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-levy-asser-asse:
Asser Levy van Swellem was one of the first Jewish settlers of New Amsterdam. He was probably born in Amsterdam and died in 1680. He reached New Netherland in 1654, most likely as a refugee from Brazil. From the start he fought for his people's rights and let no slight pass without protest.

In 1655 Governor Stuyvesant barred Jews from guard duty and taxed them instead. Levy and his comrades refused to pay. They asked leave to stand guard like other burghers. Turned down, Levy appealed to Holland and won the right to serve. He also traded at Fort Orange and held one of the colony's first butcher licenses. In 1657 he claimed the burgher right in court.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-life-9976:
Life, in Hebrew hayyim, is the subject of this entry. It denotes first the animal existence of a being. By Scripture, life begins when the breath of God is breathed through the nostrils. It ends when God takes that breath back. Life is God's gracious gift, and with God is the fountain of life.

Long life was read in old times as the reward of virtue and piety. The poets dwell on how short life is. Yet the moral view marks Judaism most, the entry says. Life is sacred and must be guarded with care in man and beast alike. The whole Law sums up in one charge: choose life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lucerne-10176:
Lucerne, a Swiss city in the canton of the same name, is the subject of a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906 by Richard Gottheil and Meyer Kayserling. Jews lived there by the middle of the thirteenth century. The town’s earliest records already regulate how meat slaughtered by Jews had to be sold.

Those rules also promised protection: no one was to injure the Jews, on pain of a fine or banishment from the city. As elsewhere in Switzerland, Jews alone could charge interest on loans, and money-lending was their trade. Even so, they were expelled in 1401. No Jew settled again until about 1864, and the community counted forty-two members in 1904. The entry gives a compact history of early protection, expulsion, and a very late return.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-magnus-markus-1:
Markus Magnus, an elder of Berlin's Jewish congregation, is profiled in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He served as court Jew to the crown prince, later King Frederick William I. That royal backing set him against his rival, Jost Liebmann. King Frederick I favored Liebmann, and the community split into two hostile camps.

The article follows the feud to its end. After Liebmann's death his widow and sons kept the quarrel alive. Magnus won in the end. He persuaded the congregation to replace the private synagogues of the old families with one public synagogue. In 1722 the government issued new rules for the congregation's management. Magnus and Moses Levi Gumpertz were named permanent chief elders, each with a salary of three hundred thalers. The entry shows how court favor and rivalry shaped Berlin's Jewish self-government.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-manresa-10376:
Manresa, a town in Spain's province of Barcelona, is given a Jewish history in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. In the twelfth century it is said to have held five hundred Jewish families. Most lived in a narrow lane by the town hall, the Grau dels Jueus. Their cemetery outside the city is still called Fossana dels Jueus.

The article describes livelihoods and mounting hostility. Manresa's Jews worked in manufacturing, trade, money-lending at twenty percent, and their own vineyards. In 1325 townspeople tried to stop them baking Passover bread, and the Jews appealed to the king. The persecution of 1391 struck Manresa too, and many Jews professed Christianity. After 1414 few remained. In 1492 the last of them sold their property for what it would fetch and left. The entry also notes the Zabarra family members who lived in the town.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meir-ben-joseph:
Meir ben Joseph ben Merwan ha-Levi was a French scholar of twelfth-century Narbonne. Richard Gottheil and S. Kahn give him an entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was the brother of the nasi, the head of the community, R. Moses ben Joseph ben Merwan. He was a pupil of Isaac ben Merwan, who headed the Narbonne academy in the early twelfth century. He was held in great respect and moved in the circle of Abraham ben Isaac, president of the rabbinical college of Narbonne about 1165.

No book of his is named. His survival in the record rests on a conjecture by Gross. Gross held that this Meir is identical with Meir ben Jacob. That man appears, among five other scholars, at the end of a rabbinical responsum dated at Narbonne in the mid-twelfth century. The bibliography sends readers to chronicles and legal collections.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mendlin-jacob-w:
Jacob Wolf Mendlin, a Russian Hebrew economist, is profiled by Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was the first Hebrew writer to take up economics for the Jewish masses of Russia. He was born at Moghilef-on-the-Dnieper in 1842. About 1862 he went to Germany. Studying the labor movement under Lassalle turned his ambition to economics and cooperation. From his first article in "Ha-Meliz" in 1879, he wrote steadily on the condition of Russian Jewry, in Hebrew, Russian, and Yiddish papers.

His books argue one remedy: "Ba-Meh Niwwashea'," By What Shall We Be Saved (1883), and "Mekore ha-Osher," Sources of Wealth (1898). With a Yiddish work on self-help, they point to mutual aid and cooperative organization. That, they argue, is the surest cure for the wretched state of the Jewish poor. He also founded charitable institutions at Odessa, where he was living in 1904.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-metatron-hebr-g:
Meṭaṭron is an angel found only in Jewish literature, powerful enough that Elisha ben Abuyah, seeing him in heaven, believed there were two divine powers. Joseph Jacobs and Ludwig Blau wrote the Jewish Encyclopedia article on him in 1906. The entry gathers his roles from Talmud, Midrash, and later mystical books.

Meṭaṭron bears God's name, consoles God after the Temple's destruction, and yet may not be worshiped, the article stresses. Later sources call him prince of the presence, heavenly scribe, and lord of secrets, and identify him with Enoch. Closing sections weigh rival accounts of his origin, from Latin metator, meaning guide, to links with Mithra, Philo's Logos, and Horus.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-micah-10776:
Micah the prophet, author of the sixth book among the Twelve Minor Prophets, heads a Jewish Encyclopedia article written by Isidore Singer, M. Seligsohn, Solomon Schechter, and Emil G. Hirsch in 1906. His name is a short form of Micaiah, meaning Who is like Yhwh. Almost everything known of him comes from his book's opening line.

He was a Morasthite, from Moresheth-gath, and prophesied under the Judahite kings Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, a span the article dates to 756-697 B.C. at the outside. Later tradition confused him with Micaiah son of Imlah and told of his death under Ahab, claims the entry reports with doubt. After the prophet, the article takes up the other biblical Micahs, including the Ephraimite whose stolen silver funded a household shrine.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moos-solomon-10:
Solomon Moos, born at Randegg near Constance on July 15, 1831, was the German ear specialist who built otology at Heidelberg, in an entry by Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He took his medical degree there in 1856 and joined its faculty three years later. From 1875 he practised otology alone.

He founded Heidelberg's otological clinic and dispensary and directed it until his death — on his sixty-fourth birthday, in 1895. With Knapp he had founded the Archiv für Augen- und Ohrenheilkunde in 1868, and he translated Toynbee's Diseases of the Ear into German. His monographs run from the Eustachian tube to fungal invasion of the labyrinth after diphtheria and measles.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-eliakim-b:
Moses Eliakim Beri'ah ben Israel was a Polish preacher born at Cozienice, where he died in 1825. The Jewish Encyclopedia entry is credited to its editorial committee and M. Seligsohn. Like his father, Israel of Cozienice, he was a disciple of Elimelech of Lysensk. Elimelech was one of the active leaders of Hasidism.

His printed book, Be'er Mosheh, gathers homilies arranged by the weekly portions of the Pentateuch. Two more works stayed in manuscript: Da'at Mosheh, a homiletic commentary on the Pentateuch, and Matteh Mosheh, on the Passover Haggadah. The entry keeps a Hasidic preacher's name and books on record for later readers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mossiri-hayyim-: Hayyim Nissim Raphael Mossiri was a Turkish rabbinical writer who died at Jerusalem about 1800. Gotthard Deutsch and M. Franco give him a short entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He had come to Jerusalem from Salonica. His one work is Be'er Mayim Hayyim, a book of responsa in two volumes, printed at Salonica in 1764 and 1814.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nahash-serpent-:
Nahash, a name meaning serpent, belongs first to a king of the Ammonites in the days of Saul. The Jewish Encyclopedia article, by its editorial committee and M. Seligsohn, tells his attack on Jabesh-gilead. He offered the town a choice: every right eye put out, or the sword. The town won seven days, and Saul came and routed him.

The article notes that fear of Nahash was itself a reason Israel demanded a king. David later sent condolences to Nahash's son, for Nahash had shown him kindness in flight. Two more Nahashes follow: the father of Shobi, who fed David in exile, and a name in Amasa's family line. The rabbis identified that Nahash with Jesse himself.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nathanson-bernh:
Bernhard Nathanson was a Russian Hebrew journalist and author. Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Satanow, Podolia, on April 15, 1832. His father guided his early Hebrew studies. When his father died in 1853, he moved to Odessa.

At Odessa he studied both sacred and secular subjects. He spent three years copying and fixing Levinsohn's manuscripts. In 1875 he went to Warsaw to publish Levinsohn's works. His own first article appeared in Ha-Maggid in 1864. He wrote a Bible name book in 1871. He also wrote Levinsohn's life and a Talmud word book.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-neumark-mirels-:
Meshullam Zalman Neumark, called Mirels, was a German Talmudist. The entry was written by the Editorial Board's Executive Committee and A. Peiginsky for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was the father of Zebi Ashkenazi. He died at Hamburg on Nov. 28, 1706. Vienna's ghetto had counted him among its most respected men.

When Vienna expelled its Jews, he moved to Berlin. There too he rose to prominence among Jews. He joined Talmud study to business and to charity. In 1678 he returned briefly to Vienna on permit. He negotiated a loan there for the elector. Soon after, he gave up trade entirely. Hamburg and Altona took him as their rabbi. The sister communities shared his rabbinate from then on.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nobah-11576:
Nobah names both a warrior and his captured town. Emil G. Hirsch and M. Seligsohn wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The man was a Manassite of the conquest age. He seized Kenath, east of the Jordan, with its villages. He then gave the place his own name.

Gideon passed Nobah chasing the Midianite kings eastward. Later ages called the town Canatha in their records. Coins suggest Gabinius restored it in Roman times. Herod met a crushing defeat there against Arabs. Inscriptions show councilors and a market clerk governed it. It also belonged, for a time, to Agrippa II. Today it is Ḳanawat, held by a few Druse families. It sits on the old Roman road to Damascus.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ohole-shem-asso:
The Ohole Shem Association was a group based in New York. Herman Rosenthal and Frank H. Vizetelly wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It was founded on October 8, 1895. Its aim was to spur the study of Hebrew. It also backed study of kindred tongues and Jewish past.

Herman Rosenthal founded the group, with help from friends. Dr. A. Radin and Dr. S. Brainin stood with him. The group set up talks in three tongues at once. Those tongues were Hebrew, German, and English. It put out a Hebrew monthly in its first years. It marked the birth days of great Jewish men. In 1901 it marked one hundred years since Zacharias Frankel was born.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ornstein-zebi-h:
Zebi Hirsch Ornstein was an Austrian rabbi of Lemberg. The board and M. W. Rapoport wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Lemberg and died there in 1888. His father was Mordecai Zeeb Ornstein of that city. His grandfather was Jacob Meshullam Ornstein, its rabbi.

Zebi was taught by his father and grandfather in youth. He showed rare talent while still a young man. Some of his replies were placed in his grandfather's book. That book was Yeshuot Yaakob, a famed work of replies. His name soon spread far past his own land. In 1855 he took his first post at Brest-Litovsk. There his great memory drew awe from all who heard him. The state forced him out of that town in 1874.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-palti-or-phalti: Palti, or Phalti, is a name borne by two men in the Bible. Emil G. Hirsch and Schulim Ochser wrote its short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The name is most likely a short form of Paltiel. The first Palti was a son of Raphu, of Benjamin. He was one of the twelve spies sent into Canaan. The second was the new husband of Michal, Saul's daughter. Michal had been the wife of David before that match.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pedat-b-eleazar:
Pedat ben Eleazar was a Palestinian teacher of the Talmud. He lived in the first half of the fourth century. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He learned the Law first from his own father.

Pedat served as the spokesman for Rabbi Assi in lecture. He passed on sayings from his father and from Rabbi Hoshaiah. He was a close friend of Zera and of Jeremiah ben Eleazar. A few of his readings of Scripture survive. One clears Moses of pride in a hard verse.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-petronius-publi:
Publius Petronius governed Syria from 39 to 42. Richard Gottheil and Samuel Krauss wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His term forced him into close dealings with the Jews. He used that contact to shield them once.

Caligula ordered his statue set inside the Jerusalem Temple. Petronius had the statue made slowly at Sidon. He stalled at Ptolemais through the winter, talking with Jewish leaders. Crowds begged to die rather than yield the sanctuary. Moved, he marched his troops back to Antioch. He wrote the emperor asking him to cancel the order.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pinsker-simhah-:
Simhah Pinsker was a Polish scholar of Hebrew antiquities. Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Tarnopol in 1801. He died at Odessa in 1864, pensioned and honored. His book later traced the rise of Karaism.

Pinsker failed in trade, then served Odessa's rabbi as secretary. His fine handwriting had won him the post. He helped found a public school for Jewish children. Then Firkovich brought strange old manuscripts from Crimea. Pinsker cracked their odd system of vowel points. Gold medals and a pension rewarded the feat.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-popper-josef-12:
Josef Popper was an Austrian engineer and author born at Kolin in Bohemia in 1838. Isidore Singer wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He wrote essays on machines for learned journals. His books range far beyond his trade, though. They treat social questions, flight, and Jewish life.

Popper wrote on the right to live and the duty to die in 1878. He wrote against anti-Semitism in a book on Bismarck in 1886. His flight book came out in 1889. Best known is his early idea for sending electric power over wires. He set out that idea in 1862. A Vienna academy printed it twenty years later.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-procurators-123:
Procurators were the Roman governors set over Judea. Gotthard Deutsch and Samuel Krauss wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. They took charge after Archelaus was banished in the year 6. From the year 44 they ruled the whole of Palestine. The land was joined to Syria in name. In fact it kept a governor of its own.

Josephus gives that governor more than one Greek title. His set title was procurator, or epitropos in Greek. At times Josephus calls him eparch or hegemon instead. The article lists the men who held the post in turn. It tells what each did in a tense land. Pontius Pilate stands among them in the full account.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rabbah-b-hana-r:
Rabbah bar Hana was a Babylonian teacher of the first set of amoraim. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was a nephew of Hiyya the Great. He was a cousin of Abba Arika, known as Rab. Like Rab, he went up to Palestine for his learning.

In Palestine Rabbah sat among the chief pupils of Judah the Prince. As he left, Judah gave him a broad right. He might rule on all points of Jewish law. He might sit as a judge in cases as well. Hiyya had asked that this honor be granted him. Back in Babylonia, his name stands with the great of his age.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rapoport-12576:
Rapoport is a family name shared by many Jewish branches. Isidore Singer, Jacob Zallel Lauterbach, Emil Jelinek, A. S. Waldstein, Peter Wiernik, M. Seligsohn, and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this article. It appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. All branches claim a common Kohenitic origin. The name Rapa appears about 1450 on the Rhine.

The article traces the family from Mayence toward Italy. Jews were expelled from Mayence in 1462. Soon a wealthy Hayyim Rappe appears near Venice. A Polish branch told a legend to explain the name. The writers argue it comes from a word for raven. The family arms bear two ravens, they note. The entry opens a long family history in several lands.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-remenyi-eduard-:
Eduard Remenyi was a Hungarian violinist born at Eged in 1830. Isidore Singer and Joseph Sohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He died at New York on May 15, 1898. He studied under Böhm at the Vienna Conservatorium.

The article says Austria banished him for joining the 1848 revolution. He spent five years in America as a traveling player. Back in Europe, Liszt taught him at Weimar. In 1854 he became solo violinist to Queen Victoria. An amnesty let him return to Hungary in 1860. He toured France, Germany, Belgium, and Holland in 1865. A world tour in 1886 reached Japan and China. His best original work is a violin concerto. He also transcribed many piano pieces for violin.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosenthal-morit:
Moritz Rosenthal was an Austrian pianist born at Lemberg in 1862. Isidore Singer and Joseph Sohn wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He studied under several teachers before the family moved to Vienna in 1875.

At fourteen Rosenthal gave a first public concert that won wide praise. Its program ranged from Beethoven and Chopin to Mendelssohn and Liszt. A tour led to his naming as Rumanian court pianist at Bucharest. From 1876 to 1878 he studied under Liszt himself. He later toured America twice and published advanced technical studies for pianists. With L. Schytte he published technical studies for pianists of the highest development.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sachs-johann-ja:
Johann Jacob Sachs was a German physician born at Märkisch Friedland on July 26, 1803. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He took his medical degree at Königsberg in 1827 and practised in Berlin.

In 1832 Sachs founded the Berliner Medizinische Zeitung, a medical weekly paper. Renamed over time, it was still being published when this entry appeared. He also issued a medical almanac and a yearly repertory of medical progress. His own books cover mineral waters, cholera on German soil, and influenza. Attacked by critics in 1842, he defended his literary work in print.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samson-ben-jose:
Samson ben Joseph of Falaise was a tosafist of the twelfth century in France. Kaufmann Kohler and Isaac Broydé wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He was grandfather of two famed tosafists, Isaac of Dampierre and Samson of Sens.

Jacob Tam, who corresponded with Samson on learned questions, esteemed him highly. Samson wrote tosafot to Shabbat, Erubin, Yebamot, and Hullin in the Talmud. His ritual decisions were cited by Joel ha-Levi under the title Pesakim. One ruling let a nursing woman remarry soon after her divorce. Jacob Tam attacked that decision severely in his Sefer ha-Yashar.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sandor-paul-131:
Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Paul Sándor. He was a Hungarian merchant and deputy. Sándor was born in 1860 at Hodmezövásárhely. He studied at the academies of commerce in Budapest and Dresden. That training prepared him for business and for public life in the capital.

In Budapest, Sándor sat on the municipal council. He also belonged to the Chamber of Commerce and Industry. In 1901 the Lipótváros district of Budapest sent him to the Hungarian Parliament. The entry is brief, and it rests on Sturm's parliamentary almanac for 1901 to 1906. It records a merchant who carried his standing in trade into national politics.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schlesinger-her:
Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Herman Schlesinger. He was a German physician. Schlesinger was born at Adelebsen, in Hanover, on April 1, 1856. He took his medical degree at Göttingen in 1879. The same university gave him a prize for a treatise. It studied what long, small doses of mercury do to animals.

After further study in Berlin, Schlesinger settled at Frankfort-on-the-Main. In 1899 he became editor of Die Aerztliche Praxis, published at Würzburg. His handbook covers hygienic and dietetic rules, water cures, and other treatments. It reached a sixth edition in 1896. Raffaelo Supino translated it into Italian at Florence in 1897. The entry rests on Pagel's biographical lexicon of physicians.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-seder-13376:
Cyrus Adler and Lewis N. Dembitz wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on the Seder. Seder is the Ashkenazic name for the Passover home service. It falls on the first night of the feast. Those who keep a second festival day repeat it then. Sephardic Jews call the service the Haggadah, the story. The book read aloud bears that same name.

Exodus pictures the first Passover as a household meal. Parents and children ate together at home. In Second Temple days only men were summoned to Jerusalem. Only city dwellers could keep the night as a family feast. The Temple's fall restored the home table. The father could again obey the command to tell his son. Four cups of wine mark the evening's joy. Roast lamb, unleavened bread, and bitter herbs anchor the meal.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shabbethai-ben-:
Shabbethai ben Moses ha-Kohen was rabbi of a town near Tikoczin, Russia, in the early eighteenth century. Gotthard Deutsch and S. Mannheimer wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. His lasting work was as an editor rather than an author. He prepared a Talmud commentary collection for print at Fürth in 1741.

That collection, Minhat Kohen, gathers fresh readings of the Talmud. Its authors were Abraham Broda, Zebi Ashkenazi, and Jacob Kohen Poppers of Frankfurt. Shabbethai added some readings of his own to theirs. The entry is short, yet it credits the quiet labor that carried other rabbis' learning into print for wider use.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shiggayon-13576:
Shiggayon is a puzzling term set at the head of Psalm seven. Emil G. Hirsch and Wilhelm Nowack wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. A plural form heads the third chapter of Habakkuk. Ancient versions read the word in differing ways.

Some old translators linked it to a word for trespass. Rashi and the Midrash took a similar view of it. The entry judges that reading incorrect, though. Shiggayon likely belongs with labels like mizmor and maskil. Those labels mark types of songs in the Psalms. Some scholars derive it from a root meaning to reel. They call it a wild, passionate lyric form. Yet Psalm seven is not unique in feeling. The term stays unexplained, and the entry says so plainly.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simeon-13676:
Simeon was the second son of Jacob, by his wife Leah. Joseph Jacobs, M. Seligsohn, and Wilhelm Bacher wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He was born at Padan-aram, far from Canaan. Genesis explains his name as God hath heard.

Leah felt herself hated, and the name marked that sorrow. Scholars offer other roots for the name as well. Simeon stands out in two famous incidents of Genesis. With Levi he massacred Shechem's men for wronging Dinah. Jacob rebuked both brothers sharply for that revenge. Later Joseph held Simeon hostage in an Egyptian prison. He stayed bound until the brothers returned with Benjamin. The entry weighs name lore against a violent, vivid story.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-singer-paul-137:
Paul Singer was a German Social Democrat and deputy born in Berlin in 1844. Isidore Singer and Max Cohen wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He went into trade after real-school. In 1869 he set up a cloak factory with his brother. The business prospered and made him a fortune.

Singer turned to politics and the study of labor. He joined the Social-Democratic party and rose beside Bebel and Liebknecht. In 1884 Berlin voters sent him to the Reichstag. He gave 5,000 marks to aid families of exiled Socialists. An expulsion order against him in 1886 was soon withdrawn. He also helped found the Refuge for the Homeless in Berlin.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solomon-ben-mei:
Solomon ben Meir was a French grammarian and Bible commentator. Crawford Howell Toy and M Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He lived in the twelfth century in France. He was a grandson of Rashi through his mother. His brothers were the famed tosafists Isaac, Samuel, and Jacob Tam.

Some authorities denied that Meir had a fourth son at all. Berliner found proof in Vatican fragments in 1874. Those fragments quote a commentary by Solomon ben Meir often. They call him brother of Jacob Tam in plain words. He was called father of grammarians for his skill. He served as prayer leader at Ramerupt and signed Tam's ordinances.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-spitzer-friedri:
Friedrich Samuel Spitzer was a French art collector and dealer of fame. Isidore Singer and Richard Gottheil wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born in Presburg in 1814, son of a grave-digger. He went penniless to Vienna to seek his fortune. A picture bought for five gulden proved to be a Dürer.

That find laid the foundation of his great wealth. He learned that old weapons drew high prices in England. He bought up old arms in Austria and sold them in London. Settled in Paris at Rothschild's urging, his business prospered greatly. Gambetta offered him six million francs for his collection. After his death in 1890 it sold for ten million francs.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-strauss-gustave:
Gustave Louis Maurice Strauss was a British author born in Canada in 1807. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He was born at Trois-Rivières and educated in Hanover and Berlin. He also studied medicine at Montpellier. He died at Teddington on September 2, 1887.

Strauss served as assistant surgeon with the French army in Algiers. France banished him in 1839 over a suspected plot. He then settled in London as author and tutor. He also worked as linguist, dramatist, and surgeon there. His books include Men Who Have Made the German Empire. His Old Bohemian tales retell his own roaming life. He wrote grammars and translated many books into English. Gladstone later secured him a small government annuity. The entry recalls a restless, many-sided writer.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-szenes-philip-1:
Philip Szenes was a Hungarian painter born at Török Szent Miklos in 1864. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He studied first at Budapest's technical school. Then he gave himself wholly to art. He lived years in Munich, Italy, and Paris.

In 1895 the Paris Academy of Art gave Szenes first prize. He returned to Budapest with that honor fresh. At once he ranked with Hungary's foremost painters. His chief works retell Bible scenes in paint. Samson and Delilah, Esther, and Judith lead the list. He also painted quiet scenes like After Dinner. His canvases hang in Budapest's National Museum. Emperor Francis Joseph kept some in his private gallery. The entry marks a painter crowned early by Paris.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-taylor-charles-:
Charles Taylor was an English Christian Hebraist born in London in 1840. Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He studied at King's College, London, and at Cambridge. He later became master of St. John's College there. His work centered on rabbinic texts in English.

In 1877 Taylor published Sayings of the Jewish Fathers. It is an elaborate edition of the Pirke Abot. A second edition followed in 1897. An 1899 appendix lists its manuscripts in full. Jacobs calls it the finest such work by a living Christian. Taylor found the Jewish source behind the Didache. With Schechter he edited the Wisdom of Ben Sira. Cambridge's Genizah gifts bear the Taylor-Schechter name. The entry honors a Christian master of rabbinic learning.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-thorn-14376:
Thorn, a West Prussian town founded in 1233, long barred Jews from living there. Isidore Singer and I. Rosenberg wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. The Teutonic Knights founded Thorn and excluded Jews. Polish rule after 1453 admitted them only now and then.

Expulsions came in 1766, 1774, 1779, and 1797. Still, families kept returning over the years. By 1823 the community counted 52 families, or 248 people. Its first rabbi served without pay until 1847. A synagogue rose that same year. Scholars such as Zvi Hirsch Kalischer lived in Thorn. A home for the aged opened in 1892. The community also kept a loan society and a literary society. By 1903 the town held 1,200 Jews among 30,000 residents.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-verdun-hebrew-1:
Verdun is a French city, capital of the department of Meuse. Gotthard Deutsch and S. Kahn wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jews lived at Verdun from the twelfth century. Its scholars included the tosafist Samuel ben Hayyim. Samuel ben Joseph and Jacob ben Joseph also taught there.

For long stretches, Jews could not live in Verdun at all. In 1433 the city asked Basel's council to let expelled Jews return. The request failed, and residence stayed banned until 1559. Later French kings let Metz Jews visit briefly for business. A Jew who stayed three days in 1774 was expelled. The entry traces this tight, shifting welcome.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wanefrieden-eli:
Eliakim Getschlik Wanefrieden was a judge and preacher at Amsterdam. Gotthard Deutsch wrote this short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He worked at the end of the eighteenth century. In 1790 he published a pamphlet called Megillat Sefer. It holds sermons and a eulogy. The eulogy honors Saul Löwenstamm, Amsterdam's chief rabbi.

His surname points to Wannfried in Hesse as his birthplace. The entry separates him from a namesake in Moravia. That other Eliakim served as rabbi in Kanitz about 1760. He was likely father to Jeremiah Wanefrieden. Jeremiah defended Jonathan Eybeschütz against heresy charges. The brief note untangles two men of one name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-west-14876:
West is one of the four quarters of heaven and earth. Emil G. Hirsch wrote this short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Hebrew calls the east kedem, meaning front. The west is ahor, meaning rear. Since the Mediterranean Sea lay west of Palestine, the word sea itself came to mean west.

Another term, ma'arab, names the sunset point. In later Hebrew it became the common word for west. Rabbis debated where God's presence, the Shekinah, resides. R. Abbahu placed the Shekinah in the west. That view opposed Babylonian belief about death's gate. Palestine itself was called Ma'araba, the West, from Babylon. Its people were the sons of the West.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wolf-gerson-149:
Gerson Wolf (1823-1892) was an Austrian historian and teacher of Jewish life. Isidore Singer and Newell Dunbar wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in Moravia, he learned Hebrew as a small boy. He later studied Talmud at Nikolsburg and went to Vienna in 1839.

At Vienna he took up teaching, thought, and new tongues. His first piece ran in print in 1845. It set Greek plays beside the plays of his own day. He took part in the street fights of 1848 and 1849. Bold pieces in two papers forced him to leave Vienna for a time. The long entry follows his books and his school work. It shows a writer caught up in the hopes of his age.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yelisavetgrad-e:
Yelisavetgrad is a town in the state of Kherson in Russia. Herman Rosenthal, Isaac Broyde, and S. Janovsky wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It was founded in the year 1754. It grew into a chief town of the south of Russia.

Its name stirs sad thoughts for the Jews of Russia. From that town came the spark for the riots of 1881. When a new czar took the throne, tales of a rise spread. The heads of the Jews asked the governor for guards. No heed was paid to their plea at that hour. On April 27, 1881, the mob broke out at last. A row in an inn on blood use served as the spark. The mob then fell on the shops of the Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zarko-judah-ben:
Judah ben Abraham Zarko was a Hebrew poet famed for fine style. Joseph Jacobs and Isaac Broyde wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He worked at Rhodes in the sixteenth century of this era. On a stay at Constantinople he wrote his chief book.

That book bears the name Lehem Yehudah in Hebrew tongue. It holds a tale on the soul in figure form. It holds verse and prose poems side by side in it. It holds sharp short verse at the great men of his day. Some of that verse is aimed at Maimonides himself. A note of his stands at the head of a style book. More of his short poems came out in a London book. That book was made by Edelmann in the year 1853.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zoan-15276:
Zoan was an ancient Egyptian city, nearly as old as Hebron in the Bible's telling. Emil G. Hirsch and W. Max Muller wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Isaiah ranks its princes beside those of Memphis, and Ezekiel names it with Thebes. Israelite embassies went to Zoan, which hints it was once a royal residence.

The Greeks called the city Tanis. It stood in the Nile Delta, on the Tanitic branch, near Lake Menzalah and Egypt's northeast frontier. Kings of the twenty-first dynasty, called Tanitic, ruled from there. Digging by Mariette in 1860 and Petrie in 1883 uncovered monuments from the sixth dynasty to Roman times. By then the great city had shrunk toward a fishing village.
legge-the-shih-king-or-book-of-poetry-sh:
James Legge Englished China's oldest songbook in The Shih King, issued in 1876 with the Chinese text beside his version. Its 305 songs date from about the eleventh to the seventh century before Christ. Love songs, war songs, and harvest hymns all stand in its pages.

Legge, a Scottish scholar and missionary, gave Victorian readers a window on ancient China. Court odes praise kings, while folk ballads sing of longing and toil. The book formed part of the Sacred Books of the East series. Few anthologies anywhere are older or more loved, and this version pairs sound learning with the original words.
life-of-johnson-volume-2-1765-1776:
Boswell's second volume covers Johnson's life from 1765 to 1776. Hill's edition places the years November 1765 to March 1776 inside. Appendices preserve Johnson's autograph records in the Bodleian Library. Another appendix gives his sentiments toward his American fellow-subjects.

The text opens with Johnson busy on his Shakespeare edition. For over two years he sent Boswell not a single letter. Yet he constantly helped friends revise works and dedications. In that courtly composition, Boswell says, no man excelled him. His sentiments toward American fellow-subjects fill another appendix section. Johnson apologised handsomely for the long epistolary silence later.
lissagaray-history-of-commune-1876:
Prosper-Olivier Lissagaray wrote this history of the Paris Commune. He composed the French original in 1876, close to events. Eleanor Marx Aveling translated it for English readers. New York's International Publishing Company issued her version in 1898.

She explains the translation follows Lissagaray's revised second edition. France's government had refused to allow that edition's publication. Lissagaray himself added nearly a hundred pages for English readers. Her father corrected the translation, and she left it as he knew it. Prisoners in New Caledonia dated some passages by 1898, she admits. Patchwork updating would spoil the work, she argues in her preface.
maskelyne-modern-spiritualism-1876:
John Nevil Maskelyne shows the tricks of the dark room in Modern Spiritualism, his bust book of 1876. Maskelyne was the top stage mage of London. He and his mate built a famed hall of feats. Seers, he says, use the same craft: hid ropes, false hands, and dark to fake the shapes and sounds that guests take for the dead at work.

He prints how each feat is done, step by step. His aim is to save the crowd from fraud. The book is the stage's best word on the theme. Its scorn still stings.
maxwell-matter-and-motion-1876:
Matter and Motion, published in 1876, is James Clerk Maxwell's short primer on the laws of moving bodies. Maxwell wrote it for beginners, not experts. In a few brief chapters he lays out the ground rules of Newtonian mechanics.

He covers space, time, velocity, force, and work, each defined with care. Worked examples show how the same laws govern a falling stone and a circling planet. Because Maxwell writes so clearly, the book became a model science primer, and students of physics still use it to meet the subject. Each short chapter builds on the last, so the logic stays easy to follow.
moliere-dramatic-works-vanlaun-vol4-1876:
Tartuffe, the most famous of all Molière's plays, leads volume four of van Laun's set, published in 1876. Tartuffe is a religious fraud who worms into a rich man's house and nearly steals all he owns. The play was banned for years in France for its daring.

Sharing the volume are Mélicerte, a pastoral piece left unfinished, and The Sicilian, a short musical comedy. Amphitryon retells the Greek myth of Jupiter wooing a mortal wife. George Dandin mocks a rich peasant who marries above his station and regrets it. Van Laun's notes trace how each play fared on the Paris stage.
moliere-dramatic-works-vanlaun-vol5-1876:
Volume five of van Laun's Molière, published in 1876, opens with The Miser. Harpagon, its grasping hero, loves his money box more than his own children. His greed drives the plot through loans, thefts, and crossed love affairs until the box itself is stolen.

The volume also gives Monsieur de Pourceaugnac, a farce about a country lawyer tormented in Paris. The Magnificent Lovers is a court spectacle in mythic dress. The Citizen Who Apes the Nobleman laughs at a rich tradesman hiring tutors to seem grand. Psyche, a grand verse tragedy with ballet, closes the volume in a very different key.
moliere-dramatic-works-vanlaun-vol6-1876:
