Validated in mouse muscle, the method's area distributions from routine pink stained paraffin sections matched those from a comparison stain and from frozen sections. In a nerve injury model it correctly registered the shrinkage of fibers cut off from their nerve. The payoff is access: decades of stored slides become measurable, and small laboratories without specialist kit can join neuromuscular research on equal terms.
plos-pone-0358576: Zuo and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on diet, sleep, and lung cancer in southwest China. They compared patients with lung cancer against people without it, in a case-control design. The focus was on polyunsaturated fats in food and on sleep patterns. Links found in such studies can shape diet and sleep advice, though they need care before being read as causes.
plos-pone-0358776: Shimagaki and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on outlook after liver cancer surgery. They tested a blood-based index, built from C-reactive protein, albumin, and lymphocyte counts, measured before surgery. The question was whether that index predicts how patients fare after part of the liver is removed. A cheap score from routine blood tests could help surgeons judge risk before operating.
plos-pone-0359776:
Joshua Vo and six colleagues published this protocol in PLOS ONE in 2026. It plans a scoping review of how medical students and residents around the world are taught telemedicine. Telemedicine, care delivered by video or phone, became a core skill during recent years, yet training in it varies wildly between schools.

A scoping review will map what is taught, where, and how it is evaluated, across countries. Medical schools building telemedicine teaching need that world map before writing their own courses. Educators and accreditation bodies are the audience for a review designed to show the gaps in training.
plos-pone-0359976:
Lei Zhu and colleagues built in 2026 a mosquito recognition system that runs on a mobile device. Identifying mosquito species matters because only some kinds spread diseases such as dengue and malaria, and control efforts differ by species. Their system uses a convolutional neural network, the image recognizing form of deep learning, trained to judge mosquitoes by two kinds of shape evidence at once, which the authors call dual morphology.

Putting the trained model on a phone moves identification out of the laboratory and into the field, where health workers and citizens actually encounter the insects. Fast, accurate identification can sharpen surveillance maps and help target spraying and breeding site removal. The study joins a growing set of phone based tools for tracking disease carrying insects.
plos-pone-0360076:
Andrew Tusubira and colleagues reviewed in 2026 how people living with HIV manage their own care when they also live with high blood pressure or diabetes. Their systematic review gathers studies from low and middle income countries, where clinics are stretched and patients carry much of the daily work of staying well. Self-care covers taking medicines faithfully, watching diet and symptoms, and knowing when to seek help.

Having three long term conditions at once multiplies that work, and health systems built around single diseases can leave such patients unsupported. By mapping what self-care looks like and what helps or hinders it, the review gives program designers a view from the patient's side of the clinic door.
plos-pone-0360376:
Jhon Zabaleta-Santisteban and a large team of collaborators mapped in 2026 where cacao could grow well in the Amazonas region of Peru. Their approach is an ensemble of predictive models, combined through a platform called BIOMOD2, that weighs many data sources at once. The maps fold in territorial management and plant health alongside climate and soil, so the result speaks to farming decisions rather than to climate alone.

Cacao is a valuable export crop and an alternative livelihood in regions pressed by deforestation. Knowing which land suits it, and which land should be left alone, helps planners steer planting toward success and away from forest clearing. The study gives regional authorities a planning tool grounded in the region's own conditions.
plos-pone-0360476:
Amine Ben Safta and colleagues ran a randomized trial in 2026 on the pressure used during a common gallbladder operation. In laparoscopic cholecystectomy, surgeons inflate the abdomen with gas, a pneumoperitoneum, to see and work, and the operation is usually done at standard pressure. Some surgeons argued that a lower pressure, eight millimeters of mercury, would leave patients in less pain afterward.

Patients were assigned by chance to the low pressure or the standard approach, and their pain was scored on a visual analog scale after surgery. The trial's headline result is plainly stated: the lower pressure did not significantly reduce those pain scores. A clear negative answer is useful, since it tells surgical teams that this particular adjustment is not where pain relief will be found.
pmc-10654176:
Monica Barr Agholme and a team of co-authors track mouth problems in children who receive stem cell transplants from donors. Their twenty twenty-three multicenter study deals with oral mucositis, a painful soreness and ulceration of the mouth lining. It is common in transplant care and can block eating and swallowing.

Sixty-eight children at three sites were enrolled, and sixty-three were followed through the low-white-cell phase until the graft took hold. Half developed mucositis of grade two to four, worst at about eight to eleven days after the infusion. Nearly nine in ten had some mouth complaint. Blisters and ulcers bothered them most, and four in ten reported severe pain that cut into daily life.
pmc-10655276:
Yaqin Yang and eight co-authors built a tool to call the risk that ovarian cancer has spread to lymph nodes, in a study from twenty twenty-three. Data came from patients at three medical centers over eight years. The team used ultrasound findings and clinical data, and built the tool with a regression model.

In the training group of three hundred sixty-eight patients, about twenty-seven percent had spread to lymph nodes. Tumor width, tumors in more than one spot, and a growth marker called Ki67 stood out as risk factors on their own. The tool scored well at telling apart patients with and without spread, in both the training and check groups, and its risk calls matched real outcomes well. The authors say it can help teams pick the right surgery and care plan for each patient.
pmc-10655476:
Hongyu Wang and Lin Zhong write to the editor about a sepsis study and a lurking virus in a 2023 comment. The study under discussion linked testing positive for human cytomegalovirus, a common herpesvirus, to worse survival in sepsis. It also found that standard biomarkers predicted outcomes only in patients carrying the virus. Wang and Zhong raise aspects they think were missed.

Their sharpest point is a puzzle in the reactivation rate. The reported share of patients whose dormant virus woke up is much lower than in earlier studies, even though this cohort held many immune-weakened patients, who should reactivate more. They ask whether some patients quietly received preventive antiviral treatment, as transplant patients routinely do. Such details could shift what the original numbers mean.
pmc-10656076:
Jessica Oster and co-authors published a climate study in 2023 on a cold span long ago. About sixteen thousand years back, the western United States was much wetter than now. Rivers of moist air from the Pacific likely fed that wet spell. At the same time, meltwater poured into the North Atlantic.

The team ran climate models of that past span. Adding meltwater to the North Atlantic cooled that ocean and slowed its great current. The models then showed more moist air rivers and more winter rain in the west. The rain came from the southeast North Pacific. The link matters now, since the same Atlantic current may be weakening again. A weaker current could shift rain patterns in the west.
pmc-10656576:
Kei Saito and Masatomo Yashima report a new proton-conducting material in two thousand twenty-three. Such materials could serve in fuel cells that run on protons. The usual way to raise conductivity, adding acceptor dopants, traps protons near the dopants and hurts performance at lower temperatures.

Their material is a cubic perovskite with built-in oxygen vacancies, stabilized by molybdenum donor doping. It showed high proton conductivity in the temperature range known as the Norby gap. It also stayed stable in oxidizing, reducing, and carbon dioxide atmospheres. The authors credit high proton mobility, less trapping, and three-dimensional paths through the crystal. They propose donor doping of such vacancy-rich oxides as a general strategy.
pmc-10660976:
Haoyu Dong and four co-authors pooled past research on a heart rhythm fault in a 2023 review. The fault lies in the heart's natural pacemaker, and its link to stroke was unclear. Some patients also have a second rhythm problem, and the team wanted to know how much that changes the risk.

They searched three databases and kept six studies covering a very large number of patients. Yearly stroke rates were about the same with or without the second rhythm problem. Prior stroke, high blood pressure, and heart failure each raised the risk. The authors say the pacemaker fault alone deserves stroke prevention attention, and call for more study.
pmc-10669176:
Ameer Zahoor and co-authors fuse, in a 2023 study, two proven anticancer building blocks into a new family of compounds and test them on liver cancer cells. The design, called molecular hybridization, welds an indole unit to a triazole ring and finishes the molecule with varied aryl tails. Six variants were synthesized and screened against the Hep-G2 liver cancer line, with two standard drugs as the yardstick.

Four variants bit hard. The one carrying a double-chlorinated tail bit hardest of all, leaving about eleven percent of cancer cells alive, level with the best reference drug. Computer docking, stability simulation, and drug-likeness profiling all pointed the same way. The authors name that variant their lead compound, fit for the long road of animal testing that separates a cell result from a medicine.
pmc-10684276:
Leonard Jack, editor in chief of the journal Preventing Chronic Disease, closes twenty twenty-three with a review of the journal's year, in work from twenty twenty-three. The column reports gains in reach and standing, new student programs, and calls for papers for twenty twenty-four.

The journal's impact factor rose for a third year and hit five point five for twenty twenty-two. Rankings placed it high among open access public health journals in the United States and worldwide. Six collections ran in twenty twenty-three, one on fighting racism through research and practice. A new student committee for writing and review training was formed. The column thanks editors, reviewers, and authors for the momentum.
pmc-10687276:
Noémie Tanguay and nine co-authors studied antidepressant use in pregnancy and child development at age two, in a study from twenty twenty-three. About one in twenty pregnant women takes these drugs. Past work cleared them on thinking skills but gave mixed verdicts on movement and language, and rarely accounted for the mother's own distress.

In a large pregnancy cohort, a small share of mothers reported antidepressant use. Their toddlers scored lower on fine and rough movement scales. Thinking and language scores showed no clear link. The team adjusted for mothers' depressive symptoms and stress during pregnancy. They also probed knock-on paths through birth complications and whether boys and girls differed. Full results are reported for each check.
pmc-10694876:
Jin Liu and colleagues link personality traits to the distorted thinking patterns seen in depression, in this case-control study from China, published in twenty twenty-three. Dysfunctional attitudes are rigid, self-critical rules of thought that feed low mood. The team asked which personality domains, from a sixteen-factor test, travel with them, in patients and in healthy people alike.

One hundred sixty-eight patients with major depression and one hundred thirty healthy controls took both tests. Across both groups, the attitudes clustered with the anxiety side of personality: emotional instability, vigilance, apprehension, and tension. The traits doing the explaining differed by group, though. In patients, stability, conscientiousness, and apprehension led; in controls, vigilance and tension led. The authors conclude that anxious personality coloring shapes faulty attitudes in everyone, but the mix shifts with illness, a point for tailoring therapy.
pmc-10694976:
Qin Huang, Yangbin Fang, Yao Lai, and Hongfei Liao report a clinical study from two thousand twenty-three on a shrunken eye socket. In a contracted socket, the space that should hold an artificial eye has tightened. All patients in the study had surgery using grafts of white-of-the-eye tissue taken from donors.

Half the patients also got low-level laser therapy after surgery, while the rest healed without it. The laser was applied once a day for five minutes over seven days, starting a week after the operation. The team then tracked both groups for six months. They watched how fast blood vessels grew into the graft and how the socket depth changed.
pmc-10696876:
Ye Yang and colleagues studied pre-surgery scans in womb cancer in 2023. Whole-body sugar scans can reveal how aggressive a tumor is. The team reviewed just over two hundred patients in Shanghai. All had scans before surgery for endometrial cancer. Three scan measures were tested against surgical findings. They were peak uptake, tumor volume, and total sugar use. Targets were deep muscle invasion and neck-of-womb invasion. Spread to lymph nodes was the third target.

All three measures linked strongly to the surgical findings. Accuracy and ruling-out power ran very high. The team built a risk model from best cutoff values. Volume and total sugar cutoffs split patients by outlook. Larger volumes marked poorer survival in follow-up. Node-positive scans with big volumes also fared worse. The authors call scan cutoffs independent warning signs. Surgeons could use them to plan wider operations.
pmc-10698976:
Mark Mohan Kaggwa and a large team study self-harm among forensic patients in Ontario, Canada. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-three. These patients are held under a review board after a court finds them unfit or not responsible. Their safety, and the public's, is a core duty of the system.

They scan a board data bank for two years. A small share of patients show self-harm acts in that span. Two system traits track with self-harm: being found unfit to stand trial, and being an inpatient. The kind of offence, the victim's link to the patient, and past crime do not track with it. The authors call for close watch and care plans shaped to each inpatient.
pmc-10700276:
Sakib Hossen and seven colleagues published a computational vaccine design study in two thousand twenty-three against human parainfluenza virus 3. The virus causes serious respiratory illness with no vaccine or specific therapy. The team used immune-informatics to assemble a multi-piece peptide vaccine on paper.

Three stable viral proteins supplied the building blocks. Chosen immune-triggering fragments covered over ninety-nine percent of the world population and avoided any match to human proteins. The stitched construct ran four hundred seventy-eight amino acids and scored stable, antigenic, and non-toxic in simulations. It bound immune sensors firmly in docking models. A bacterial production plan was drafted virtually. Lab testing remains entirely ahead.
pmc-10700376:
Parvez Anwar and seven co-authors test how mixing two rice varieties, and staggering their planting dates, affects yield and profit. Their study came out in 2023 and was run at a farm university in Bangladesh. One variety is tall, late, and fine-grained, while the other is shorter and coarse-grained.

In the first trial, mixed plantings yielded more than either variety grown alone. The best profit came from one of the mixed ratios, well above the fine variety alone. In the second trial, planting the coarse variety a week before the fine one gave the highest return. The authors advise that mixed planting with a head start for one variety.
pmc-10702076:
Haiyi Long and co-authors report a single-center experience from two thousand twenty-three using heat ablation for liver cancer that returned in children. Recurrent liver cancer in children is rare and hard to treat. Radiofrequency ablation burns tumors through the skin under ultrasound guidance, avoiding open surgery.

The team reviewed ten children, aged six to seventeen, treated between two thousand seven and two thousand twenty-one for fifteen recurrent tumors. The first ablation cleared fourteen of the fifteen lesions. No local regrowth appeared over an average follow-up of about five years. Survival was seventy-eight percent at one year and forty-four percent at three years, while five children died, mostly of disease progression. The authors conclude the method is safe and feasible for these young patients.
pmc-10702276:
Uchenna Ajoku and Linda Iroegbu-Emeruem present a case series from two thousand twenty-three on a common brain bleeding condition that showed up in uncommon ways. Chronic subdural haematoma is a slow blood collection under the skull lining, frequent in the elderly. Its signs are often vague. They are often blamed on pressure or irritation of the brain surface.

The series covers four patients whose stories did not point to the diagnosis at first. They include a young woman with a drooping eyelid and wide pupil, and an elderly man unable to move his legs. Another man had an isolated foot drop, and a young soldier had no injury history. In each case only brain imaging revealed the collection. The authors stress early scanning for odd neurological signs.
pmc-10704876:
Ana Nunes Santos and her five co-authors, publishing in 2023, describe a new parasitic worm species from a Brazilian Amazon tree frog. The worms belong to a genus that infests the guts of frogs and reptiles across the Neotropics. Under light and electron microscopes, the specimens showed a signature mix of traits. Both sexes carry side flanges and surface bumps. Males have short, equal mating spines and no steering plate. The count of tail bumps around the vent is distinctive.

The find is the genus's first record in this frog host and its fifty-eighth known species. The team also tidies the family tree. Adding a missing trait pattern for one known species, they argue another, long filed in this genus, belongs in a neighboring one instead. Taxonomy papers like this one build the reference shelf that parasite surveys and biodiversity counts depend on.
pmc-10708976:
Paulo Henrique Schmidt Lara and co-authors review, in a 2023 study, shoulder surgery outcomes for high-demand athletes with an unstable shoulder joint. In these injuries the socket loses bone, and a bone block operation rebuilds it. The authors asked whether bigger bone loss leads to worse motion, function, or more complications after the operation.

Over five years, 41 shoulders had the surgery. Twenty had bone loss up to fifteen percent, and twenty-one had losses between fifteen and twenty-five percent. The two groups showed no clear differences in complications, new dislocations, or return to sport. Motion ranges and function scores also matched between groups. The authors conclude that bone loss size alone did not drive results, and that the operation served both small and large losses well.
pmc-10710576:
Keiko Nomura, Hisato Tagawa, Shuji Yamaguchi, and Laureline Gatellier report, in a 2023 paper, what a patient alliance does all day, and what its members still lack. A brain tumor diagnosis shocks patients and families across body, feelings, money, and social life, and the needs outlast treatment. The Japan Brain Tumor Alliance, founded in 2006, runs monthly gatherings where patients and families share daily problems. It circulates current information, works with other patient groups at home and abroad, and brings patient voices into research planning.

The alliance helped produce a support book with rehabilitation therapists and nurses and leaflets on supportive care, including planning ahead. Its survey, running since April 2023, found that patients and caregivers struggle to voice their concerns. They also rarely meet the range of professionals who could help. The authors conclude that daily-life support must grow beyond the hospital's walls.
pmc-10714476:
Seda Cinar, Dilek Isik Tasgin, and Canan Unaleroglu published a 2023 study of a switch in chemical synthesis. The same starting materials can end in two kinds of ring. The substituent chosen decides which kind forms. Rings of this family sit at the heart of dyes, drugs, and light-based goods. One ring kind holds four building blocks of one sort and two of another. The other holds three and one.

The team ran the syntheses with a copper salt as the catalyst. They then traced the steps with a sensitive mass spectrometry tool that reads the mixture as the reaction runs. Short-lived intermediate forms showed up in the readings, in two-block and three-block chains. Those intermediates feed the two pre-ring shapes, the team says. The work shows how the starting choice steers the ring, with the pathway read live.
pmc-10715976:
Ki Park and Natalie A. Bello wrote this two thousand twenty-three review of cardio-obstetrics, the field where pregnancy care meets cardiovascular medicine. They note that cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of pregnancy-related death in the United States. Maternal deaths and complications have risen over recent decades. Contributing factors include older mothers, more obesity and other risk factors, and better survival of patients with congenital heart disease.

The authors explain that most patients with heart conditions can be guided safely through pregnancy with careful risk management. The problem is a shortage of clinicians trained for this work. They call for cardio-obstetrics care teams spanning cardiology, obstetrics, maternal-fetal medicine, and family medicine, covering care from preconception through the postpartum period.
pmc-10716976:
Ghaidaa Khalifa and co-authors published a 2023 survey study on how adults in Saudi Arabia view alternative medicine for autism. Autism is a developmental condition affecting social and communication skills. Alongside standard care, many families try other practices, from special diets to local traditions such as Zamzam water and black seeds. The authors asked the wider public what it thinks of these options.

An online questionnaire reached 4,311 adults across the country. Two-thirds of those who answered were women. Just over half said they knew about autism. Many believed some non-drug approaches could help, led by art therapy and physical exercise. About half doubted that traditional treatment alone can help autism. Only a fifth backed some of the other practices asked about. The study maps public attitudes that clinics and health campaigns in the kingdom need to work with.
pmc-10729976:
John Hunyara and co-authors study a molecule that shapes how the eye connects to the brain's daily clock, in a paper from 2023. Some eye cells sense light directly and send signals to a small brain area that runs the body clock. How those wires find their target was not well known.

The molecule, called teneurin-3, is common in one cell type in the clock area. In mice that lack it, the wiring from the light-sensing eye cells to that area was reduced in one zone. Links between two cell groups inside the area also changed. Yet the mice were more sensitive to light, not less, and reset their clocks faster after a shift. The work shows the molecule both guides wiring and tunes response.
pmc-10731176:
Moonhwan Kim and co-authors present a 2023 case report on liver transplant artery spasm. Artery blockage after transplant can doom the graft. A 57-year-old man with hepatitis B liver disease and liver cancer got a living donor transplant. The blood types were incompatible, a harder setting. Right after the artery join, the pulse weakened sharply. A second join through another artery still gave a poor pulse.

Scans showed diffuse spasm along the artery, like beads on a string. The team infused a fat-carried prostaglandin drug straight into the artery. That route targets the spasm at its site. Transplant surgeons get a worked rescue for a feared early complication. Spasm differs from clot, and the fix differs too. A case that names the pattern and the response can save grafts when minutes count.
pmc-10733176:
Keisuke Saito and co-authors traced how a signal travels across a key gap inside photosystem II, the plant protein complex that splits water and releases oxygen. A tyrosine unit called TyrZ passes electrons between the water-splitting manganese cluster and the rest of the machinery. When TyrZ is oxidized, a proton ends up moving about eleven angstroms away, and the route was puzzling.

Quantum and molecular simulations show the message travels through water, not direct force. Oxidation breaks one unusually strong hydrogen bond. A nearby water molecule swings to donate a new bond to the cluster. That shift frees a proton to hop along a second strong bond to a distant aspartate. The authors call the linked chain a Grotthuss-like network, echoing how protons relay through water.
pmc-10735176:
Many people carrying the COVID virus have few or no symptoms, yet they can still spread it, and emergency rooms rarely test them. Judith Leblanc led a large team that ran a trial in eighteen emergency departments across the Paris area in early twenty twenty-one. In turns, each site either kept its usual testing, aimed at the sick and admitted, or added nurse-led testing offered to everyone else who walked in.

The trial covered more than one hundred and thirty-eight thousand visits across both periods. At the added-testing sites, over six thousand symptom-free patients filled in a risk questionnaire, and nurses tested more than four thousand of them. The study weighed whether that extra reach raised the share of infections found among all visitors.
pmc-10736476:
Pablo Martinez Amezcua and co-authors (2023) tested whether hearing loss travels with frailty in older Americans. Frailty brings weakness, slowness, and exhaustion, and raises the risk of disability and death. Hearing loss touches about two-thirds of older adults and links to isolation and poorer function. The team analyzed 2,361 participants from a national aging study in 2021. Hearing was measured by tone testing; frailty by the standard five-part phenotype.

Seventy-three percent of participants had some hearing loss. Those with moderate or worse loss had notably higher odds of being frail rather than robust, with an odds ratio near 1.8. The pattern strengthened with worse hearing. The authors suggest hearing loss may be a genuine risk factor for frailty, not just a fellow traveler of age. Trials of hearing treatment as frailty prevention, they argue, could matter for public health.
pmc-10736576:
Han, Lee, and Kim present a study from twenty twenty-three on contact-free sports and self-rated health in older Korean adults. The pandemic closed sports facilities, which threatened older adults' bodies and minds. Data come from a national survey of adults over sixty-five who exercise regularly. Over eleven hundred people enter the analysis. Age links to worse self-rated health and stamina in their models. Taking part in contact-free sports changes that age link, though. The age penalty shows only among non-participants.

Participants keep steadier health and stamina ratings with age. The authors read this as a buffer against age-related decline. Contact-free activity is urged as vital during outbreaks. The findings speak to keeping older adults active when facilities close.
pmc-10737376:
Zainab Toteh Osakwe, Michelle Odlum, Amarilis Céspedes, and Sasha Perez study how home health aides view telehealth for patients with dementia, in a paper from 2023. The pandemic pushed home care visits onto video at speed. Patients with dementia lean on aides to voice their needs to the care team. The team asked whether remote visits truly work for that group.

They interviewed twenty-five aides from four agencies in the summer of 2020. Aides favored platforms with live video, since faces make the talk feel human. They saw telehealth as a supplement, never a swap, for in-person nurse visits. Handling a tablet while giving hands-on care added strain. Many also felt their training on the tools was too thin. The authors urge agencies to plan telehealth with aides, not around them.
pmc-10737576:
Aya Yoshikawa and Richard Fortinsky wrote this research paper, published in 2023, on pain medicine and falls among older adults who live at home. It focuses on people with arthritis, who often take pain medicine and already face a higher risk of falling.

The authors studied Medicare beneficiaries in a 2015 national survey on health and aging. People with arthritis reported far more pain and pain medicine use than those without arthritis. Among those with arthritis, taking pain medicine was linked to a higher chance of falls. Taking it every day raised the risk more. Balance problems were an even stronger factor. The paper flags daily pain medicine use as a fall risk worth watching in arthritis care.
pmc-10738576:
Maia McLin and Danielle Nadorff compare how a child's belief in self-control relates to grades, depending on who is raising the child. Their study appeared in 2023. About six million American children live with grandparents, many without a parent present. The team surveyed 323 caregiving grandparents and 105 foster parents nationwide. Grandchildren reported a stronger sense of control over their schoolwork than foster children did, though reported grades did not differ between the groups.

The link between control beliefs and grades was strong in both groups but stronger for foster children. After accounting for caregiver age and means, the difference between groups held. The authors say caregiver type changes how much a child's mindset matters, which interventions should respect.
pmc-10738876:
Erica Fan and co-authors study how living in a deprived area shapes the link between brain markers of Alzheimer's disease and thinking skills, in a paper from 2023. Most past validation of these markers came from White groups. Black adults face higher risk and more social disadvantage, so the gap matters.

The cohort held just under two hundred adults aged fifty and older, half of them Black. Brain scans measured thinning of the cortex and white matter damage, and a second scan measured amyloid, a protein tied to the disease. Higher area deprivation, more brain shrinkage, and more white matter damage each linked to worse thinking scores. The mix of deprivation and shrinkage shaped memory recall in a pattern the authors explore.
pmc-10739376:
Tobi Abramson, Jo Anne Sirey, and Jacquelin Berman present new ways to give mental health care to older adults in a session report from twenty twenty-three. The work deals with the triple burden of age bias, mental health stigma, and race bias. It sums up results from three service models used in community settings.

One program gave brief help to older victims of abuse or crime, and video care worked as well as care in person. A peer-led program helped most people with low food access feel less depressed. A third program placed care inside senior centers and saw clear gains in mood and less loneliness.
pmc-10741876:
Christina Schröder and colleagues compare two focused radiation schedules for prostate cancer, five sessions against seven, in this matched analysis from twenty twenty-three. Nearly two hundred men with intermediate or high-risk disease were treated at two centers: the five-fraction group on a robotic platform, the seven-fraction on a standard machine. Propensity matching balanced one hundred twenty for the head-to-head.

Both schedules controlled the cancer well early, with few relapses. The difference was collateral damage in the gut. The seven-fraction patients suffered significantly more moderate bowel toxicity, acute and late, including one severe bleed in an anticoagulated man. Urinary toxicity ran similar. PSA fell further in the five-fraction group. Follow-up is short, a median of thirteen months, and the authors withhold a final verdict, but the gut signal favors five.
pmc-10742076:
Andrea Alberti and co-authors audit side effects of prostate biopsy at a large Italian center in a 2023 paper. The biopsy style studied passes the needle through the rectum, guided by MRI targets. European guidance now favors a route through the skin instead, mainly for its lower infection risk.

The center tracked 458 patients biopsied from 2020 to 2022 under a strict shared pathway. About forty-four percent reported some problem afterward. Most were mild, led by blood in the urine, while about nine percent had moderate issues such as blocked urination. The audit sets a fair baseline for judging the switch: the older route, done carefully, was safer than its reputation. Centers can weigh that record against the newer route's gains.
pmc-10742976:
Julia Wittenborn and a team of co-authors piloted a new mark to triage a hard cervical case. Their pilot study, from twenty twenty-three, deals with patients whose transformation zone in the cervix cannot be seen. That type three zone brings strife in colposcopy care, since harm can hide from view. The team asked if tiny RNA bits, called miRNAs, could flag high grade cell change in such cases.

They took mucosa samples with a brush at routine visits. Patients were split by tissue and cell results and by a standard virus test. Groups with high grade change were set next to clear ones. Readers who screen for cervical cancer get a first read on a bloodless mark for a blind spot in care.
pmc-10743176:
Fenghao Liu and co-authors present a 2023 journal article on genes behind queen fertility in the red imported fire ant. The invasive ant breeds fast and spreads damage, so its reproduction is a target. The team compared gene activity across queens, winged females, and males, then zoomed in on genes loud and specific in queens. Two vitellogenin genes, egg-yolk protein makers, stood out.

Both genes ran highest in queens and winged females, above all in the thorax. Silencing either gene, or both, shrank ovaries and cut egg laying. The authors present the pair as proven fertility factors and candidate targets for ant control.
pmc-10744076:
Rafael Salido-Vallejo and five co-authors compare outcomes of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma in organ transplant patients versus people with sound immune systems, in a look back cohort study. This skin cancer is the second most common skin tumor, and weak immunity raises its risks. The study came out in twenty twenty-three.

Cases came from one Spanish hospital across many years, with age, clinical, and tissue data logged. Rates of local return and spread were higher in tumors from transplant patients than in others. The team also read progression free survival and hunted for risk factors within the transplant group by single factor tests.
pmc-10744576:
Manuela Manziuc and co-authors wrote a review from 2023 on a new ceramic used for crowns and other dental fixes. The material blends two known ceramics. One gives a glass-like look that suits front teeth. The other, a hard white oxide, adds strength. The mix aims to give both looks and strength in one block that machines can mill.

The team searched three large databases for studies on the material's look, strength, and gluing. Its inner structure makes it tougher than older glass ceramics but less clear, so light passes less well. Tooth color below and glue shade both shift the final look. Strength scores beat those of plain glass ceramics and hybrid types, though not the strongest oxide alone. Acid etch and sand blasting are the main ways to prep its surface for glue. The team notes that long-term mouth data are still thin.
pmc-10747976:
Peng Zhang, Hongyuan Wen, Zhiyong Xu, and Zhao Zhao present a noise-hardy way to measure the time gap between two sensors hearing the same sound, in this 2023 paper. That gap pins down where a sound came from, but background noise scrambles it. Their method leans on a simple split: noise splashes arrive with random delays, while true signal points share one lag.

A four-step routine roughs out the delay, rearranges the time-frequency picture to part signal from noise, keeps the points flanking the delay ridge, and then refines the estimate. A sharpened second-order variant packs the signal energy tighter. In simulations and bench tests, the approach beat existing methods on both accuracy and robustness.
pmc-10749476:
Kim Greis and co-authors read the infrared fingerprints of fluorenyl cations held in ultracold helium drops, in a study from two thousand twenty-three. The ions are classic cases in the old puzzle of ring systems that break the aroma rule. Bare ions were made by spray, sorted by mass, then trapped in cold drops.

A tunable laser scanned a wide infrared band at fine detail. Matched with density functional math, the sharp spectra show all ions sit in their singlet state. The result pins shapes for a textbook antiaromatic family in the gas phase. Readers in physical chemistry get clean spectra where warmth and solvent blur are gone.
pmc-10754676:
Szu-Chi Chen and co-authors present a 2023 community study from Taiwan on a blood protein and later cancer risk. The protein, called VAP-1, helps white cells stick to vessel walls and plays a part in inflammation and tumor growth. The team asked whether its level in healthy people predicts cancer or death over the long term.

The study enrolled 889 cancer-free adults from 2006 and tracked them to 2018 through registries. In about twelve years, 69 people got cancer and 66 died. Those with the highest third of protein levels faced clearly higher risks of cancer, cancer death, and death from any cause. The links held after the team weighed other factors. A cheap blood test of this kind could one day help flag people for closer watch.
pmc-10782476:
Takeru Takahashi, Koshi Nagai, and Kazumasa Kotake weigh whether a Japanese herbal formula can prevent diarrhea from cancer drugs. The diarrhea can be severe and can force treatment to stop. Past trials of the formula disagreed, so the team pooled the proof from randomized trials. Three studies, all using the same cancer drug, met their bar.

Pooled results showed no clear cut in severe diarrhea against mixed comparison groups, and no change in mild diarrhea. Against no treatment alone, though, severe diarrhea did fall. The authors judge the proof thin and of low quality, and call for larger trials before the formula is trusted for this use.
pmc-10827976:
Hach, Bertsch, and Nonell published in twenty twenty-four a study of psychiatric drug use in suicidal teenagers. Few psychiatric drugs are approved for adolescents, so off-label use is common. The team checked urine and blood samples from teens admitted for acute suicidality. Samples reflected the drugs they took as outpatients before admission. More than two hundred cases were included, most of them girls.

Over half the teens took at least one prescribed psychiatric drug. Off-label use was far more common for one drug class than for antidepressants. Depressed teens were more often treated within approved labels than teens with stress disorders. Girls showed high drug blood levels much more often than boys. The authors urge blood-level checks to improve safety. They also call for more real-world evidence in this age group.
pmc-10834876:
Jun Li and co-authors published this study in 2023. It tests a two-drug combo against acute myeloid leukemia, a fast blood cancer. The drugs are azacitidine and homoharringtonine, both already used in blood cancers. In lab leukemia cells, the pair arrested growth more than either drug alone. Formal scoring confirmed true synergy. Colonies shrank, and cell death rose sharply in two cell lines.

Gene reads traced the effect to a stress pathway inside the cells. The combo lowered a growth driver called c-MYC while raising a death chain through DDIT3 and PUMA. Blocking parts of that chain blunted the synergy, confirming the route. The authors propose the pair as a candidate regimen worth clinical testing. The paper appeared in a Chinese journal, with an English abstract.
pmc-10877376:
Kubota and co-authors lay out a trial plan for schizophrenia care in a protocol paper. Thinking problems are a core part of the illness and linked to poor outcomes, yet drugs or social training alone help only a little. The trial tests pairing brain training with one of two drugs.

Patients will be assigned by chance to get either lurasidone or paliperidone, each paired with the same training program. The first six weeks use drug treatment alone, followed by twenty-four weeks of combined care. The main measure is change in a tablet-based thinking score. The team will also track social function, symptoms, quality of life, and safety. The plan was published in two thousand twenty-four, with the study dated two thousand twenty-three in its head.
pmc-11531876:
Iara Diamela Rodriguez and Leonardo Ariel Saravia weigh the strength of links in an Antarctic food web in this twenty twenty-four study. Warming has shifted the species mix around the West Antarctic Peninsula in recent decades. Knowing which species hold the web together helps judge how the system copes with change.

The pair studied Potter Cove, off the South Shetland Islands. They estimated how strongly each species affects the ones it eats or feeds, then removed species one by one on a computer to see how stability and web break-up changed. Strong links were unevenly spread. The work names the heavyweight species whose loss would shake the cove most.
pmc-11531976:
Huang, Chen, and Lin published in twenty twenty-four an editorial on a leech-based traditional medicine for high uric acid. The medicine is a freeze-dried powder from a medicinal leech species. A recent study found its protein extract lowers blood uric acid in tests. It blocks an enzyme that makes uric acid in the body.

It also adjusts transport proteins in kidney and gut to clear more uric acid. The editorial weighs that study's strengths and weaknesses. The authors hope gut microbe targeting may extend the approach to related metabolic conditions. Their piece is a commentary, not new experimental data.
pmc-11539276:
Farah Khalida Abdul Rahman and two co-authors hunted traits that drive dengue deaths in a Malaysian state. Their study, from twenty twenty-four, deals with dengue fever. Cases and deaths have climbed in Malaysia as the disease spreads in poorer lands. Past work stuck close to the clinical signs of severe infection. This team widened the lens to traits of the person, the clinic, and the setting.

They drew data from the state's e-dengue system, a live registry. A case control design set deaths next to matched survivors. Readers who fight dengue in city states get a fuller map of who dies and why. Such maps can aim scarce care at the highest risk first.
pmc-11542476:
Yu Sun and co-authors search for protein markers of papillary thyroid carcinoma, the most common thyroid cancer. The study draws on five patients, comparing cancer tissue with nearby normal thyroid tissue from each. A tagging method called TMT proteomics measures thousands of proteins at once. The team then flags proteins whose levels differ between the paired tissues and annotates what they do.

In total, 639 proteins differ: 278 run higher in cancer and 361 run lower. Six of the higher proteins stand out as potential specific markers for this cancer. The authors argue these proteins and their pathways may reveal how the disease develops. The findings offer candidate markers for later validation in larger patient groups.
pmc-11547876:
Mohammed Al Bahri and co-authors test, by simulation, how to keep magnetic whirlpools stable at high temperatures inside nanowires, in a 2024 paper. The whirlpools, called skyrmions, are tiny swirls of magnetization that could store data at very small scales. Heat is their enemy: it can scramble a skyrmion's shape or spawn stray ones at random, corrupting stored data.

The team varied three magnetic properties of the wire material and the wire's own size. For some settings of magnetization strength and directional stiffness, the skyrmion's shape held steady above 800 kelvin, well above room temperature. Wider or longer wires also protected the structure against heat. Random skyrmions only began appearing on their own above about 700 kelvin. The authors conclude that with the right material tuning and geometry, skyrmion memory can survive the heat of real devices.
pmc-11551476:
McMullen and ten co-authors explored social prescribing for Pakistani carers in this study from twenty twenty-four. Social prescribing connects people to community support instead of medicine alone. Pakistani carers in Britain face deeper isolation than white British carers, yet services rarely fit their culture. The team interviewed twenty-seven carers and ten stakeholders in London and Sheffield.

Carer identity itself proved complicated, tangled with family duty and stigma. Many carers had never heard of social prescribing. Stakeholders cited funding gaps and weak links between doctors and community groups. Both sides wanted culturally aware staff and education pitched to the community. Two carer advisers shaped the study throughout. The authors urge collaboration to close the gap.
pmc-11570276:
Enrique Hernández-Jiménez and co-authors test a new way to predict positive blood cultures in sepsis, by gauging how worn down the immune system has become. Blood culture is the standard test for bacteria in the blood, but it is slow and can mislead both ways. Sepsis itself can blunt the immune response, a state called endotoxin tolerance, and the team reasoned that this blunting might flag true infection.

Blood was drawn from emergency patients who met the Sepsis-3 criteria, at admission. In the lab, samples were challenged with bacterial endotoxin, and the cytokine reply was profiled. Clinical facts, immune cell markers, and five cytokine levels were recorded. Patients whose cultures grew bacteria showed a clearly weaker TNF-alpha response to the challenge. A sluggish immune reply could flag true infection days before the culture dish answers.
pmc-11570676:
Madeline Hawke, Linda Sweet, and Julie Considine published a 2024 study of shared decision-making in pregnancy care. Good care should involve women in choices. The team recorded real clinic consultations in Australia. Women with higher body weight formed one group. A leaner group allowed comparison.

Trained raters scored each talk with a standard scale. Scores were low across the board. Women were rarely drawn into decisions. Body weight made no difference to the scores. A case example covered induction of labor. The findings show a gap between policy and practice. Training and time may both need attention.
pmc-11570776:
Amwas and three co-authors wrote a review in twenty twenty-four on adoptive T cell therapy for solid tumors. In these treatments, a patient's own immune cells are collected, changed or grown in a lab, and given back to fight cancer. The authors focus on why solid tumors, such as brain tumors, resist such care.

The review compares three main types: tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte therapy, engineered receptor therapy, and CAR T cell therapy. Each type has strengths, such as hitting many tumor targets or sensing very low levels of a target. The authors then survey ways to help cells reach tumors, stay active, and work inside the harsh space around a tumor.
pmc-11577076:
A shrub found only in Mali's Dogon Country is a mainstay of local healing, yet science had never examined it. Mamadou Konare and co-authors interview forty-five residents across three villages about Acridocarpus monodii and test its chemistry in the lab. Most healers were older men, and malaria topped the list of treated illnesses.

Leaves were the most used part, usually boiled and drunk or used in baths. The plant proved rich in flavonoids and polyphenols, the compound families behind much plant medicine. Its extracts also quenched free radicals strongly in two standard tests. The authors warn that harvesting roots and bark, favored by more educated users, threatens the species. They present the work as a first scientific record of the plant.
pmc-11585276:
HanYu Wang and six co-authors test whether a waist index adjusted for weight predicts obstructive sleep apnea, in a two thousand twenty-four cross-sectional and genetic study. The weight-adjusted waist index is meant to capture central obesity independent of body weight.

In national survey data from two thousand seventeen to two thousand twenty, higher index values tracked higher apnea risk even after full adjustment, with the top quartile at clearly elevated odds. The index outperformed other measures as a predictor, with a saturation point in the relationship. Mendelian randomization, using genetic instruments, supported a causal reading. The authors propose the simple index as a screening aid for apnea risk.
pmc-11587676:
Nine doctors led by Tomasz Czarnik set out the plan for a trial on vitamin D dosing in very ill patients whose blood is cleaned by machine around the clock. Such patients often run low on the vitamin, and the cleaning process can strip more of it away. No guide says how much to give them.

The trial, run across up to five Polish university hospitals, gives one very large single dose or a slightly smaller one, by mouth or feeding tube. It checks how many patients reach a healthy blood level three and seven days later. About one hundred thirty-eight patients will join. The plan paper explains the design and its reasoning.
pmc-11588776:
Mecca and co-authors map dust particle shifts across Turin over three years. Monitors ran from 2018 to 2021, spanning the COVID lockdown. Three particle sizes were tracked: PM1, PM2.5, and PM10. Background sites read 28 to 30 micrograms for PM10. Traffic sites read higher at 36 micrograms.

PM2.5 peaked at traffic sites with 24 micrograms. Daily peaks fell in the late morning hours. The lowest values came in the late afternoon. Source direction tests pointed to the Po Valley from the north. Saharan dust paths from the south added a second source. That long window let the team set lockdown readings against normal years.
pmc-11591576:
Fabio Casciano and colleagues published a 2024 review on exercise and cancer immunotherapy. Exercise helps prevent several cancers. It can also support cancer treatment. The biological reasons are still being mapped. The review focuses on immune effects.

Exercise changes blood flow inside tumors. It releases signaling molecules from muscle and fat. These signals can wake up anticancer immunity. They may also alter tumor metabolism. The authors assess exercise given before or during immunotherapy. They suggest where future trials should look. The goal is turning a healthy habit into a planned treatment partner.
pmc-11596476:
Chan Ho Lee and co-authors map where kidney cancer spreads and how that shapes survival in Korea in a study from two thousand twenty-four. Spread sites have been tied to survival gaps elsewhere, but Korean data were unclear. The team drew on a national study group database.

Over seventeen hundred patients who began targeted therapy were analyzed. The lung was the most common spread site, then lymph nodes and bone. Liver, adrenal gland, and brain followed. Median cancer survival ranged from about fourteen months with liver spread to about twenty-nine with lung spread. Liver, bone, and pleural spread marked the shortest survival. The authors offer the map for prognosis talks.
pmc-11603176:
Mengistu and three co-authors measured suicidal thoughts among pregnant women at an Ethiopian hospital clinic in twenty twenty-four. Suicide is a leading cause of death in people of reproductive age, and local evidence on pregnancy was thin. The study surveyed women attending antenatal care at Gondar's specialized hospital in twenty twenty-two.

Of one hundred sixty-eight participating women, about five percent reported suicidal ideation and about five percent a past attempt, rates the authors call low. Several factors were significantly tied to ideation: unplanned pregnancy, a history of abortion, a history of stillbirth, being HIV positive, and lifetime substance use. The authors say these predictors can help antenatal services spot women who need extra support, and they call for solution-oriented follow-up research in the region.
pmc-11603976:
Johanna Heugenhauser and nine co-authors link brain tumor images to blood immune profiles in glioblastoma, in a 2024 study. Glioblastoma is the deadliest common brain cancer, and up to a third of its mass is immune cells. Imaging and immunology each describe the disease well, but nobody had fused the two views.

The team reused data from an earlier immunotherapy trial. Seventy-six patients were screened, and forty-one had both baseline tumor scans and blood immune data. Scans yielded twenty-seven measures of size and shape under a standard visual scoring system. Blood yielded sixty-seven immune variables from cell sorting and gene tests. Cross-mapping the two sets hunts for blood signatures that mirror what the scan shows, a step toward choosing therapy from a blood draw.
pmc-11605476:
Jinglin Wang and co-authors review a promising bacterium for blocking dengue and Zika viruses in a 2024 commentary. Both viruses spread through mosquito bites and cause many infections each year, while vaccines and treatments remain limited. The commentary discusses a study that found the bacterium living in the gut of wild Asian tiger mosquitoes in Yunnan, China.

The bacterium, a strain of Rosenbergiella, was able to block both viruses from passing through the mosquito. Wang and co-authors explain why this matters and what it could mean for dengue prevention. They present the gut microbe route as a fresh biological strategy against mosquito-borne disease. Questions of scale and field use remain, but the approach offers a new direction beyond sprays and vaccines.
pmc-11605576:
Ryosuke Matsujda and co-authors report a way to watch leg motor pathways during brain tumor surgery, in a conference abstract from 2024. Damage to those pathways can leave a patient unable to move a leg well. A strip of contacts placed in the fold between the brain's two halves can stimulate the leg area directly.

The method was used in eighteen operations on sixteen patients. A six-contact strip was placed after the skull was opened, and a standard signal method located the central groove of the brain. Stable signals from three leg muscles were recorded in most cases. A drop of more than half in signal size was set as the warning line. In the monitored cases, no such lasting drop occurred. Follow-up lasted at least three months.
pmc-11607076:
Ramadan A Geioushy and colleagues report a two thousand twenty-four study of antibacterial paper coated with metal-decorated zinc oxide particles. Paper for packaging and records could gain germ-fighting power from such coatings. Silver and copper were added to tune the effect.

Higher metal loadings strengthened the paper noticeably. Tensile strength, stretch, energy absorption, and burst resistance all rose. Silver versions kept the paper bright, while copper dimmed whiteness. The coating attacked Staphylococcus aureus, a common contaminant. Long-term antimicrobial behaviour was also projected over decades. The work targets sustainable paper with built-in protection for archives and hygiene uses.
pmc-11607976:
Tao Li and colleagues published a 2024 case report on treating extra heartbeats during pregnancy. Extra beats strained the expectant mother's heart. They caused palpitations and risked reducing blood flow to the baby. Her faulty focus sat in an unusual spot. It lay within the right chamber's muscular ridges.

Doctors mapped the focus without X-ray imaging. A heated catheter then destroyed the tiny faulty site. Avoiding radiation protected the fetus during the procedure. The ablation succeeded despite the tricky location. The report details her symptoms, tracing, procedure, and recovery. Radiation-free ablation deserves wider use in pregnancy.
pmc-11608476:
Hongliang Hui and co-authors published this trial in 2024 on finding small lung nodules before surgery. When a patient has many nodules, marking them all so the surgeon can cut true is hard. The team tested a new guide, electromagnetic navigation, against the standard CT scan guide. Fifty patients were split by lot between the two methods.

The new guide's marks landed about as close to target as the scan's, within the set margin for a tie. The new method also ran faster, taking about sixteen minutes against twenty-two. Patients felt less anxiety before surgery with the new guide. Harms did not differ by a clear mark. The authors say navigation marking can stand in for scan marking when many nodules need flags at once.
pmc-11609576:
Chen Feng and his five co-authors, publishing in 2024, study a protein called LMAN2 in breast cancer. The protein normally helps move and sort other proteins inside cells, but its role in tumors was unclear. The team measured it in cancer samples and cell lines, then raised and lowered its levels to watch what changed, and searched for partner proteins it touches.

They found LMAN2 levels higher in tumors than in nearby healthy tissue, and higher levels tracked with worse outcomes for patients. In lab cells, extra LMAN2 sped growth, spread, and resistance to the chemotherapy drug cisplatin, while blocking cell death; silencing it reversed those effects and even re-sensitized resistant tumors in mice. LMAN2 binds a partner called MAPK9 and switches on a known growth pathway. The authors propose it as both a warning marker and a drug target.
pmc-11609876:
Anna de Jong, Anna Von Wachenfeldt, Lennarth Nyström, and Anne Andersson wrote, in two thousand twenty-four, on how women in Sweden stick to hormone pills after breast cancer. The pills are adjuvant endocrine therapy, taken for years after surgery. In cancer that feeds on estrogen, they cut the chance the ill comes back. They help only if women keep taking them.

The team found 10,422 women with that type of cancer in two thousand eight to two thousand ten, in the breast cancer list. Drug lists showed who picked them up. Good use was 94.4 per cent at one year, 87.6 at three, and 81.6 at five years. The South scored best. Zones with a cancer clinic beat zones with none at five years. Women aged past seventy-five stuck to the pills least. Help should aim at them and at women under forty.
pmc-11610076:
Rachel Canaway and five co-authors ask whether software prompts could raise alcohol screening in Australian general practice. Their feasibility study was published in twenty twenty-four. The prompt would target patients who are pregnant or planning pregnancy, a group where drinking carries extra risk.

The team reviewed literature and interviewed twenty-three stakeholders: software vendors, clinicians, and others. At least eighteen software packages serve Australian general practice, which complicates any add-on. A further twenty-two stakeholders sense-tested the recommendations. The study weighed what a fitting tool looks like, when a prompt should fire, and what helps or blocks uptake. Its findings guide how such a prompt could be built into real clinic systems.
pmc-11611476:
Jacob Msando and co-authors survey medical staff on a blue card concussion rule in semi elite Australian football, in work from twenty twenty-four. Under the rule, umpires can send a player off for a head check. The league hoped the rule would help medical teams catch concussions.

Staff from the men's and women's leagues replied at a rate near half, split among doctors, physios, and trainers. Most did not find the rule helpful and did not want it kept. Two thirds said umpires are not trained to spot concussions on field. Only a third felt fully sure in their sideline checks. Most asked for more policy teaching before each season. Ties with other staff were not much harmed by the rule.
pmc-11613776:
Ruiyin Zeng and co-authors report a 2024 study of slow-healing wounds in diabetes. Such wounds heal poorly because new blood vessels and nerves grow back too slowly. The team built a soft gel that can be injected into the wound. The gel carries stem cells from fat tissue plus tiny packets with two active factors. One factor draws the cells to the injury site.

The gel forms under light and holds its parts through weak links. Once in place, it aims at three systems at once: defense, vessel growth, and nerve growth. The cells are guided toward nerve-like roles as healing goes on. The authors present the mix as a cocktail therapy in one dressing. Wound care teams get a single tool that tackles several blocks to healing at once. The work is a lab study, so patient use would need more tests for safety and dose.
pmc-11615376:
Yuxi Chen and co-authors test a common antibiotic as a treatment for retinitis pigmentosa, a genetic eye disease, in work published in 2024. The disease kills light-sensing cells over time, and immune cells in the retina speed that loss. The drug, minocycline, calms those immune cells and protects nerves in other settings.

The trial gave 35 patients a daily tablet for twelve months, with no control group. The main test measured an electric signal from the eye. About a third of patients improved on that signal at one year. Vision measures such as field, sharpness, and colour also improved. Side effects appeared in most patients but all cleared without extra treatment, and none were severe. The authors call the results promising while noting the open design.
pmc-11615676:
Elizaveta Kuznetsova, Anastasiia Liashenko, Natalia Zhozhikashvili, and Marie Arsalidou review how gifted children differ from their peers, in a paper from 2024. Schools still debate how to spot giftedness and what marks it. A shaky picture leads to missed children and weak programs. The team gathered studies from more than twenty-five countries.

In all, they reviewed 104 papers covering more than seventy-seven thousand children. Gifted children beat peers on memory, focus switching, and shape problems. Their brains also fired faster and harder on tough tasks. They scored higher on inner drive, self-belief, and openness, and earned better grades. Tests are growing more fair across cultures, the authors note. The review gives schools a firmer base for spotting and teaching gifted youth.
pmc-11615876:
Paramesh Shamanna and six colleagues describe a digital twin platform for personalizing diabetes nutrition, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-four. Type 2 diabetes involves insulin resistance and failing beta cells. Standard diets ignore how differently individuals' blood sugar responds to the same meal.

The platform learns from continuous glucose monitoring, dietary records, and other body signals. It predicts each patient's post-meal glucose response. Recommendations then steer meals toward better predicted control. The stated goals include improved insulin sensitivity and support for remission. The paper presents the technology's development and its application in practice. Personalized nutrition of this kind aims to replace one-size-fits-all diet sheets with feedback tuned to one metabolism.
pmc-11618376:
Ryan Feathers, Ryan Vignogna, and Christopher Fromme reveal how a protein complex switches on Rab6, a traffic controller for the Golgi apparatus. Rab proteins cycle between off and on states. The Ric1-Rgp1 complex turns them on by swapping nucleotides. How it does so had never been seen in structural detail.

Their cryo-electron microscopy structure catches the complex mid-swap with Rab6. A helical region not characterized before proves to be the exchange domain, with key residues confirmed by mutation. In a surprise, an arrestin fold grips Rab6's loose tail. That suggests activators often hold Rab proteins by their tails. The findings give a detailed picture of how cargo flow through the Golgi is controlled.
pmc-11618876: Dieter Schollmeyer and Heiner Detert report the structure of a small selenium ring compound in a short paper from 2024, made from a semicarbazone starting material and selenium dioxide. The ring joins a ten-membered carbon loop to a selenium and nitrogen unit, with a double bond on one side. The flat parts of the molecule sit almost at right angles to each other, and the chain linking them is nearly free of strain. The note records the makeup and shape for chemists who study such rings.
pmc-11625876:
Yojiro Ishikawa and four co-authors published a case report in twenty twenty-four on a cancer side effect so rare it earned a syndrome name: tumor-induced oblique abdominal muscle paralysis. Their patient, a man in his seventies with malignant pleural mesothelioma, developed a bulge on his left side that appeared when he stood and vanished when he lay down.

Scans showed the oblique muscles wasted and the navel pulled rightward, consistent with the tumor invading the intercostal nerves. Abdominal wall paralysis is usually blamed on disc problems, shingles, or nerve injury, almost never on cancer. The authors urge positional examination, standing and supine, whenever tumor nerve invasion is suspected. A bulge that keeps office hours, they show, can be a neurological sign in disguise.
pmc-11626976:
Chunyan Weng and a team of co-authors review TRIM proteins in gut cancers, in a paper dated twenty twenty-four. TRIM proteins tag other proteins for disposal, a system gut tumors lean on heavily. The family steers growth signals, cell death, and tumor spread.

The review lays out what each member does in gut tissue, healthy and cancerous. Some TRIM proteins act as brakes; others feed tumor growth. Their levels may serve as warning markers for diagnosis and outlook. The authors also weigh the family as a set of drug targets for future therapy.
pmc-11628176:
Huanhuan Li and co-authors fed zinc oxide nanoparticles to rare minnows to test their value as a feed additive. The particles are prized for being easy for the body to absorb, but their effects on fish growth and health are little studied. The team measured growth, zinc buildup in tissues, blood cells, and gene activity over sixty days.

The supplemented fish ended lighter, with zinc levels and a liver injury index clearly above the control group. Blood cell counts first rose, then fell. In muscle, growth genes were dialed down after sixty days, while liver tissue switched immune genes up. The authors read a split story: short feeding may help growth and immunity, but long feeding lets zinc build up and harms both.
pmc-11630776:
May van Schalkwyk and co-authors published a 2024 essay on how harmful industries pollute public debate. Companies whose products damage health and the environment do not just sell goods; they sell stories. Those stories shape science and policy in their favor. The authors name the effect discursive pollution, drawing a parallel with the physical pollution the same industries cause.

The piece catalogs the tactics across industries: casting doubt on evidence, framing regulation as overreach, and presenting industry-friendly claims as common sense. It also exposes contradictions inside those stories. The second half turns to defense. The authors propose how the health community can push back: naming the tactics, refusing the loaded terms, and building clearer counter-narratives. The essay adds a cross-industry lens to research on the commercial drivers of health.
pmc-11631776:
Muthukumar Santhanakrishnan and three co-authors set three tooth root set times head to head in the front top jaw. Their trial appeared in twenty twenty-four. Seventy-five patients were split by lot to fast set, fast set with a socket shield, or late set. Scans and pink gum scores tracked bone and soft gum shifts for a year.

The shield group lost the least bone rim girth by far at one year. Late set lost the most. Pink scores ran best in the shield group, then fast set, then late set. Pain and joy marks were taped too. The team backs the shield path when front bone is thin.
pmc-11631876:
Cuiwen Zhang and colleagues identify a single enzyme gene as the disease factor of a bacterium causing potato common scab. Their 2024 study examines a Streptomyces strain whose suspect gene switched on during potato infection.

The gene was cloned and shown to encode a protein of over four hundred building blocks in an enzyme family that breaks down pectin. The purified protein alone caused disease when placed on healthy potatoes. Deleting the gene slowed bacterial growth and shrank the clear zone the mutant formed on pectin plates. Colony appearance and pigment stayed unchanged in the mutant. Gene loss also reduced the strain's ability to infest potatoes, confirming the enzyme's central pathogenic role.
pmc-11634176:
A large team of co-authors presents a study from two thousand twenty-four building a rat model of combined scalp and skull wounds. Such composite defects, where soft tissue and bone are missing together, are hard to rebuild in layers. A good animal model is the first step toward testing engineered repairs.

A three-dimensional printed plug kept the scalp wound open and slowed its healing, preserving the skull defect and mimicking a chronic wound. Alongside, the team set up a repair using the animal's own tissue as a positive control. That control healed its skin reliably within three weeks, with varied bone integration, matching clinical experience.
pmc-11638776:
Emily Greenfield, Natalie Pope, and Tonya Roberts ask what age-friendly community drives change, read as system change. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four. Since the early two thousands, a world move has pushed towns to fit old age in built space, social life, and services. Proof of what such drives yield is still young.

They read talks with key staff at eight grown drives in the northeast of the United States through a six-part lens of system change. Strong proof shows for office practice, resource flow, ties across groups, and views of older adults. Proof for shifts in power and in policy is thin. The lens can guide how drives are judged and led.
pmc-11639776:
Emily Jessop and co-authors test whether blocking an enzyme can make an aggressive breast cancer cell less able to invade. Their 2024 paper studies triple-negative breast cancer, a subtype with no hormone targets and high spread rates. Soft nuclei help these cells squeeze through tight spaces, so stiffening the nucleus could slow them.

The team blocked the enzyme SIRT2 with a specific drug in a standard cell line. Treated cells built a more organized cage of fibers around the nucleus. Their nuclei resisted collapse under osmotic shock better than untreated cells. In scratch tests, the treated cells showed polarity faults that hamper directed movement. Confined models showed reduced invasiveness. The work is cell-level, but it names a mechanical route against metastasis worth testing further.
pmc-11640376:
Laetitia Cloutier and co-authors compare feeding plans for pregnant sows across three cycles. Their 2024 study tests precision feeding against simpler constant plans. Two standard plans kept feed mix fixed, with amounts flat or bumped late in pregnancy. Two precision plans tuned the mix to each sow's parity or weight.

In the first cycle, piglet deaths before weaning ran lower under precision feeding than under bump feeding. The second cycle showed no litter gaps between plans. By the third cycle, stillbirths were lowest under one precision plan. Precision plans also cut nitrogen intake by about a tenth and phosphorus by slightly less. The results favor tailored feeding for both piglet survival and lower waste.
pmc-11641476: Kan Katayama and Kaoru Dohi introduce a set of new findings on kidney diseases in this 2024 editorial overview. The piece frames chronic kidney disease as a lifestyle-related condition affecting about nine percent of the world's population as of 2017. Beyond that framing line, the hosted text carries only the opening of the overview, so the specific new insights it announces are not set out in the text provided here.
pmc-11641576:
The authors review how hormone-disrupting chemicals harm the lungs in a paper from 2024. These chemicals are widespread in the environment and in food. They interfere with the body's hormone system and can raise the risk of diseases such as asthma, chronic lung disease, and lung scarring, with exposure before birth a special concern.

The review lays out the ways these chemicals act inside lung tissue. They can drive oxidative stress, change how cells grow and mature, slow repair, and stir inflammation. They can also weaken the barrier between blood and air, letting harmful substances reach the lung. More work on mechanisms and prevention is urged.
pmc-11642376:
Jessica Cusato and co-authors wrote a study from 2024 on whether gene variants in the vitamin D pathway predict who answers to two biologic drugs for bowel disease. Vitamin D helps steer the immune system, and its handling genes vary from person to person. The team followed just over a hundred patients with Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis on one of the two drugs. They checked responses at three and twelve months and a stool marker of gut healing.

One drug answered more often at twelve months. An early response strongly foretold a late one. One variant in a vitamin D carrier gene marked most patients who failed to respond at a year. Another marked those who missed the gut healing target. The team offers the variants as leads for personal drug choice.
pmc-11642976:
Meijing Ren and six colleagues model how short-range order changes crystal plasticity in a chromium-cobalt-nickel alloy, in a study from twenty twenty-four. Medium-entropy alloys have become a materials research hotspot. Recent work shows they contain short-range order, which alters how they deform. The team built that effect into a crystal plasticity framework.

Their non-local constitutive model evaluates short-range order effects within mesoscale continuum mechanics. A slip model incorporating order was combined with nanoindentation and multi-level grain tensile simulations. Load-displacement and stress-strain curves showed order increases the alloy's hardness. Shear strain and dislocation distributions revealed growing heterogeneity as order increased. The study enriches crystal plasticity theory. It also offers guidance for tuning microstructure and performance in multi-level grain materials.
pmc-11643076:
Juan Xia leads a team studying diet and health among breast cancer survivors in China, in this twenty twenty-four paper. Survivors face a raised risk of other long-term diseases. Gaps in food knowledge and diet quality may add to that risk.

The team surveyed more than fifteen hundred women in a Shanghai cancer recovery club. Most were in their mid-sixties, and food knowledge was low in about half of them. The study linked food knowledge and diet quality to the chance of having other chronic diseases at the same time. The findings point to diet teaching as a fair way to protect survivors' long-term health.
pmc-11643176:
Barbara Sciandrone leads a team that tests a plant compound's safety in worms. Their study from twenty twenty-four deals with justicidin B. The compound is a lignan with anti cancer traits in cells.

Finding safe new cancer drugs is a clear need, they note. Worms got two doses of the compound in tests. The low dose did not harm worm life, short or long term. The high dose cut life span in short daily use only. Build up in throat granules may explain that harm. Chem tests found changed forms of the compound too.
pmc-11643376:
Grzegorz Łysiak and Ryszard Kulig published a study in twenty twenty-four on what happens inside the press when farm waste is squeezed into pellets. The waste is the solid left from biogas making. Pellets store and ship well and can serve as food for soil or as fuel. The snag: once the press lets go, the pellet springs back a bit, and that spring can spoil its strength.

The pair pressed samples at five levels of wetness and five force levels, ten squeeze cycles each. Spring-back grew with wetness and force, and shrank with each added cycle. Yet spring-back barely tracked pellet strength. The energy locked in for good was the true mark of a strong pellet. The authors say watching the squeeze-release loop is the best way to judge a batch.
pmc-11643676:
Ewelina Szaniawska-Białas and co-authors review work from two thousand twenty-four on membranes made of tiny tubes of titanium oxide. The tubes are grown in neat rows by a process called anodizing. When the layer is lifted free and its tube ends are opened, liquids and gases can flow through it.

The review covers how the membranes are made, what shapes the tube growth, and how the freed films are treated for different uses. It then surveys recent work that uses them to make hydrogen, clean polluted water, store energy in cells and batteries, sense chemicals, and serve medical aims. The authors weigh what helps the material work and what still limits it.
pmc-11645276:
Violeta Raverdy and co-authors used data-driven grouping to show that fatty liver disease tied to metabolic problems comes in two distinct types. The disease, shortened to MASLD, affects many people with obesity but follows very different courses. Working from six simple clinical measures in nearly fourteen hundred patients, the team found two clusters, then checked them in biopsy cohorts and a national biobank.

One type is driven mainly by the liver itself, progresses fast toward chronic liver disease, yet carries limited heart risk. The other is cardiometabolic, marked by blood sugar problems and high triglycerides, with higher risks of heart disease and diabetes. Gene, tissue, and blood profiles differed sharply between the types, which suggests treatment should be tailored to each.
pmc-11647076:
Theresa Ackfeld leads a team with a tumor that mimicked a heart attack. Their case from twenty twenty-four deals with a woman of forty-three. She came in with chest pain, head pain, and sweat.

Heart traces looked like a major heart attack at first. Yet vessel scans showed no blocked heart arteries at all. A heart chamber scan showed a balloon like tip instead. High blood pressure raised doubt of an adrenal tumor. Blood tests proved it, and surgery took the tumor out. Such tumors should be weighed in odd cases.
pmc-11648776:
Lisa Maurer and her team asked if special insoles help people with Parkinson's disease walk more safely, in two thousand twenty-four. The disease often makes walking unsteady and raises the risk of falls. The insoles aim to boost feel in the foot and steady the step.

Sixteen people with the disease walked while wearing the special insoles and plain insoles in turn. The team timed their steps, tracked brain waves, and asked how steady they felt.
