None of the gains reached a level the team could trust. Step speed and length did not change in a clear way. The authors say the group was too small to settle the question, and longer studies are needed.
pmc-11649676:
Rodrigo Vieira, Plinio Moreno, and Athanasios Vourvopoulos test brain signals for predicting human action in a 2024 pilot study. The setting is human-robot teamwork, where a robot that sees a move coming can work more safely. Brain waves, read by EEG sensors on the scalp, can show signs of a planned move more than a second before it happens.

The team trained deep learning models on a data set where people imagined movements. Their best model sorted the signals with accuracy near eighty-one percent. In a live pilot test, actions were forecast a few hundred milliseconds before they were carried out. The authors say pairing brain signals with modern learning methods could make shared tasks smoother. They frame the work as an early step toward safer joint work with robots.
pmc-11650176:
Shadi Ghaemi and three colleagues pool clinical trials to ask whether vitamin D supplements ease depression, in a meta-analysis published in two thousand twenty-four. Earlier trials disagreed, leaving the dose question open. The authors searched three databases for randomized trials in adults through December two thousand twenty-two.

Thirty-one trials with 24,189 participants qualified. Each extra thousand international units of vitamin D3 per day slightly reduced depressive symptoms. The effect appeared in people with and without diagnosed depression and grew more pronounced at higher doses in some groups. Certainty of evidence was graded moderate. Anxiety outcomes were also examined. The authors present vitamin D as a modest adjunct, not a stand-alone antidepressant.
pmc-11652876:
Siyi Chen and co-authors study a 2024 question about how the gut handles a choline-bearing compound sold as a supplement. The compound, called GPC, has been studied as a source of choline inside cells and has been hoped to guard the brain. Yet high intake of choline compounds is tied to making a liver product, TMAO, that is linked with artery disease.

The team focuses on an enzyme in the gut, Gpcpd1, and its role in breaking down GPC. In lab tests with a layer of gut-like cells, added GPC was split into choline on the outer side, and the choline then crossed into the cells. Tracing that path helps explain how much of a supplement turns into the raw material for TMAO, and where control points may sit.
pmc-11653576:
Jiaqi Zhang and co-authors published a 2024 study building a questionnaire to measure how much patients feel they gain from China's family doctor contracts. Under the scheme, residents sign with a family doctor team and receive broader primary care. Whether patients themselves feel better served was unmeasured: no instrument captured their sense of medical gain. The team set out to build and test one.

Scale development followed the standard craft: draft items from the concept, refine them with patients and experts, then check the questionnaire's structure and consistency in survey data. Preliminary validation asks whether the scale hangs together and measures one thing rather than noise. Such a tool lets managers compare districts and programs by the patient's own ledger, not just visit counts. The authors frame felt gain as a missing metric in judging a flagship reform: a service can be comprehensive on paper and thin in experience.
pmc-11654276:
Dawson and a large team studied how health and social services work as partners for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander clients in twenty twenty-four. Many clients deal with several groups at once. When services work in silos, on their own, clients can find care hard to get. The study was set on Kaurna Country in northern Adelaide, Australia.

Fifty-nine service providers took part, through interviews and yarning circles. Yarning is a discussion method grounded in the culture. Two thirds of participants were Aboriginal. Acts of partnership included advocacy, referrals, shared information, and case meetings. People said these acts improved client access and how staff felt about work. Keen staff, shared goals, and formal agreements helped. Racism, red tape, short-term funding, and high staff turnover got in the way. The authors list reforms, from steady funding to coordination led by Aboriginal people.
pmc-11655876:
Zengzhuang Yuan and co-authors show how a gene called ELF3 helps lung cancer grow when a guard gene is missing, in this 2024 study. The guard gene, PTEN, is often lost in tumors. A cell death route named ferroptosis can block cancer, and the team asked how ELF3 affects it. Extra ELF3 alone in mouse lung cells caused overgrowth but also more ferroptosis.

With PTEN removed as well, tumors formed and ferroptosis dropped. The reason was a gene, SLC7A11, that ELF3 switches on and that holds ferroptosis back. A drug blocking that gene restored cell death and curbed tumors. Human lung tumors showed matching patterns, and high ELF3 with its partner gene tracked with worse survival. The authors propose triggering ferroptosis as a treatment angle.
pmc-11657176:
Okagbue and nine co-authors review whether Nigerian girls in villages reach puberty later than girls in cities. Ages at first menstruation are falling worldwide, faster in poorer countries. The review gathered studies spanning 1976 to 2023 under standard reporting rules.

Ten studies qualified, with a low overall risk of bias. First periods came at about 13.4 years in rural areas and 13.0 in urban ones. The gap, though, was not statistically firm, and it seems to be shrinking over time. The authors note the steady downward trend in both settings. They frame the work as a base for health planning for adolescent girls.
pmc-11657576:
Suzanne Cosh leads a team that sets cut scores for climate anxiety. Their study from twenty twenty-four deals with eco anxiety in young adults. Fear and worry on climate change are seen world wide.

Such anxiety can be helpful at times, but can also harm health. No good way yet flags who needs support for it. A large sample of Australian young adults filled forms. Distress scales scored low mood, anxiety, and stress in each. Those scores set what counted as a true case. Cut scores on the climate scale were then derived.
pmc-11659976:
Kuang-Yu Wei and a large team compare two transplant drugs in rats in a 2024 paper. Both drugs are calcineurin inhibitors that affect how the kidney handles salts and blood pressure. The newer drug, voclosporin, seems to disturb magnesium and calcium less than tacrolimus, but lab proof was missing.

Rats received one of the drugs or a plain vehicle for 28 days. The team tracked salt handling, blood pressure by telemetry, and the levels of transport proteins in the kidney tubule. Tacrolimus raised calcium loss more than four-fold and lowered blood magnesium. Voclosporin did not. Tacrolimus also cut several transport proteins that voclosporin spared.
pmc-11663576:
Pablo Calzadilla and Fernando Unrein present a study the catalog lists under 2025. Cyanobacteria harvest light in waters where light swings wildly. Clouds and wind stir shallow lakes, so cells spend long spans in dark water. Brief trips to the bright surface punctuate that darkness. Too much light can damage the harvest machinery. Cells must balance capture against protection as light jumps.

The study centers on a protein called RppA in that balance. Pigment production is regulated in tight coordination during acclimation. The authors trace how the protein helps cells adjust to dark-light cycles. Lake ecology and biofuel work both care: pond-grown cyanobacteria face the same swings. A strain that acclimates fast wastes less light and survives gusts of sun. The work speaks to basic photosynthesis science in a realistic light regime, not steady lab lamps.
pmc-11663876:
Katharina Gryksa and seven colleagues compare social and emotional behavior in two common lab mouse strains, in a twenty twenty-four study. The strains, a black line called BL6 and a white line called CD1, differ in genes and in stress responses. The team tested males as teens and as adults on anxiety, fear, social acts, and pain sense. They also mapped the oxytocin system, a hormone web tied to social behavior.

BL6 mice were more anxious, less social, and more shaken by trauma at both ages. CD1 mice calmed with age, while BL6 mice grew more fearful. Oxytocin receptor patterns differed by strain and age. The authors urge care in picking strain and age for stress research.
pmc-11664276:
Wang and eight co-authors pinpoint which chemicals give stored grass carp its spoiled smell. Freshwater fish spoil fast at room temperature, and the smell drives buyers away. The team measured odor chemicals in fresh, spoiled, and badly spoiled fish cubes.

Nineteen odorants mattered across the stages. Mixing and removal tests confirmed five key culprits in spoiled fish, including trimethylamine and ammonia. Badly spoiled fish added five more, among them putrescine and histamine. Twelve amino acids and ten fatty acids fed the formation of these smells. The authors say the map of odor sources can guide fresher storage methods.
pmc-11665776:
Yunhan Wang and colleagues published a plant biology study in 2024 on how a potato viroid copies itself. Viroids are tiny circular RNA strands that infect crops. They carry no protein-coding genes of their own. Instead they borrow the host plant's machinery to multiply.

One borrowed enzyme joins the cut ends of viroid RNA into circles. The team tracked that enzyme and the viroid inside plant cells. Both gathered together near the nucleolus, the cell's dense core region. The viroid RNA itself was highly condensed in that same spot. The authors argue the pair forms a droplet-like condensate for processing. The finding extends condensate biology to these minimal pathogens.
pmc-11665876:
Somya Mehra and four co-authors model how sleeping malaria parasites wake in the liver, in a paper published in twenty twenty-four. One malaria species, Plasmodium vivax, hides as dormant forms called hypnozoites. They can stir weeks or months after a bite and cause fresh illness. What sets their timing was unknown.

The team fitted a simple math model to a rich cohort study on the Thailand-Myanmar border. Over thirteen hundred children were watched daily for twenty-one months, logging thousands of malaria bouts. A model where each sleeper wakes at a steady random rate fit the relapse patterns well. It put the average dormancy near six months. The team also tested what a blood test for hidden infection could add in quiet regions.
pmc-11668576:
Antonia Wambsganz and co-authors published this health psychology study in 2024. Only about half of Germans meet the World Health Organization's activity recommendations, despite exercise preventing many illnesses. The team surveyed 1,119 mentally healthy adults online to find what separates regular exercisers from the rest, hoping to spot levers for public health.

Regular exercise went with stronger motivation of both kinds, inner and outer, plus higher self-efficacy, resilience, and belief in one's own control. Exercisers also scored higher on conscientiousness, extraversion, and agreeableness, and they took more risks. Circumstances mattered too: money, sports facilities nearby, and having active family members in childhood. Many people preferred outdoor group exercise yet actually trained alone indoors. The authors recommend cheap, low-threshold exercise options in public spaces and childcare settings, aimed at disadvantaged groups.
pmc-11672076:
Chen and a large team target an RNA editing enzyme in liver cancer in twenty twenty-four. The enzyme, FTO, removes a chemical mark from RNA and drives several cancers. Its role in liver cancer was unclear. The team also asked how it relates to small vesicles that cancer cells release.

FTO levels were higher in patient liver tumors than in normal tissue. It boosted cancer cell growth, movement, and invasion in lab tests and in animals. Lowering FTO helped immune T cells enter tumors and attack them. A protein called GPNMB was found to be a key target of FTO. Vesicles carried GPNMB to T cells and damped their activation. An FTO blocker curbed cancer growth and improved response to other drugs.
pmc-11672776:
Connie Allen Wild, Lisa Yon, and Peter Henzi wrote this commentary, published in 2024. It looks at how group mates in social mammal species gather around and support a female while she gives birth.

Such support has been seen in primates, elephants, whales and dolphins, and bats, in groups with very different social setups. In humans, support during birth is known to help both mother and baby. The authors ask whether the same holds for other mammals. A calmer birth may lower the risk of a hard delivery and help the mother bond with her newborn. Both factors shape whether the young survive. The paper weighs ideas such as kin selection to explain why helpers might gain from lending support.
pmc-11673276:
Eleonora Fini and a large team of co-authors study clotting risk in endometriosis in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. The chronic inflammatory condition affects women of reproductive age and has been tied to thrombosis. The molecular link was unclear.

Seventy-one patients and matched controls were compared. Patients showed higher oxidative stress across blood cell types and in plasma. Their fibrinogen, the protein that builds clots, was oxidized and structurally altered. That damage made clots form oddly and resist breakdown by the usual enzyme. The authors read this as a pro-clotting state driven by oxidative stress. They propose the fibrinogen changes as a target to cut cardiovascular risk in these patients.
pmc-11673476:
Haima Yang and co-authors build a computer model that sorts vaginal lesions in medical images, in a paper from 2024. The lesions, linked to a common virus, are often missed when doctors inspect the cervix and focus less on the vaginal area. Missed cases can delay care.

Their model, called DLRNet, was designed to learn from small sets of images. One part finds the lesion in the image. A second part then reads both the raw image and the marked map to make its call. A third part guides focus to the right features. The team built the model on a known image network and tuned it at several levels. By reading cervical and vaginal signs together, the model aims to sort lesion types more exactly than a single-path model.
pmc-11673976:
Han Sol Kang and colleagues present ARS, an artificial intelligence driven recovery controller that helps a quadruped robot get up after falling. Their 2024 study addresses a basic problem, since falling is inevitable for legged robots on rough terrain.

A single neural network model was trained in two steps in simulation using reinforcement learning. It was then applied directly to a real quadruped robot with twelve degrees of freedom. Experiments showed recovery within five seconds from varied postures, even when the robot was completely turned over. The robot also recovered after a fall caused by a disturbance. The approach avoids separate controllers for each fall type.
pmc-11674976:
Marie Quiriny and a large team build a molecular signature to sort thyroid nodules before surgery. Their prospective study was published in twenty twenty-four. Needle biopsies leave many nodules in a grey zone, and surgery is often the only way to know.

Biopsy samples were taken from nodules during thyroid removal, across all biopsy categories. Tiny RNA molecules and gene mutations were measured in each sample. The true diagnosis came from the removed tissue. Learning algorithms trained on half the samples classified the rest. The best model leaned mostly on the small RNAs, reaching high accuracy with strong specificity. The signature could cut unneeded thyroid surgery.
pmc-11675176:
Hans Fuchs, Elisabeth Dumont, and Federico Corni revisit Sadi Carnot's waterfall picture of heat, two centuries on. Their essay appeared in twenty twenty-four. Carnot, founder of thermodynamics, pictured heat as a force of nature that works like falling water.

In his image, heat's drop from hot to cold drives an engine the way a waterfall drives a wheel. The authors read the picture as an archetype: a deep pattern in how humans grasp causes. They show how the same pattern maps onto fluids, electricity, magnetism, gravity, and motion. From it they build a unified way to talk about power and energy across physics. The essay honors the analogy as a tool for building theories, not a mere metaphor.
pmc-11675476:
Aristeidis Mystakidis and co-authors use math planning to build nurse rosters in a 2024 case study. Rostering in a cancer ward is hard, since patient needs are sharp and hard to predict. Bad rosters tire staff and can lower the quality of care. The team built a model based on integer programming, which picks the best whole-number plan under set rules.

The rules cover legal work hours, staff skills, and personal wishes. In a real clinic trial, the model spread work more fairly among nurses. It met most wishes and kept all rosters within the law. Staff satisfaction rose along with smoother running of the ward. The authors present the model as proof that operations research can aid daily health care management.
pmc-11675976:
Endre Csaki, Antonia Foldes, and Daniel Campos present open questions about anisotropic random walks, a topic in probability theory. Their 2024 article gathers intriguing unresolved problems and the background needed to understand them.

Between twenty oh seven and twenty eighteen, the authors collaborated extensively with two senior colleagues on many of these problems. Over the following six years they continued exploring the same issues. The article compiles key results from a dozen of their previous works. That compilation frames the open questions for other researchers. Readers get both a progress report on anisotropic random walk theory and a map of what remains unsolved in the area.
pmc-11676776:
Pintarič and co-authors published a 2024 study of how fertilizers shift the links between soil microbes and soil enzymes across three farming systems. Microbe and enzyme activity together signal soil health. The team sampled soils from conventional-integrated, organic, and biodynamic farms across seasons. Each soil received one of three feeds: standard fertilizer, spent mushroom substrate, or a composed fertilizer. They then tracked how microbe groups and eight enzymes moved together.

The biodynamic soil changed least under the different feeds. Standard fertilizer created negative links between one microbe group and one enzyme in the organic and biodynamic soils. Other links flipped sign depending on the feed, whatever the base soil. The authors suggest some microbe-enzyme links could serve as general soil health indicators, while others reflect the farming system.
pmc-11677076:
Qingxuan Qiao and a large team of co-authors study gut bacteria from a crop pest moth, in two thousand twenty-four. When the moth caterpillar feeds, it spits gut fluid onto the plant, and the bacteria in that fluid can sway the plant's defenses. The balance among plant, insect, and bacteria shapes who wins.

Six bacterial strains were grown from the fluid and tested on a model plant. Two strains stood out: they weakened a moth enzyme that normally helps the insect blunt plant defenses. Caterpillars with those strains grew worse on the plant, though not on artificial food. The authors suggest adding such bacteria could become a tool for pest control.
pmc-11677376:
Nevena Todorovic and four co-authors reviewed how gut microbes split by cause in liver cancer growth. Their review, from twenty twenty-four, deals with hepatocellular carcinoma, the top form of first liver cancer. Long liver disease runs through swelling, scar, and cirrhosis to that end. Gut microbe balance is now known to sway that path in both germ and non germ causes. A newer field reads the microbes that live in the tumor it self, the oncobiome.

The team sets the microbe tale by root cause of the liver ill. That split is their core claim: one tale does not fit all roads to this cancer. Readers get a cause wise map for a hot new field.
pmc-11679076:
Sherif Fakher and others tested polymer gels for underground flow control in 2024. Directing fluids underground is technically hard and costly to get wrong. Carbon dioxide behaves compressibly down there. Water and gas flow together often. Two crosslinked polymer systems were compared. Loose sandstone formations hosted the tests.

Both polymers cut water flow more strongly. Carbon dioxide flow fell less overall. Salt levels changed performance markedly. One polymer loved salt conditions greatly. The other weakened in salty water. Oil recovery could benefit from such diversion in the field. Carbon storage could benefit as well. Future work targets storage improvement.
pmc-11679376:
Balachandran Nair Premakumari Sreeja and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-four study on securing location finding in wireless sensor networks. Networks of small sensors must know where each node sits. Malicious anchor nodes can feed false positions and wreck that map.

Their algorithm borrows the bat search method from nature-inspired computing. Clustering and probability checks help it spot and isolate bad anchors. Simulations pitted it against six existing secure localization methods. It beat them across the performance measures used. The work targets safer sensing for security systems and environmental monitoring where position errors carry real costs.
pmc-11680376:
Justin Smith and co-authors test vaccine antibodies in monkeys in a 2024 paper. A mucosal HIV vaccine should raise IgA antibodies that block the virus at entry sites. No immunogen had yet produced IgA that neutralizes hard-to-kill tier 2 strains.

The team purified IgA and IgG from the blood of six vaccinated rhesus macaques. The vaccine used a stabilized envelope trimer with a strong adjuvant. IgG carried more antibody overall. Yet per unit of binding antibody, IgA from some animals neutralized the matched virus as well as or better than IgG. Potency tracked with the share of certain antibody forms.
pmc-11688376:
Danish, Suhail, and Farooq teach a deep learning tool to outline the gestational sac in ultrasound scans and call the age of the unborn, in a study from twenty twenty-four. The shape of the sac and its mean width help foresee miscarriage and tell how far along a mother is, early on. By hand, the measures are slow work and swing with the sonographer who scans. Five hundred scans, from four to ten weeks, form a fresh data set.

Four nets of the CNN kind, built on ResNet cores, vie in cross-check rounds. ResUNet wins, with overlap and Dice scores near the top of the scale. A new biometry trick calls gestational age by machine, straight from the outlines. Its miss next to sonographers is just seven hundredths of a week, on average. The chain can stretch with ease to other parts of the unborn.
pmc-11688976:
Zhan Yu and co-authors study how the pandemic changed older adults' use of digital tools in China, in a mixed-methods study from 2024. China's zero-case policy leaned on mandatory QR codes, which pushed many older people online for daily needs. The team asked what that forced shift left behind.

Survey data showed internet use among older adults jumped sharply in 2020 against 2015. Focus groups in Shanghai added texture: many felt compelled to go digital to shop and stay in touch. In the post-pandemic era, some felt digital demands had invaded daily life. Belief in their own tech skill now drives whether they keep using it. Prior community tech classes shaped how people fared, a lead for policy.
pmc-11689676:
Vonetta Dotson gives a career talk, in twenty twenty-four, on brain health research and outreach. Dotson is a brain and aging specialist. Her work studies what helps or harms brain health in diverse older adults. Gains come from acts such as exercise. Harms come from states such as low mood. Her aim is to cut gaps in brain and mood disorders in late life, so all can age well.

She credits two bodies, a national aging institute and a national aging society, for support across her career. That support spans early training to large grants. She also shares newer outreach: a start-up firm and a book that give the public plain, science-based facts on keeping the mind sharp.
pmc-11690976:
William Evans asks how sarcopenia, the age-related loss of muscle, reached a state with no agreed definition, no diagnostic criteria, and no approved drug, in a symposium paper from 2024. Muscle is far more than a motor: it disposes of blood sugar, drives resting metabolism, supports bone, and stores amino acids for hard times.

Losing muscle therefore feeds chronic disease, disability, and death, and drug makers have chased muscle-building therapies for decades. Yet none has won approval for this condition. The symposium sets out to explain the stall. Science on muscle protein control has leapt ahead, the author notes, while the field's basic terms stayed unsettled. The piece frames the talks that follow on why translation into care has failed.
pmc-11692676:
Megan Siebecker and four co-authors chart, in a 2024 study, health disparities for Native American older adults in Wyoming. Accumulated inequities leave this group at higher risk for many chronic conditions than non-Hispanic White peers. The team drew on state healthy aging reports, census data, and COVID-19 death counts to compare the state with Fremont County, home to the largest share of older Native adults.

About twenty-four hundred Native adults aged 55 and up live in the state, and over half of them live in that county. Life expectancy there runs five years below the state mean. Deaths in the COVID-19 years ran about half again as high as the state rate. Maps built with small-area methods show the gaps in place. The authors call for policy steps aimed at these disparities.
pmc-11692876:
Ray-Yuan Chung and three co-authors build a chatbot to raise technology and health literacy in a retirement community. Their study came out in 2024. Many residents struggle with digital tools, which blocks their access to information and services.

The chatbot, powered by a large language model, was designed with the residents in mind: large text, high contrast, voice input, and simple navigation. It answers practical questions such as dining menus and contact details. It also gives step-by-step guides that teach digital skills as residents ask. In trial sessions, residents completed the set tasks successfully. They reported high satisfaction and said they would recommend the chatbot to peers. The authors propose it as a friendly front door to the community's existing app.
pmc-11693076:
Ai Iizuka and seven co-authors describe a 2024 trial of a team form of the board game Go for older adults in Tokyo. In Pair Go, two players share one side, so wins and losses are shared too. The team built a class around the game to test if shared play could lift mood and build social ties.

Twenty-eight adults aged seventy-one to eighty-six met once a week for twelve classes of ninety minutes. Each class mixed short talks, practice tasks, and full games in pairs. Scores for loneliness fell after the course, and half the group made new friends they kept seeing outside class. The authors say shared play may help in ways that the solo game does not.
pmc-11707476:
Remmele and coauthors compare vaccine cover in twins where one has a heart defect. Children born with heart defects face higher infection risk. Long hospital stays add exposure to germs as well. Twin pairs let the team control genes and home setting.

The study recruited twins across Germany from 2019 to 2022. Ages ran from 3 to 99 years in the pairs. Vaccine records were checked against German national rules. Cover for early shots and lung germ shots was logged. Pairs showed where the heart twin lagged or matched. Gaps may guide catch-up vaccine plans for heart patients.
pmc-11709576:
Gonzalo Sánchez-Benavides and co-authors test whether phone-call speech can flag hidden Alzheimer's changes in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Speech shifts can be early signs of the disease. People with memory complaints but normal test scores may already carry its biology.

Forty-one such Spanish and Catalan speakers did memory and fluency tasks on an automated call. Software scored their speech on memory, executive function, and speed. Those free of the amyloid marker scored higher overall than those with it. The gap was strongest for speed and middling for executive function, with no gap for memory. Tau groups showed only a trend. The authors see a cheap, remote screening path.
pmc-11709776:
Christian Haass presents a 2025 conference abstract on a gene therapy plan for frontotemporal degeneration. Too little progranulin, a growth-related protein, drives one inherited form of the disease, with TDP-43 clumps in the brain. Direct brain delivery of gene therapy spreads poorly, so Haass's team aimed a virus at the liver instead.

The virus makes a progranulin variant that can cross into the brain and stay there after one dose. In two mouse models, treatment eased motor deficits, TDP-43 faults, cleanup failure, and nerve loss. A human cell model showed the same rescue. The work offers early proof for this delivery route.
pmc-11709876:
Zahra Rostami and co-authors share a 2025 conference abstract on empathy-like behavior in rats given amyloid. Empathy rests on reading the feelings of others, a skill that frays in brain disease. The team injected amyloid into the hippocampus of rats and tested whether they still worked to free a soaked cage mate.

Fourteen rats took part, tracked over twelve days of the helping task. The time to open the door fell in the amyloid group, both when the soaked mate reacted and when it did not. The authors read the shift as a break in picking up social cues. The work probes how disease proteins warp social behavior.
pmc-11710076:
Edoardo Marcora and Hao Sun share a 2025 conference abstract on fine-mapping gene control sites in the human brain. Small DNA variants can tune how genes switch on, how their messages are spliced, and how chemical marks sit on DNA. The team used new math tools to pin down which variants drive these effects at single-letter detail.

The team found variants that play two or three roles at once, tuning marks and gene output across nearby genes. They also sorted splicing events that doom a message to decay, and tied one such event to an Alzheimer's risk signal. The results show how gene control layers interact in brain tissue.
pmc-11710876:
Omar Namiq and Namir Al-Tawil report a rare case of a rib broken by coughing, in work from two thousand twenty-four. A woman aged fifty-four had a dry cough for sixteen days after a chest infection. Sharp pain then set in on the right side of her chest.

The break sat in her right fifth rib, caused by the force of hard coughing. Her bone health showed no clear signs of the thinning disease often blamed for such breaks. Care without surgery led to a good outcome. The authors urge doctors to weigh rib breaks when a long, hard cough pairs with chest pain.
pmc-11712176:
Elizabeth A Boots and co-authors pilot a self-run thinking test in people with progressive supranuclear palsy in a 2025 Mayo Clinic study. The disease, called PSP, is a rare brain disorder that affects movement and thought. Self-run tests work well in Alzheimer's disease, but their fit for other diseases was untested. The platform, Mayo Test Drive, runs on phones and tablets.

Eleven patients took both the self-run test and standard paper tests. Ten finished the self-run test in about twenty-two minutes on average. Users rated ease of use near nine out of ten, and all said they could manage alone, though some needed help with links or codes. Those with the worst movement symptoms struggled most with tablets. Score links with the standard tests were also checked.
pmc-11713176:
Ramachandra Reddy and a large team study the safety and composition of an Ayurvedic herbo-mineral tablet proposed against COVID-19. Their 2024 study follows laboratory evidence that the tablet kills the virus in cell assays.

Safety was tested in fruit flies and their larvae, which stayed healthy and active at tested doses with normal activity rhythms. Elemental composition was measured with several spectrometry methods. Microscopy and diffraction examined the tablet's microstructure. The tablet proved safe in the fly model up to the highest dose tested. The authors argue the findings support an accessible, safe traditional therapeutic approach, with composition data guiding quality control.
pmc-11715276:
Pontus Eriksson and co-authors published this study in two thousand twenty-five on a spinal fluid protein called GFAP and its power to tell dementias apart. GFAP marks a kind of brain support-cell reaction, and labs are often asked to measure it, but its worth for diagnosis was unclear.

The team merged lab records with the Swedish dementia registry, covering more than nineteen hundred people across ten diagnoses. GFAP levels did differ by disease. Parkinson's dementia ran lowest, while vascular dementia and late-onset Alzheimer's ran high. The protein split some pairs of diseases cleanly, like vascular dementia from frontotemporal dementia. It failed to split others. The authors say GFAP can help on a group level in hard cases. It is one more clue for the clinic, not a stand-alone test.
pmc-11726876:
Shen and co-authors review a herb part, Z-ligustilide, as a care pick for wall fat ill. Wall fat, called AS, is a chief spark of brain vessel ills. Death and loss from it climb year by year in counts. The part comes from two herbs used in China care past. First, its stuff traits and body pace get told in the text. Then its acts on AS and brain kin ills get swept.

Acts span fat burn lift, rust fight, and flare calm in hosts. It guards wall coats and curbs scar, thick, and lime in plaques. In brain ills tied to AS, it shields nerve cells in hosts. Stroke, short stroke, and mind loss form that kin set. Paths span flare calm, rust fight, and cell death curbs.
pmc-11728676:
Philip Hicks and co-authors wrote a study from 2024 on a vaccine candidate against a deadly tick-borne virus of east Asia. The virus has sickened tens of thousands and kills a high share of its victims, yet no vaccine or therapy is approved. The team built the candidate on a proven vaccine platform: a mild livestock virus reworked to carry the target virus's surface proteins. They tested it in three mouse strains, including ones with weak immune defenses.

The vaccine proved safe even in the fragile strains and showed no nerve harm when placed in the brain. Vaccinated mice made strong neutralizing antibodies and survived a lethal dose of the virus. Serum from vaccinated mice also protected fresh animals, before or after exposure. The vaccine even shielded mice against a close American relative of the virus. The team calls the profile promising.
pmc-11784776:
Syed Mohammed Shafi and Sathiya Kumar Chinnappan propose a hybrid deep learning pipeline that first outlines diseased lung regions in scans and then names the disease. Lung disorders kill millions each year, and their scan appearances vary unpredictably, which makes automated reading hard. Writing in twenty twenty-four, their system cleans images with a noise filter, segments the affected area with an improved transformer and convolution design, and pulls out texture, shape, color, and learned features. A linked memory network then classifies the case, with the segmenter and classifier sharing a modified design.

Tested on two CT data sets, one covering COVID cases, the hybrid beat a long list of earlier models in the authors comparisons, with accuracy rising as more training data was used. The paper is aimed at builders of diagnostic support tools.
pmc-11789476:
Marta De La Plaza San Frutos and co-authors measure how fatigue, breathing, balance, and core muscles relate in multiple sclerosis in this study. People with MS often report deep fatigue, and it may drag on breathing and stability. Ultrasound now lets clinicians inspect trunk muscles directly.

The team studied 27 people with MS, 17 women and 10 men. They scored fatigue with a standard impact scale and measured lung capacity and forced exhalation. Balance was tested with two clinical scales. Ultrasound captured the size and behavior of abdominal muscles and the diaphragm. Comparing all these measures shows which problems travel together. Such links could shape rehab programs that train breathing and trunk strength together.
pmc-11841676:
Maboko and five co-authors screen fresh drug shapes for blocks on a brain enzyme tied to Alzheimer's disease. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. Drugs that block this enzyme are first-line care, but they ease signs more than they cure and can harm. The team sought shapes that block well, cross into the brain, and spare cells.

More than fourteen hundred shapes were screened in lab and by computer. Twelve blocked the enzyme well at low dose, and five could cross to the brain on the model. One shape plus a known drug gave the best joint gain. One shape, called C53, stood out as safe and strong, alone and paired, and is flagged for more work.
pmc-11894576:
Maria Christofidou and colleagues published a 2025 legal study of consent for health data reuse in Europe. European privacy law demands informed consent. Research uses are often impossible to specify in advance. Genomic studies and trials expose the tension clearly. Different groups have improvised different consent models.

The authors reviewed these models and the surrounding debate. A newer idea is data altruism. People could donate data for public good under safeguards. The study asks whether altruism frameworks solve the research problem. Clearer lawful paths would help studies share data responsibly. Patient trust must anchor any solution.
pmc-12099076:
Shota Fukuda and five colleagues published a 2024 study on friendly mouth bacteria that block a gum disease germ. The germ, Porphyromonas gingivalis, invades gum cells and drives periodontal disease. Healthy mouths host many harmless bacteria, but their protective roles are rarely tested in the lab.

The team focused on Neisseria, a common harmless mouth resident. They built a flow-based test to count how many germs get inside gum cells. Neisseria cut that invasion down in their tests. The result suggests some mouth residents act as guards, not just bystanders. Harnessing such guards could add a new line of defense against gum disease.
pmc-12110476:
Yusuf Karaşin and Yalçın Karagöz build a survey scale for abortion attitudes in Turkey, in work from 2024. Abortion is lawful there under set terms, and views on it split by culture and era. A shared scale can make those views plain to study. The team drafted items, took expert notes, piloted the draft, and tested it on three hundred three women in Istanbul.

The final scale holds twenty-three items in three groups. The groups were named stigma, exclusion, and heed for respect. Fit scores for the three-group shape passed standard bars. The authors offer the scale as a sound tool for future work on this charged topic in Turkey.
pmc-12284476:
Rubromycins are bacterial aromatic polyketides with a signature spiroketal core, known for killing cells and germs by striking nucleic acids. One member bears a ring change that an amide bond synthetase installs. The six authors mined genomes for clusters with that enzyme but without the usual ring-building enzymes, in hope of finding a new compound. One strain, Lentzea tibetensis, was the hit.

Grown in culture, it made a new family member fused to an aminocoumarin group, which the team named coumarubrin. Mass spectrometry and NMR pinned down its structure, and its absolute configuration matches the family. First assays show strong activity against Gram-positive bacteria. The head dates the paper to 2024, though the catalog lists 2025.
pmc-12692276:
Eight researchers study how melatonin protects goat fertility cells from heat in a paper from 2025. Heat stress is a growing threat to male fertility in livestock as the climate warms. Sertoli cells support sperm production but are easily hurt by heat. The team exposed goat cells to heat and tracked gene activity and carbon flow through cell metabolism.

Heat damaged the cells' energy hubs and slowed the main energy cycle. Pre-treatment with melatonin restored hub function and chemical balance. It also shifted metabolism into a protective pattern and kept more cells alive. The authors say melatonin could help protect breeding animals in hot climates. The work also informs human heat and fertility research.
pmc-12695476:
Shintaro Yamagami and co-authors check whether slow blood flow in a heart pouch predicts clots after a rhythm procedure in a 2025 study. Atrial fibrillation lets blood pool in the left atrial appendage, a small pouch where clots form. Ablation can restore rhythm, but stroke risk may linger. The speed of flow in that pouch, seen on an ultrasound through the esophagus, was already known as a warning sign before treatment.

The team reviewed more than fifteen hundred ablation patients who had that ultrasound first. About one hundred had reduced flow speed; the rest had preserved speed. They then tracked clot events, rhythm relapse, and major heart outcomes over the long term. If a slow pouch still warns after ablation, those patients may need longer clot protection than the standard plan.
pmc-12695676:
Kruthika Reddy and co-authors report an unusual case of Wilson disease in a 2025 article. Wilson disease is an inherited disorder where copper builds up in the body and can damage the brain. It usually shows with tremor, stiffness, or behavior change, which makes it easier to suspect.

Their patient was a twenty-four-year-old Indian man whose only problem was nine months of slurred speech, plus drooling and trouble moving food with his tongue. He had no tremor, stiffness, or thinking problems. Eye rings typical of copper buildup, blood tests, and brain scans pointed to the diagnosis. Treatment with copper-removing drugs and speech therapy brought marked improvement by his own account. The authors urge a full work-up when slurred speech stands alone.
pmc-12699376:
Asma El Kaourat and eight co-authors published a 2025 study making silver nanoparticles the green way, from argan oil waste. Saponins drawn from argan press cake, the residue of oil making, drove the synthesis of silver and silver chloride grains. A battery of instruments confirmed the product: round grains 12 nanometers across on average, with the expected light absorption band.

The grains killed both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria in standard assays. They also showed moderate toxicity against three cancer cell lines, breast and cervical among them. The authors present the waste-to-grain route as sustainable and biocompatible, with medical promise. Turning a regional waste stream into a medical material is the study's wider pitch.
pmc-12702276:
Yueping Zhou and colleagues compare three ways of preparing the womb lining for a frozen embryo transfer in women whose ovaries respond poorly, in this study from twenty twenty-five. Over four thousand six hundred women with diminished ovarian reserve had their first transfer between twenty sixteen and twenty twenty-four. The options were a natural cycle, hormone replacement, or hormone replacement preceded by a drug that quiets the ovaries first.

The pretreatment won. Women who received it had better live birth and clinical pregnancy rates than hormone replacement alone, with the clearest gain in those thirty-five and older. Natural cycle and hormone replacement performed alike. Babies born as singletons fared similarly whichever route was used. The authors suggest the quieting pretreatment deserves a place for older patients with low reserve, while noting the evidence is retrospective.
pmc-12706876:
Tadesse Sheleme and co-authors ran a cluster randomized trial of medication therapy management in southwest Ethiopia. Their 2025 study took in adults who had both diabetes mellitus and hypertension, and who went to outpatient clinics.

Hospitals were placed by chance in a group that got the new care or a group that did not. Each group had two hundred one patients. The new-care group got medication therapy management as well as the usual care. Staff gauged how well patients stuck to their drugs with the Adherence in Chronic Diseases Scale. In the new-care group, the share who stuck to their drugs rose by fifty percent. The control group showed a unlike result. The trial tests if set, pharmacist-led help can keep people on long-term drugs.
pmc-12714576:
Lorenzo Peri, Alberto Gomez-Saiz, Christopher Ford, and Fernando Gonzalez-Zalba made small models that let staff run quantum dots in plain circuit tools. Quantum machines of the years ahead must join with plain circuits. To run that joint face true in tests is key but hard. Their Verilog-A models copy sound quantum acts and loss of sync in a stock circuit tool. The 2025 work aims at chip based and Majorana based quantum kits.

Joint tests in a trade stock design tool showed quantum acts run side by side with plain parts. The models aim for no trade off past quantum truth and true circuit feel. Years of chip design work could then serve quantum builds. The team frames this as a new design way. Quantum chips get built with the same flows that made plain chips.
pmc-12716476:
Shota Imai and seven co-authors engineered tiny cell-made parcels that teach the immune system to stand down against one chosen target, in this 2025 study. Lasting tolerance would help autoimmune and allergy patients, but blunt drugs suppress everything. Their parcels display three signals on the surface: the target antigen on its presenting molecule, plus two calming messengers.

In dishes, the parcels turned naive immune cells into antigen-specific regulatory T cells carrying the classic calming markers. In mice, pairing the parcels with a low dose of rapamycin boosted those cells further. The induced cells actively suppressed other immune responses in tests. The authors present the design as a modular, cell-free route to precise tolerance.
pmc-12718176:
Herminia Torelló-Sentelles and four co-authors show how cities slow storms down, and so pile up rain and flood risk. Their study, from two thousand twenty-five, joins radar reads with storm sims.

How storms move over towns may sway how much rain falls and how floods rise. The team tracked lone rain cells over eight towns, and matched their pace by the town to a pace up-wind. Next they simmed ten heavy rain runs over one town, with and sans the town's build. Cells slowed over and past most towns. The sims showed the same: winds at cloud height eased. Warm town ground lifts drafts, which brake the winds. More rain, not just pace, drives most of the flood gain.
pmc-12720476:
Bethany Davey and colleagues pool trials on whether numbing a nerve can spare hip fracture patients the confusion of delirium, in this review from twenty twenty-five. Postoperative delirium is common and harmful after hip surgery. Peripheral nerve blocks ease pain without heavy sedation, which might protect the brain.

Twelve randomized trials, eleven hundred fifty-seven patients in all, compared blocks against none in patients without prior cognitive problems. Delirium struck about a third less often with a block, a pooled risk ratio of zero point six eight. The authors are careful: block techniques varied, trial designs differed, and the patients most at risk, those already impaired, were excluded by design. They call for standardized trials stratified by risk. Still, in a frail population where every avoided delirium counts, the signal favors the block.
pmc-12722476:
Suus van Noort, Deborah Sival, and Dineke Verbeek present a 2025 study of hindbrain faults. The hindbrain is the back part of the brain, home to the cerebellum and brainstem. Gene-based faults there are found more often as scans and gene tests improve. Why so many gene faults strike this region is still unclear. The team builds a fresh gene list for hindbrain faults.

Genes are sorted by where the fault shows most: cerebellum, both regions, or brainstem. Brain gene networks then reveal shared paths among the genes. The networks also flag new genes not yet tied to hindbrain faults. Shared paths hint at what hindbrain growth cannot do without. Child brain doctors get a map that may speed diagnosis in odd cases. A gene on the flag list can guide the next lab test. The study is data analysis, so flagged genes still need bench proof.
pmc-12723076:
Thomas Klak and six colleagues published a tree restoration study in two thousand twenty-five on the American chestnut. A blight fungus from abroad wiped out this once-dominant forest tree. Engineered blight-tolerant trees may restore it, but breeding them outdoors is slow and tightly regulated.

The team grew trees indoors, where both male and female flowers formed quickly. They also rescued embryos from young seeds and grew them in the lab. These steps produced the first fully transgenic chestnut trees carrying the trait in both copies. Pollen from them passed the trait to nearly all offspring in outdoor crosses. DNA markers now identify each engineered line. The authors say indoor speed breeding could speed the tree's return.
pmc-12727876:
Jin-Hua Li and four co-authors test how layer thickness governs the strength of rock made of soft and hard bands. Their twenty twenty-five article deals with laminated rock masses, common in tunnels and slopes. The mix of soft and hard layers makes the mass uneven and directional in its behavior.

The team made samples with soft shares from ten to ninety percent and crushed them under one-axis load while listening for acoustic cracks. As the soft share rose, peak strength fell by about sixty-three percent and stiffness fell too. Failure shifted from splitting, led by the hard layers, to shear sliding, with a longer plastic stage. An energy account of the breakage rounds out the model.
pmc-12728076:
Eichler, Kruse, Schob, and Lenz review what makes links between brain cells in the top layers of the human cortex special, in a review from twenty twenty-five. These links both send and store signals, which underpins learning and memory. Human brains have extra thick top layers and more long links than other species. That hints their links may work in distinct ways.

Recent work uses thin slices of human cortex taken in surgery. The review pulls that work together on link shape, strength, and change. It shows traits that set human links apart from those in lab animals. It also maps gaps that still need study. The goal is to grasp how human brain webs work as a whole.
pmc-12729076:
Yisong Yang and co-authors published this cancer review in 2025. Tumors burn through cholesterol as they grow, and one enzyme throttles its production: HMGCR, the target of statin drugs. The review gathers evidence this enzyme acts as a hub in many cancers. It supplies cholesterol and building blocks, feeds growth pathways, and helps tumors hide from the immune system. It tunes how sensitive cancer cells are to a form of iron-driven cell death.

The story has a twist. An inflammatory signal, TNF-alpha, can suppress the enzyme, while the enzyme in turn shapes that inflammation. Statins block the enzyme and show anti-tumor effects in the lab. In patients, the needed doses can be toxic, and resistance and tissue targeting pose problems. The authors argue for precision approaches aimed at the enzyme's web of interactions, and for better inhibitors that hit tumors without the costs.
pmc-12729576:
Anne-Sophie Jung and five colleagues published a 2025 study of how antibiotics move from makers to patients in rural and peri-urban India. Antimicrobial resistance grows partly because of how antibiotics are accessed, distributed, and used along complex supply chains. Most research has focused on manufacturing and regulation, not on the last miles to the consumer.

The study mapped the human antibiotic value chain in West Bengal. Formal and informal sellers, distributors, and prescribers all play roles, sometimes following rules and sometimes breaking or remaking them. The authors analyze how this governance actually works on the ground. Stewardship programs that ignore the real chain risk failure; this mapping gives them a realistic starting point.
pmc-12730876:
Wouter De Brouwer and co-authors compare, in a 2025 pilot study, three sources of tumor DNA for tracking multiple myeloma, a cancer of plasma cells in bone marrow. Even after deep remission, traces of disease usually remain and later drive relapse. Marrow sampling hurts and cannot be repeated often, so blood-based checks are in demand.

The team used gene sequencing of the antibody locus on marrow DNA, free DNA in blood, blood cell DNA, and DNA from tumor cells fished out of blood. In active disease, the fished-out cells scored best, finding tumor DNA in every case. In remission patients, half of those positive in marrow were also positive in the enriched blood cells. Patients negative in blood cells but positive in marrow progressed about as slowly as those negative in both. The authors see promise in the blood method.
pmc-12731176:
Katerina Konikkou and colleagues tested whether a fast burst-pattern brain stimulation shifts attention toward or away from emotional images. Theta-burst stimulation, or TBS, is a faster cousin of standard magnetic stimulation. Here it was aimed at the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. Ninety-one healthy young adults were randomized to real or sham TBS over the left or right side. They then did a dot-probe task with distressing, pleasant, and neutral pictures.

Those who got real TBS responded more slowly to probes that replaced neutral images than to emotional ones. The sham groups showed no such gap. The pattern suggests the pulses tilted attention toward emotional material. Such biases in emotional attention matter in anxiety and depression research. This twenty twenty-five trial refines where and how brief TBS protocols can move that bias.
pmc-12733076:
Suchanski and co-authors trace how a membrane lipid, sulfatide, controls death signals in breast cancer cells. Odd sugar coating on cell surfaces is a hallmark of cancer and aids tumor growth. Sulfatide levels shift often in breast cancer, with mixed effects seen before.

Prior work showed sulfatide helps tumors spread through blood vessel contact. Yet high levels also made cells more prone to die and less tumor-forming. Using two cell lines with altered sulfatide output, the team found BOLA2 dropped as sulfatide rose. Raising BOLA2 made cells resist a chemo drug's killing effect. Integrin and STAT5 signals also enter the control path.
pmc-12733176:
Sharon Hadad and Ohad Shaked surveyed small business owners in Israel about mental distress during the war that began in October twenty twenty-three. Their study, published in twenty twenty-five, treats owner well-being as a public health issue, not just a business concern. A nationwide survey asked about money pressures, personal resources, trust in institutions, and background traits. The team then modeled how those factors combined to shape distress levels during the conflict.

Uncertainty and lost income raised distress the most. Resilience, hope, and trust in government lowered it, acting as protective resources. Patterns differed between men and women owners. The authors argue that helping entrepreneurs cope during armed conflict supports whole communities, since small firms anchor jobs and daily life. They frame support for owners as part of national recovery and health promotion.
pmc-12734776:
Szczygiel and Radon-Kobus test how print orientation affects a steel-filled plastic composite made by filament printing, in a study from twenty twenty-five. The composite holds ninety-five percent steel powder by weight, far above typical loadings. Such heavy filling may behave very differently by print direction. Samples are printed flat and upright for comparison.

Tensile tests measure strength in each orientation. Surface roughness is read with a contact profilometer. Wetting is judged from contact angle, and size accuracy from caliper checks. Results link orientation to both strength and surface traits. The data guide printing choices for metal-rich polymer parts where direction cannot be ignored.
pmc-12735176:
Tanya Pereira-Riveros and colleagues grow a finicky gum bacterium using extract from another bacterium. Their methods paper from twenty twenty-five targets Tannerella forsythia culture. The periodontal pathogen cannot make a key wall ingredient itself. Pure cultures need that ingredient supplied from outside.

The team extracted wall material from a staph strain instead. Measurements standardised the extract strength with calibration curves. Plates seeded with the extract went into an oxygen-free chamber. The target bacterium grew on those plates over a week. Results confirm the substitute source supports isolation work. Simpler culture opens this pathogen to more labs. Gum disease research depends on growing such organisms reliably.
pmc-12735276:
Boyanka Angelova and co-authors map the bacteria that live at the edges of three glacial lakes in the Rila Mountains of Bulgaria, in work from twenty twenty-five. High lakes are rich in life yet hard to reach, so their microbes stay poorly known. Seasons and warming may reshape those small communities fast.

Water samples came from ice free months in twenty twenty-three and twenty twenty-four. Gene reads found more than a thousand bacterial groups across the lakes. Richness peaked in June, just after ice melt, most of all in the highest lake. Warmth and carbon in the water drove the main shifts. The study warns that cold loving types may fade as the region warms.
pmc-12736376:
Sofía Fernández-Godino and co-authors report a small study from two thousand twenty-five on diet and daily function in multiple sclerosis. The disease inflames and damages nerves in the brain and spinal cord, often in young adults. Diet may shape its course, since foods differ in how much they stir inflammation.

The team studied nineteen patients, scoring their diets with an index of inflammatory potential. They also rated function with a scale made for this disease. Patients on the more inflammatory diet reported a heavier symptom burden, with more fatigue and more muscle and gut complaints. Those on the calmer diet reported fewer symptoms and more energy. The authors treat the work as a first step that needs larger samples.
pmc-12737076:
Sérgio Ivan Lopes and co-authors published a 2025 perspective article on low-cost air sensors for indoor rooms, and how to build and trust systems around them. Tight new buildings hold air in, saving energy but fouling the air people breathe. People spend most of their lives indoors. A sick building syndrome grew from that: illnesses with no single cause, tied to time spent in a place.

Low-cost sensors can now monitor indoor air in real time, at fine detail. They flag pollution sources and help cut heating and cooling use. They do not match the reference instruments, and the team is plain about that. The article gives a shared design model for such sensor networks, from the sensing head to the network link. It then weighs the strengths and weaknesses of the cheap path, and looks ahead to how their reliability can be proven.
pmc-12738076:
Chowdhury and coauthors give a lab method for sharp imaging of cell fibers. A method called expansion microscopy puffs samples up for fine views. It lets plain lab scopes show tiny cell parts. Fiber labels can blur or shift during sample prep, though.

The new method strips cell fluid and skins while it keeps fibers intact. Growth steps then cut fibers into small bits for dye tagging. Dyes tag the cut ends, so no antibody step is due. Tag shift stays at about one nanometer or less. The method works for lab-grown fibers and for fibers in cells.
pmc-12738576:
Azine Datlibagi and a team of co-authors built a lab model of a scarring eye disease, in two thousand twenty-five. The disease grows membranes inside the eye that can harm sight. Their model uses a human retinal cell line grown in a dish, with or without a water channel protein added.

Certain treatments pushed the cells to change type, stretch out, and move more, like cells in the disease. Cells with the added protein, under the harsh treatment, matched real patient membranes most closely in gene use. The protein also seemed to aid cell movement and invasion on its own. The authors offer the model as an easy tool for study.
pmc-12739176:
Louis-Marie Paget and four co-authors published a check-up study in twenty twenty-five on how well code-based rules spot mild head injury in French emergency rooms. France has no dedicated watch system for these injuries. A large ER data network could fill the gap, if its diagnosis codes can be trusted.

The team read over five thousand charts by hand and scored each rule against the charts. Rules worked well in children but fell short in adults, and none met the bar set for a watch system on its own. Scores shifted with age and other traits of the patients. The authors show both the promise of the data and the work still needed before it can count cases with care.
pmc-12743476:
Eddie Nagadi and co-authors published a 2025 study of how to rinse the root canals of a tooth so a deep bacterium dies in the walls. The bacterium in view often feeds root infections. The rinse is a mixture of three fluids, activated in the canal by one of three ways: sonic shaking, ultrasonic shaking, or a laser beam. A plain needle rinse was the control.

Nearly forty extracted teeth were seeded with the bacterium and split into four groups. Live-dead dye and a fine microscope measured how deep the kill ran. The laser way won by a wide gap: its kill depth ran past a thousand tiny units, micrometers. The sonic way came next, then the ultrasonic. The needle control ran least by far. Statistical checks held the gaps as firm.
pmc-12748576:
Patoo Withatanung and co-authors characterize a new virus that infects a staph bacterium in this 2025 paper. The host, Staphylococcus pseudintermedius, infects animals and can pass to humans. Drug resistant forms with strong biofilms are a growing problem. The virus, called VL4, was isolated from sewage using a resistant clinical strain.

Its genome holds 68 reading frames and no toxin, resistance, or virulence genes. Family analysis placed it as a new species in its genus. The virus reproduced fast and stayed stable at body temperature and neutral acidity. It suppressed host growth and attacked 27 of 31 clinical isolates. It also blocked new biofilms and partly broke down mature ones. Such phages may become backup treatments.
pmc-12749976:
Murata and co-authors wrote a study from 2025 on delayed bleeding after removal of bowel growths in patients on blood thinners. The drugs, a class of direct oral blood thinners, are gauged poorly by standard tests. Their strength in the blood varies a lot from person to person. Delayed bleeding days after the snip is a known risk of the procedure. Whether the drug's measured strength predicts that bleed was unknown.

Centers across Japan followed users of these drugs through the procedure over four years. About one in ten suffered delayed bleeding. Blood levels of the drugs swung widely between patients on the same dose. A lab gauge of the drug's anti-clotting action tracked the blood levels closely. In the pooled math, patients whose drug action ran high faced far greater odds of a delayed bleed. The team advises care with patients whose readings run strong.
pmc-12751676:
Francesca Conca and a large team mapped how the brain supports picture naming in people with brain disease that gets worse over time. Their 2025 study had 178 patients in the frontotemporal dementia group and the Alzheimer's disease group. Each patient took an Italian picture naming test and had an FDG-PET brain scan. The team cut ten word traits, such as word length and how often a word is used, down to four groups. They linked naming scores to brain use in eleven zones on the left side of the brain.

Short, plain word forms went with better naming. One brain zone, the fusiform gyrus, backed both the look and the sense of the pictures. Front and side zones linked word sense and word sound. The two disease groups used distinct zones for the same traits. That hints each disease finds its own way to make up for loss.
pmc-12751976:
Xue Zhong and co-authors mine health records for conditions that precede Alzheimer's disease in a 2025 study. Some conditions are known to raise risk, but a systematic scan had not been done. The team used two huge record databases, covering 153 million people, and tracked the ten years before diagnosis.

They found over forty-four thousand cases matched against hundreds of thousands of controls. Hundreds of conditions appeared more often in future patients, led by mental and nerve disorders. More than seventy conditions repeated in both databases, including depression, sleep disorders, artery hardening in the brain, and type two diabetes. Nineteen of them tied to known genetic risk signals for the disease. The authors see chances for early action in the list.
pmc-12752976:
Jing Lin and four co-authors ran a trial on pain relief after womb surgery in a 2025 paper. Deep internal pain after keyhole removal of the womb remains hard to control. A neck nerve block, guided by ultrasound, is used for other pain but was little tested for this kind. The team split ninety patients into three groups.

One group got both blocks, one got a belly wall block alone, and one got no block. The combined group reported much lower deep pain in the first hours and needed rescue pain drugs far less often. Cut pain did not differ between groups. The authors back the neck block as an addition to standard pain plans.
pmc-12753476:
Megan Wolfe and co-authors compare glucose in spinal fluid with glucose in blood, in healthy dogs and dogs with brain and cord disease. Spinal fluid glucose is easy to measure and might track inflamed disease of the central nervous system. The team used the ratio of fluid glucose to blood glucose. Records came from one hospital.

The study held 41 healthy dogs and 359 with nervous system disease. In healthy dogs, fluid glucose averaged 78.4 milligrams per deciliter and the ratio 0.80. In healthy dogs the ratio rose with age. Dogs with non-inflamed structural disease had higher fluid glucose than healthy dogs, near 87.8, but a like ratio. Dogs with epilepsy had a like ratio too. Dogs with inflamed disease had a mean ratio of 0.70, significantly lower. A cheap fluid test will not name a disease, but a low ratio adds a clue for inflammation.
pmc-12753976:
Lingang Xu and four co-authors build a machine learning model to forecast how well stem cell care will work in plastic surgery. The care shows promise, but results vary a lot by person and no trusty forecast tool exists. The study came out in twenty twenty-five.

Records of hundreds of patients treated over three years were split into training and test sets. The team screened traits by single factor checks, then by joined models and a shrink method that picks key traits. Three learning models were built and checked on the held back set. About three in five patients in both sets had good outcomes, which sets the base the models must beat.
pmc-12754176:
Hai-fei Zhou and colleagues find a way to grade stomach cancer from scans alone, without a blood draw, in this study from twenty twenty-five. Doctors can estimate how much of a tumor is fluid space outside cells, a clue to how nasty the cancer is. The standard method needs the patient's blood count from a lab sample, which is not always on hand at scan time.

The team used one group of patients to build formulas that infer the blood value from plain CT images of two large vessels. In a second group with stomach cancer and dual-energy CT scans, the inferred values matched the lab-based ones closely. Both versions sorted tumors by their grade under the microscope about equally well. The authors say the scan-only method can stand in when blood results are missing, keeping the grade clue available for care planning.
pmc-12756476:
Xinyuan Han, Zhijun Huang, Jing Ning, and Wenhui Shang published this case report in 2025. It describes a 47-year-old man with high blood pressure who fell into a coma from bleeding inside his brainstem. Scans showed a bleed of 10.3 milliliters, a size that usually ends in death. The report follows the mix of treatments the hospital team used over the following weeks.

Doctors drained the pooled blood through a small guided puncture and opened a breathing tube in his neck. Care also covered drugs to stop bleeding, steps to lower pressure inside the skull, and treatment for repeated infections by drug-resistant bacteria. After two months the man woke up and regained some limb strength, though speech and swallowing stayed impaired. The authors present the case as a sign that combined care can save some patients, while noting that one case cannot prove the approach.
pmc-12766576:
Jens Bager Christensen and co-authors published this developmental neuroscience study in 2025. A signaling pathway called WNT pushes cells from the first state into the second. Both factors also run separate side jobs in cell division and survival. pmc-12780176:
Ana Raquel Cruz and co-authors wrote a study from 2025 on gut bacteria that cling to the bowel wall and help train the immune system. The bacteria grow first as single teardrop cells, then stretch into long threads. The tip of the young cell is the part that grips the gut wall. The team froze the bacteria and viewed them with a fine electron scope to see that grip up close.

Young cells wear a neat, tiled coat. At the tip, it gives way to a messy fringe of hairs. As the cell grows into a thread, a new hair-like coat takes over. The same switch showed up in bacteria from mice and rats. One key protein sits all over the wall but can be reached by immune cells only at the tip.
pmc-12780376:
Li and a large team build in twenty twenty-five a scan-based model to spot hidden air trapping in lungs that standard breathing tests miss. Trapped air signals small-airway trouble, defined here by an inflated leftover air volume. In a single-centre group of several dozen adults, each person had low-dose scans at full inhale and exhale plus breathing tests within a week.

About a third met the trapping definition. Their scans showed distinct density ratios and more very-low-density lung area than the rest. A model built on scan measures sorted the groups well in training and fairly in internal checks, led by three measures. The authors say paired-phase scans could aid early risk sorting and follow-up.
pmc-12783176:
Guoshan Li and six colleagues engineer a nerve repair tube loaded with a drug and stem cells, in a study published in two thousand twenty-five. Peripheral nerve injuries after fractures often heal incompletely. A guidance conduit that also delivers therapy could close the gap.

Laboratory tests checked structure, mechanics, cell survival, and blood compatibility. Rats with severed sciatic nerves then tested real recovery. Motor and sensory function, muscle preservation, and axon regrowth were measured. The menstrual blood cells are an accessible, ethically simple stem cell source. The design stacks several healing aids into one implant.
pmc-12788576:
Mohammed Rashid and colleagues measured jaw bone density during orthodontic treatment sped up with low-level laser light. Laser treatment can move teeth faster, but its effect on the dense outer bone of the lower jaw was unclear. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team ran a randomized study of adult patients with fixed braces. Half received laser sessions on alternating days during the first month, aimed at the lower jaw bone. Three-dimensional scans at the start and after twelve weeks gave density readings near a molar and a canine tooth.

The laser group lost clear density at both sites by twelve weeks, while the control group barely changed. Lower density fits the idea that light loosens bone so teeth can shift sooner. The authors present the finding as support for laser-assisted treatment, within the short window their scans covered.
pmc-12791176:
Nilesh V Joshi and six colleagues review what happens when dental implants sit very close to natural tooth roots, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Bone loss and implant gum disease appeared in up to four percent of very close placements. Cavities and structural defects were reported less consistently, mostly in back teeth. pmc-12800176:
L. Szelerski and colleagues compared surgical techniques for healing upper arm bone breaks that had failed to knit, using an external frame method named for Ilizarov. The frame slowly adjusts bone position while new bone forms. Records before and after surgery included X-ray classifications and validated shoulder function questionnaires, plus standard scoring systems for bone and function.

About nine in ten patients achieved bone union that held over a year of follow-up. Shoulder scores improved by large margins on every scale used. The most common problem was infection around the frame wires. The authors recommend the frame especially when nonunion comes with deformity or shortening, and favor a closed approach for chronic cases at risk of wound trouble.
pmc-12801576:
Wan, Hamid, and Krishna study mental health and identity growth among medical students in Singapore, in a study from twenty twenty-five. Those clashes test students' inner compass, meaning their core belief system. Students with a mature compass and strong support cope in healthy ways. Those without support fall into harmful coping and deeper strain. The team urges long-term, personal support over brief fixes.
pmc-12805776:

They then tested it on 526 elderly pain patients at a large hospital in Shanxi Province.

The final Chinese version kept sixteen items. Expert ratings of content quality were high. Factor analysis found four themes: disability, confidence for physical activity, movement avoidance, and self-perceived ability. Together they explained about sixty-nine percent of the variation in answers. Consistency and repeat-test scores were all solid, above 0.84. The authors conclude the translated scale is reliable and valid for studying how pain relates to movement behavior in this patient group.
pmc-12807976:
Anna Braspenning and seven colleagues interview users of a blended phone-based fatigue program for young patients, in a study from twenty twenty-five. No such blended program had yet reached pediatric care.

Eleven patients, eleven close others, and twenty professionals were interviewed. Patients wanted improvement yet found the sampling burdensome. Three themes ran through their accounts. Families valued the insights the sampling produced. Support and ownership shaped how the program landed. The study maps what implementation must solve. Effort must be balanced against insight for young users.
pmc-12810176:

Seven databases were searched through April two thousand twenty-four; five studies qualified and two entered the meta-analysis, most at low bias risk. In class two malocclusion, patients with heavier lower crowding had mandibles about four millimeters shorter than lightly crowded peers. Crowding ran moderate to severe with short class two bases and minimal with the longer bases of class three. The authors frame jaw length as a diagnostic input for tailored orthodontic plans.
pmc-12811976:
Adibul Chowdhury and four co-authors report a liver illness that mimicked an autoimmune disease, in this twenty twenty-five case paper. Tests found immune markers and tissue signs that pointed to autoimmune hepatitis. Yet he lacked other traits of that disease, and his virus stayed controlled. A team of specialists judged the long-used drug the true cause and swapped it for another. The case warns that drug harm can arrive late and wear a good disguise.
pmc-12816576:
Shehla Yasmeen, Aaron DiFilippo, and Marius Orlowski explain a strange effect in copper-based memory devices: stopping a reset halfway makes them conduct better. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. The devices store data in a tiny metal filament whose shape sets the resistance.

pmc-12821176:

Sequencing the parcels' small RNAs then profiled their cargo. The authors offer the pipeline to other hard plant tissues.
pmc-12821276:
Tianci Yao and a team of co-authors studied how changes in frailty link to new chronic disease, in two thousand twenty-five. Frailty is a state of weakness that grows with age. The team used a large Chinese study of adults aged forty-five and older, with frailty checked twice, two years apart.

pmc-12829276:
