pmc-12834976:
Gökhan Yüksek, a solo author, designs a motor controller that bakes time delay into its own rule, in a 2025 engineering study. The target is the brushless DC motor, a workhorse in robots and vehicles, whose speed must hold steady when signals lag. The controller blends the present error with a weighted delayed error, and two knobs reshape how it chases the set speed. A physics-inspired search method tuned the gains.

On a standard test rig, the tuned design settled eight percent faster than rival tuned controllers and cost less on a mixed score. Overshoot stayed under three percent. Lab runs on a real drive kept the edge under noise, drift, and outside pushes. The author offers the design for motion jobs where lag cannot be dodged.
pmc-12835476:
Chenchen Yang and four co-authors mined single-cell data for a prognostic gene in pancreatic cancer in a 2025 paper. Pancreatic cancer is among the deadliest cancers, and chemical tags placed on proteins after they are built may drive its course. One tag, S-nitrosylation, had never been profiled in this disease.

The team combined bulk and single-cell data from several cohorts and raced 101 machine learning combinations to build a survival model. Their winning model split patients into high- and low-risk groups across nine cohorts. Among tag-linked genes, LAMC2 tracked the risk score most strongly. Lab tests in a pancreatic cancer cell line backed its role. The authors propose LAMC2 as a key driver worth targeting.
pmc-12836976:
Henrik Thomassen and Villy Våge report one center's results with a repair for reflux after weight-loss surgery, in a 2025 paper. The surgery, sleeve gastrectomy, is the most common weight-loss operation, yet it often leaves patients with heartburn. The usual fix is a gastric bypass, but some patients still need daily acid pills.

The Hill repair rebuilds the valve area between stomach and food pipe without wrapping the stomach around it. Ten patients had the repair between 2019 and 2022 for reflux after sleeve surgery. Symptom scores improved at one and three years, and pill use fell from all patients to under a third. Pressure at the valve rose sharply after surgery. Two patients later needed another operation for returning symptoms.
pmc-12838476:
Klaus Widhalm, Sebastian Durstberger, and Peter Putz report a two thousand twenty-five crossover trial on downhill walking and knee control. Poor leg alignment while walking can feed into knee osteoarthritis. Live visual feedback might help walkers correct their movement.

Twenty-eight healthy adults aged eighteen to thirty-five walked on a sloped treadmill. Conditions mixed self-paced walking, inward focus, and screen feedback, plus a matched-speed repeat. Feedback changed left knee sideways motion and load balance between the legs. Effects were moderate to large. The findings support testing feedback training for people who need better knee control.
pmc-12840076:
Awele Ndubisi, Felix Agyapong-Opoku, and Belinda Agyapong review past reviews on social media use and sleep quality in teens and young adults, in a paper from 2025. Heavy social media use is now a normal part of young life. Many studies link it to poor sleep, through late use, light, and mental arousal.

The team used a five-stage scoping method and searched five databases for reviews from 2020 to 2025. Ten reviews met all the rules and were studied. Across them, social media use had a small but steady negative link to sleep quality. Problem use, where habits feel out of control, linked more strongly than normal use. Some platforms tied more to short sleep and late bedtimes than others. The authors map gaps for future studies.
pmc-12840776:
Tatiana Tikhonova and five colleagues turn a drop of finger blood into a calcium measurement using a smart gel, in a study published in two thousand twenty-five. Blood calcium flags parathyroid, kidney, and bone disorders. Point-of-care testing needs methods without a full laboratory.

Their platform is gelatin hydrogel loaded with Arsenazo III, a calcium-sensitive dye. A blood drop placed on the gel separates into plasma and cells as it soaks in. Calcium binding shifts the gel's absorption spectrum, readable optically. Six candidate gel materials were compared; only gelatin performed suitably. The approach promises rapid total calcium readings at the bedside or clinic. Simplicity is the selling point: no centrifuge, no large analyzer.
pmc-12846476:
Mario García-González and four co-authors report a detailed guinea pig case in a 2025 paper. Diseases of the reproductive tract are common in pet guinea pigs, but two conditions found together are rarely written up. Their patient was a two-year-old female with a tender belly.

Ultrasound showed cysts on both ovaries and a thickened, cyst-filled womb lining. Surgeons removed the ovaries and uterus under combined pain control, and lab tests confirmed both diagnoses. The guinea pig healed fully within 21 days. The authors also stress the value of writing up animal cases under standard reporting guidelines, so other vets can trust and reuse the details.
pmc-12847876:
Gholam Hossein Hamedi and co-authors test whether two nano additives guard warm-mix asphalt against water harm as it ages, in a study from two thousand twenty-five. Twenty mixes faced freeze-thaw rounds in a strength test, with surface energy reads beside. Warm mixes age less in laying but still fear water.

Both additives raised the energy cost of water-driven peeling, in fresh and aged states. Self-grip energy of the binder jumped by over half in the two binders tried. Grip on stone rose about a tenth on average. Lab strength and energy reads agreed strongly in late freeze rounds. Readers in road work get a physics-backed case for nano lime and chalk.
pmc-12853876:
Sara Larsson and colleagues ran a two-year trial on wrist arthritis exercise in two thousand twenty-five. Wrist arthritis causes lasting pain and weak grip. Education and exercise help other joints first-line. Proof for the wrist stayed thin. Patients joined a twelve-week self-management program. Half trained nerve and muscle control. The rest did motion-only exercises.

The team tracked wrist scores, grip strength, and pain. They also counted who later chose surgery. Follow-up lasted a full two years. Such long tracking is rare in wrist research. Results guide a real choice patients face. Many hope to delay or avoid an operation.
pmc-12853976:
Neah Albasha and six co-authors explore what helps and what blocks fall prevention for older adults in Saudi Arabia. Their qualitative study was published in twenty twenty-five. Falls lead injury and hospital use in this group, and local barriers tied to culture, schooling, and resources were underexplored.

The team interviewed sixteen health professionals, nurses, therapists, and doctors from public and private hospitals. Talks ran in Arabic and were analyzed with a mix of open coding and a theory framework. Themes covered knowledge, beliefs, setting, and means. The mapping gives structure to scattered complaints. The authors aim to guide fall programs that fit Saudi homes and clinics rather than copying foreign models wholesale.
pmc-12858676:
Shahed Salehzehi and co-authors build a graph neural network that reads breast MRI scans and patient facts together to assign several cancer labels at once. Care teams judge receptor status, tumor stage, and grade side by side, not one by one. The authors turned five kinds of MRI volume into 3D graphs. Each voxel and each clinical variable became a node, with radiomic features and patient data as its traits.

Edges link nodes by closeness in space and by likeness in brightness. A graph isomorphism network then sharpens each node's profile by pooling its neighbors. Rare classes were balanced with synthetic samples, and five-fold cross-checks tested firmness. The labels sought were HER2 status, TNM stage, and the parts of histological grade. A model that gives these jointly, with an eye on structure, fits how oncologists in fact weigh a case.
pmc-12858976:
Seunghun Song, Jueun Baek, and Sangjae Seo present a 2025 journal article introducing LNP Atlas, a dataset of lipid nanoparticle recipes for delivering genetic medicines. These fat bubbles carried mRNA vaccines to fame, yet design knowledge lies scattered across papers. The team extracted formulations from the literature with an AI-assisted workflow, then standardized everything with automated checks.

Each entry holds lipid types and ratios, chemical codes, particle size and charge, synthesis settings, and biological results. The authors expect the shared resource to speed data-driven design of delivery particles for vaccines and gene therapies alike, replacing scattered reading with searchable evidence.
pmc-12883776:
Yu Xu and colleagues built prediction tools for death within twenty-eight days among intensive care patients. The SOFA score, which grades organ failure, is widely used to judge outlook in critical illness. Whether tracking how the score changes over time, alongside age, sharpens prediction was the open question behind the study of several hundred patients at one hospital.

Change in SOFA between early time points added real predictive value, especially for patients whose starting scores sat in the middle range. A simple chart tool combining change and age gave an easy bedside estimate, while a machine learning model also performed well. Outside testing showed more multi-centre work is still needed.
pmc-12915676:
Sivasankar and Markkandan present a 2025 paper on keeping wireless links private with the help of intelligent reflecting surfaces. These surfaces are panels of many small elements that bounce signals in chosen directions. The risk is that a stray listener may catch the signal while conditions change as users move. The authors propose a hybrid method with the short name SGP-DARE that tunes both the sender's beams and the panel's settings.

One part of the method handles the joint tuning at low computing cost. The other part guards against errors in channel knowledge and user movement. The scheme works within hardware limits such as fixed phase steps. In simulations it beat rival methods on secrecy and energy use. The authors aim at networks where eavesdropping risk and power cost both matter.
pmc-12920676:
Ahmed Abdelmoaty, Maha Alsadik, and Khaled Abdel-Sater wrote a review in two thousand twenty-five on lung problems in celiac disease. Celiac disease is a long-term gut disorder set off by gluten in people with a genetic risk. It mainly harms the small intestine, but signs keep appearing in other organs.

The review gathers evidence that the lungs are one of those organs, a link summed up as a gut-lung axis. It covers lung conditions reported in celiac patients, from asthma to rarer lung disease. It also lays out the paths that might connect gut harm to lung harm, and what the link means for doctors and for future studies.
pmc-12946076:
Lindiwe Modest Faye and four co-authors study community-led governance for tuberculosis care in a rural district. Their paper is dated two thousand twenty-six in the pack, while its text head says the year before. The district, in South Africa's Eastern Cape, bears a high TB load with few means. Their frame blends clinic rules with community voice.

They use patient data from twenty eighteen to twenty twenty. Treatment success climbs from about two in five patients to about two in three across those years. Machine learning models are used to explain, not to forecast, and they mirror the governance marks by design. Scenarios show a steady pace could hit the world target of ninety-five percent success by twenty thirty, while a slow pace would fall short.
pmc-13018376: Monika Gandhi and co-authors published a 2025 study of three infusion plans for patients fresh from abdominal surgery. Sharp pain after surgery slows recovery and triggers stress. Two drugs were in view: a sedative and a numbing drug, each given by infusion. The team compared them head to head, and as a pair. Ninety patients were observed, with pain and recovery scores taken at one and two days. The combination group showed the lowest pain scores, used the least backup pain drug, and led in recovery.
pmc-13094576:
Debra Winberg and co-authors interview diabetes patients about taking their medicines in this 2026 paper. Type 2 diabetes control depends on steady medication use. Some health plans now offer a zero dollar copay for these drugs. Whether cost is the main barrier, and what else helps or hurts, was the focus.

Semi structured interviews were held with plan members with and without the zero copay benefit. The interview guide was built with patients, clinicians, and plan leaders. Barriers named went beyond price, into routines, side effects, and beliefs. Supports included reminders, family help, and trust in the care team. Comparing the two groups shows what a copay waiver alone cannot fix. Plans can target the remaining barriers directly.
pmc-13127676:
Cammies, Cavaciuti, and Montgomery build a hands-on class to teach brain size scale rules. Scale rules sit at the core of how brain form shifts by kind. Yet the rules prove hard for class youth to grasp cold. They force a merge of growth thought with math ties. Part-wise scale shifts through deep time add more load still. Few lab tasks let youth probe the rules in brain terms.

Their task pairs sheep and pig brain cuts with plain dye steps. Free scan tools let youth view and weigh part shares in shots. Youth can trace scale ties in one kind and cross kinds. Test scores on scale asks rose sharp past the lab meet. That rise hit a firm mark by test norms in class. Most youth, 93 percent, urged the class stay on.
pmc-13130276:
Cajsa Aranäs and co-authors report a rat study from two thousand twenty-four on pairing two gut-hormone drugs to cut alcohol drinking. Alcohol use disorder has tangled brain roots, so combining drugs may help where single ones fall short. Two gut-brain peptides, amylin and GLP-1, each reduce drinking in rodents on their own.

The team paired activators of both receptors in rats of both sexes, in two drinking experiments. Adding the amylin drug to ongoing GLP-1 treatment lowered intake in males and females. Starting both at once cut intake at first, but tolerance then developed. Food intake and body weight fell consistently in both sexes. Inflammation markers did not change. The results support combined gut-hormone treatment as a lead for alcohol research.
pmc-13151776:
Martyna Świerkowska and co-authors report a marathon runner whose fitness masked heart disease in a 2026 case paper. The man, fifty, was an amateur long-distance runner with high blood pressure and cholesterol. Breathlessness struck near the twentieth kilometer of marathons, forcing brief rests. His exercise test looked superb: oxygen uptake above the predicted value, with no symptoms at peak effort.

Yet his heart tracing during the test showed warning shifts. A CT scan of the coronary arteries found a soft plaque in the main front artery, first read as a possible tear. Catheter imaging confirmed severe narrowing at two spots of that artery. Two drug-eluting stents opened them in one session. The authors draw three lessons: top fitness can hide advanced disease, electrical warning signs deserve imaging, and early CT scanning suits athletes with new exertional symptoms.
pmc-13152376:
Sukaynah Khetani and colleagues recount a fertility treatment that flooded a young woman's abdomen with fluid, in this case report from twenty twenty-six. Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome is the feared overshoot of assisted reproduction: pushed ovaries swell and leak. Their patient, thirty, came to the emergency department nauseated, vomiting, belly distended, and short of breath.

Scans confirmed the picture: large fluid collection in the abdomen and enlarged ovaries studded with cysts. She was admitted for five days under the gynecology service, treated with intravenous fluids and drainage of the abdominal fluid, and recovered. Beyond the story, the report reviews how the syndrome presents, how its severity grades are sorted, how it is managed, and how clinics try to prevent it, with imaging examples. It serves as a compact teaching case on a complication every fertility team dreads.
pmc-13155776:
Larissa Bianchini is first author on a 2026 review offering practical guidance for surveys in clinical research. Surveys capture what patients and other stakeholders know, believe, and do, and can measure how treatments are put into practice. They are versatile and cheap, but weak design ruins their value.

The review walks through each decision, from setting aims and choosing a sample to writing clear questions and picking how to deliver them. Knowledge, attitude, and practice frameworks can structure questionnaires. Online platforms widen reach and ease data handling. Low response rates and uneven engagement are named as key practical risks, with planning strategies offered to lift participation without harming data quality.
pmc-13156876:
Abou Bakr Salama and twelve co-authors test whether adding nitric oxide during machine resuscitation helps or harms the restarted heart. Their animal study was published in twenty twenty-six. Heart muscle failure after arrest drives deaths, and nitric oxide was proposed as a protector.

Rats underwent cold cardiac arrest, then resuscitation on a life-support circuit with or without nitric oxide gas. Heart tissue was read for gene activity, oxidative damage, and cell death. The gas turned on oxidative and inflammatory signaling and suppressed metabolism genes, a profile more warning than rescue. The detailed pathway map tempers enthusiasm and points at what a safer adjunct must avoid.
pmc-13165476:
Su Peng, Juan Zuo, Zhangyi Wang, Kang Zheng, and Feng Lu study a sugar-transport gene in bowel cancer in a 2026 paper. The gene, SLC2A3, helps cells pull in glucose, and hungry tumors often raise it. The team asked whether its level in a tumor predicts spread to the liver, return of the cancer after surgery, or other complications.

Records and tissue from one hundred fifty surgical patients were analyzed. The gene's message ran far higher in tumors than in nearby healthy tissue. High levels tracked with liver spread, recurrence, and complications after surgery. In adjusted models, the links to recurrence and complications stood on their own. The link to liver spread faded once tumor grade was counted, hinting it works through that path. The authors propose the gene as a marker for sorting risk after surgery, with caution.
pmc-13172776:
Eun Jae Lee and Woojoong Kim review wearable tools for tracking children with brain development disorders, in work from two thousand twenty-six. Symptoms shift over time, while clinic scales and parent diaries are brief and subjective. Wearables can watch motion, heart signals, skin response, and brain waves in daily life.

Motion tools sorted posture and gait with high accuracy and flagged repetitive acts well. Wearable brain sensors scored high on autism sorting and sleep staging. Wrist signals even warned of aggressive acts minutes ahead. Smart glasses coached social skills, and smart shoes tracked gait in cerebral palsy. Clinic fit and privacy remain open hurdles.
pmc-13180876:
Veerapaneni, Delhibabu, Subbotin, and Zhukova built a fast in-memory database in twenty twenty-six for smart video surveillance in critical patient care. Hospital video systems produce data at high speed. Standard databases can be too slow, delaying decisions about patients who need urgent care.

Their system, named SubDataBase-0.91s, keeps all data in memory and saves to disk in the background. They tested it against six major database products using scripts that mimic video data streams. It read and wrote far faster than the slowest rival and beat the fastest commercial in-memory rival on some tasks. Dropping strict safety rules of general databases gave the speed. The authors offer it as a base for smart hospital systems.
pmc-13181876:
Giovanni De Antoni and co-authors wrote a study from 2026 on access to rare disease drugs in Switzerland. The drugs, called orphan drugs, treat diseases that few people have, among them faults in body chemistry passed down at birth. The team looked back at adults cared for at one Swiss center over five years. They tracked who was offered such a drug, who got it, and how long the wait was.

Of one hundred and ninety patients, forty-one had a reason to get an orphan drug, and thirty-nine did get one. The wait from need to first dose was about a month in most cases. It stretched to more than six months for drugs not yet cleared for sale in Switzerland. Swiss clearance also came close to two years after clearance abroad. The team urges simpler pay and approval paths so care is not held up.
pmc-13185676:
Jiying Ling, Ethan Yaroch, Yingcen Xie, Kenneth Resnicow, and Jennifer Baumgartner present a study dated 2026 on family body measures and preschoolers' social behavior. A child's behavior at school reflects home life, and the team asked whether parents' and children's body and health measures track with how the children act.

Data came from 168 preschoolers, about forty-seven months old, and 154 parents at sixteen Head Start centers in the Midwest. Parents and teachers rated behavior problems and social skills. Trained staff measured height, weight, body fat, skin carotenoids, and parent blood pressure. Children's body mass scores linked positively with teacher-rated social skills. Other links, including parents' body mass with self-centered behavior, were explored in the full analysis.
pmc-13186076:
Huiyuan Ye and co-authors build a tiny delivery system to treat lupus, an immune disease that attacks many organs, in a paper from 2026. Current drugs can cause harm with long use. The team sought a gentler option that calms inflammation and clears harmful oxidants.

Their system starts with very small particles of a dark polymer. Immune cells of a calming type take the particles in as they mature, then shed them inside small parcels called exosomes. Those parcels carried a rich protein load and entered target cells well. In tests they cut oxidant stress and inflammatory signals better than plain parcels from the same cells. In mice with lupus, kidney damage eased and disease markers fell, with no clear toxicity.
pmc-13186176:
Pfeil and six colleagues give a protocol for preparing mouse bladder and urethra for microscopy in twenty twenty-six. Seeing cells in their three dimensional tissue setting aids understanding. Whole mount preparation keeps the organ intact instead of slicing it. Their method starts with mice perfused through the heart.

Steps cover dissection, tissue clearing, and antibody labelling. Cleared tissue becomes transparent for confocal laser scanning microscopy. Three dimensional processing of the images is also detailed. The protocol suits the urethra and urinary bladder of mice. It lets researchers map cell networks across whole organs. The authors point readers to an earlier study for full usage details.
pmc-13186276:
Takahiro Hadano and two co-authors report a 2026 pilot study from a Japanese university hospital on pain diagnoses that are easy to mix up. Many patients sent in with diagnosed or suspected fibromyalgia may in fact have myofascial pain syndrome, a muscle pain condition with tender trigger points. The team re-read the charts of patients seen from 2018 to 2022 and checked each final diagnosis.

Of the patients in the final set, the large share were judged to have the muscle condition, not fibromyalgia. That group was older, felt less fatigue, and responded better to local care. Yet many also had upper back pain and wide pain, traits linked to fibromyalgia. Careful exams and response to local care may help sort the two apart.
pmc-13190276:
Chia-Yuan Chang and colleagues audit antibiotic prescribing for migrants in British Columbia, in this population study from twenty twenty-six. Migrants face language and access barriers that can skew care. The team used province-wide health records to grade each outpatient antibiotic course as fitting, maybe fitting, or never fitting its diagnosis.

Prescribing fell by nearly half between the year two thousand and twenty twenty-two, for migrants and non-migrants alike. But migrants still got a higher share of never-fitting prescriptions and a lower share of fitting ones, even after accounting for patient and doctor traits. Bad fits clustered in the youngest patients, the poorest groups, and prescriptions from surgeons and urologists rather than family doctors. The authors say stewardship programs should watch equity, not just totals, and coach the specialties and clinics where poor fits concentrate.
pmc-13190776:
Ahmed and coauthors study word use in young patients with a brain tumor. The tumor sits in the back lower part of the brain. Some patients find it hard to pull up the right word. Few past studies test word skill before surgery or probe speech in depth.

The team tested 38 patients aged about 3 to 18, before and after surgery. Each child named pictures in a timed word game. Scores tracked both right words and speed of speech. The team also sought speech traits that flag who will struggle. Their aim is care that spots word loss early and plans speech help.
pmc-13196176:
Mustafa Al-jarshawi and colleagues offer a 2026 projection for oral semaglutide in the United States. Semaglutide is a drug for type 2 diabetes that also protects the heart. The team applied results from the SOUL trial to national survey data to estimate broad impact.

They estimate about six point one million adults would qualify for the drug. Over four and a half years, wide use could prevent about 118,664 major heart events. Those events include heart-related death, heart attack, and stroke. Gains held across sex and race groups. Even at half uptake, tens of thousands of events could be avoided. The authors argue that better access could bring large public gains.
pmc-13197376:
Albrecht Lindemann and colleagues report a 2026 case series on stopping leukemia therapy after remission. Older patients with acute myeloid leukemia often get two drugs long term until the disease returns. Past work hints that stopping in deep remission may not hurt survival, so the team offered a fixed six-month course.

Seven patients reached full remission and chose to stop therapy. Five cleared their mutation traces to very low levels. Six of the seven stay in remission, from seven to fifty months so far. One patient relapsed after fourteen months and regained remission once therapy resumed. The authors suggest time-limited therapy may suit select patients, though the group is tiny.
pmc-13197476: Xiaoming Wang and colleagues issued a 2026 author correction to a study on forecasting the strength of permeable cement road base. The original source data file was an older, less complete version. The notice explains how one figure's results were built, adding nine outside strength values to three lab values for one mix design. It gives the full value list, the mean and spread used, and why a population formula was chosen for that larger set.
pmc-13200976:
Xun Huang and co-authors mapped two decades of research on college student suicide with bibliometric tools. They gathered 2,262 publications from 2002 to 2022 and charted who publishes, where, and on what themes. Output grew fast and may keep growing steeply. The United States led the field, and the ten most productive institutions were all American, yet cooperation between institutions was weak. Two journals carried the most work in the area.

Hot topics included suicidal thoughts, prevention, medical students, mental health, stigma, and mobile health approaches. The most published and most cited authors were identified for newcomers. The authors conclude that interest in student suicide research is rising, but the field needs stronger collaboration across countries, institutions, and authors. Their maps are meant to guide researchers choosing directions, showing both the crowded centers and the thinly studied edges of the field.
pmc-13202076:
Dementia care research rarely asks which questions matter most to affected families, and a 2026 plan by Elena Michel sets up a partnership to do exactly that. The plan presents GenderDem, a priority setting study on diversity-sensitive psychosocial programs for behavioral and psychological symptoms of dementia.

Following the James Lind Alliance approach, people with dementia, caregivers, and health professionals will serve together on a steering group as co-researchers. Two rounds of online surveys will gather and rank candidate research questions from wider participants, supported by a literature review. A final workshop will settle a top ten list meant to guide future dementia care research funding.
pmc-13202676:
One molecule hitting two cancer targets is the design goal of a 2026 study by Joydeep Chatterjee, which synthesizes eighteen new imidazoquinoxaline compounds. The research article uses a Pictet-Spengler route to build carboxamide-bearing molecules aimed at both the EGFR growth signal and the tubulin skeleton of cells.

Two compounds beat the approved drug erlotinib against breast cancer cells in culture and blocked EGFR enzyme activity at low concentrations. One of them also stabilized microtubules much like paclitaxel, raised reactive oxygen species, and arrested cells before division. Docking and dynamics simulations showed both compounds sitting stably in the two target pockets, supporting the dual-action design.
pmc-13202976:
Matthew Chen and four co-authors use language models to sort mild from severe symptoms in cancer patients on radiation care. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-six. Symptom watch during and after such care is key, but past machine tools cost much to retrain and give no clear reasons.

They frame the task as anomaly spotting and write six prompts with a chance-based design. The models read scant patient data and call each symptom mild or severe. Tests on prostate patients cover bowel pain, low mood, and sexual trouble. Scores are checked by standard marks and charts, and sample reason chains are shown so staff can see how a call was made. The path offers live, explainable watch.
pmc-13203076:
Huanhuan Zhou and five co-authors published a pig study in twenty twenty-six on a gene that helps muscle stem cells turn into muscle. The cells came from week-old piglets and were grown in dishes. The gene, TEAD4, rose step by step as the cells matured, in step with known muscle genes.

When the team shut the gene off, the cells still grew at the same pace. But they failed to fuse into muscle tubes, and their muscle genes stayed low. Gene-wide reads pointed to energy balance as the weak spot, with one energy-sensing path turned up too high. The authors say TEAD4 keeps the cells' energy use in tune while they build muscle, a hint for both farm and basic science.
pmc-13203876:
Fernandes, Fernandes, and Gehrke set out a score tool in twenty twenty-six to guess if a tooth implant will do well before surgery. Implants last long in most cases, but body, habit, and build flaws still cause strife. Their tool sums six fields into a score out of one hundred.

Fields cover body health, habits, hard jaw bone, soft gum, the implant, and the false tooth plan. High scores mean a bright outlook and low scores mean high risk. Chart views let a dentist read the result at a glance. The tool is a design plan for now and needs clinic tests to prove it.
pmc-13206176:
Daiyi Zhao, Kaiyue Bi, Dongsheng Niu, Xuewen Li, and Feng Li track how 'French' plums change as they ripen. Plums are sold fresh, but softening and rot after harvest cost growers money. The team read fruit at six stages of growth, checking firmness, sugars, acids, color, and health-linked compounds. Firmness fell as fruit ripened, while sugars rose and acids dropped. Skin moved from green to deep purple-red.

Two health-linked compounds peaked mid-way, before the skin turned. At the purple stage the fruit struck the best balance of sweet, tart, and firm. At full ripeness the walls of the fruit cells broke down. The paper pins the best stage to pick and eat.
pmc-13206676:
Fatma Soylu Çakmak, Yeliz Yıldırım Varışoğlu, and Meserret Aslan study menopause symptoms, faith-based coping, and resilience in a 2026 paper. They asked whether resilience, the ability to bounce back from strain, carries the effect of religious coping onto how strong symptoms feel. The study surveyed postmenopausal women in Türkiye aged forty-five to sixty.

Negative religious coping, such as feeling punished, went with lower resilience. Resilience itself did not link clearly to symptom strength, and positive coping showed no clear link to resilience either. The model explained only a small share of why symptoms differ. No carrying effect of resilience was found. The authors say symptoms likely depend more on body and life context, and they urge studies that follow women over time.
pmc-13209476:
Evidence favors cemented hip implants for broken femoral necks, yet surgeons rarely use them, and a 2026 study authored by Hamed Tayyebi quantifies the gap. The retrospective cohort covers 4,407 patients over fifty who received partial hip replacement for intracapsular fractures across a hospital system between 2009 and 2018.

Only about one patient in nine received a cemented implant, despite cemented cases showing significantly fewer fractures around the implant during and after surgery. Surgeon background predicted the choice: trauma specialists used cement far more often than arthroplasty specialists in the data. The authors call the mismatch a stubborn evidence-practice gap needing stronger guideline uptake.
pmc-13209576:
Yin Shang, Fengqin Li, and Chunhong Yang model electric-driven flow of an elastic fluid in a tiny channel in a paper from 2026. The channel walls carry a polymer brush and a charge pattern that varies along them. A time-varying electric field drives the fluid, a Maxwell fluid with spring-like behavior. The team solves the governing equations with a superposition method. They track how oscillation strength, elasticity, and electric parameters shape speed and solute spread.

Wall charge patterns plus the pulsing field create swirling, back-and-forth motion. Moderate pulsing boosts both flow and transport. Stronger pulsing, though, makes transport less efficient. The results give design guidance for lab-on-chip devices that move samples electrically.
pmc-13210176:
HIV infections among people who inject drugs in Kyrgyzstan have fallen sharply, and a 2026 modeling study authored by Ainura Moldokmatova asks what really drove the drop. The research article runs a deterministic compartmental model under three scenarios, switching needle programs, substitution therapy, prevention, and antiretroviral treatment on and off.

The simulations point to a shrinking population of people who inject drugs as the main engine of the decline. Prevention programs and treatment still reduced the overall burden meaningfully, the model suggests, even if they were not the primary trend drivers. Reported case patterns, meanwhile, likely mirror changing testing behavior more than true swings in new infections.
pmc-13212876:
Douglas V. D'Agati and Donald C. D'Agati write in 2026 an essay on living well with a bipolar temperament, drawn from the lives of six exceptional historical figures. Their subjects, who lived before psychiatric medicines existed, achieved greatly while suffering severe depressions.

The figures range from Samuel Johnson and Winston Churchill to explorer Meriwether Lewis and physician William Osler. Five of them wrote down lessons from their experience in strikingly similar terms. Each, the authors argue, found rescue in total commitment to a demanding, absorbing, spiritually satisfying challenge. pmc-13213076:
