pmc-13371876:
Amaya Daniels and co-authors tell of a huge gallstone that moved in an odd way in a 2026 case report. An 82-year-old woman had a drain tube path from her gallbladder to her skin. Such paths are used when surgery is too risky for a sick patient.

A stone about 65 mm long moved through the path and got stuck just under the skin. Scans can miss how much hard stone sits in such a lump, the team warns. They cut the path open and took the stone out, and her symptoms eased fast. The case is said to be the first of its kind with a stone this large.
pmc-13372376:
Eanna Johnston and co-authors built a fine eye scan to track burns in a 2026 study. Alkali burns are a harsh type of eye harm and can blind. Plain scans see shape well but miss tiny shifts in the clear front window of the eye.

The new scan reads light in a way that picks up shifts far below the plain scan's limit. The team used it on a burn model and on care with cell-based drops. Scan shifts tracked harm and heal steps as they changed. A tool that watches heal steps without touch could help eye teams time care and test new drops in trials.
pmc-13373276:
Gina Chowa and others centre the lived experience of adolescent girls and young women in Burundi in a 2026 study of mental health. The work moves beyond counting cases to trace the conditions that shape well-being in a low-resource, conflict-affected setting, using phenomenological qualitative methods. Structural inequality, gender norms, economic precarity, and violence contact all feature.

The study also identifies barriers to care and locally grounded facilitators of resilience, from community ties to social protection systems. Its help is practical: actions should be culturally responsive, gender-sensitive, and built into existing community structures. The authors present the voices of Burundian girls and young women as the foundation for fairer mental health policy and programming.
pmc-13373676:
Shuroog Nabhan and co-authors summed up switch data for a gut drug and its copies in a 2026 review. The drug calms bowel swelling, and cheaper copies are now in wide use. Doubts stay on what switch steps do to health in daily care.

The search found seven studies with 5,721 adults in all. Three were planned ahead, three looked back, and one took a one-time snapshot. Watch time ran from six months to just over two years. The sum-up weighs if health held firm after a switch, and in which ways. Such proof helps clinics and patients trust a switch made to cut costs.
pmc-13374176:
Li Zhang and co-authors mapped a view-sort method in long ill work in a 2026 review. The method asks people to sort views into piles, which shows how groups truly see a point. It suits the mix of tales that long ills bring, where one fixed plan fits few.

The team used firm review steps and searched four data banks to late 2025. Each past use was logged for its ask, its craft twists, and its gains. Use has spread across many long ills, from pain to heart and mind care. The map shows where the method shines and where reports are thin, to guide new work.
pmc-13374276:
Caiping Liu and co-authors linked long calm-drug use to thought skill in a 2026 study in China. The drugs in view calm nerves and aid sleep, and are often used long in mind care. The group came from a large watch study of a grave mind ill.

Fifty-seven long users were matched to 57 non-users by age, sex, ill span, and main drugs. A set test scored thought, and scales scored signs, weight of ill, and daily life skill. Long users scored worse on thought tests in the match. The team says long use should be weighed with care, and thought should be checked in this group.
pmc-13379376:
Noel George, Usha Arcot, and Bruntha Devi Palanisamy published a 2026 mathematics paper on six common plastics, treated as chains of repeating units. They use a formula called the M-polynomial, which captures the structure of a molecular graph in algebraic form. From that single formula, many numerical measures of structure can be derived.

The plastics covered are polyethylene, polypropylene, PVC, polystyrene, nylon-6,6, and PET. For each chain the authors work out the formula as a function of chain length, then compute eleven standard measures, including the Zagreb and Randic indices. Graphs comparing the plastics show how the measures grow and differ, which can help predict material properties from structure alone.
pmc-13379976:
Yecheng Chen and colleagues present a 2026 study of blood sugar stress measures in critically ill patients with heart failure. Illness can push blood sugar up sharply, and that rise is linked with worse outcomes. One measure corrects the rise for a patient's usual sugar level, but people differ in how their blood sugar marks long-term control.

Records for 2,488 patients came from three intensive care databases. The team grouped patients by a glycation index, which captures that personal difference, and tracked how the stress measure changed over time against death rates. The link between the stress measure and death differed across the groups, so the same reading may not mean the same risk for every patient.
pmc-13382776:
Eric N. Enyong and co-authors examine caveolin-1 outside its usual membrane pockets in retinal support cells in 2026 work. In Müller glia, the main support cells of the retina, caveolin-1 is plentiful while its pocket-forming partner is scarce. Microscopy confirmed that the flask-shaped pockets themselves are almost absent in these cells.

Without pockets, caveolin-1 boosted signals from a bacterial sensor and raised levels of the messenger IL-6 after stimulation. Silencing the protein, or forcing pockets to form, calmed that response. In vessel cells where pockets are normal, silencing had the opposite effect, a contrast that may guide care for inflamed eye disease.
pmc-13385576:
Zheng Wei's team observed coupled Kondo clouds in a mirror-symmetric nanotube-molybdenum device, in a 2026 physics study. Magnetic impurities in metal are screened by conduction electrons into a spin cloud, but detecting that cloud in dilute alloys stayed hard. The team built mirror-symmetric carbon nanotube arrays separated by a molybdenum strip.

The Kondo effect hinged sensitively on strip width. Widths of roughly one-third to just over one micrometer gave a Kondo temperature plateau near 108 kelvin, while one and a half to three micrometers gave about 16 kelvin. A two-spin model reproduced both plateaus and their crossover, explained by intra-edge and inter-edge cloud coupling. The result opens routes in spintronics and quantum computing.
pmc-13385876:
Anh Cong's team solved structures of protein kinase C-beta and its allosteric regulation, in a 2026 structural study. PKC isozymes direct diverse cell pathways and matter as drug targets in cancer and neurological disease, yet their auto-regulation mechanism stayed enigmatic for lack of full-length structures. The team determined structures of human PKC-betaI and PKC-betaII.

The structures reveal how PKCs hold an auto-inhibited state and switch to an ordered active form through a lipid-lever mechanism, and how isoform differences alter allosteric control. Endoxifen, a newly identified PKC-betaI inhibitor, shifted the allosteric mechanism, proving that allosteric regulators of PKCs are feasible. The work gives a foundational model for second-messenger control of PKC function.
pmc-13386676:
Bilal Aygün's team tested serum TIE-2 as a diagnostic marker in newly diagnosed multiple myeloma, in a 2026 case-control study. Angiogenesis drives myeloma pathophysiology, and TIE-2 regulates vessel growth, but its diagnostic value was unclear. The team compared 38 newly diagnosed, untreated myeloma patients with 37 healthy volunteers at Adana City Hospital.

Serum TIE-2 ran significantly higher in myeloma patients at 1.4 versus 0.9 nanograms per milliliter. Receiver operating analysis gave about 76 percent area under the curve for distinguishing patients from controls. TIE-2 shows promise as an adjunct blood marker, pending validation in larger cohorts.
pmc-13386776:
Trent Benedick's team built and validated a radiotherapy planning aid that matches new cases to similar past cases, in a 2026 paper. Radiotherapy planning still leans on individual experience plus dose-based tools, and finding a good reference case can guide plan creation. The team built a multi-step method that measures geometric similarity between cases from overlap volume histograms and spatial target signatures, comparing features with Earth Mover's Distance and a hybrid cluster-then-predict machine-learning model.

Validation on 192 head and neck cancer cases showed a strong link between the model's geometry score and actual dose similarity, with a correlation of about four-fifths. Clinical review plus receiver operating analysis gave an area under the curve of about 88 percent for spotting cases clinicians judged useful as planning templates. The tool aims to standardize plans, raise plan quality, and help clinicians at the first planning step.
pmc-13386876:
Benjamin Hafey and Liangqi Xie review hybrid viral-human DNA circles in HPV-driven cancers in a 2026 article. When human papillomavirus integrates into host DNA, it can spawn circular elements mixing viral and human stretches. Such hybrids appear in roughly 30 percent of HPV-linked throat cancers, with parallels in cervical cancer models.

The circles amplify viral drivers together with captured human genes and build new enhancer hubs from scratch. They also drive very high gene output and can act as roaming activators elsewhere in the genome. The authors discuss how these traits may open treatment angles tailored to hybrid-carrying tumors.
pmc-13386976:
Erasmus N. Kotey and a large team build a glowing, traceable version of a monkey virus related to Epstein-Barr in 2026 work. Rhesus lymphocryptovirus mirrors human EBV infection in macaques, making it a prized vaccine test model. Until now it lacked the green fluorescent tag that speeds EBV cell tracking in the lab.

The engineered virus kept its full genome intact and infected blood cells from several primate species. A mutant missing the entry protein gp350 infected B cells and surface cells far less well in their tests. That result confirms gp350 as the key to entry, matching its human counterpart.
pmc-13388776:
Andrea Delbarba's team reviews how low testosterone reshapes male body makeup and how dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry, the standard bone-density scan, can track it. Testosterone loss cuts lean mass and raises fat mass, especially around the organs. It weakens muscle, feeding frailty and heart-metabolism-linked risk through disrupted signals between bone, muscle, and fat.

The review explains the scan's three-compartment model, which quantifies fat, lean tissue, and bone with low radiation. It weighs evidence that testosterone replacement partly reverses the changes. Practical guidance covers reading scans in hypogonadal men so clinicians can spot osteosarcopenic obesity, the joint loss of bone and muscle with excess fat.
pmc-13388976:
Joshua Conrad Jackson's team tracked sixty years of civil rights lawmaking in the United States with text analysis of legislative archives, asking whether support grew gradually or in bursts. Civil rights bills became more common over time, but sponsorship split sharply by party.

Divergence sped up in the early 1990s and again in the mid-2010s, the second surge driven by racial minority Democrats as the Black Lives Matter movement rose. The split centred on bills for racial minorities, women, and LGBTQ people, while focus to older adults and disabled people faded in both parties.
pmc-13390576:
Victor Pokorny's team tested whether people at risk of mind illness over-spot faces and speech in faded stimuli, studying over eight hundred teens and young adults, with extra mind-illness-risk recruits. Humans by nature spot faces and voices in noise, but over-spotting under doubt may seed false sights.

Those who saw more faces in two-tone images also heard more speech in filtered audio. Both detection rates independently model doctor-rated positive signs, with a joint score predicting sense quirks alone, beyond mistrust or jumbled thinking. A cross-sense over-spotting tendency may thus mark mind-illness risk.
pmc-13391476:
Nadja Deflorin and colleagues run, in 2026, a randomised crossover trial on whether a short trip to low altitude improves night breathing for people who live higher up. Sleep-disordered breathing is common at moderate altitude, where thinner air lowers blood oxygen overnight.

Forty-four healthy residents living above one thousand metres had sleep studies in random order. Each person spent two nights at home and two nights at a laboratory in Chur at 590 metres. A two-week washout sat between the blocks. The main outcome was time spent below ninety percent oxygen saturation, with overall saturation and apnoea counts as secondary measures. Altitude medicine readers gain controlled evidence on descent as a simple remedy.
pmc-13392676:
Qianru Jiang leads a large structural study showing that ketamine and its older cousin phencyclidine, better known as PCP, can plug directly into human opioid receptors and switch them on. Both drugs are famous for blocking a different brain receptor, yet their mix of helpful and harmful effects hinted at more targets. The team froze receptors with each drug bound and imaged them at near-atomic detail.

The pictures, backed by targeted mutations and chemical variants, pinpoint the grips each drug uses inside the receptor's binding pocket. A drug-free view of the kappa opioid receptor shows the pocket before any guest arrives. Ketamine shifted around more inside the pocket than PCP did, a looseness that may explain its distinct clinical behaviour. The authors argue opioid receptors belong in any full account of ketamine.
pmc-13393276:
Xiaoyun Wu and five colleagues review how re-engineering the flanking groups around diketopyrrolopyrrole, a workhorse pigment-turned-semiconductor, unlocks functions far beyond its classic roles in transistors and solar cells. Standard synthesis fixes aromatic rings on both sides of the core, and those rings dictate energy levels, packing, and charge flow. Decades of swapping them delivered steady gains but boxed in the possible shapes.

Newer work breaks the mould with naphthalene motifs, vinyl links, and fused backbones that reshape how molecules couple and stack. Those moves stretch the material family toward flexible electronics, intelligent skins, and biological sensors that demand softness and responsiveness classic designs lack. The review organises the field into a structure-property-application map, presenting flanking-group design as the unifying lever for next-generation multifunctional organic electronics.
pmc-13393876:
Wu Weinian and Li Yongjun build a nomogram to predict chronic pain after keyhole lung surgery in a 2026 study. Chronic postsurgical pain after video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery burdens recovery, and early identification of high-risk patients could personalize perioperative care.

In a retrospective case-control study of 500 patients operated on from 2022 to 2024, 92 had pain at three months and 408 did not. Daily pain scores, surgical details, and demographics fed variable selection and logistic models, validated in a split cohort. Clinicians gain a bedside chart for estimating who needs intensified pain prevention.
pmc-13394776:
Feldman and co-authors assess, in 2026, whether the seizure drug cenobamate can be restarted at full dose after a short break without triggering hypersensitivity reactions such as rash. Slow dose escalation is normally required when starting the drug, leaving restart rules unclear. They exploited a natural experiment: epilepsy patients whose medicines were paused during intracranial EEG monitoring at a tertiary center, then restarted before discharge.

Thirty-two patients, median age 29 years, had cenobamate withheld for a median of seven days and restarted at a median of 200 milligrams per day. A quarter resumed at 300 milligrams or more, and 44 percent had a prior history of rash from some cause. Even so, no hypersensitivity reactions or rashes attributable to the drug appeared during hospitalization or two weeks of follow-up. The authors suggest previously tolerant patients may skip retitration after brief interruptions, easing management of missed doses.
pmc-13395276:
Vendhan and Mysore survey, in 2026, how Indian dermatologists use narrowband ultraviolet B phototherapy for vitiligo, the skin condition that destroys pigment in patches. The light treatment is standard care, but real-world dosing, upkeep schedules, and pre-treatment dose testing vary widely. Their survey, checked by three senior dermatologists with over 15 years of phototherapy experience each, drew 80 replies from doctors in practice.

The response rate was only 5 percent, itself a finding about survey fatigue among clinicians. Among respondents, 65 percent had more than ten years of experience with the treatment. Just over half, 52.5 percent, used whole-body phototherapy units exclusively, while the rest combined whole-body cabinets with targeted devices for limited areas. The authors use the snapshot to argue for more standardized practice, since inconsistent dosing strategies and upkeep plans can change outcomes for vitiligo patients receiving the same nominal therapy.
pmc-13395376:
Lawrence Ejike Ugwu and co-authors expose, in 2026, an age penalty in blood pressure and diabetes care across Africa. Data came from a world risk factor pool built on 2,309 studies and 245 million people. Country-year figures ran from 1990 to 2022. Care steps, from diagnosis to control, were compared across age bands.

Older adults had more hypertension yet less control of it than fifty-year-olds. Diabetes treatment coverage fell after age seventy, dropping further past eighty-five. Severe untreated hypertension was most common in Central and West Africa. The authors say health systems built for infections and acute care miss older needs. They urge age-split tracking in coverage goals.
pmc-13395476:
Joachim P. Sturmberg and Carmel M. Martin argue, in 2026, that generative AI fits poorly with the heart of family medicine. Many patients now ask AI first when ill. The editorial grants that AI spots patterns and sums records fast. Good primary care, though, rests on knowing a patient over years and judging through doubt across visits.

Much illness arrives vague, and time itself is a diagnostic tool in this setting. No data set can supply moral judgement or healing ties, the authors say. Tests of AI should weigh continuity, skill loss, patient feel, and fairness, not accuracy alone. Family doctors must steer AI use, not just adopt it, they urge.
pmc-13395976:
Damian Lewis and colleagues set out to put number values on life with open wounds in dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa, a rare condition where skin blisters and tears easily. Their 2026 study fills a gap, since such values are needed when new wound treatments are judged for cost and benefit.

The team wrote short health descriptions, called vignettes, that varied in wound number and size, pain, itch, and hours spent on wound care. A United Kingdom public sample of 1,139 people and 44 people with the condition rated these states with a standard quality-of-life tool. Patients rated their own states, while the public rated states as if caring for someone affected.
pmc-13396076:
Naoko Sanno and others check real-world safety and worth of lasmiditan for migraine in Japan in a 2026 post-sale study. Lasmiditan, a picky serotonin 1F trigger, gives a choice for patients who shun or spurn triptans.

A one-arm, multi-site, forward watch study tracked 550 new lasmiditan patients from 53 sites. From mid-2022 to late 2024, harms and two-hour pain-free and pain-eased rates were logged via case forms, day books, and forms. Prescribers gain Japan real-world proof on a newer fast migraine drug, straight from clinics, not just trials.
pmc-13396176:
Wang and team report, in 2026, evidence that microwaves can push electrons in a semiconductor into superballistic flow, a regime where a viscous electron fluid conducts better than free flight allows. Working with point contacts carved from ultrahigh-mobility two-dimensional electron gas, they used photoconductivity, the change in conduction under microwaves. That let them probe how edge magnetoplasmons, waves running along the sample edge, stir the electron fluid.

Weak microwaves at low magnetic fields produced photoconductivity matching superballistic flow, while strong fields flipped the signal negative as phonon scattering took over. The key evidence was geometric: photoconductance scaled with the square of the point contact width, the fingerprint of viscous flow. Edge waves that reinforced each other sharply enhanced the signal, while waves that cancelled were strongly suppressed. A conductance plateau near 35.6 units of e-squared over h implied an effective channel width of 0.44 micrometers, measured with error below 1.5 percent.
pmc-13396476:
Chalie Mulugeta and Abebaw Alamrew study how mothers in an Ethiopian town feed babies past six months. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-six, based on field work some years before. The first two years of life are a key window for growth and brain build. Added foods, next to milk, must start on time and be varied and rich enough.

They survey mothers of children under two in the town. Fewer than half feed in line with world health advice. Mothers who stay at home, who had care after birth, who gave birth in a clinic, and whose child had shots are more apt to feed well. The authors urge feeding advice in postnatal and shot visits.
pmc-13396576:
Georg Evers and co-authors gathered records from 12 German lung cancer centers on what happens after a common modern treatment path fails. Their 2026 study follows patients with locally advanced non-small cell lung cancer whose disease returned after chemotherapy with radiation and a follow-on year of the immunotherapy drug durvalumab.

Charts for 145 such patients were reviewed for tumor traits, later treatments, and survival. No standard approach exists for this relapse point, since the drug sequence is recent and trials have not settled the next move. Real-world series like this one show what doctors actually choose and what those choices deliver.
pmc-13396676:
Tiankai Di and co-authors restored the blood-vessel-growing power of aging dental pulp stem cells by delivering two gene messages into them, in a 2026 study. Older pulp cells lose their ability to support new vessels, which stalls attempts to regrow living tooth pulp instead of filling dead teeth.

The team traced the loss to weak sugar metabolism, with low levels of a glucose transporter and an enzyme called HK2. A branched polymer carrier delivered the instructions for both proteins, entering over 90 percent of cells without harm. Fluid from the treated cells doubled the length of vessel tubes grown in the lab and brought branch points back to youthful levels.
pmc-13397576:
Sajni Parikh and co-authors compare short and extended blood-thinner cover after breast rebuilding with the patient's own belly tissue. Their 2026 chart review covers DIEP flap cases at one centre from January 2017 to June 2025. Blood clots in veins kill many patients each year, yet national guidance on longer cover never covered this operation.

Patients went home on enoxaparin, sold as Lovenox, for either two weeks or a longer course after a practice change. Anyone with past clots, clotting disorders or regular anticoagulant use was left out. Rates of lung and leg clots, plus procedure problems, were compared across the switch to judge whether longer cover helps or harms.
pmc-13398476:
Ziyin Huang and colleagues map the gene-activity states inside metastatic melanoma and test which states forecast survival. Their 2026 study profiles tumour samples from 111 patients with in-transit metastases diagnosed between 1990 and 2020, using digital spatial RNA profiling. Melanomas fall into distinct internal states, but how those states track with how long patients live was unsettled.

Clean profiles emerged for 105 patients, including 30 who received checkpoint immunotherapy and 20 with acral melanoma in the set described. Four main axes separated the states, from undifferentiated to melanocytic patterns, with immune and stromal signals on other axes. The melanocytic state tied to poorer overall survival on its own, a warning sign pathologists may add to staging.
pmc-13399576:
Michal Zielinski and Kamila Dziemianowicz report a fatal case of re-expansion pulmonary edema in 2026, a rare complication that can follow the draining of a collapsed lung. Scans showed a complete left-sided pneumothorax with the left lung nearly fully collapsed. On arrival he was walking, stable, and holding 95 percent oxygen saturation on room air.

A large chest tube was placed and connected at once to active suction at minus 20 centimeters of water pressure. Roughly thirty minutes after decompression he crashed into fast-worsening oxygen failure. A new chest X-ray showed dense, one-sided clouding filling the re-expanded left lung, with blood-tinged frothy secretions in his airway. The authors present the timing and one-sided picture as strong evidence for fulminant re-expansion edema. They urge especially close monitoring after drainage when a lung has been down for a long time in diseased tissue.
pmc-13400276:
Thomas Bieganowski and Zorica Buser comment on a survey of public views on spine surgery techniques. Their 2026 commentary discusses a study of 493 online respondents, mostly women under 40, who were asked which spine operation they would choose for themselves. Spine surgery now includes robotics, less invasive, and endoscopic options, heavily marketed with reassuring phrases, yet public understanding had been little studied.

Less invasive surgery was chosen by 72 percent and laser spine surgery by 61 percent, matching earlier work that links less invasive labels to hopes of less pain and faster recovery. The commentary warns that preference may reflect marketing and misunderstanding rather than proof, since laser surgery is not a distinct standard operation. It calls for clearer patient education before preference shapes demand.
pmc-13400476:
Anastasia Kolesnikova, Andrew Armitage, Klara Hajdu and Helen Cockerton review, in 2026, how the recombination pathway could help breed better crops. During sexual reproduction, matching chromosomes swap segments, mixing parental genes into new combinations. Breeders depend on that mixing, yet crossover events are few and tightly controlled in most plants.

The authors assemble an up-to-date network of the plant proteins that run recombination, covering how crossovers form and how chromosomes separate cleanly. They assess how far breeders already alter the process, survey new tools that could raise or redirect crossover rates, and weigh the gains on offer. More crossovers, in theory, mean more new trait combinations to select from.
pmc-13400576:
Caviglia Marta and an international group reflect, in 2026, on trauma stabilization points, small forward clinics set up in war zones to treat the wounded near where injuries happen. Moving care forward matters when normal evacuation breaks down. The World Health Organization convened experts to draft guidance drawing on deployments including Gaza.

Between February and July 2024, three such points in Gaza handled over 4,000 consultations. Though built for trauma, they soon treated minor injuries and everyday illness too, reflecting what people could actually reach. Referral success varied with hospital distance, ambulances and shifting front lines, and insecurity forced mobility. Lessons echoed other conflicts: stay near injury points, link into a working referral chain and keep clear staffing and records.
pmc-13400876:
Sagaidac Irina, Cemortan Maria and Cernetchi Olga review, in 2026, the World Health Organization Labor Care Guide for monitoring childbirth, with a focus on adoption in Moldova. The older partograph chart, used for decades, relied on rigid thresholds for how fast the cervix should open. Newer evidence favors care tailored to each woman.

The guide, launched in 2020, supports monitoring tailored to the woman. It cuts needless interventions and promotes respectful care without harming safety, according to global experience. Moldova approved a new national guideline on care in labor in 2025, aligned with the guide. The authors trace the science behind it, its global uptake and the Moldovan policy steps.
pmc-13401576:
Svatava Kubickova, Halina Cernohorska, Hana Hradska, and Miluse Vozdova developed a 2026 rapid molecular method for sexing primates, aimed at managing captive populations of endangered species where males and females look alike. Knowing a newborn's sex early helps zoos plan breeding and group composition.

Their PCR test targets the male-specific SRY gene with a c-myc control gene found in both sexes. It was validated on blood DNA from adult Sumatran orangutans, western lowland gorillas. Silvery gibbons, then applied to non-invasive samples from four newborns, two orangutans, a gorilla, and a gibbon, using umbilical cord material collected after birth and hair. The method also worked in adult chimpanzees and pig-tailed macaques. Non-invasive sampling means infants need no handling for an early, reliable sex result.
pmc-13401676:
Fardina Rahman Omi, Farhana Zaman, and SM Saidur Rahman Mashreky wrote a 2026 systematic review of how chronic diseases affect health-related quality of life in South and Southeast Asia. Chronic illness in the region imposes a double burden of sickness and economic hardship on patients and health systems alike.

The search covered studies from 2014 to 2024 measuring quality of life in chronic disease patients, spanning cross-sectional, observational, cohort, and economic designs. Conditions ranged across lung disease, kidney disease, diabetes, sarcopenia, cardiovascular disease, breast cancer, and hepatitis C. Twenty-five studies from multiple Asian countries were included. For each, the reviewers charted the population, disease, methods, sample size. Which validated quality-of-life instruments were used, exposing both the weight of the burden and the variety of tools used to measure it.
pmc-13401876:
Herong Wang and colleagues ran a large survey of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in Tianjin, China, reported in 2026, measuring prevalence, associated factors, and public awareness of the disease. Smoking is the best-known driver, but biomass fuel smoke and other exposures matter too, and big surveys guide prevention.

Between January 2023 and December 2024, a cluster-sampled cross-section enrolled 65,680 adults aged 35 to 75. Diagnosis rested on breathing tests after a bronchodilator, with the standard ratio threshold defining obstruction. The team assessed age, sex, body mass, smoking history, biomass fuel use for cooking and heating, and chronic cough, then used multivariable regression to isolate independent associations. Awareness questions probed how much the public knows about a disease many carry undiagnosed, rounding out a prevention-oriented snapshot of one Chinese city.
pmc-13402276:
Liu Yang and colleagues used eye tracking to test whether first-person shooter gaming sharpens visual-motor speed and control. Their 2026 study compares 29 experienced shooter players with 32 non-players on a gamified Go/No-Go target task with shooter-like spatial demands. Shooter games require fast seeing, spatial awareness, and stopping unwanted responses, yet their cognitive correlates remain debated.

Shooter players executed responses reliably faster, while Go-trial accuracy did not differ. No-Go errors showed no overall group effect but varied systematically with target quadrant and distance, and eye tracking showed shorter saccade latencies and durations, clearest in one quadrant. The findings link shooter experience to faster visuomotor responding and distinct gaze patterns, while inhibitory accuracy appears shaped more by spatial layout than by gaming history.
pmc-13402576:
Debojyoti Chowdhury and colleagues built ACSCeND, a deep learning framework that reads cancer stem-like cell states from gene activity data, in both single-cell and bulk tumor samples. Stem-like cells drive tumor variety, drug resistance, and relapse, yet profiling them evenly across data types has been hard. One part of the tool sorts single cells into pluripotent-like, multipotent-like, or unipotent-like states; a second part, guided by attention, unmixes bulk samples into those same shares.

Put to work on more than 25,000 tumor profiles from atlas and outcome datasets, the tool linked higher stem-like shares to shorter disease-free survival and weaker response to checkpoint immunotherapy. It also recovered known growth hierarchies in healthy tissue, supporting wider relevance. The authors offer the package freely in Python and pitch stem-like state as a pan-cancer marker that could guide stemness-aware treatment choices.
pmc-13402676:
Tian and co-authors name, in 2026, the protein LRP4 as an entry receptor shared by several encephalitic alphaviruses, including Eastern equine encephalitis virus, whose human case fatality rate approaches 40 percent. Known receptors from the lipoprotein receptor family left some infection unexplained. The team ran a CRISPR activation screen in cells stripped of several attachment factors to find what else the virus uses.

LRP4 handled viral attachment and entry directly, its binding domain gripping the virions, and it served Western equine encephalitis, Semliki Forest, and Sindbis viruses as well. Soluble LRP4 decoy proteins strongly blocked Eastern equine encephalitis virus in primary mouse neurons, in live male mice, and in human brain organoids, a possible treatment route. Mammalian and avian versions of LRP4 both promoted infection, fitting the virus's bird-mosquito-human cycle. The authors say the shared receptor reshapes understanding of alphavirus tissue targeting and defense design.
pmc-13402776:
Kazuki Ohashi and colleagues map who actually used telemedicine in Hokkaido, Japan, from 2022 to 2024, as pandemic rules relaxed. Claims data followed more than 1.48 million people with regular outpatient care, and only 0.4 percent, or 5965 people, ever had a remote visit. The analysis stacked 34 personal and municipal factors under Andersen behavioral model of health service use.

Where a person lived mattered hugely: 39 percent of the variation sat at municipal level, rising to 54 percent among people aged 75 and older. Sicker patients, women, prior telemedicine users, and those with opioid or psycholeptic prescriptions used remote care more; older age itself pulled use down. Towns with more single-parent households and stronger finances saw higher uptake. The authors call for infrastructure and caregiver-friendly policy to reach older, digitally left-behind patients.
pmc-13403276:
Matheus Henrique Sicupira Lima and team report a heart-cancer bind: treating endometrial cancer in a woman with Eisenmenger syndrome. Their 2026 case concerns a 66-year-old with an uncorrected atrial septal defect, fixed high lung pressure, and chronic clot disease, who grew endometrioid adenocarcinoma with life-risking womb bleeding. Surgery was far too risky.

pmc-13427876:

pmc-13434276:

pmc-13435476:

pmc-13435676:

pmc-13437676:

pmc-13439476:

pmc-13441776:

pmc-13442876:

pmc-13443676:

pmc-13443876:

pmc-13444176:

pmc-13445076:

pmc-13445376:

pmc-13452276:

pmc-13453576:
Rasolofomamonjy Rasoamiadana Volanirina and five co-authors probe the link between problem internet use and depressive symptoms in Quebec adults at high risk of cannabis use disorder. The problem internet group also skewed younger and male, with more problem drinking and higher anxiety scores. pmc-13453976:

pmc-13454176:

pmc-13454276:

pmc-13455276:

pmc-13457076:

Their chance to check came during heart catheter procedures, where a wire already tracks true aortic pressure beat by beat. As an arm cuff inflated, the team watched the inner pressure in 234 patients, averaging about sixty-one years old.

Most patients, about seventy percent, barely reacted. The rest split. About twelve percent surged, gaining near ten points of systolic pressure the moment the cuff squeezed. About eighteen percent dropped by a similar amount. People with higher starting pressure and jumpier readings reacted more, yet no trait predicted who would react. The authors say a third of patients may be misread by an amount that matters for treatment choices, and they call for prospective work on the cuff effect.
pmc-13457176:
Yang Zhao and colleagues argue in a 2026 essay that artificial intelligence lacks a shared basis for judging whether systems deserve trust. The essay closes by sketching a two-layer design linking shared trust foundations to practical deployment.
pmc-13457376:
Irfan Ali, Liliana Lo Presti, Marco La Cascia and Igor Spano' published this 2026 computational linguistics study on splitting Sanskrit compound words. Sanskrit glues words together and the joining process, called sandhi, changes sounds at the seams, hiding the boundaries. A splitter must find multiple hidden seams and rebuild each piece, and several answers can look plausible. The authors built a neural model that predicts boundaries and generates the split text, tracking its own uncertainty.

On benchmark tests it reached an exact-match boundary accuracy of 84.39 percent and exact segmentation accuracy of 79.34 percent across the dataset used. Boundary precision and recall both sat above 91 percent. The authors argue that uncertainty-aware coupling makes decoding more robust where boundaries are ambiguous, aiding humanities work on Sanskrit texts.
pmc-13458376:
Varshini Odayar and colleagues read the blood of patients starting immune checkpoint therapy for metastatic lung cancer, hunting signals of who will thrive. Two inflammatory signals spelled trouble: each doubling of interleukin-6 raised the death hazard by 34 percent, and interleukin-8 by 36 percent. pmc-13458476:
Maximilian Schulze and colleagues check lung function during anti-TNF therapy for bowel disease in a 2026 study. pmc-13458776:
Muhammad Waheed and colleagues pit the two front-of-neck operations for a worn cervical disc against each other across a decade of follow-up. Disc arthroplasty preserves motion; fusion, the standard, locks the segment and is blamed for stressing its neighbors. Their 2026 retrospective study draws on a national administrative database and propensity-matches 3,138 arthroplasty patients to 3,138 fusion patients with no prior spine surgery.

The trade-offs cut both ways. Arthroplasty patients suffered fewer clots and nerve injuries early and fewer infections and nerve problems later. Yet they returned for more cervical surgery at two years (1.5 against 0.7 percent) and five years (1.9 against 1.1 percent), a gap that closed by year ten. pmc-13459276:

pmc-13459376:

pmc-13459676:

Given the small sample, the authors call for larger studies that follow people over time.
pmc-13459776:

pmc-13461476:

pmc-13462776:

pmc-13464076:

pmc-13464376:

pmc-13464876:

pmc-13464976:

pmc-13465176:

pmc-13465476:

pmc-13465876:

pmc-13466876:
Eitetsu Koh and Yasuo Sekine respond to an editorial about their case of a collapsed lung in a patient whose other lung was destroyed by tuberculosis, writing in 2026. pmc-13466976:

pmc-13467376:

pmc-13467476:

pmc-13468076:

pmc-13468776:

pmc-13468976:

pmc-13469576:

pmc-13470376:

pmc-13471176:

pmc-13471276:

At matched tumor dose, the optimized plan improved recovery for the voice box, saliva gland, and swallowing tube, with small gains elsewhere. pmc-13471376:

pmc-13471576:

pmc-13471676:

pmc-13472876:

pmc-13473176:

Gaps showed in plain view. Near a third of the doctors rated their skill at spotting high risk patients and planning care by risk as weak. More than half said they ask about patient fears on safety at best now and then. Doctors in town clinics felt the gaps more than those at big schools. Folk in both camps pled low grasp of how to tame side effects. The authors call for set teach plans, shaped by work place.
pmc-13473276:
Nemcová and colleagues report a 2026 qualitative study of people who use child sexual abuse material but have never been caught, a group rarely heard from directly. Through anonymous chat-based interviews in an EU prevention project, 32 help-seeking users assessed as low to medium risk described their experiences in four languages.

Participants described their use as deeply distressing, marked by a felt loss of control, inner conflict, threat to their identity, and heavy stigma. The explanations they gave for their behavior served to manage shame and responsibility. Secrecy, isolation, and scarce support blocked help-seeking. Stable relationships, emotional well-being, and structured daily life helped people engage with services. The authors argue prevention should address stigma and ambivalence directly, with low-threshold, culturally sensitive support.
pmc-13473376:
Li surveyed in 2026 how family resources shape the grades of music students at Chinese universities, a fairness question rarely studied in arts education. Drawing on Bourdieu's theory of capital, the study split family advantage into money, culture, and social ties. It asked which kind matters most for music majors.

Cultural capital, such as books, art exposure, and taste formed at home, proved the strongest driver of achievement. Money helped directly, while social ties helped only through two middle steps: how engaged students were and how much they believed in their own skill. School type and rural or urban origin also bent some of the paths.
pmc-13473476:
Wen-Di Jiang and fifteen colleagues investigated in 2026 a gene regulator that may drive pulmonary arterial hypertension, a disease in which lung arteries narrow and the heart strains. Silencing also curbed cell growth through the mTOR/P70S6K pathway in cells and in animals. A drug that blocks Nrf2 likewise slowed growth, but losing Brg1 removed that effect. The authors nominate Brg1 as a possible treatment target.
pmc-13473576:
Xiaobing Xie and eight colleagues mapped in 2026 the germs behind male reproductive tract infections in Hunan Province, China, using targeted gene sequencing. pmc-13473976:
Naina Kumar and colleagues describe a 2026 case where bowel cancer spread hid behind signs of ovarian cancer. Scans showed masses on both ovaries, coated organs, and fluid in the belly, all classic for ovarian cancer. Tumor marker tests were high, with one marker far above the usual range.

Care then switched to a bowel cancer drug mix. The case warns that twin mucus-type ovary masses with poor chemo response deserve a gut check.
pmc-13474176:

pmc-13474376:

No donor reported regret, family disruption, financial burden, or job change, and rates of depression, anxiety, and fear of kidney failure stayed low. Yet one in ten said they would not donate again, rising to one in three among donors whose kidney function had fallen below 45 on the standard scale. The findings support careful donor selection and long-term kidney monitoring.
pmc-13474576:
Mary E Hackbarth and co-authors model a rare storage disease in mice in 2026 by copying its most common gene fault. The disease blocks exit of a sugar acid from cell recycling units, harming the brain over time. Mice with two copies of the fault built up the sugar acid as patients do. They showed unsteady gait, tremors, seizures, and shorter lives.

Genes for making myelin were broadly turned down, and the back brain showed a distinct inflammatory mark. Support cells swelled and a class of movement cells died off step by step. The model gives drug tests a faithful test bed.
pmc-13474676:
Zhenning Feng and colleagues probe blood antioxidants and thinking skills in 2026 in people with schizophrenia who had never taken antipsychotic drugs. Just over two hundred patients and about one hundred healthy peers gave blood for four antioxidant measures. Thinking was scored with a standard battery, and symptoms with a standard rating scale. Models tested links while accounting for age, sex, and clinical traits.

About half of the patients met the bar for cognitive impairment. Two protective blood measures ran lower in patients than in peers, while one waste product ran higher. Within patients, higher levels of the two protective measures tracked with lower odds of impairment. Diet and metabolic care may deserve a place beside drug care.
pmc-13474776:
Uhawenimana and colleagues asked eye care users in Rwanda in 2026 how primary eye services felt after the country folded them into performance-based financing, a system that pays clinics partly on results. The team ran six focus group talks at six health centers with 72 people, including older adults and people with disabilities. They asked about travel, cost, quality, and how satisfied users felt with the care they received.

Users said bringing eye care into local health centers cut travel time and made visits easier to reach than before the program began. Cost still blocked many people, mainly the price of eyeglasses and some medicines that community health insurance did not fully cover for them. Stock-outs of basic supplies, limited equipment, and few service days also hurt quality, yet many users praised staff attitudes and described respectful, supportive care during their visits to the centers.
pmc-13474876:
Batuhan Aydın and co-authors test a dissolving membrane in 2026 for guiding bone regrowth in rat skull defects. The membrane layers two plastics, one slow to dissolve and one fast, printed in three dimensions. Twenty-four paired defects were split across four setups, mixing membranes with graft types or blood alone. Bone growth was measured at four and eight weeks.

The layered membrane with blood alone led all groups at four weeks by a clear margin. At eight weeks it still beat two groups and tied the control. Early speed matters where a membrane must hold space before it dissolves. The design earns larger animal tests before human use.
pmc-13476076:
Ellison and colleagues measure how fast liver cells clear 207 chemicals, data needed to set an internal safety threshold for exposures. Safety limits today rest on doses fed to animals, but harm depends on the level that reaches blood and tissue. Their 2026 study uses frozen, thawed liver cells from several species at two low doses. Rates at the two doses tracked each other closely, which supports the assay's reliability. The data will help regulators judge combined exposures from food, skin, and air together. They can screen exposures from many routes at once and read the chemical traces found in people's blood, all with fewer new animal tests.
pmc-13476576:
Kinan El Husseini and co-authors chart research themes in 2026 for chronic lung transplant failure, the top cause of late death after transplant. Just over eighteen hundred papers from 1990 to 2025 were screened with machine help checked by blinded experts. Topic modeling with a biomedical language model found twenty-four themes. Trend math sorted themes into falling, steady, rising, and emerging sets.

A mixed subtype of failure drew far less study than its patient share warrants. Funding can use the map to close blind spots.
pmc-13477076:
Harrison R Herrera and co-authors show in 2026 how follow-up quality warps reported harms after mechanical aortic valve surgery. A group of 558 patients from 2000 to 2023 split into local and referral patients by distance from the center. Bleeding and clot events were counted by chart review and by billing codes. Matched groups of local and distant patients were compared.

Local patients were followed far longer and showed higher raw event rates. Careful time-based math shrank but did not erase the gap. Billing codes stretched the gap wider than chart review did. Distant patients are not safer; they are simply watched less closely.
pmc-13477776:
Singh and co-workers in India reported in 2026 a rare appendix cancer that wore the mask of plain appendicitis. Their patient was a woman of 64 with right low belly pain for a week. Scans showed a plump appendix with small stones, a classic sign of a blocked, sore organ. The team took the organ out, as is standard for such a case.

The lens told a split tale. The wall held a signet ring cell cancer, named for cells that look like signet rings, spread through the full wall and into the fat pad. Stains for three marks came back plus, and a fourth came back minus, a code that points to the lower gut as the source. The cut edges still held tumor. The authors stress that each removed appendix needs a full tissue read, since this fast cancer needs more care than the first cut.
pmc-13478176:
M E Annadorai and M Ramakrishna tested in 2026 how fibre layout affects wear in magnesium-carbon fibre sandwich composites for aerospace use. They made panels with one-direction, two-direction, and multi-direction fibre stacks and ran pin-on-disc sliding tests.

Fibre layout decisively shaped wear resistance, with the multi-direction stack showing the lowest wear rate, about 44 percent better than the one-direction layout. It also showed lower friction, minimal roughness growth, and higher cross-section hardness, pointing to better load sharing. Microscopy showed mainly abrasive wear with less damage in multi-direction panels. The work links structure to wear performance for lightweight design.
pmc-13479476:
Peng and co-workers in China sifted in 2026 what shapes a heart patient's full day of motion, rest, and sleep. They hunted wearable based studies of adults with coronary heart disease, the clogged artery ill. No study had yet traced all three day parts at once in this group. Twenty four studies fit, most of them on motion alone, and the team sorted each driver by scale, from the self out to home, streets, and state rules.

The authors urge plans that push rehab sign up and home backing first.
pmc-13479576:
Jun Liu, Jun Sun, Huanyu Li, and Jingyu Zhao published a 2026 systematic review and network meta-analysis comparing physical activity programs for people with autism spectrum disorder. Exercise is a promising drug-free support, yet families face a confusing menu of types and doses. Seven databases were searched through December 2025 for controlled studies.

Forty-five studies covering 1,479 participants met the criteria. Outcomes were social communication, repetitive behaviors, and motor skills. Network methods let the authors rank programs that were never tested head-to-head, by borrowing strength across the whole evidence web. The ranking approach gives therapists and parents a comparative map for choosing activity type and dose, rather than another single-program verdict.
pmc-13479976:
Chenxi Jin and coauthors published a 2026 retrospective MRI study checking whether jaw disc positions after surgery are actually sensible. The operation, arthroscopic disc repositioning done on both sides, treats jaw joints where the cushioning disc has slipped forward and will not return. Ninety consecutive patients with scans were screened for the analysis.

After exclusions, fifty-nine surgical patients covering 101 joints were compared with thirty-one symptomatic patients whose discs were not displaced. Scans at one, three, and six months after surgery measured both disc position and joint mobility. The authors call their yardstick rationality: a disc can sit correctly yet still fail to move with the jaw. The graded follow-up shows whether early good positions hold or drift.
pmc-13480076:
Fumio Kurosaki and co-authors present a 2026 review of an inhaled drug used for stubborn lung infection with Mycobacterium avium complex. The drug, a liposomal form of amikacin breathed in through a nebulizer, serves patients whose infection resists standard care. Faulty use also mattered, covering stretched-out dosing gaps and late swaps of nebulizer parts. Voice hoarseness was the most common side effect and at times drove the dosing gaps. Teaching patients steady technique and checking their routine often may lift success rates without new drugs.
pmc-13482576:

pmc-13482876:
Gider and colleagues asked whether newer deep-learning tools beat a standard method at spotting the rare crashes that kill people. Their 2026 study used 5,676 crashes recorded in Batman province, Türkiye, from 2013 to 2022. Fatal crashes made up only 0.8 percent of records, so a lazy model could look accurate while missing every deadly case. The team compared XGBoost with two neural designs, TabNet and FT-Transformer.

Its precision-focused score ran nearly four times the random baseline the authors computed for comparison. XGBoost and TabNet trailed close behind each other. pmc-13483376:
Zirui Wang and others build a prediction model for recurrence in triple-negative breast cancer, an aggressive form that lacks three common treatment targets. Their 2026 study joins medical and pathology data with quantitative traits from magnetic resonance imaging in a cohort of seven hundred patients. The model adds two novel elements: variation inside the tumour and traits from tissue just around it.

By capturing tumour variety that staging systems miss, the tool aims to help doctors tailor treatment intensity and follow-up schedules to each patient. Oncologists gain a fuller picture of biological aggressiveness from scans they already collect.
pmc-13483576:
Karen Redhead and co-authors separate the effects of sleep apnea and low mood on pregnancy outcomes in a 2026 observational study. pmc-13483676:
Hou and colleagues filmed pelvic organs in motion to map how prolapse actually unfolds inside the body. The uterus traced a reversed S with four turning points. By the third strain, the uterus had traveled about 83 percent of the reference line's length, far beyond its first-push distance. pmc-13484876:

pmc-13484976:

pmc-13485076:

The authors call for shared practice guidelines.
pmc-13485676:

pmc-13487276:

pmc-13487976:

pmc-13489076:

Gene material showed in a share of the urine set. Blood tests found both early and past infection marks. Types and clinical signs of infection were mapped. Early finds matter for pets and their owners.
pmc-13490376:

pmc-13490576:

pmc-13491676:

The author advises caution because the measures did not behave identically across sexes.
pmc-13491776:

Women with the syndrome carried more Lactobacillus, Roseburia, and Escherichia-Shigella, and less Akkermansia, a microbe often tied to metabolic health. pmc-13491876:

Tests in urine worked directly without sample cleanup. The authors pitch the platform for quantitative point-of-care testing beyond pregnancy as well.
pmc-13493776:

pmc-13493976:

No deaths, fluid buildup, or visible damage to the abdominal lining followed, and microscopy showed the surface cell layer intact apart from mild flattening and slight scarring beneath. pmc-13494076:

Bone density was tracked with a high-resolution scanner at the shin and wrist plus standard density scans, alongside blood markers of bone turnover.

Both groups lost a little bone over the twelve months, but the probiotic group unexpectedly lost slightly more at several sites rich in spongy bone, including the shin and spine. The main comparison reached statistical significance. The authors urge caution: the differences were modest and outside factors may have crept in despite randomisation. Their practical message runs against the supplement's promise, since sound nutrition and regular activity remain the dependable defences.
pmc-13494476:

Raising the strand's level in two ovarian cancer cell lines cut growth, spread, and invasion. It also raised cell self-eating and cell death, and it shut down a major growth pathway. In mice, tumors with more of the strand grew less. Patient tissue checks backed the pattern. The authors propose the strand as a partner that deepens the drug's lethal effect.
pmc-13495376:

Instruments led the top hundred, then fixation devices, healing biologics, implants, access tools, and computer-guided systems. Fixation patents drew the most citations and the fastest yearly citation rate. Across eras the mix shifted: instruments dominated the earliest years, then shrank in share, while implants and biologics climbed. Near half the patents had expired at the time of study. The authors read the map as a record of where shoulder scope invention has concentrated and where it is heading.
pmc-13495476:

Single-port surgery took about ten minutes longer, yet patients lost less blood and left hospital about seventeen hours sooner. Complication rates and bladder control at three months did not split. pmc-13498776:
Tetsuo Kon and his team review how chromosome-level genome assemblies are changing life science. Their review from twenty twenty-six marks a shift in genomics. Long-read sequencing and contact maps made full assemblies cheap for one lab to build. Those who study life now pick species by their question, not by data at hand.

The review steps through the making, checks, and marking up of assemblies. Case studies show four big gains from this way of work. Structural variation and deep chromosome change over ages come into view. Doubled genomes of tangled build can at last be sorted. Traits tie to genome layout in new ways. Life forms far from the pet kinds gain study tools of the same rank. The authors cast assemblies as base tools for new finds.
pmc-13499176:
Christian Summa, Daniel Swink, Joseph AbouAyash, and a wider team wrote this case report, published in 2026. It describes a full repair, done entirely through the leg artery, of a torn and bulging aorta in a sixty-six-year-old man.

The patient had a long-standing tear of the upper aorta with ballooning near the gut arteries. A branched stent graft was chosen to fix the segment while keeping those arteries fed. Because of an earlier neck bypass, the team avoided arm access and worked only from the leg. An electric cutting step opened a controlled channel between the tear's two layers so the graft could pass. All gut branches received stents through nested tubes. Final imaging showed no leaks. The authors present the case as proof that even complex aortic repairs can be done from the leg alone.
pmc-13499676:
Hamzah M Javed and colleagues describe in 2026 a delayed, whole-body collapse after a large overdose of a common HIV treatment tablet that combines four antiviral drugs. Published overdose reports had mostly described mild courses handled with supportive care alone. Their patient was a 35-year-old man with HIV, high blood pressure, and amphetamine use who intentionally swallowed about 90 tablets and arrived awake, alert, and stable.

Within the next day his course changed sharply. He developed shock needing drugs to support blood pressure and breathing failure needing high-flow oxygen. Acid build-up in the blood followed, along with a heart rhythm warning sign on tracings, mild kidney injury, and newly weakened heart pumping seen on imaging showing fluid in the lungs. Infection tests stayed negative throughout, and intensive supportive care brought gradual recovery over several days, adding a severe pattern to the sparse overdose literature.
pmc-13500376:
Sugiyama, Morimoto, and Asai report finding drug-resistant bacteria in an Asian black bear in Japan, a worrying sign of human pollution in nature. From droppings collected in a persimmon orchard in 2025, they isolated an Escherichia coli strain carrying ESBL, an enzyme that defeats several frontline drugs. The 2026 genome analysis showed the resistance genes were built into the bacterium's chromosome. The strain resisted five tested drugs, including ampicillin and tetracycline.

Its genes sat close to isolates from a pig farmer in Vietnam and from Japanese slaughterhouse wastewater. They sat within a few dozen DNA letter differences, hinting at recent shared ancestry across the human-animal boundary. Dropping DNA showed a mostly wild plant diet, so the bear likely picked the bacterium up from its surroundings. The authors warn wildlife can become a reservoir spreading such bacteria back toward people.
pmc-13501576:
Yazhou Li leads an eight-author team comparing two endoscopic operations for far lateral lumbar disc herniation, where a slipped disc pinches a nerve root at the spine's side. The study reviewed 122 patients treated between January 2022 and July 2024 by one surgical team. Of these, 62 received percutaneous endoscopic lumbar discectomy through a single channel, and 60 received unilateral biportal endoscopy, which uses separate viewing and working channels. Everyone was followed for at least twelve months.

Both groups improved markedly in pain and disability. The biportal operations took longer, averaging about 132.77 minutes against 86.61 minutes in clock time, and involved more blood loss, near 270 millilitres against roughly 37 millilitres on average. Long-term pain scores, disability scores, and excellent-or-good outcome rates, 91.9 percent against 93.3 percent, were comparable. A cumulative sum analysis placed the learning curve turning point at 24 cases for the biportal method and 38 for the single-channel one.
pmc-13501776:
Tianlong Wang leads a twenty-three-author team reporting a 2026 multicentre validation of a transfusion risk score for heart surgery on bypass. The FW-TRIC score was built earlier at Fuwai Hospital to forecast which patients will need red blood cell transfusion, a common event tied to worse outcomes. This study tested it externally in 3,287 adults operated on at nine Chinese cardiovascular centres during 2024, excluding transplant, mechanical support, and pre-transfused cases.

The overall transfusion rate reached 40.1 percent, giving the test plenty of events to judge. Discrimination was good, with an area under the curve of 0.713, and calibration was excellent, meaning predicted rates matched observed ones closely. Every single ingredient of the score, from age to surgery type, predicted worse alone than the combined score did. Performance held across all nine centres, with each centre's area above 0.65 on that measure. The authors back its use for blood management planning.
pmc-13502576:
Arpan Mondal and Richard A. Layfield report a 2026 study in which rare-earth complexes chop white phosphorus step by step. White phosphorus, the P4 molecule, is industry's gateway chemical, but rare-earth reagents stop at cage anions that resist use. The team's yttrium and gadolinium dinitrogen complexes, sources of divalent reactivity, instead cleaved P4 into a series. First came a four-atom dianion, then a two-atom dianion, then a phosphorus atom carrying an electron.

Structures and spectra characterized each stop. The four-unit ligand adopts a bicyclobutane-like shape, the two-unit ligand binds side-on as a double bond of the element, and the atom behaves as an element-centred radical. Paramagnetic resonance confirmed coupling to the element and yttrium, while the gadolinium version showed antiferromagnetic exchange with the radical. Calculations placed the spin on the element, extending its multiply bonded chemistry into the rare earths.
pmc-13502776:
Wang and colleagues described a sixty-one-year-old woman with breast cancer that spread into the membranes around her spinal cord. She regained leg function and nearly three and a half years of disease control, in a 2026 case report. Her tumor was triple-negative, lacking the drug targets, and had returned after two quiet years, paralyzing both legs.

Wang profiled her genes and found an mutation in PALB2, a DNA-repair gene that makes tumors vulnerable to a drug class called PARP inhibitors. After chemotherapy and a checkpoint immunotherapy drug had failed, they added the PARP inhibitor olaparib. Her leg strength improved from paralysis to partial movement, and scans showed shrinkage of the spinal-membrane and bone lesions. Progression-free survival reached forty months with side effects. The authors caution that one case cannot separate drug's contribution, but argue the strategy merits study in patients.
pmc-13503276:
Emma Elizabeth Sabu Kattuman leads an eight-author team with a 2026 melanoma study that unmasks an inflammation receptor as a self-fuelling tumour driver. Mining TCGA data, the team found the cysteinyl leukotriene receptor CysLT1R far higher in metastatic than primary tumours. In mouse and human melanoma cells, activating the receptor with leukotriene D4 drove growth and invasion through two pathways, ERK and YAP. Crucially, the melanoma cells make their supply: they express the synthase and secrete the leukotrienes themselves.

That autocrine loop keeps the receptor switched on without help from surrounding tissue. Deleting the receptor, or blocking it with the drug MK571, clearly slowed tumour growth in animals and shut down the YAP-LOXL-2 axis. Experiments in receptor-deficient mice showed the host's own receptor in nearby tissue contributes too. The authors nominate CysLT1R as a druggable target in a cancer starved of options.
pmc-13503476:
Basri and a large team review how bile acids, the detergents the liver makes to digest fat, may help or harm the brain in Alzheimer's disease. Beyond digestion, bile acids act as hormones, and gut bacteria constantly remodel them before they circulate to distant organs. Their 2026 narrative review pulls together biochemical, animal, and clinical findings on two bile acid receptors that sit at the crossroads of metabolism, inflammation, and brain health.

People with Alzheimer's or mild cognitive impairment show altered bile acid profiles. The review sorts the family into villains and protectors. Water-hating secondary bile acids are linked to blood-brain barrier leaks and direct nerve toxicity, while water-loving types appear anti-inflammatory and protective in the cited evidence. Bile acids also trigger gut hormones, including GLP-1, the target of blockbuster diabetes drugs, giving them indirect routes to the brain.
pmc-13503876:
Chao Ma leads a team that glued crystal sponges into gas-sorting sheets with a plastic-like bond, in a 2026 study. The crystals, called metal-organic frameworks, sort gases by pore size and chemistry. Sheets made from them leak through gaps where grains meet, which ruins the sorting.

Heat and a helper compound triggered a linking reaction right at the grain faces of one crystal type, UiO-66. The sheets ended up almost all crystal by weight, with few leak paths left. They passed carbon dioxide fast while holding back nitrogen, beating a known quality line for that pair. The sheets also shrugged off damp air and could be refreshed. The same trick worked for three more crystal types of the same family.
pmc-13504776:
Nan Sun and others propose a federated distillation model for cell type classification from medical single-cell transcriptomes. In 2026, the plan, called scKSFD, lets institutions collaborate without pooling raw patient data, a constraint imposed by privacy rules such as GDPR and HIPAA. Standard federated learning exchanges model parameters; this approach instead shares probability-level soft labels on a reference data set.

Stratified proxy sampling preserves rare cell groups, while probability-level aggregation mitigates batch-specific levels shifts without explicit feature correction. Across forty-two medical data sets, the method matched or beat centralized and current federated baselines under heterogeneous settings, with clear paired improvements. A multi-hospital COVID-19 case study improved classification over local-only training without sharing patient-level levels data.
pmc-13505076:
Yaodong Zhang leads a team testing a newer anesthetic against propofol for preventing sickness after surgery, in a 2026 trial. Nausea and vomiting after operations strike about a third of patients and most high-risk ones. Propofol helps but can sting on injection and drop blood pressure.

The trial enrolled 334 women having keyhole gynecologic surgery, split between the two drugs for sleep induction and upkeep. Sickness rates in the first day were near equal, at about 58 percent in each group. The new drug did not prove itself no worse within the set margin. It did win on safety: far less injection pain, less early low pressure, and less slow heart rate during surgery. Pain scores and satisfaction matched. The authors offer it as a gentler option.
pmc-13505176:
Denzel L Q Drop leads an international team that tested a virtual reality video made to help intensive care survivors understand what happened to them. Many survivors develop stress symptoms, anxiety, or low mood after critical illness. Across eleven hospitals, 344 adults who had spent at least three days in intensive care were split among standard care, an early video viewing, and a late viewing.

Six months later, stress symptom scores did not differ between either video group and standard care. Anxiety, depression, and quality of life also showed no group differences. Patients still rated the video highly, giving it a median eight out of ten for improving understanding and for satisfaction. The authors warn that a single viewing should not be expected to work like longer, guided, or personalised programmes, and they suggest future trials focus on high-risk patients.
pmc-13506576:
Kanako Kasuya and colleagues review, in a 2026 study from Japan, how often older patients with womb lining cancer received care that matched national guidelines. Records covered 130 patients aged 70 or older treated between 2010 and 2019 at one hospital. Guideline care meant main surgery, node checks when needed, and added chemotherapy based on risk.

Patients aged 75 or older met the full standard far less often than those aged 70 to 74, mainly through fewer node checks and less added chemotherapy. Missing the standard linked to worse outcomes even after other factors were counted. The authors advise judging fitness by full assessment, not age alone.
pmc-13506976:
Tsuboi and a large team offer a simple bedside test to split two look alike tremor diseases in twenty twenty-six. Dystonic tremor and Parkinson's disease can be hard to tell apart when signs are mild. A brain scan can help, but it is costly and not always at hand. The team measured tremor with motion sensors in one hundred two patients.

Tremor while drawing a spiral ran higher in dystonic tremor, while tremor at rest ran higher in Parkinson's. Posture tremor did not split the groups. A plain rule, spiral shake beats rest shake, named the disease with high accuracy. Three blind raters using their eyes alone matched the sensors well. The authors urge wider testing of the rule.
pmc-13508276:
Asima Khan and six co-authors map how proven type 2 diabetes care gets put into practice at primary clinics in poorer countries, in a 2026 scoping review. Diabetes is rising fast in low- and middle-income nations, where tight budgets make clinic care uneven. The team searched eight databases for studies from 1996 to late 2024. Papers had to describe rolling out, adapting, or judging evidence-based diabetes care in primary settings. Ninety-two articles covering 85 studies in 27 countries qualified.

Rollout tactics clustered most often around engaging patients, changing clinic infrastructure, and using feedback to adjust course. Tactics tailored to local context appeared less often. The team also coded what helped and what blocked progress, using a standard framework. Readers get a map of which strategies clinics actually use, where the gaps lie, and which hurdles planners must clear before diabetes care can improve at scale in resource-poor settings.
pmc-13508376:
Sofia Kaloper and four co-authors study how accurately people report the places tied to HIV risk and care in Los Angeles, in 2026 work. Prevention programs lean on location data to find hotspots, yet self-reported places carry error. Data came from a long-running study of gay, bisexual, and other sexual minority men in the city. Mapping checks and statistical models then weighed which traits, activity types, and areas predict reporting accuracy.

Personal traits, the kind of activity reported, and geography each shaped accuracy in a meaningful way. Places inside a person's home region were reported more accurately than places outside it. That regional tilt could quietly bias hotspot maps built from surveys alone. The authors plan sharper models with confidence ranges around reported points. Their goal is fairer targeting of prevention work, so that areas with fuzzier reporting do not get overlooked in funding maps.
pmc-13510376:
S. Fouziya Sulthana, U. Mohammed Iqbal, B. S. Sreeja, and Rajesh Anbazhagan review flexible wearable sensors that track body chemistry and body signals at the same time, in 2026 work. Most wearables today cover one side only, either movement and electrical signals or chemical measures such as glucose and lactate in sweat. Joining both sides in one soft, skin-fitting patch could give a fuller picture of health between clinic visits.

The review covers new flexible materials and building methods, then weighs progress in physical sensing, chemical sensing, and ways to merge them on one platform. Gains include steady tracking of chronic conditions and earlier warning of changes. Hurdles remain in accuracy over time, power, data handling, and the step from lab demos to approved medical use. The authors close with directions for the next wave of combined wearables.
pmc-13510576:
Marinos Chatzikonstantinou, Kyriaki Michailidou, Marios Pantzaris, Gavriella Alexandrou, Charalambos C. Charalambous, and Dimitris Sokratous pilot a two-arm exercise program for people with progressive multiple sclerosis, in 2026 work. Five participants with primary or secondary progressive forms took part in a twelve-week program of in-phase movements, where both arms move in the same pattern together. Sessions ran thirty to sixty minutes, and the study used a single-case design with staggered starts.

The program proved safe, workable, and well tolerated across the group. Three of the five participants showed clear gains in the excitability of pathways from brain to muscle, plus gains in some clinical measures. Earlier work had shown similar gains in the relapsing form of the disease. The authors call the low-cost program a candidate for routine and group rehabilitation, while stressing that five cases can only point the way.
pmc-13512776:
Koraj and colleagues redesigned inhibitors of ST6GAL1 to fix their flaw: they could not cross cell membranes. ST6GAL1 is an enzyme that decorates cell surfaces with sialic acid and helps cancers spread and hide from immunity. Their 2026 medicinal chemistry study started from a known non-sugar inhibitor bearing a sulfonic acid group. They replaced that group with look-alike substitutes called bioisosteres.

Koraj found that sulfonylurea substitutes restored passive membrane crossing in an artificial membrane test while keeping enzyme inhibition. An expanded series improved potency, with the best compound reaching low micromolar strength. Binding measurements confirmed the new compounds engage the enzyme at similar strength to the parent. Magnetic resonance mapping showed which parts of the molecule touch the enzyme, with the strongest inhibitors making extra contacts through their aromatic arms. The work supplies a design framework for cell-permeable versions of this cancer target.
pmc-13514676:
Teresa Sinicropi and four co-authors present a 2026 case report of a giant desmoid tumour in the small bowel of a 27-year-old man. Desmoid fibromatosis is rare, grows invasively where it starts, and almost never spreads, yet its behaviour is unpredictable and no standard treatment pathway exists. The patient arrived with fever and worsening abdominal pain five years after sleeve gastrectomy weight-loss surgery, and a CT scan revealed a large abdominal mass arising near the small intestine.

Surgeons removed the mass along with the right colon and the end of the small intestine, and laboratory examination confirmed the desmoid diagnosis. The man left hospital on the fifth day after surgery in good condition, with no sign of the tumour returning at the time of writing. Sinicropi's team reviews the wider literature and finds their full-removal approach matches current thinking.
pmc-13515876:
Mikołaj Maga and six colleagues translate and validate a Polish version of the Walking Impairment Questionnaire in a 2026 study. The questionnaire scores walking distance, speed, and stair climbing for people with intermittent claudication, the leg pain of narrowed arteries that strikes during walking. One hundred patients lined up for vessel-opening treatment completed the Polish form, two quality-of-life surveys, and a six-minute walking test.

Scores on the Polish questionnaire lined up with both quality-of-life surveys across every domain. They also tracked the distance walked before pain began and the maximum distance reached. Repeating the test gave near-identical results, and the questions hung together strongly as a set. Maga's team concludes that the Polish version, built on metric units, is a reliable and clinically useful gauge of walking limits in this patient group.
pmc-13515976:
Gulnur Nakhanova leads a twenty-two-author team developing a quality-control test for a brucellosis vaccine candidate, in a 2026 study. The vaccine uses a lab-made protein, superoxide dismutase, as its antigen. Standard antibody tests can misread such proteins after the chemical steps used in vaccine making, so the team built an older-style diffusion assay instead. First they raised rich antibody serum in sheep, comparing two booster additives.

The aluminium-based additive produced far stronger antibody levels than the rival by day forty-two. With that serum, the diffusion assay formed rings whose size grew in a straight, predictable relation with antigen amount. It detected the protein down to a fraction of a microgram per millilitre, measured precisely, and ignored unrelated proteins. Nakhanova's team presents the assay as a sturdy tool for checking antigen strength in future vaccine batches.
pmc-13516676:
Rejoice Nyarku leads a ten-author team validating a rapid Salmonella test for poultry settings in a 2026 study. Salmonella in chickens is a top food-safety threat, and knowing which strain is present guides the response. The platform, GenoPATHX, runs two multiplex gene panels, one tuned to chickens and one to turkeys, each spotting priority strains plus a general Salmonella marker in a single same-day workflow.

Bench validation showed strong, straight-line readings and detection down to tens or hundreds of genome copies per reaction. The panels caught every target strain in the test set and excluded off-target germs cleanly. On naturally contaminated farm samples, the direct workflow reached about eighty-one percent sensitivity and ninety-one percent specificity against the reference culture method used by United States inspectors. Nyarku's team presents the assay as ready support for poultry surveillance and risk-based food safety action.
pmc-13518776:
Inka Romero-Ortells, Manuel Perea, Eva Gutierrez-Sigut, and Jon Andoni Duñabeitia report 2026 eye-tracking experiments on how subtitles steer attention in bilingual teaching videos. University students watched two-speaker lessons while researchers varied the spoken language and the subtitle language. The learners were Spanish speakers studying English, with native English speakers as a comparison group.
