The team drew on records for 36,340 outpatients from community pharmacies between twenty sixteen and twenty twenty-one.

About one in ten patients had leftover drugs. Those patients tended to be older, take more drugs, have longer prescriptions, and use more prescribing departments. Yet the weight of each factor changed with age group in a clear pattern. The authors say support for patients should fit their stage of life, not follow one rule for all ages.
pmc-13587276:
Farhad Heydari and colleagues put four bedside stroke scales head to head in an emergency department study. Brain scans settle a stroke diagnosis, but they are not always at hand in the first minutes, so short checklists of face, arm, and speech signs do the early work. The team scored 655 adults with suspected stroke between 2021 and 2023 and checked every score against MRI results.

Close to three quarters of the patients truly had an ischemic stroke, a blockage type. All four scales sorted patients well, with no firm winner overall. The Cincinnati scale caught the most true strokes, which suits roadside use, while the detailed NIH scale wrongly cleared the fewest healthy patients, which suits hospital confirmation. The authors advise picking the tool by setting, time pressure, and the user's training.
pmc-13587376:
Adekunle Ayomide Adegoke and colleagues compare two immune signals in Nigerians living with HIV on treatment. Antiretroviral therapy quiets the virus but often leaves the immune system partly stirred up. One signal, IL-6, marks inflammation, while IL-10 marks the calming side. Their 2026 study drew 81 people at a Port Harcourt teaching hospital: some on treatment under six months, some for two years or more, plus HIV-negative controls.

IL-6 ran highest in the short-term group, lower in the long-term group, and lowest in controls, with each step clearly apart. Years of treatment thus cool inflammation without fully matching the uninfected state. IL-10 ran higher in treated patients than controls but did not track time on treatment. Age and sex shifted neither signal. The authors back cytokine profiling as an extra gauge of immune health on therapy.
pmc-13588176:
Seh Hoon Park and co-authors present Protea-Tac in this 2026 study, a new way to destroy chosen proteins inside cells. Cells clear proteins through a machine called the proteasome, which usually grabs proteins tagged with ubiquitin. The team skips the tag step. Their chimera joins a proteasome receptor part with an antibody that binds the target, dragging the target straight to the machine.

The chimera slots into proteasomes without harming their shape or function. With matching antibodies it cleared several targets, including a cancer-linked protein and tau. Tests showed the platform is modular, tag-free, and highly specific. In animals, it slowed tumor growth by clearing the cancer-linked target. Delivery worked by virus and by other routes. The authors frame it as a fresh platform for targeted protein removal.
pmc-13590476:
Desirée I. Gracia and colleagues released an electrospinography database of spinal-cord signals during walking tasks and motor imagery. Spinal-machine interfaces promise closed-loop control of leg exoskeletons for gait rehabilitation, but need rich spinal signal data. Their 2026 dataset records high-density surface electromyography from the spinal cord region in 14 able-bodied volunteers across baseline, movement, and imagery trials.

Three protocols covered electrode arrays over brachial and lumbar plexuses and nearby muscles. Sessions ran 10 for the first experiment, 10 for the second, and 5 for the third. Preprocessing reduced heart and motion artefacts. The authors offer the pioneering resource for refining exoskeleton control and artefact-removal methods in neurorehabilitation research.
pmc-13591476:
Naseer Khan and colleagues survey fellows' perspectives on the interventional cardiology fellowship match after it moved into the national matching program. Their 2026 study follows an earlier analysis of program directors, adding the missing applicant viewpoint.

Ninety-six fellows responded, a thirty-eight percent response rate. Most had applied to over thirty programs and received more than fifteen interview invitations. Rank lists most commonly held six to ten programs, with many ranking over fifteen. Prematch offers were rare, at about thirteen percent. Most applicants preferred particular training settings canvassed in the survey. Fellows generally viewed the new transparent system positively despite the heavy application volumes described.
pmc-13592476:
Romain Bouet leads a 2026 study asking what magnetic brain imaging adds when surgeons hunt the seizure source in stubborn focal epilepsy. Their cohort followed 101 patients in a prospective imaging study; those who went on to implanted electrodes or surgery formed the test group. Magnetic source imaging was stacked against standard MRI and metabolic PET scans, with electrode findings and the removed zone as the truth standard.

Magnetic imaging flagged extra source regions beyond MRI in over half the cases, and beyond both older scans in a third. Using all three scans together gave the best detection rate, well above any single scan. Bouet and the team say the gain comes without extra false alarms, which matters most in complex or scan negative cases.
pmc-13592576:
Toshio Narimatsu and five colleagues measure low contrast vision in healthy adults to test whether ordinary short sight quietly dulls sight. Standard eye charts use bold black letters, which can miss subtle loss. Their records covered 43 healthy eyes from checkups at a Tokyo center, all with normal best corrected scores and no eye disease history. Grey chart acuity was tested under best correction.

Low contrast scores worsened with age and ran clearly worse in more short sighted eyes. Better low contrast scores tied to shorter eye length and milder prescriptions, among other factors. Narimatsu and the team conclude that even non diseased myopic eyes carry a real visual penalty, and they commend the grey chart test for clinic studies hunting subtle change.
pmc-13592876:
Chunliu Zhuo and six co-authors map the gene switches behind a special plant fiber in a 2026 study. The plant Cleome hassleriana makes a rare fiber called catechyl lignin in its seed coats. That fiber is a plain chain with traits that suit chemical and material making, but the seed coat switches to it mid-growth by turning off two methylation enzymes.

Using gene activity data, the team rebuilt the web of switches around those enzymes. Tests with a light-based reporter assay named one switch as an activator and another as a repressor. Two further switches shut the enzymes down while waking the genes of the new fiber path. Work in hairy roots backed the model, which the authors present as a wiring diagram.
pmc-13593176:
Gurmehr Brar and Brian Lee review the burden, across the world, of metabolic and alcohol-associated liver disease, known as MetALD. Their 2026 review draws as one the work on its spread, its results in clinics, and what it means for public health. It is a class set out not long ago.

The class takes in two drivers that act as one: metabolic dysfunction, and use of alcohol. Roughly ten to twenty percent of people across the world who have fatty liver meet its marks. When both are at play, the links are to fibrosis that moves fast. They are also to more cirrhosis and decompensation. And they are to a higher rate of liver cancer than for each one on its own. Death rates are raised too. The burden splits by region and is set to rise in lands with high and middle incomes.
pmc-13594076:
Xiao and colleagues published a 2026 study on forcing drug-resistant stomach cancer cells to self-destruct. Some stomach cancers survive platinum drugs by dodging a rust-like cell death called ferroptosis. A surface protein, EphA2, helps them keep that death route switched off. pmc-13605676:

pmc-13606476:

pmc-13608776:

It lays out the models used to judge which patients face high risk. It also covers results so far and newer ideas for keeping the cancer out of the central nervous system.
pmc-13626776:
Bernhard Scheiner and nine colleagues published a review in two thousand twenty-six on liver cancer trends in Europe. Hepatocellular carcinoma makes up most primary liver cancers. Cases tied to viral hepatitis are set to fall, yet total cases keep climbing.

The authors project new cases and deaths to rise by over thirty percent by two thousand fifty. Fatty liver disease linked to metabolism, plus an ageing population, drives the growth. Most cases grow out of long-term liver disease, and over half look preventable by tackling changeable risks. The paper maps what this means for care at each disease stage and for health policy. It also notes that treating the root cause improves outlook.
pmc-13628576:
Jayanta Dey and Dmitry Katayev review nitrooxylation, the chemistry of attaching a nitrate ester group to organic molecules, in a 2026 survey that runs from classical methods to the newest catalytic strategies. Nitrate esters matter as medicines that release nitric oxide, as energetic materials, and as versatile building blocks, yet the traditional mixed-acid route is harsh, poorly selective, and hazardous.

The review follows the field's shift toward gentler tools: stable transfer reagents, catalytic systems, and light-, electricity-, and grinding-driven methods that generate the reactive nitrogen species in place. These approaches widen the range of workable reactions, from modifying alcohols to functionalising carbon-hydrogen bonds. The authors tie the progress to a clearer mechanistic picture and aim the field at safer, more sustainable synthesis.
pmc-13629776:
Chaohui Huang and nine colleagues chart sixty years of listeriosis in China, pairing a literature review of cases from 1961 to 2020 with genomic analysis of the foodborne bacterium Listeria monocytogenes. Published in 2026, the study divides the record into three eras, from scattered sentinel cases to a high-incidence plateau after 2010.

Overall fatality ran near a quarter of cases, and higher still among pregnancy-related infections, which also brought frequent miscarriage and newborn deaths. One clone, CC87, dominated clinical isolates and formed its own evolutionary branch carrying two virulence islands; family-tree timing places its origin around the late 1960s, with nationwide mixing rather than local clusters. The authors flag this hypervirulent clone as a priority for food safety action.
pmc-13630276:
Shahana Alasgarli and co-authors wrote a case report from 2026 on a heart sac that stiffened two years after a throat stent. The patient was a woman of seventy-four with two months of growing breathlessness. Two years before, she had a stent placed for throat cancer, then drug and radiation care. A stiff heart sac can trap the heart and mimic other causes of failure.

Heart scans showed the stiff pattern with no large fluid pool. Chest scans found dense fluid with air bubbles in the sac, a hint of a past throat leak, though no open tract showed. Surgeons cut the sac away and found a large mass of firm, cheese-like pus. Lab tests grew a gut germ from the sample. Tissue checks showed long-term swelling, scarring, and calcium deposits. With surgery and matched drugs, her marks of infection settled and her heart signs cleared.
pmc-13632476:
Xianzheng Liu and five co-authors review solid electrolytes for all-solid-state lithium batteries through the lens of practical cells. Their review was published in twenty twenty-six. The field's chase for raw conductivity has outrun the harder problems.

A useful electrolyte must pass ions, hold contact with electrodes, block stray electrons, flex or resist cracking, and be made thin at scale. Oxide, sulfide, halide, nitride, polymer, and mixed types are compared on all these axes at once. Contact loss, surface films, voids, and lithium spearing get particular attention. The authors argue the winner will be chosen by factory floors and interfaces, not by conductivity records.
pmc-13632576:
Katherine Bunch, Simon Ammanuel, and Bradley Schmidt describe a combined minimally invasive spine surgery technique, in work published in 2026. The operation fuses two lower spine bones while also clearing pinched nerve channels. Standard fusion reaches one side well, but patients pinched on both sides and in the centre need more.

Their technique pairs the fusion with a keyhole removal of bone over the canal, all through a one-sided approach that preserves the midline structures. That pairing decompresses both sides while still stabilising the spine. Guidance from CT scans during surgery cuts radiation exposure for the team compared with standard live X-ray methods. The authors suggest the approach for patients with a slipped vertebra and instability who want midline structures kept intact. The paper is a technique report rather than an outcomes trial.
pmc-13632876:
Eight researchers test whether alpacas can catch a dangerous bird flu virus in a study from 2026. The virus, H5N1 of a fast-spreading clade, has moved from birds into mammals around the world. In 2024, infections in young goats and alpacas were reported in the United States. The team gave six alpacas the virus through the nose in a controlled experiment.

Illness stayed mild, with slight fever and lower food intake for a few days. Virus RNA appeared in nose swabs, and live virus was confirmed. Traces were found only in nose and throat tissues at day four. The authors conclude alpacas can host a productive infection. They urge surveillance and tighter biosecurity on farms.
pmc-13633176:
Mohammad Nafeli Shahrestani and colleagues measured sixty immune-related proteins in blood to find which ones predict later stroke. Their participants came from the Northern Manhattan Study, a long-running community cohort. All were at least fifty years old and stroke-free when blood was drawn. The team used a selection method to sift the sixty markers, then tested the survivors against strokes recorded over a median of fourteen years.

Of nearly twelve hundred participants, one hundred thirty suffered a stroke, most of them the ischemic kind, where a clot blocks blood flow. Only two markers passed the first sifting, and just one, a signaling protein called CXCL10, held its link after full adjustment. Higher levels meant roughly a fifth more stroke risk per standard step upward. The link survived accounting for white matter damage too. The authors propose CXCL10 as a marker of immune activity that leaves vessels vulnerable.
pmc-13633576:
Brian Ireland and colleagues present a 2026 case report of two problems striking one patient at once. Respiratory syncytial virus, or RSV, is best known as a childhood infection, but it also sickens adults, mostly in winter. It usually stays in the airways. A sixty-five-year-old man arrived short of breath and with belly pain, and he tested positive for the virus.

Scans revealed a second, hidden problem: a tiny hole in his sigmoid colon where an inflamed pouch had burst. Surgery was judged too risky, so doctors treated him with strong antibiotics instead. Abscesses later formed in his belly and were drained through tubes guided by scans. The authors note the virus has weakened bowel walls in children. They raise the possibility it played a part here too, and urge doctors to watch for gut trouble in adults with RSV.
pmc-13634576:
Nour Abdelrahman and many colleagues published a 2026 study on growing crystals of a layered magnetic material. The material mixes chromium with niobium diselenide, in a one-to-four ratio. Such layered crystals host gaps where magnetic atoms can sit, which tunes their electronic and magnetic states.

Good single crystals of this mix have been scarce. Past reports on its magnetism even clash with each other. The team grew high-quality crystals and tracked how their antiferromagnetic states change. In such states, nearby atomic magnets point in opposed directions. Clean crystals let the group settle what the material truly does. That base is needed before any device use.
pmc-13641676:
Wonseok Lee and colleagues review the biology of steatotic liver disease through a lens in a 2026 paper that separates subtypes. The umbrella covers metabolic dysfunction-associated disease, alcohol-associated disease, and a mixed form where moderate drinking joins metabolic dysfunction, yet the subtypes share much of their appearance. The authors argue that distinctions in pathology and molecular features are needed to build models that capture how alcohol and metabolic stress amplify each other.

The review draws on multi-omics and single-cell profiling of genes, epigenetics, spatial patterns, and proteins to map cell diversity and disease drivers. It follows progression from simple fat buildup through inflamed steatohepatitis to fibrosis, driven by fat-laden liver cells, inflammatory myeloid cells, and scar-making stellate cells. It also weighs human liver spheroids as experimental models. The result is a framework for classifying the disease and for targeting therapy to its drivers.
pmc-13642376:
Bruno Riccio and seven co-authors review a drug formulation trick for non oral delivery in a 2026 article. Amorphous solid dispersions keep a poorly soluble drug in a high energy glassy state mixed with a polymer, boosting how fast it dissolves. The approach is well studied for pills, but evidence for skin, lung, eye, and other routes is scattered and mostly early stage.

The review covers how drug and polymer interact, how molecules move in the mixture, and how water uptake can trigger crystallization that ruins the boost. Evidence is summed up route by route, including injections and implants as special cases. The authors map what blocks translation into real products.
pmc-13644176:
Danielle Tracey and two colleagues present a 2026 study of a shared gardening program in at-risk areas of New South Wales, Australia. Shared gardens are known to help health and mood. Less clear was whether such a program can be run as planned and grown wider.

The study used thirty-three survey replies, thirty-nine talks with people, and case notes from seven sites. People in the program had strong needs tied to health and jobs. Those with disability had the most need. Turnout rose and fell, with clear aids and blocks. People liked the program and gave ideas to improve it. Delivery stayed true to the plan, the authors found.
pmc-13646076:
Aobo Zhuang, Bin Zhou, and Mengmeng Xiao introduce a journal collection of twenty-one articles on tumors of the retroperitoneum, the deep space behind the abdominal organs. Such tumors are hard to reach, often found late, and tangled with major vessels and nerves. The editors sort the collection's lessons along one care pathway. Six original studies, fourteen case reports, and one review make up the set.

The first lesson is that good surgery starts with sharp diagnosis, and the editors cite ultrasound scores, imaging patterns, and tissue tests that separate look-alike tumors. A deep learning model trained across twelve Chinese centers also gets attention for sorting tumor types from scans. Later pieces turn to planning operations around each patient's anatomy and matching treatment scale to tumor biology. The editorial closes by tying surgical care to long-term team follow-up for these rare cancers.
pmc-13646276:
Niamh O’Malley and five colleagues solve the three-dimensional structure of a human potassium channel called Kir7.1, in a 2026 study, to explain a rare inherited eye disease. The channel helps cells keep their electrical balance and is switched on by a membrane fat. A mutation in its gene causes snowflake vitreoretinal degeneration, which has no cure. Using cryo-electron microscopy, the team imaged both the normal channel and the disease variant.

In the variant, the swapped building block swings into the channel's pore and blocks potassium flow, which explains the loss of function. A second finding surprised the team: binding of the activating fat widened the channel's gate even without a part usually seen docked in other channels. That hints this channel opens through a halfway shape of its own. The structures give drug designers a concrete target for restoring channel function.
pmc-13648776:
Nicholas Summerfield and ten colleagues taught a deep learning tool to trace heart parts on scans of patients who carry heart devices. Metal in these devices blurs CT scans with streaks. The tool serves two groups: people set for heart-sparing radiation, and people set for burn therapy that stops wild heart rhythms.

The team retrained the tool with device cases mixed in, then tested it on held-out device scans. Scores rose for both the rhythm group and cancer patients with devices. Scores on scans with no device barely moved. Dose maps showed the heart's lower chambers, one valve, a key nerve node, and the left heart arteries took the most dose in rhythm cases. The authors back device-aware training.
pmc-13649376:
Haoyang Jiao and two colleagues argue that care for polycystic ovary syndrome should pivot to insulin sensitivity and weight-neutral risk checks. A world accord has renamed the ill the polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome. The swap will count for little, they say, if care still fixates on ovary shape and body size.

Weak insulin response can serve as a hub for care in a large share of patients. It is not the sole cause, though, and it should not turn into a test that gates diagnosis. Their path keeps checks on blood sugar, fats, pressure, heart risk, pregnancy plans, and mind health, open to all body sizes. Drugs keep their guidelined roles. If the new name lifts care, time will tell.
pmc-13649976:
Hao Pang and three colleagues follow patients with a form of chronic hepatitis B who receive pegylated interferon alpha, a timed course of immune-based treatment. The team tracks two genes, IFI44L and SAMHD1, measured in blood immune cells, to see whether their levels during treatment line up with later response.

Patients were treated for 48 weeks, and gene levels were measured before treatment and at weeks 12 and 24 using a standard laboratory test. Higher levels at the mid-treatment checks went with larger falls in viral markers. The week 24 readings separated responders from non-responders most clearly among the time points tested. The results point to both genes as possible early signals of how well interferon therapy is working, though the authors frame them as candidates needing further proof.
pmc-13650676:
Hongzhi Cao and five colleagues report a 54-year-old man whose liver held two cancers growing side by side: a hepatocellular carcinoma and a bile duct cancer. That pairing is called a collision tumor. They stay distinct under the microscope rather than mixing, a rare entity confused with blended tumors or spread from elsewhere.

The man, a long-term hepatitis B carrier, came in during June 2024 feeling tired, eating poorly, and with a swollen belly. Scans first suggested widespread spread of one cancer, while a specialized scan hinted at two primaries, and biopsies aimed at both lesions confirmed the split diagnosis. Surgery was ruled out because lymph nodes were involved, so the team combined artery-delivered chemotherapy for one tumor with immune therapy, a vessel-blocking antibody, and chemotherapy cycles. At the check in April 2026 he had lived over eighteen months with tumors shrunk and no severe side effects.
pmc-13650976:
Lin Guo and five colleagues ask whether rising above one's parents in education protects functional health in old age, and whether the answer depends on the country. Their outcome is intrinsic capacity, the World Health Organization's composite of thinking, movement, energy, senses, and mood, which reframes aging around function rather than disease.

Harmonized data from five national aging studies covered over one hundred thousand people past fifty, about half a million observations in all. Upward educational mobility was robustly tied to higher capacity everywhere. In China, Europe, South Korea, and Mexico, mobile adults also declined more slowly with age, a pattern of delayed aging. The United States broke the pattern: mobility raised the starting level sharply while the pace of decline matched everyone else's. Wealth, behavior, and chronic disease carried part of the effect. The authors keep mobility central to healthy longevity policy.
pmc-13655476:
Chang Kyung Kang and Jonathan Li review a tricky problem in HIV care: virus levels that stay low but never fully vanish on treatment. Modern drugs suppress the virus for most people, yet this lingering trace is common. It can mean missed doses or drug clashes, or virus leaking from hidden reservoirs with no real growth.

The review lays out a step-by-step workup, starting with adherence, food and drug interactions, and resistance tests. Fixes differ by cause: better adherence or a drug switch for true growth, but watchful waiting for reservoir leak. The authors also cover new long-acting shots and note sex transmission risk stays very low in this range.
pmc-13662876:
Tomoki Asano led a 2026 study using deep learning on CT scans to ask whether muscle quality or muscle quantity better reflects walking ability before hip fracture in older women. Muscle loss and fatty infiltration both accompany aging and fracture risk, yet which matters more for function was unclear. The team studied 170 women with intertrochanteric or femoral neck fractures, automatically segmenting muscles on the unfractured side into gluteal, adductor, quadriceps, and hamstring groups.

Pre-injury walking ranged from outdoor walking to being chairbound or bedridden. Across all muscle groups, poorer walking tracked with lower muscle attenuation, higher comorbidity burden, and lower body mass index, while muscle volume did not reach significance. The authors conclude that CT muscle quality, reflecting fatty infiltration, mirrors functional decline better than size alone. Geriatricians get support for reading muscle quality into fracture risk and rehabilitation planning, not just muscle bulk.
pmc-13677076:
Maria Michali and seven co-authors measured how patients feel after nose-straightening surgery in a 2026 study. A bent nasal septum blocks airflow and drags down quality of life. Forty-three patients had septoplasty combined with radiofrequency shrinking of the swollen lower turbinates on both sides, and answered two validated symptom questionnaires before surgery and six months later.

Twenty healthy volunteers provided a comparison baseline. Both questionnaire scores improved significantly after surgery. The prospective design, with the same patients tracked across the operation, strengthens the reading. The authors present patient-reported outcomes as the honest test of this surgery, since anatomy alone does not say how well a nose breathes.
pmc-13678676:
Kanu Garg and colleagues published a 2026 review of ultrasound treatment for wheat proteins. Wheat feeds much of the world. Heat processing can damage its nutrients. Ultrasound offers a gentler, non-thermal alternative. Sound waves reshape protein structure and behavior.

The review covers chemical and structural changes. Function in foods can improve after treatment. Storage life may also lengthen. Evidence spans many wheat products and studies. Sustainability and precision are recurring themes. Food makers want quality without heavy energy use. Ultrasound fits that demand well. The authors map what is known and what remains untested.
pmc-13680476:
Nathan Vaudiau and a large team of co-authors show how two kinds of guide cells team up to train tumor-fighting cells, in a study published in twenty twenty-six. Some killer T cells settle in tumors like resident guards, and patients who hold more of them fare better. How those guards get specified was unclear.

The team used a mouse model of lung cancer and removed each guide cell type in turn. One type proved vital for making the main attacking and worn-out killer cells. Both types, though, helped shape the resident-like guards in the lymph nodes that drain the tumor. The second type shows tumor parts sparsely, which favors guard training, while the first type drives guard growth and adds a homing signal. Teamwork, not a single teacher, builds the guards.
pmc-13682476:
Tianhao Wang and co-authors give a recipe for growing bone organoids with plant-based ink in a 2026 protocol paper. Organoids are lab-grown mini tissues. Bone versions often lack immune signals, though immunity steers bone repair. They also rest on animal-derived gels that vary batch to batch and are poorly defined.

The team's ink mixes aloe vera gel, a printable gelatin derivative, and a clay-like additive, with no animal matrix and no added cytokines. In dishes, the ink steadily reprogrammed macrophages, immune cells that set the tone for healing. That built an immune setting in which bone organoids matured well. The protocol walks through ink preparation, organoid printing, and tests in skull bone defect models. The authors offer the platform as a defined, repeatable swap for gel-based systems. They suggest it can adapt to other immune-responsive tissues.
pmc-13685776:
Samantha Thomas and co-authors ask how women in Australia view the growing business around menopause. Their study appeared in 2026. Firms now sell many products and services aimed at menopause, and shape how it is understood. The team ran an online survey with open questions for 362 women aged 45 to 64, then grouped the answers into themes.

Three themes stood out. First, some women welcomed the attention as a sign their experiences count. Second, many feared firms were profiting from women's weak spots, and doubted the motives behind the marketing. Third, women felt flooded by online content and struggled to judge what to trust. The authors argue that policy and health advice must reckon with this crowded, profit-driven setting.
pmc-2247476:
Drummond and Rambaut present BEAST, software for Bayesian evolutionary analysis by sampling trees. Studying how sequences change is a statistical task at its core. Use of probability models for family trees, alignments, and population genetics was growing when they wrote.

BEAST is described as a fast and flexible package that samples many possible trees and weighs each by likelihood. That approach yields not just one tree but a sense of how sure each branch is. BEAST became a central tool for dating species splits and tracing the spread of viruses through time.
pmc-3012676:
Du, Zhang, Huang, and co-authors compare two ways of expressing DNA methylation levels from microarray data. Measuring methylation across CpG sites is crucial for understanding how genes are switched without changing the DNA code. Illumina's Infinium assay offers cheap, high-throughput profiling for that purpose.

Results can be reported as Beta values or as M values, and the choice affects statistics. The authors test both methods side by side to show where each behaves well. Their guidance helps researchers pick a scale that supports valid comparisons in studies of cancer and development.
pmc-3445676:
Elwyn, Frosch, Thomson, and co-authors present a practical model for shared decision making in clinical practice. The principles of sharing decisions between doctor and patient were well documented by 2012. Guidance on how to actually do it during routine care was lacking, though.

The authors translate earlier theory into a practical three-step model that clinicians can easily remember. The steps move from introducing choice, through describing options, to reaching a decision together. Their model gave clinicians a teachable routine for respecting patient preferences without lengthening visits unworkably.  Training programmes for doctors now teach the three steps as core communication skill.
pmc-3447976:
Friedman and Alm present methods for building correlation networks from genomic survey data. High-throughput methods such as 16S rRNA gene profiling promise to reveal the inner workings of natural microbial communities, from ocean water to the human gut. A key step is finding which microbes vary together.

Raw correlations mislead because community data are proportions, not absolute counts. Their method, SparCC, was designed to handle that trap. Better networks help ecologists guess which microbes cooperate or compete, shaping hypotheses that lab work can then test directly.  Ocean surveys used network maps to predict which microbes thrive together seasonally.
pmc-5340976:
Smith, Heger, and Sudbery made UMI-tools in 2017 for more exact gene counting. In many sequencing tests, each starting molecule gets a random tag, called a UMI, before copies are made. Copies that share a tag came from one molecule; copies with new tags were new molecules.

The catch is that the tags themselves pick up read errors, so true groups can split or merge. UMI-tools models those tag errors and groups the reads the right way. That fix makes counts of gene activity far more true to the sample. As tagged tests spread through labs, tools like this became part of the basic kit.
pmc-6366976:
Ake Lu, Austin Quach, James Wilson, and coauthors built the GrimAge aging marker in 2019. It was unclear whether blood protein levels could be guessed from DNA methylation marks. It was also unclear whether such guesses could forecast lifespan.

The team built methylation-based estimates for several plasma proteins tied to health and smoking history. Combined into GrimAge, the score strongly predicted time to death and to major diseases. It beat earlier methylation clocks on those outcomes in their tests. Researchers now use it to gauge biological aging in large cohort studies.
pmc-7619276:
Dena Matalon and a large team of colleagues report clinical, molecular, and gene-expression findings from a major cohort of people with RNU4ATAC-opathy. The rare condition comes from faults in a small RNA gene involved in splicing, the editing step that prepares gene messages for use. Because so few patients are known, each family's features help define what the condition includes and how severe it can be.

Pooling many patients let the team connect specific genetic changes to patterns of symptoms and to measurable shifts in how genes are read out in cells. That three-way view, covering the body, the molecule, and the transcript, sharpens diagnosis for children whose features overlap with better-known syndromes. It also gives families firmer information about prognosis, and gives researchers defined molecular effects to target in any future treatment work.
pmc-7857476:
Jeanne Bertuit and two colleagues study how pregnancy changes walking in women with pelvic girdle pain, and whether a pelvic belt helps. The study enrolled women with the pain condition, healthy pregnant women, and non-pregnant women, measuring the timing and spacing of their steps on an instrumented walkway. Two belt designs for pregnant women were tested on the same measures.

Women with pelvic pain walked with shorter stance and cycle times than healthy pregnant women, and pregnancy itself slowed walking and shortened steps compared with the non-pregnant group. Wearing a belt measurably changed speed, single-support time, step length, and step width. Results like these let midwives and physiotherapists recommend belts on evidence about gait, and let designers see which support style changes walking the most.
pmc-9825576:
Brian Alcock and colleagues presented the 2023 update of CARD, a database that collects what is known about how bacteria resist antibiotics. CARD pairs a set of standard terms for resistance with checked gene sequences and the gene changes known to cause resistance. Together they let a lab read a bacterium's genome and say which drugs it can likely withstand.

The update adds more curated records, support for machine learning, and better tools to predict a sample's resistome, the full set of resistance genes it carries. Health teams use CARD when they sequence bacteria from hospitals and towns. Knowing resistance genes with care is key to picking the right drug and to spotting dangerous strains early.
polano-talmud-selections-1876:
Polano's Talmud: Selections, published in 1876, offered English readers early and easy access to rabbinic literature. The Talmud itself is a vast record of Jewish law and debate in Hebrew and Aramaic. Polano chose and translated passages for a general audience.

The selections range over prayer, charity, family duty, court rulings, and tales of the rabbis at work. Readers could meet the Talmud's mix of strict law and warm story without facing its full bulk. The book served as an influential introduction for English readers curious about Jewish tradition. Victorian readers met a living tradition here, not a dead code.
price-observations-civil-liberty-1776:
Price's Observations on the Nature of Civil Liberty appeared in 1776 and made him famous in a night. The dissenting minister wrote as Britain moved toward war with its American colonies. His pamphlet defended the American cause on principle, and it sold by the thousand in the year of independence.

Price defines liberty as self-government, for nations as for persons, and argues that Britain's claim to tax and bind the colonies was a form of slavery. He extends the argument to Ireland and India, which widened both the book's reach and its enemies. The government of the day considered prosecuting its author. The tract carried deep thought to the barricades across the sea, and it stands as the English voice of the American Revolution at its birth.
proudhon-what-is-property-tucker-1876:
Benjamin R Tucker published his translation of Pierre-Joseph Proudhon's What is Property? in 1876. Proudhon, a French printer and self-taught thinker, had issued the memoir in 1840 and shocked France. His answer to his own question became famous at once: property is robbery.

Proudhon distinguished property, the right to use and abuse and charge rent, from simple possession of what one works. He attacked rent, interest, and profit taken without labor. Judges and economists denounced the book, and Proudhon answered them in later memoirs. The work is widely read as the founding text of anarchism, the first time a writer claimed that label with pride.
shi-king-book-of-poetry-legge-1876:
James Legge published his complete translation of the She King, the Book of Poetry, in 1876. It forms volume three of his Chinese Classics, in a revised edition with the Chinese text, prolegomena, and notes. The Shih Ching holds 305 songs and hymns, gathered in China more than two thousand years ago.

Court odes, temple hymns, and folk songs of love, harvest, and war stand side by side. Tradition credits Confucius with choosing and ordering the collection. Legge's prose renderings favor exact sense, while his notes carry the learning of Chinese commentators. The songs remain China's oldest poetry anthology and a school text for ages. English readers meet them whole in Legge.
smith-chaldean-account-genesis-1876:
George Smith, a bank note engraver turned Assyriologist at the British Museum, wrote this book in 1876. He had taught himself to read the clay tablets of Babylon from the museum's vast store. Four years past, he had read out a flood tale from the tablets to a stunned London crowd.

The book sets the Babylonian tales of the making of the world and man by the side of Genesis. A flood tale far older than the Bible stands in its pages in clay writ form. The find shook the firm faith of Victorian Britain in the lone truth of its own text.
spina-quaestio-de-strigibus-latin-1576:
Bartolomeo Spina, a Dominican who served as master of the sacred palace at Rome, wrote his Quaestio de strigibus early in the sixteenth century. This edition of 1576 kept his answer in print. Spina writes against Ponzinibio, the skeptical jurist who had called the sabbath an illusion.

Point for point, Spina defends the sabbath's reality with scholastic logic and old texts. The witches fly in body, he insists, and their assemblies truly meet. His book is the Counter-Reformation's learned reply to early doubt. Orthodoxy strikes back here with full armor. Reading Spina against Ponzinibio shows the sixteenth-century debate at its sharpest, lawyer against theologian over the same frightened women.
taine-ancient-regime-durand-1876:
Hippolyte Taine's The Ancient Regime appears in John Durand's translation of 1876. The book opens Taine's Origins of Contemporary France, his study of the Revolution's causes. Taine applies his method of race, milieu, and moment to old France. Taxes, privilege, and a rigid central state crush the peasantry and starve reform.

He paints the court, the tax farmer, and the village in hard detail. The old regime, in his account, made revolution near certain. Taine wrote after the Paris Commune, and fear of crowds colors his work. Historians debate his science, yet respect his research. The volume is a classic of analytical history in the French style.
the-dare-boys-of-1776:
Stephen Angus Cox wrote The Dare Boys of 1776, with pictures by R. Mencl, published in New York by the Platt and Peck Company under a 1910 copyright held by the A. L. Chatterton Company. Its contents send the Dare boys through a night attack, dangerous work, spy missions, a haunted house, and the Battle of Long Island, with General Washington pleased along the way.

Chapter I, The Clang of the Liberty Bell, opens on the fourth day of July, 1776. Excitement runs through all the colonies, for on this day the people's representatives, gathered in Philadelphia, are to decide whether the Declaration of Independence, already drawn up, should be adopted and signed. In Philadelphia the feeling runs so high that business stops and crowds throng the streets, talking and waiting for the decision.
the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-seing:
Spain, the opening part of Spanish Passions in Jacques Casanova's memoirs, follows the 1894 London edition translated by Arthur Machen, with chapters discovered by Arthur Symons. Chapter One opens with a hard maxim: whoever punishes a knave and leaves him alive invites vengeance. Casanova has survived a den of thieves, three against one, and lost his purse. At dinner, a police agent summons him to Count Schrotembach, the governor at Vienna.

The governor shows him a watch and sets the hour: be gone from Vienna by that time tomorrow, or face expulsion. Casanova protests the injustice of the order, issued before he could lay his robbery complaint. The chapter's summary promises the empress moderating the order without annulling it, then Munich, Augsburg, and Aix-la-Chapelle. Readers see the adventurer's luck turn on official suspicion, with Spain still ahead of him.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i:
Number 478 of the Mirror, dated Saturday, February 26, 1831, illustrates autographs of eminent persons and resumes the theme of character in handwriting. Shenstone's quaint wish, to see Mrs. Jago's handwriting and judge her temper, supplies the motto. The signatures come from an engraved plate of forty-three autographs published with the Edinburgh Literary Journal, No. 28. Anecdotical traits only are selected here.

Anne Grant of Laggan's present hand shows a little instability of advancing life, yet keeps a well-rounded breadth and distinctness matching her clear, judicious mind. General Stewart of Garth writes a free, bold, military hand, taken from a letter praising Chambers's History of the Rebellion of 1745. Allan Cunningham's writing flows easily and tastefully, the reviewer adds, from a man who handled the chisel as Hogg handled the plough. Readers are taught to read temper and trade from ink strokes.

The Mirror's number for Saturday, May 21, 1831, No. 490, records an old house in Southwark, taken down the previous autumn for the New London Bridge approach. The crazy but picturesque building stood on the High Street's eastern side. Its style belongs to Henry VII's time, with florid carvings on the first and second stories' fronts. The upper stories had later been covered with plaster, and the windows mix periods.

The house carries a historic claim beyond its architecture: it was the residence of Anne Boleyn, the article states. Its interior was finished in palatial style, with the royal arms conspicuous in one apartment. The editors regret that Southwark's ancient history remains unwritten despite the suburb's celebrity. The Mirror's stated object is rescuing such relics from oblivion, and here demolition supplies the deadline. Readers get a doomed house photographed in prose weeks after its fall.
the-old-bell-of-independence-or-philadel:
Henry C. Watson wrote The Old Bell of Independence, a book for young Americans about Philadelphia in 1776. Lindsay and Blakiston entered it for copyright in 1851. Watson had already written The Camp-Fires of the American Revolution and a book on Boston in 1773. His preface says he hopes to stir respect for the patriots of the War of Independence.

Stories of chief men of the Revolution are linked by veteran storytellers gathered around the old State House bell. The contents promise a story of General Washington, The Spy's Fate, and a story of a sermon. Watson praises devotion and resolve while calling war itself a horror.
the-principal-navigations-voyages-traffi: Volume III of Hakluyt's Principal Navigations, in Edmund Goldsmid's edition, covers North-Eastern Europe and Adjacent Countries, Part II. Its subject is the Muscovy Company and the North-Eastern Passage. The notes explain the kept sixteenth-century spelling and the editor's footnotes. Other records hold Volumes II, VIII, X, and XII of the same set. The pages shown here reach only the title pages, so the Muscovy voyages themselves stay out of view.
the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volume-22:
Headed volume twenty-four in its own pages, this portion covers three years. The record title calls it volume twenty-two instead. Its years run from 1574 to 1576 in chapter three. The summary matches the closing complete portion in theme. Blood Council decline leads the account here. Insincere peace talks follow the council's latter days. Secret meetings between Leoninus and Orange test the Prince.

Orange refuses resignation when the Estates press him. He accepts near-unlimited power from them instead. A union of Holland and Zealand follows his elevation. Talks at Breda stall in adroit insincerity afterward. His Bourbon marriage succeeds Anna of Saxony's fate. Tortures by Sonoy darken the summary's close in North Holland. Readers should expect the same ground as before. The complete record's final chapter covers it too.
the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volume-23:
Headed volume twenty-five in its own pages, though the record calls it volume twenty-three, this portion covers 1576 in chapter four. The state council at Brussels takes up affairs amid Madrid hesitation and maladministration, while Orange watches vigilantly and Holland and Zealand draw closer under a new union.

Zierickzee falls on honorable terms after Admiral Boisot dies relieving it, Spanish troops mutiny in Schouwen from deep discontent, and rebel regiments spread alarm. Elizabeth's policy and secret French talks hover at the summary's edges. Mutual exhaustion pushes the provinces toward each other.
the-valley-of-fear-pg3776:
Arthur Conan Doyle's The Valley of Fear appears again in this separate edition, and its contents and opening match the other library copy of the novel. Part one, The Tragedy of Birlstone, runs from The Warning through Darkness and A Dawning Light to The Solution. Part two, The Scowrers, moves to Lodge 341, Vermissa, and ends with the trapping of Birdy Edwards.

The first chapter begins with Watson starting a sentence and Holmes cutting in impatiently. Watson confesses himself long-suffering yet annoyed by the sardonic interruption. Readers get the familiar partnership at work before the Birlstone case unfolds, first in England and then in an American valley ruled by fear.
tob-0076:
Edmund T. Whittaker wrote the classic history of how physicists explained light and electricity before Einstein. His subject runs from Descartes, who filled space with spinning whirlpools of fine matter, to the aether theories of the Victorian age. Maxwell's equations and the discovery of the electron close the long story.

Whittaker was a working mathematician who lived through the upheaval he describes, and it shows in his grasp of detail. Generations of students have treated the book as the standard history of field theory. It also reminds readers that the aether, now discarded, once organized the best science of its century.
tob-0176:
G. Horner's translation presents Pistis Sophia, a Gnostic text preserved in Coptic, in which the risen Jesus teaches his disciples over an extended period after the resurrection. Mary Magdalene stands foremost among the questioners. At its center, Pistis Sophia, Faith-Wisdom personified, has fallen into chaos and repents her way upward through thirteen aeons, singing psalms of repentance in each.

Hostile archons, hymns, and detailed maps of higher and lower realms fill the dialogues. The Christianity shown here is stranger and richer than the creeds that won, built on secret knowledge and cosmic drama. Scholars prize the text as a major surviving witness to late Gnostic teaching.
tob-13329-15476:
Books eight to twelve form volume three of Ganguli's Mahabharata, the epic's dark second half. The great battle grinds to its end as champion after champion dies. A shameful night raid kills the last sleeping warriors of the beaten side.

Aftermath fills the rest: grief on the field, funeral fires, and the slow, unwilling work of rule. Yudhishthira must be coaxed to govern the kingdom he has won at such cost. Long discourses on duty replace the clash of arms. Ganguli's translation turns elegiac with the poem itself. Seldom has a war story spent so much strength on sorrow.
tob-4146-15476:
Books eight through twelve fill volume three of Ganguli's Mahabharata, and the war burns toward its end. Great champions fall one by one. A night attack slaughters sleeping warriors, an act the epic itself treats as shameful. Victory, when it comes, tastes of ash.

Widows mourn on the field, funerals follow, and Yudhishthira, the eldest Pandava, takes the throne with a heavy heart. Long talks on duty and grief slow the pace on purpose. The epic turns from deeds of war to their cost. Ganguli's steady translation lets the sorrow build, page after page, without relief.
tob-4176:
Teresa of Avila, the Spanish nun and reformer, described the soul as a crystal castle in The Interior Castle, her mature masterpiece of 1577. Benedict Zimmerman translated her guide for English readers. Seven sets of mansions lead inward, room by room, toward the King who waits at the center.

Each mansion marks a stage of prayer, from stumbling effort to quiet union. Teresa writes from her own trials, with humor about distractions and dry spells that still disarms readers. Nuns under her rule received the book first; the world claimed it next. Many judges call it the greatest guide to the life of prayer ever written.
tob-4276:
William Hickling Prescott wrote his History of the Conquest of Mexico in the 1840s, and it became the most widely read history of its time. Volume one of four sets the scene before Hernan Cortes lands. It describes the Aztec empire at its height, ruled by Montezuma from Tenochtitlan, a great lake city of temples, markets, and canals.

Prescott explains Aztec government, religion, warfare, and daily life in detail drawn from Spanish and native sources. He writes history in the manner of a novel, with vivid scenes and strong characters. Readers get both a rich portrait of a lost civilization and the background they need for the clash that follows in later volumes.
tob-9052-15476:
Grief rules volume three of Ganguli's Mahabharata, as the war of Kurukshetra ends. The field lies covered with the dead of both houses. Widows and mothers search the corpses, and the victors find their crown brings no joy.

Funeral rites, laments, and hard reckonings take the place of battles. The epic turns, by design, from action to mourning and reflection on what violence costs. Yudhishthira rules a kingdom of ashes and doubts his own part in winning it. Ganguli carries the slow, somber books with patience. Readers feel the full weight the Sanskrit poem places on victory.
tob-9776: A. J. Maas wrote this Catholic Encyclopedia article on the Hexaemeron, the six days of creation described in the first chapter of Genesis. It sums up how early Church writers and later theologians read those six days, whether as plain days, ages, or figures of speech. Maas writes as a scholar for general readers who need a clear map of a long debate. Short and factual, the piece works as a starting point on how Christians have understood the creation story.
transactions-of-the-american-society-of-:
W. B. Gregory reports strength tests on creosoted southern pine in Paper No. 1168 of the society Transactions. The beams had served 26 years in a railroad trestle near New Orleans. Each 30-foot stringer was cut in half for testing.

Gregory notes that Forest Service research had mapped treated and untreated timber properties, yet little was known about time's effect on creosoted wood. Despite heavy rain, humid air, and hard train service, the specimens showed no visible decay. The treatment rules called for long-leaf or southern pine, with sap surfaces preferred on two or more sides. Engineers designing wooden structures gain rare long-service evidence here.
tumulus-hermetis-apertus-in-quo-ad-solem: Tumulus Hermetis Apertus, dated 1676 in its record, survives through badly garbled lines in which its Latin title page can still be read. The title promises an opened tomb of Hermes, in which the hidden physical truths of the most ancient sages are to be seen in full daylight. It also promises the mistaken opinions of some more recent writers. The subject is the much-praised liquor called the mercury of the philosophers. Only this damaged title page is present here, so the treatise itself does not appear.
twain-tom-sawyer-1876:
Mark Twain published The Adventures of Tom Sawyer in 1876, complete in the first edition text. The beloved Mississippi boyhood novel drew on Twain's own youth in Hannibal, Missouri, on the river. Its sunny mischief made Twain famous on both sides of the Atlantic at once.

Tom, raised by Aunt Polly, dodges school and chores for swimming, pirates, and treasure hunts. He whitewashes a fence by making the chore look like rare sport to his friends. At night he sees Injun Joe murder Dr. Robinson in the town graveyard in secret. Lost in a cave with Becky Thatcher, Tom finds both terror and buried gold there. The book's glow of boyhood hides sharp satire of village piety and pride.
un-ga-res-376:
Korea's division hardened into war, and Resolution 376, adopted by the General Assembly on 7 October 1950, restates the UN aim. Past votes of 1947, 1948, and 1949 had set the goal: a free, united Korea. The UN Commission on Korea had now reported. The goals, the text admits, had not been met. Worse, an armed attack from North Korea had tried to wipe out the Republic of Korea by force.

The Assembly recalls its 1948 ruling on the south. A lawful state, the Government of the Republic of Korea, held real rule over the part of Korea the UN team could reach. That state rested on votes the team had watched. The text holds to the goal of one Korea, free of outside force.
un-ga-res-a-69-76:
The world's sole forum for arms talks gets a review in Resolution A/69/76, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The Conference on Disarmament, based in Geneva, holds the prime role in hard talks on arms cuts. The Assembly had the conference's own report before it. Word from the Secretary-General, and speeches by foreign chiefs, had each voiced both support for the body and worry at its stall.

Real talks on firm points are needed, the text holds, and the state of the world should give them fresh push. Yet worry runs deep: for all the hard work of its member states, the conference had long failed to agree a plan of work. That deadlock, unbroken for years, hangs over the whole text.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 376 (V), adopted on 7 October 1950, addressed Korea in the first months of the Korean War. The Assembly noted that an armed attack from North Korea sought to wipe out the Government of the Republic of Korea by force. United Nations forces were fighting under Security Council calls. They were to repel the attack and restore peace.

The text urged steps for calm across Korea. It urged elections under United Nations watch. It urged one united, free, and democratic government. United Nations forces were to stay only as long as needed. It created the United Nations Commission for the Unification and Rehabilitation of Korea, a seven-state body. It ordered plans for relief and rebuilding once the fighting ended.

Resolution 69/76 of the General Assembly, adopted at the sixty-ninth session in 2014, takes up the report of the Conference on Disarmament. It records that the Conference again failed in 2014 to begin substantive work or agree on a programme of work. That extended a deadlock of well over a decade. It notes the re-established informal working group. It notes consultations among its successive presidents meant to find a way forward.
un-sc-res-1376:
Congo's peace process gained its third MONUC phase on 9 November 2001. The Lusaka parties' political committee met the Council in joint session that day. The ceasefire generally held, though fighting went on in the east. Some foreign forces had left, including the whole Namibian contingent. The Secretary-General's report of 16 October set out the next deployment plan.

The Council welcomed the ceasefire's broad respect and called on the parties to stop backing armed groups in the east. It demanded again that Kisangani be demilitarized rapidly and without conditions, noting the RCD-Goma pledge on the city. The Council backed the inter-Congolese dialogue as a key part of the peace process. It approved phase III of MONUC's deployment, on the concept in the Secretary-General's report, with weight on the east and within the set ceiling. Grave concern was voiced at rights abuses and the country's humanitarian state.
un-sc-res-1476: Adopted in 2003, Resolution 1476 adds one more entry to the Security Council's long numbered run. The copy here is transcribed from the official record on English Wikisource. Like its neighbors in the sequence, it states the Council's grounds first and then records the decision in numbered operative paragraphs for governments to carry out and report on.
un-sc-res-1576:
Haiti's mission gained six months and a push on aid money in 2004. On 29 November 2004 the Security Council extended MINUSTAH until 1 June 2005. The transitional government was preparing free elections for 2005. The Council praised the Secretary-General's special representative and his support for dialogue. Political reconciliation and rebuilding were called essential and urgent. The mission's mandate stayed as set that April.

Transitional leaders had to widen the political process. Haitians who rejected violence should be brought into the transition. The Council endorsed the Secretary-General's latest recommendations. It urged donors and banks to release pledged funds fast. That money had been promised at a Washington conference in July.
un-sc-res-1676: Resolution 1676 is a formal Security Council text held here through a Wikisource copy of the official record. Its shape is the standard one, and the standard is the story: the same architecture carries ceasefire orders, mission mandates, and court referrals alike. The entry lets readers see that architecture at work in one complete act.
un-sc-res-176:
Security Council Resolution 176, adopted on October 4, 1962, recommended Algeria for membership in the United Nations. Algeria had won independence from France that July, after a war of eight years that shook both lands and killed vast numbers of people. A seat at the UN marked the new state's arrival on the world stage in formal terms.

The General Assembly admitted Algeria four days after the council acted. Few admissions carried such weight: France had long claimed Algeria was part of France itself, not a colony. The short resolution thus sealed a verdict that the war had already rendered, and Algeria soon became a leading voice for other peoples still under colonial rule.
un-sc-res-1776:
Afghanistan stood before the Council as it adopted Resolution 1776 on Afghanistan on 19 September 2007. The vote passed with fourteen in favor and one abstention. Attacks by the Taliban and other armed groups had grown sharper. Roadside bombs, suicide blasts, and seizures of hostages struck civilians and soldiers alike.

The text extends the mandate of the International Security Assistance Force for twelve months beyond 13 October 2007. States in the force may take all needed steps to carry out that mandate. Members are urged to send more troops, gear, and funds. The Council also presses for faster training of Afghan soldiers and police, so Afghans can guard their own country in time.
un-sc-res-1876: Resolution 1876, from 2009, records a decision of the fifteen-member Security Council in official form. The collection's copy follows the record held by English Wikisource. Inside the act, the preamble does the explaining and the operative clauses do the obliging. Both parts survive here, giving the decision its full context and its full force.
un-sc-res-2076:
M23's seizure of Goma drives Resolution 2076 of the United Nations Security Council, adopted on 20 November 2012. The rebel group had taken the city after fresh attacks in North Kivu. Reports said outside support kept flowing to the rebels. Crowds of displaced people were growing again across the east.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council demands that M23 leave Goma at once. The group must halt all advances, disband, and lay down its arms for good. All outside support to M23 must stop now. The sanctions committee should review two named M23 commanders for listing at once. More targeted sanctions are under active consideration. The Secretary-General must report within days on the claims of foreign backing.
un-sc-res-276: Within the United Nations official record, Resolution 276 is the Security Council text catalogued for 1970. The Council is the UN body charged with world peace and security, and it speaks formally through texts like this one. For students of the UN, the record offers the Council's language itself rather than a summary written later. The entry belongs to the library's DECLASSIFIED group of public official records.
un-sc-res-476:
Jerusalem's status was defended by the Security Council on 30 June 1980. Pakistan, chairing the Organization of the Islamic Conference, had written on 28 May 1980. Israel kept changing the city's physical character, population makeup, institutions, and status. Steps in the Knesset toward a law on Jerusalem caused the Council grave concern.

The Council restated the overriding need to end the occupation of Arab lands held since 1967, Jerusalem included. It strongly deplored Israel's refusal to obey the Council and the General Assembly. All Israeli laws and acts meant to alter Jerusalem's character and status were declared without legal validity. They broke the Fourth Geneva Convention and blocked a full, just, and lasting peace. Such changes were named null and void. Israel was called urgently to drop them, and the Council vowed to examine practical steps if it did not.
un-sc-res-676: Kept in the official record of the United Nations, Security Council Resolution 676 is catalogued here as dating from 1990. Voting in the Council requires support from its permanent members, so each adopted text marks a point of agreement. Readers will find the full wording here, taken from the English Wikisource transcription of the UN official record. The entry belongs to the library's DECLASSIFIED group of public official records.
un-sc-res-76: A wire from Batavia is passed on in Security Council Resolution 76, passed on 5 October 1949. The Consular Commission at Batavia had cabled the Council's president on 5 August. It asked that the United Nations take over the future costs of the armed watchers in Indonesia, the men who kept eye on the truce between Dutch and Indonesian forces. The Council rules, in full, that the wire be sent to the Secretary-General.
un-sc-res-976:
Angola's new peace operation, UNAVEM III, was created on 8 February 1995. The Lusaka Protocol of 20 November 1994 promised peace after years of war. The ceasefire was generally holding, and the two armies' chiefs had met at Chipipa and Waco Kungo. Yet the protocol's timetable was slipping. Angola's offer of large in-kind support for the operation was welcomed.

The Council authorized UNAVEM III to help the parties restore peace and win national reconciliation. Military and police observers would deploy fast to watch the ceasefire. Infantry units would follow only on the Secretary-General's word that the conditions on the ground were met. A full mine clearance program for the country was named vital. The new force needed a strong public information voice, the Council agreed. The Secretary-General had to report each month on deployment and on the Lusaka Protocol's progress.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Resolution 1376, adopted unanimously on 9 November 2001, reviews the Congo war's slow thaw. The Lusaka ceasefire was generally being respected, the Council found, though fighting continued in the east, where it told the parties to stop backing armed groups. Some foreign forces had withdrawn, including Namibia's whole contingent, which the Council counted as a real step.

Other states that had not yet begun pulling out were asked to start. The Council took note of the Secretary-General's October report and recommendations, and welcomed a joint meeting held that same day with the Lusaka agreement's political committee. Congo's sovereignty, including over its natural resources, was reaffirmed even as foreign armies still occupied much of its territory.

Emergency relief arrangements for Iraq are kept in force a little longer on 24 April 2003. Acting under Chapter VII, the Council decided that paragraph 4 of its resolution 1472 of March 2003 would remain in force until 3 June 2003. Those provisions gave the oil-for-food machinery flexibility to deliver humanitarian relief after the outbreak of war, and the Council noted the measures could be renewed again.

Haiti's climb back from chaos took a new step in late 2004. A stand-in regime ran the land. Polls were set for 2005, with power to pass to elected hands. The UN force, MINUSTAH, kept the peace. The chief's report of 18 November 2004 drove the talks. Resolution 1576 passed on 29 November 2004.

The force's term ran to 1 June 2005. More terms were meant to come. Armed bands that played at police work drew blame. A swift arms hand-in drive was called urgent. Rights abuses were damned, as was jail with no charge for one's politics. Donors were told to pay pledges made in Washington that July at speed. Word on the work was due each three months.

Somalia's arms embargo monitoring team is set up once more on 10 May 2006. The country's transitional federal institutions were still struggling to build real national governance. The embargo, dating from 1992, continued to be broken, and the previous monitoring group's term had run out.

The Secretary-General is asked, in consultation with the sanctions committee, to set the Monitoring Group up again to track violations and gather evidence. Support for the transitional institutions and for the African Union and regional efforts behind them is repeated. Somali leaders are urged to keep up political dialogue, and all states are reminded of their duty to respect the arms embargo in full.

Algeria's admission to the United Nations is recommended in Resolution 176, adopted on 4 October 1962 by ten votes to none, with China abstaining. The Council had weighed the bid of Algeria, filed under the state's full formal name. Algeria had won independence from France that July, after a brutal eight-year war that reshaped both countries.

The Council asks the General Assembly to admit Algeria to membership. The recommendation capped a remarkable reversal: a state whose liberation movement the UN had debated for years now joined as a member. Algeria quickly became a leading voice for colonized peoples in the Assembly, and this short admission text is where that career formally begins.

Afghanistan's international force is renewed by Resolution 1776, adopted on 19 September 2007 by 14 votes to none with one abstention. The International Security Assistance Force, ISAF, had completed its expansion across the whole country under NATO leadership. Taliban, Al-Qaida, and other extremist attacks, including suicide bombings and abductions, were rising, and civilian casualties were a growing concern. Counter-narcotics and security-sector reform were tied to the fight.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends ISAF's authorization for twelve months beyond 13 October 2007 and authorizes its member states to take all necessary measures to fulfil the mandate. It calls on states to contribute personnel, equipment, and funds, and stresses training and mentoring the Afghan National Police and army so Afghan forces can take over in time. ISAF must work closely with the Afghan government and the UN mission, UNAMA, and report quarterly through the Secretary-General.

Guinea-Bissau's peacebuilding office is extended on 26 June 2009, and its upgrade is ordered. Political assassinations had rocked the country that year, showing again how fragile its institutions are. A presidential election was set for 28 June 2009, two days after adoption, and a free and fair vote is treated as the key step back to constitutional order.

The office's mandate is extended, and the Secretary-General is asked to establish a United Nations Integrated Peacebuilding Office in Guinea-Bissau in its place, with a strategic workplan. All sides are called on to respect the election result and keep the process peaceful. The armed forces, including their leaders, are urged to stay under civilian control, and security sector reform is restated as a national duty.

The fall of Goma draws condemnation and a withdrawal demand in Resolution 2076, adopted in November 2012. The 23 March Movement, M23, resumed attacks in North Kivu and entered Goma on 20 November 2012. It displaced people and committed abuses including summary executions, sexual violence, and child recruitment. Reports alleged external support to the rebels.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council condemns the M23's attacks and demands its immediate withdrawal from Goma. It demands an end to advances, disbanding and disarmament of its members, and restoration of Congolese state authority in North Kivu. It demands all outside support cease. It asks the Secretary-General to report within days on the support allegations and on redeploying MONUSCO forces. It intends to consider sanctions against the M23 leadership and external backers under the Resolution 1857 (2008) criteria. The Great Lakes conference's joint verification mechanism is tasked with investigating the support reports.

South Africa's presence in Namibia is declared illegal by Resolution 276, adopted on 30 January 1970. The United Nations had ended South Africa's mandate over the territory in 1966. South Africa stayed anyway. It enforced its own laws there and put Namibians on trial in its courts.

The Council strongly condemned South Africa's refusal to obey the United Nations decisions on Namibia. It declared that South Africa's continued presence was illegal. Every act South Africa had taken for Namibia since the mandate ended was illegal and invalid. The occupation was said to have grave effects on the rights of the Namibian people. All states were told to avoid dealings with South Africa that clashed with that ruling. A special sub-committee was set up to study how the decisions could be carried out.

The Comoros, an island chain between Madagascar and Mozambique, declared independence from France in July 1975. Its UN application moved quickly. Resolution 376 was adopted on 17 October 1975 by fourteen votes to none. The Council met for its 1848th session that day.

Members recommended the Comoros for membership. The General Assembly admitted the islands the next month. One island, Mayotte, voted to stay French, splitting the new state. That quarrel shadowed the Comoros for decades. Even so, admission confirmed the archipelago's statehood in law. This resolution preserves the moment. A tiny island nation took a seat equal in voting weight to the largest powers in the Assembly.

Jerusalem's fate is the theme of Resolution 476, passed on 30 June 1980. Pakistan, then chair of a bloc of Muslim states, had raised the matter in a May letter. The Council said land seized by force can never be owned by right. It stressed the city's rare place in three faiths. The holy sites, it said, need care and respect above all.

The Council deplored Israel's drive to change the city's shape, its people, its rules, and its status. It voiced grave fear at bills in Israel's Knesset that aimed to lock those changes in law. It told Israel to end its hold on Arab lands seized since 1967, Jerusalem among them. It deplored its refusal to obey past rulings.

Two more months for the Iran-Iraq observer group were granted on 28 November 1990. The group, called UNIIMOG, watched a cease-fire that still held, although no full peace had followed it. A report from the Secretary-General, dated 23 November, had recommended the step. Resolution 676 records the renewal.

The Council extended UNIIMOG's mandate until 31 January 1991, as the Secretary-General had advised. He was asked to report during January 1991. His report would cover his further talks with Iran and Iraq about the observer group's future. Short renewals had become the pattern for the mission by then. Each one kept the observers on the ground for a few more weeks, while the Council waited to see whether the mission should continue at all.

A cable about the costs of military observers in Indonesia reached the Council in 1949. The Consular Commission at Batavia had written to the Council's president on 5 August that year. It asked that the United Nations take over the future costs of the observers working in Indonesia. Resolution 76, adopted on 5 October 1949, does a single thing with that request. The Council transmitted the message to the Secretary-General. No sums were set, and the Council gave no answer on the request itself.

Angola's peace deal takes shape in Resolution 976, adopted on 8 February 1995. The government and UNITA had signed the Lusaka Protocol on 20 November 1994, and the ceasefire was broadly holding. Military chiefs from both sides had met to move the plan along. Still, carrying out the deal had fallen behind its timetable.

The Council sets up a new peacekeeping operation, UNAVEM III, to help restore peace and national unity. It allows up to 7,000 troops, plus 350 military observers and 260 police observers, with a first mandate until 8 August 1995. Infantry units deploy only once the Secretary-General confirms a real ceasefire, shared military data, and named quartering areas for UNITA forces. A mine clearance program and a UN radio station are backed. The mission is meant to end once the Lusaka goals are met, with completion expected by February 1997.
uslaw-usc-t2-s476:
Section 476 of Title 2 of the United States Code sets up a council for the Office of Technology Assessment. It sits in Chapter 15, on that office. The Office is to set up a Technology Assessment Advisory Council. The Council is to be made of twelve members in all. Ten of those members are to come from the public, and they are to be named by the Board. Those ten must be men of note in a field of science or of the work of tools, or men fit by their gifts to schools or to public life.

The two last members of the Council are named by their posts. One is the Comptroller General. The last is the Director of the Congressional Research Service of the Library of Congress. A second clause deals with the duties of the Council.
virginia-declaration-rights-1776:
Virginia's Declaration of Rights was made on June 12, 1776. The people's representatives made it in full and free convention, as the basis and foundation of government. Its first section holds that all men are by nature equally free and independent. They hold rights no compact can strip from their children. Among those rights it names life and liberty, the means of gaining and holding property, and the pursuit of happiness and safety.

Later sections build the frame of free rule. All power rests in the people. Rulers are their trustees and servants, answerable to them at all times. Government exists for the common benefit and safety. When a government fails those ends, the majority holds a clear right to reform, change, or end it. The text stands behind much of the American language of rights that followed.
wallace-geographical-distribution-animal:
Alfred Russel Wallace, co-founder of the theory of evolution by natural selection, published the first volume of his Geographical Distribution of Animals in 1876. Wallace had spent years collecting in the Amazon and the Malay islands. He asked why each region holds the animals it does.

Volume One sets out the rules: how climate, seas, and land links shape where species can live. Wallace divides the world into six great regions, a scheme still in use. His maps and lists turned scattered facts into zoogeography, the study of animals across the map. Collectors and travelers supplied much of the raw data behind it.

Volume Two of Wallace's Geographical Distribution of Animals, also from 1876, puts his system to work region by region. Alfred Russel Wallace had catalogued thousands of species on his travels. Here he applies his rules to the lands of the Old World and beyond.

The volume works through Europe, Africa, Asia, and the islands of the Pacific in turn. For each region Wallace lists the families present and asks how they got there. Land bridges, past climates, and vanished seas all play a part. It completes the founding text of zoogeography. Readers meet the faunas of lands few had seen described before.
zola-his-excellency-1876:
Macmillan issued His Excellency in 1897 as the sole authorized English version, with Vizetelly's preface. Chapter heads run from The Corps Legislatif and Resignation to An Imperial Christening. Passion and Matrimony, In Retirement, and Recalled to Power follow in turn.

Eugene Rougon, the family's political genius, claws toward the top of the Second Empire. Minister and power broker, he masters the backroom deal and its price. Flatterers, mistresses, and favors traded like coin crowd around him. Zola dissects how power truly works with a razor edge. Few political novels match its grasp of influence, ambition, and the hunger that drives public men.
